en: Now begins the Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by its two commentaries: the Viṣṇucittīya and the Śrīdharīya known as Ātmaprakāśa.
Homage to the venerable Rāmānuja!
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
Then one should recite the victory of Goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa.
Śrī Sūta said:
Oṃ. Having prostrated and offered salutations to Parāśara, the best of sages, who had already performed his morning rites, Maitreya questioned him.
For from you, O Guru, the study of the Vedas has been mastered in its entirety,
as well as all the Dharmaśāstras and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) in their proper sequence.
O best of sages, by your grace, even those who are my enemies will say that I have not labored in vain regarding all the scriptures. (ViP 1.1.3)
O knower of dharma, O illustrious one, I desire to hear from you how the world came into being and how it will come to be again.
And from what was this world and Brahman born, and wherein this world of moving and unmoving beings was dissolved;
as it was dissolved, and wherein it will go to dissolution?
O best of sages, [tell me] the configuration and dimensions of the sun and other celestial bodies,
as well as the lineages of the gods and others, the Manus, and the Manvantaras.
The kalpas and the divisions of the kalpas as conceived within the four ages,
the essential nature of the end of a kalpa, and the duties of each age in their entirety.
O great sage, [I wish to hear] the life stories of the gods, seers, and kings,
as well as the division of the Vedic branches exactly as performed by Vyāsa.

And I wish to hear from you, O delight of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, everything regarding the duties of the Brahmins and others, as well as those of the residents of the various stages of life (āśramas).
O Great Sage, direct your mind toward me with favor toward Brahmā,
so that by your grace I may understand this.
The venerable Parāśara said: "Well done, Maitreya, knower of dharma! I have been reminded of that ancient account which my father’s father, the blessed Vasiṣṭha, once related."
O Maitreya, having heard that my father was formerly devoured by a Rākṣasa instigated by Viśvāmitra, an incomparable anger arose within me.
Then I commenced a sacrificial session for the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
and in that sacrifice, hundreds of night-stalkers were reduced to ashes.
Then, as those Rākṣasas were being completely destroyed,
my highly fortunate grandfather Vasiṣṭha spoke to me.
"O dear one, do not give way to excessive anger; subdue this wrath.
The Rākṣasas have committed no offense; for that was ordained by your father."
Anger occurs only in the ignorant; how could it exist in those possessed of knowledge?
For whom, O dear one, is anyone slain by whom? Since a person experiences the fruits of his own actions.
O child, even for those who have intentionally acquired great fame and ascetic merit through immense hardship, anger is the supreme destroyer.
O dear one, the supreme sages always avoid anger, which is the cause that obstructs both heaven and liberation; do not fall under its power.
Enough with these wretched, harmless night-stalkers who have been burnt;
let this sacrifice of yours cease, for the virtuous have forgiveness as their essence.
Thus, having been thus entreated by that high-souled father,
I immediately brought the sacrifice to a conclusion out of respect for his words.
Then the blessed Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was pleased;
and at that time Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, arrived there.
Having been offered the guest-offering by my grandfather and having accepted a seat,
the illustrious Maitreya, the elder brother of Pulaha, spoke to me.
Pulastya said: Since you have today resorted to forgiveness despite this great enmity because of your teacher’s word,
you shall therefore know all the scriptures.
"Since even when enraged you have ensured that my lineage is not cut off,
therefore, O highly fortunate one, I grant you another great boon."
"O child, you shall become the author of the Purāṇa-saṃhitā,
and you shall understand the ultimate nature of the deities exactly as it is."
And regarding both active and ceased karma, O child, your stainless intellect shall become free from doubt through my grace.
Then my grandfather, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, said to me:
"Everything that was told to you by Pulastya shall come to pass."
Thus, everything that was previously spoken by Vasiṣṭha and the wise Pulastya comes to my memory in its entirety through your question.
Therefore, O Maitreya, I shall relate to you in its entirety that ancient, uncomposed narrative which you have rightly requested; understand it exactly as it is.
He has arisen from the presence of Viṣṇu, and he remains established in that very same place;
he is the agent of the maintenance and the dissolution of this world, and he is the world itself.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: To the changeless, pure, eternal Supreme Self;
Salutation to Viṣṇu, who is of eternally uniform form, the conqueror of all.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara;
to Vāsudeva, the Savior, who brings about the preservation and the end of all things.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, who possesses the nature of both the one and the many, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and whose form is both unmanifest and manifest.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is himself composed of the world.
Having bowed down to the Imperishable, the Supreme Person, who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and who dwells within all beings; ViP_1.2.5.
That which is, in ultimate reality, the very nature of knowledge and absolutely pure,
appears through erroneous perception as having the nature of an object.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu— the devourer of the universe, the Lord of its maintenance and creation, the sovereign of the worlds, unborn, undecaying, and immutable— [he spoke].
I shall relate how, in the past, when questioned by Dakṣa and other most excellent sages, the Blessed One, the lotus-born Grandfather, spoke.
And they told it to King Purukutsa on the banks of the Narmadā;
he, in turn, told it to Sārasvata, and by that Sārasvata, it was told to me.
He is the highest of the high, the supreme Self abiding within the self;
He is devoid of all specific designations such as form, color, and other such qualifiers.
He who is devoid of diminution, destruction, transformation, increase, and birth can be described only as "always existing."
Because he dwells everywhere and everything dwells within him,
for that reason he is recited by the wise as Vāsudeva.
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
it is always of a single nature and stainless because there is nothing to be discarded.
All this is indeed that very same [reality], possessing the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time.
O twice-born one, Puruṣa is the first form of the supreme Brahman;
likewise, the manifest and the unmanifest are other forms, and time is yet another.
That which is the supreme among primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), the manifest (vyakta), and time (kāla)—
that pure state which the wise behold is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla, according to their respective divisions,
are the causes of the existence of forms and of the states of maintenance, dissolution, and manifestation.
The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and even Time—behold his activity, which is like that of a playing child. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2.18)
That which is the unmanifest cause is called *pradhāna* by the best of sages; it is the subtle primordial nature (*prakṛti*), eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
It is inexhaustible, without any other support, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal;
it is devoid of sound and touch, and is not composed of form or the other [sensory qualities].
That womb of the world, which is composed of the three qualities and is without beginning in its origin and dissolution,
pervaded everything at the outset, even after the dissolution.
O learned one, those who know the declarations of the Vedas, who are self-restrained, and who discourse upon Brahman,
recite this very same meaning which establishes the Pradhāna.
There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth; there was no darkness nor light, nor anything else.
At that time, the Supreme Brahman alone existed—the Primal Being, unperceivable by the intellect through the senses such as hearing. ViP_1.2.23.
O Brahmin, two forms, Pradhāna and Puruṣa, have arisen beyond the essential nature (svarūpa) of Viṣṇu;
O twice-born one, when those two are held apart by him through another form, that other form of his is designated as Time (kāla).
That which was manifest and established in primordial nature (prakṛti) during the past dissolution is therefore called the "primordial" (prākṛta) reabsorption (pratisaṃcara).
O twice-born one, the Blessed Time is beginningless and its end does not exist;
therefore, these processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution proceed without interruption.
Then, O Maitreya, while that equilibrium of the qualities remains established separately from the Person (puruṣa), the nature of time belonging to that Viṣṇu revolves.
Then that Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, who consists of the universe, who is all-pervading, the Lord of all beings, the Soul of all, the Supreme Lord; // ViP_1,2.28 //
And when the time for creation had arrived, Hari, by his own will, entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the perishable and the imperishable— and agitated them.
Just as a fragrance causes agitation by its mere presence,
even though it does not actively assist the mind, so too is that Supreme Lord.
O Brahmin, that very Puruṣottama is both the agitator and the object of agitation;
he abides even in the state of Pradhāna through the processes of contraction and expansion.
And likewise, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, exists both as the nature of the expansion and the subtle, as well as in the form of Brahman and so forth, and as the manifest form.

Therefore, O sage, best of the twice-born, from that state where the gunas are in equilibrium, once presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), there arises at the time of creation the manifestation of the gunas.
The principle of Pradhāna, having manifested, enveloped the Mahat;
and that Mahat is threefold: consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Together with the principle of Pradhāna, he is enveloped like a seed by its skin;
these are Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi, which is indeed Tāmasa.
This threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) was born from the principle of the Great One (mahattattva);
it is the cause of the apprehension of the senses because it consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), O great sage.
Just as the Great One was enveloped by Pradhāna, so too is that [ego] enveloped by the Great One.
Then the *bhūtādi*, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*);
from that subtle element of sound, it created space, which is characterized by sound.
Space, which consists of sound alone, enveloped that [subtle element] consisting of the gross elements;
then space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch.
The wind became powerful, and its touch is considered subtle;
space, consisting of sound alone, then enveloped the element of touch alone.
Then the wind, undergoing transformation, emitted the subtle element of form;
light was produced from the wind, and it is said that its quality is form.
The wind, indeed, enveloped the mere element of touch;
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the mere element of taste.
From that, waters arose which were the supports of taste;
those waters consisted of the subtle element of taste alone, and [the ego] enveloped the subtle element of form.
The waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate (the earth) is born, and fragrance is considered its quality.
In each of those [subtle elements], there is only that [specific quality]; therefore, they are known as "tanmātras" (the state of being merely that).
The subtle elements are non-specific; therefore, they are called "non-specific."
They are neither peaceful nor wise, nor are they deluded or undifferentiated;
this creation of the gross elements and subtle essences proceeds from the tamasic ego.
They say the ten sense organs are the deities born of *tejas*,
while the eleventh, the mind, is here recorded as the deity born of *vaikārika* (the mode of goodness).
O twice-born one, my skin, eyes, nose, tongue, and ears— these five, joined with the intellect, exist here for the purpose of perceiving sound and the other sense objects.
O Maitreya, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth— these are said to be the organs,
and their functions are excretion, procreation, manipulation, locomotion, and speaking.
O Brahmin, space, wind, fire, water, and earth are each joined with their respective qualities, beginning with sound, in successive order.
They are remembered as being distinguished by that [quality] into the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded.
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create living beings without a collective effort, as they had not come together in their entirety.
Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent,
they form a single composite whole, attaining complete unity.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of Pradhāna,
they produce the cosmic egg, beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣas).
Gradually increased by that process, O great-minded one, a cosmic egg was formed from the elements, resembling a water bubble; it rested upon the waters and was the primordial,
unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu in his form as Brahmā.
There, that Lord of the World, Viṣṇu, who is both unmanifest in his essential nature and manifest in his form, abides by himself in the form of Brahmā.
The navel-string of that Great-Souled One became Mount Meru, the mountains became his placenta,
and the oceans were the amniotic fluid of that supreme being.
O Brahmin, within that egg were contained the mountains, islands, and oceans, along with the collection of worlds including the luminaries, as well as gods, asuras, and humans.

Then the egg is surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, each ten times greater than the preceding; and the egg is likewise surrounded by the source of the elements (bhūtādi), which in turn is surrounded by the Great Principle (mahat).
O Brahman, the Great One (Mahat), together with all those [elements], is enveloped by the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
This cosmic egg is covered by these seven natural coverings,
just as the seed within a coconut fruit is enclosed by its outer husks.
Delighting in the quality of rajas there, Hari himself, the Lord of the Universe,
becomes Brahmā and proceeds with the creation of this world.
And having created [the world],
the Lord Viṣṇu, whose prowess is immeasurable, protects it age after age until the end of the kalpa-cycle.
And at the end of the kalpa, Jṛmbhaṇa, in the form of Rudra, overflowing with darkness and exceedingly terrible,
devours all living beings, O Maitreya.
And having devoured all beings when the world has been reduced to a single atom,
the Supreme Lord reclines upon his serpent-couch.
And having awakened, he again effects creation, assuming the form of Brahmā.
The Lord Janārdana, though he is one alone, assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who perform the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction.
As the Creator, he creates himself; as Viṣṇu, he protects that which is to be protected;
and at the end, the Lord himself withdraws it and acts as the Destroyer.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as all the senses and the internal organ— that world which is indeed designated as the Puruṣa.
He alone is the self of all beings, the universal form, from whom he is imperishable; yet his very nature, abiding within all beings, performs the creation and other acts for their benefit.
He alone is the object of creation and He is the creator; He alone sustains and devours, and He is sustained Himself.
With all forms through states beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu is the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the one worthy of being sought.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Maitreya said:
[Tell me] of Him who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and whose nature is stainless.
How is the status of being the creator of the creation and so forth attributed to Brahman?
Śrī Parāśara said: Since the powers of all entities fall within the scope of inconceivable knowledge,
therefore the powers of existence, such as creation and the rest, belong to Brahman.
O best of those who radiate heat, they exist just as heat exists in fire.
Understand how that Blessed One,
known as Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, proceeds at the time of creation.
O learned one, he is always spoken of as "born" only in a figurative sense.
By its own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years;
that is called a *para*, and half of that is designated as a *parārdha*.
O sinless one, understand from that which I have told you regarding the nature of time and of Viṣṇu, the demonstration of its measurement.
And also of other beings, both those that move and those that are stationary—
of the earth, the mountains, the oceans, and all others without exception, O best of men.
O best of sages, fifteen nimeṣas are said to constitute one kāṣṭhā;
thirty kāṣṭhās make one kalā, and thirty kalās constitute the duration of a muhūrta.
A human day and night is said to consist of that same number of muhūrtas;
a month, consisting of two fortnights, comprises that same number of days and nights.
By those six months, an *ayana* (solstice) is formed; two *ayanās*, the southern and the northern, constitute a year (*varṣa*).
The southern *ayana* is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day.
A cycle of four ages, known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consists of twelve thousand divine years; learn from me their specific divisions.
Those who know the past have declared that in the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, the durations are respectively four, three, two, and one thousand years of the twice-born.
The preceding twilight is said to consist of as many hundreds of years as those [thousand],
and the subsequent twilight of the Yuga is likewise equal to that number.
O best of sages, that period of time which lies between the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the twilight-interval (saṃdhyāṃśa) is to be known as the "yuga," designated by the names Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali together constitute the four ages;
O Sage, a thousand such cycles are declared to be a single day of Brahmā.
During the day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus;
hear now about their transformation brought about by time.
The seven ṛṣis, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons, the kings,
are indeed created at one and the same time, and are likewise withdrawn, as before.
O best of beings, a period consisting of seventy-one cycles of four yugas, plus a little more, is called a Manvantara, the time of a Manu and of the gods and others.
By divine reckoning, it is recorded as eight hundred thousand,
with an additional fifty-two thousand more.
O twice-born one, O great sage, they are calculated by number to be a full thirty crores, as well as sixty-seven other hundred-thousands (niyutas).
O twice-born one, twenty thousand years, without any addition,
is the reckoning of a *manvantara* by human years.
This period of fourteen guṇas is indeed remembered as a day of Brahmā;
at its conclusion occurs the dissolution known as the "occasional" (naimittika) of Brahmā.
For then the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvar, is consumed by fire;
and the inhabitants of Maharloka, afflicted by the heat, depart for Jana-loka.
When the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa,
lies upon the bed of the serpent, nourished by the swallowing of the triple world.
O God, while being meditated upon by the yogis dwelling in Janaloka,
he who is born from the lotus creates [the world] again at the end of that night, which is of equal duration.
Thus is a year of Brahmā, and thus a hundred years;
for the lifespan of that great-souled one is indeed one hundred such years.
O sinless one, one half of Brahmā’s lifespan has already passed;
at its conclusion occurred the great kalpa renowned as the Pādma.
O twice-born one, this first Kalpa of the current second Parārdha is proclaimed as the Vārāha.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said: O Brahmin, [tell me] how that Lord, known as Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, [appeared] at the beginning of the kalpa.
He created all beings; tell that to me, O great sage.
Śrī Parāśara said: Listen to me as I describe how the Lord Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, the divine Lord of the Prajāpatis, created all beings.
At the conclusion of the past kalpa, the Lord Brahmā, having arisen from his night's sleep and being overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), beheld the world as empty.
Nārāyaṇa is supreme and inconceivable; he is the Lord even of those who are supreme.
The Blessed One, whose nature is Brahman, is without beginning and the source of all things.

And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman, the source and the dissolution of the world: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4.5: "They say that he who is the creator of the universe, who is the cause of its preservation and its destruction, who is the supreme lord of all worlds, and who is the eternal, immutable, and imperishable—him alone do the wise know as Nārāyaṇa."
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first place of motion (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Having realized through inference that the earth was situated within the waters when the world had been turned into a single ocean, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) desired to lift it up.
Just as in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas he assumed other bodies such as those of the Fish and the Tortoise, so too did he take recourse to the form of the Boar.

For the sake of the maintenance of the entire world, the Lord of Creatures, the Supreme Self, the Soul of All, whose nature is eternal, remains established as the form consisting of the Vedas and sacrifices.
Then, praised by the Siddhas such as Sanaka and others who had gone to Janaloka,
the Supporter of the Earth, whose own self is his support, entered the waters.
Then, beholding him who had arrived from the depths of Pātāla, the goddess Vasundharā,
bowing down and humbled by devotion, offered praise.
The illustrious Earth said:
"Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace!
Lift me up from this today; for I was raised by you in the past."
I was raised up by you in the past; I am composed of you, O Janārdana, as are all other beings, including the sky and everything else without exception.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Self, O Self of the individual soul, O Self of the Puruṣa; salutations be to you, who have become the Pradhāna and the Manifested, and who have become Time.
O Lord, you are the creator of all beings, their protector, and their destroyer;
at the beginning of creation and other cosmic cycles, you assume the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
After having consumed everything when the world has been turned into a single ocean,
you alone remain, O Govinda, being meditated upon by the wise.
No one knows that supreme reality which belongs to you;
the inhabitants of heaven worship only those forms which you assume in your incarnations.
Having propitiated you, the Supreme Brahman, those seeking liberation have attained release;
without propitiating Vāsudeva, who shall obtain liberation?
Whatever is to be grasped by the mind, whatever is to be grasped by the eyes and other senses,
and whatever is to be discerned by the intellect— all that form belongs entirely to you.
"I am composed of you, I have you as my support, I was created by you, and I have you as my refuge;
therefore, this world calls me 'Mādhavī'."

Victory to you who consist of all knowledge! Victory to you, the imperishable one composed of the gross! Victory to the infinite! Victory to the unmanifest! Victory to the Lord who consists of the manifest!
O Supreme and Inferior Self, O Universal Self, O Conqueror, O Lord of Sacrifice, O Sinless One!
You are the sacrifice; you are the *vaṣaṭkāra*; you are the *oṃkāra*; you are the sacred fires.
You are the Vedas, you are their auxiliary limbs, and you are the Person of Sacrifice, O Hari;
you are the sun and other planets, the stars, the lunar mansions, and the entire world contained within space.

O Supreme Person, O Supreme Lord, that which has form and that which is formless, that which is invisible and that which is visible, that which has been spoken by me here and that which has not been spoken—all that is You. Salutations to You; again and again, salutations unto You.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus being praised by the Earth,
the glorious upholder of the world roared with a deep, rumbling sound like the resonance of Sāman chants.
Then, having lifted up the earth with his tusk, the Great Boar, whose eyes were like blooming lotuses,
rose from the subterranean realm like a great mountain of sapphire, resembling the petals of a blue water-lily.

As he rose up, the water produced from that [lotus] was struck by the breath from his mouth and washed those highly effulgent sages— Sanandana and the others— who were free from all taint and dwelt in Janaloka.

As he proceeds, the waters, having suppressed the continuous roar [of the ocean] by the sound produced when the tips of his hooves strike the surface of the netherworld (rasātala), flow away on all sides, driven by the wind of his breath; and the Siddhas who dwell there, being self-restrained, depart.
As the Great Boar, his flanks still wet with water, rises up having grasped the earth and shakes his body composed of the Vedas, the sages dwelling within the pores of his hair offer hymns of praise.

Then those yogis who dwell among the people of the world, their hearts overcome with devotion, praised him along with Sanandana and others; with heads deeply bowed, they lauded the Upholder of the Earth, whose steady gaze was both profound and majestic.
O Supreme Lord of lords, Keśava, Master, wielder of the mace, conch, sword, and discus;
You alone are the Lord who is the cause of birth, destruction, and sustenance. There is nothing else that is higher than Your supreme state.

The Vedas are your feet, O Lord, and the sacrificial posts are your fangs; the *jajñas* are in your teeth and the sacrificial altars (*citayas*) are in your mouth; you have fire for your tongue, the *darbha* grasses for the hair on your body—you alone, O Master, are the Person of Sacrifice (*Yajñapumān*).
O Great-Souled One, night and day are Your two eyes; the supreme Brahman, the refuge of all, is Your head;
O God, the entire collection of hymns is the mass of Your mane, and all sacrificial oblations are Your sense of smell.

O God, whose body is the sacrificial hall (*prāgvaṃśa*) and whose joints are the various *satra* sacrifices, with a voice as steady as the sound of the *mukha*, *tuṇḍa*, and *sāman* chants; O Lord, eternal Self, you who are the hearing of the merit of *pūrta* and *iṣṭa* rites—be gracious!
O you whose form is the universe of syllables, we know you to be the one who stands at the beginning, whose feet have traversed the earth;
you are the Supreme Lord of the universe. Be gracious, for you are our protector, both the highest and the lowest.
O Lord, this entire circle of the earth is perceived by you as resting upon the tips of your fangs,
like a lotus leaf covered in mud when you plunge into a lotus grove.
O Lord of incomparable power, that space between heaven and earth is pervaded by your very body;
O All-pervading One, whose radiant splendor is capable of filling the universe, become the benefactor of the whole world.
O Lord of the world, you alone are the ultimate reality; there is no other.
This entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by your own majesty.
This which is seen as a material form belongs to you, whose self is knowledge;
those who are not yogis perceive it in the form of the world through erroneous cognition.
Those of unawakened intellect, perceiving this entire universe— which is in its true nature pure consciousness— as being composed of material objects, wander in the deluge of ignorance.
But those who know through wisdom and possess pure minds perceive the entire world as consisting of knowledge— your very form, O Supreme Lord.
Be gracious, O All, O Soul of all! For the welfare of the worlds, lift up this earth, O Immeasurable One;
grant us shelter, O Lotus-eyed One.
"O Blessed One, Govinda, you are preeminent in the quality of goodness (sattva); O Lord, lift up this earth!
O lotus-eyed one, grant us protection."
May this engagement in creation of yours, which is beneficial to the worlds, come to pass;
salutations to you! O lotus-eyed one, grant us prosperity.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus being praised, the Supreme Self, the upholder of the earth,
quickly raised the earth and placed it upon the great waters.
Upon that flood of water, the earth stands like a boat capable of bearing the weight;
yet, because the body [of the world] is so vast, the earth does not undergo submersion.
Then, having leveled the earth, the Lord, the beginningless Supreme Sovereign, arranged the mountains upon the ground according to their respective divisions.
With his unfailing power, he whose desires were never in vain created all the mountains upon the surface of the earth, which had been burnt during the previous dissolution.
Then, having divided the earth into its seven continents exactly as they are,
he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before.
Then that Lord Hari, assuming the form of Brahmā and enveloped by the quality of passion (rajas),
being the four-faced one, performed the work of creation.
He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating those things to be created,
since the powers of the objects to be created are indeed the primary causes.
"O best of those who radiate heat, having set aside the mere sign (nimitta), nothing else is required; a thing is led to its true state of being by its own power."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Elevation of the Earth," in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said: "In what manner did that Lord create the gods, ṛṣis, ancestors, and givers?"
Humans, animals, trees, and so forth, as well as those dwelling on earth, in the sky, and in the waters.
O twice-born one, tell me in its entirety what qualities, what nature, and what form the world had when Brahmā created it at the beginning of the creation.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen with a well-composed mind as I relate how that all-pervading Lord created the gods and all other beings.
As he was contemplating creation as it had been in the past at the beginning of the kalpas,
a creation consisting of darkness (tamas) appeared, arising without prior conscious intent.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and indeed andhatāmisra—
this fivefold ignorance arose from the Great Soul.
The creation existing in five states is conscious for one who meditates;
it is without external or internal light, its nature being concealed and consisting of immobile beings.
Since the principal mountains were spoken of first, this is therefore called the primary creation (mukhya-sarga).
Having seen that unsuccessful creation, he then thought of another one again.
As he was thus meditating, a creation consisting of those who flow horizontally (tiryak-strotas) emerged;
because its movement was directed horizontally, it is therefore known as Tiryak-strotas.
These are known as beasts and the like; they consist mostly of darkness, are devoid of knowledge, follow wrong paths, and, being ignorant, imagine themselves to possess knowledge.
Pervaded by egoism and characterized by the twenty-eight forms of self-conceit (ahaṃmāna),
all these [evolutes] are luminous, yet they mutually obscure one another.
Considering that [the fire] also to be ineffective, another arose from him as he meditated;
the third was Tretā, which was sattvic and moved upwards.
Abounding in happiness and joy, they were unobstructed both internally and externally;
being luminous within and without, they are remembered as those born from the upward-streaming class.
With their souls satisfied, that third creation is known as the divine (deva-sarga);
when that creation was accomplished, there was then joy for Brahmā.
Then,
having realized that those born from the primary creation and the others were ineffective, he meditated upon another, superior creation that would be effective.
As he was thus meditating with truthful intent,
there emerged from the Unmanifest the effective fire of the Tretā age.
Because they turned back from that point, they are called arvākstrotas (those with downward-flowing currents);
they are characterized by an abundance of light, yet are dominated by darkness and an excess of passion (rajas).
Therefore, those humans who perform [their duties] repeatedly and with great effort,
being manifest both outwardly and inwardly, are indeed practitioners (sādhakas).
Thus, O best of sages, these six creations have been described here;
the first is to be known as the creation of Mahat, which belongs to Brahmā.
The second creation is indeed known as that of the subtle elements (tanmātra),
while the third creation is known as the elemental (bhūta) and the sensory (indriyaka), which is the transformational (vaikārika).
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) arose preceded by intelligence;
the fourth, however, is the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), for the immobile beings are indeed known as the "primary" ones.
That which is called the horizontal-stream (tiryakstrotas) is said to be the animal creation (tairyagyonya);
the sixth, however, is traditionally remembered as the divine creation (devasarga) of those with upward-streams (ūrdhvastrotas).
Then followed the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is the human race.
The eighth is the creation of grace, which is both characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).
These five are known as the secondary creations (vaikṛta), while three are considered primary creations (prākṛta).
The Prākṛta, the Vaikṛta, and the Kaumāra is recorded as the ninth;
thus indeed these nine creations of Prajāpati have been fully described.
The primary and secondary elements are indeed the root causes of the world for the Lord of the World as he creates it; what else do you wish to hear?
The illustrious Maitreya said:
"O Sage, you have described the creation of the gods and others in brief;
O best of eminent sages, I wish to hear it from you in detail."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Perfumed by their previous virtuous deeds, those [beings] are indeed virtuous;
yet, not being liberated from that very fame, they are withdrawn at the time of dissolution.
The fourfold progeny, beginning with the gods and ending with the immovable beings,
were born as mental creations from Brahmā while he was performing the act of creation.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold [world]— the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans— he joined his own self to these waters.
For the Prajāpati, whose self was disciplined, the quality of darkness (tamas) became predominant;
from his posterior, as he desired to create, the Asuras were first born.
Then he cast off that body whose nature consists of the quality of darkness (tamas); O Maitreya, that manifested body became the night.
Desiring to create while residing within another body, he then attained joy; from the mouth of Brahmā, O twice-born one, the gods were born, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva).
Having abandoned even that body, the day became filled with the quality of goodness (sattva);
for the asuras are strong at night, while the gods are strong by day.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of sattva;
as he regarded it as his father, from that [body] his ancestors were born.
Then, even after having created the ancestors, that Lord released her;
and once released, she became the twilight (saṃdhyā), situated between day and night.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas;
from that, O best of the twice-born, human beings were born, characterized by the predominance of rajas alone.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) also quickly abandoned that body;
it immediately became the moonlight, which is designated as the morning twilight.
O Maitreya, humans are strong at the onset of moonlight, and likewise the ancestors are strong at the time of twilight; therefore, these [two groups] indeed prevail during those times.
Moonlight, night, day, and twilight— these four, O Lord,
are indeed the bodies of Brahmā, which rest upon the three guṇas.
Thereafter, he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of passion (rajas);
from that, hunger arose in Brahmā, and from her, desire was born.
Then, in the darkness, the Blessed One created those emaciated by hunger;
they were born with hideous forms and beards, and they rushed toward the Lord.
"Do not do so, sirs; let him be protected. Those who said this were called *rākṣasas*.
Others said, "We shall devour him," and they were the *yakṣas*, so called from the act of eating (*jakṣaṇāt*).
But seeing them with displeasure, the hair of the Creator fell out;
and being deprived of their place on the head, they grew back again upon that same head.

Because of their crawling (*sarpaṇa*), they became serpents (*sarpas*); because of their inferiority, they are known as *ahis*. Then the Creator of the world, being enraged, produced from his anger those fierce flesh-eaters with a brownish hue.
O twice-born one, at that very moment, the Gandharvas were born from his meditative limb;
they were born drinking his speech, and for that reason they are called Gandharvas.
Having created these, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, impelled by that power,
then spontaneously created other birds from his own body.
From his chest, Prajāpati created Apas; from his mouth, he created Agni;
from his belly, he created the waters (Sarasvatī); and from his two sides, he created the cows.
And from his two feet [he created] horses along with elephants, donkeys, gavayas, deer,
camels, mules, nyankus, and other species.

At the beginning of the Kalpa, O best of the twice-born, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga, Brahmā produced herbs with roots and fruits from his body hairs; having created them, he then properly employed them in the sacrifice.
The cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule, and donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn from me those that are wild.
Wild beasts, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth;
aquatic creatures as the sixth class of animals, and reptiles as the seventh.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī, the Ṛg-veda, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteen-fold Stoma, as well as the Bṛhat Sāman and the Uktha.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman chants, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
From his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmāṇa, as well as the Anuṣṭubh and the Vairāja meters.
Having created the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans, Prajāpati produced from his limbs various beings, both high and low.
Then, at the beginning, the Grandfather again created from his volition the Yakṣas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases.
He created the hell-beings, kinnaras, and rakshasas; birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents; and all that is stationary and moving, both the imperishable and the perishable.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the original creator and sovereign, emitted them;
whatever actions they had undertaken in a previous creation,
those very same actions they assume again and again as they are created anew.

Whether violent or non-violent, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, true or false—impregnated by those very qualities, beings enter [into new births]; therefore, that which they have been conditioned to prefer is what pleases them.
In the sense objects, the elements, and the bodies, that Lord,
the Creator himself, thus released diversity and their respective functions.
In the beginning, he fashioned from the words of the Veda itself the names and forms of all beings, as well as the expansion of their activities, for the gods and others.
Just as the names of the sages were indeed heard in the Vedas, he likewise assigned appropriate names for others as well.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons are seen to recur in each season,
so too do all things appear in the same way at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Thus, at the beginning of each kalpa, he repeatedly creates such a world;
endowed with the power of the desire to create, he is impelled by the creative power inherent in that which is to be created.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said:
You have described that human race which flows downwards.
O Brahman, tell me in detail how Brahmā created that darkness.
Tell us how Prajāpati created the social classes and their respective qualities,
and what the traditional duties of those beginning with the Brahmins are said to be.
Śrī Parāśara said: O best of the twice-born, when Brahmā first desired to create the world while meditating upon Truth, beings characterized by an abundance of *sattva* were born from his mouth.
From the chest of Brahmā, those characterized by an abundance of rajas were born;
likewise, from his thighs, those characterized by an abundance of both rajas and tamas were produced.
O best of the twice-born, Brahmā created other beings from his feet;
they were all dominated by tamas, and from them arose this fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya).
O best of the twice-born, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
and Śūdras emerged from his feet, thighs, chest, and mouth respectively.
O highly fortunate one, Brahmā indeed created all this—
the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya)— as the supreme means for accomplishing sacrifice.
O knower of dharma, the gods, nourished by sacrifices, nourish the subjects through the release of rain; thus sacrifices are the cause of all prosperity.
These are always brought about by those men who are devoted to their own duty,
who are endowed with pure conduct, who are virtuous, and who walk upon the path of the righteous.
O Sage, O twice-born one, through human birth men attain both heaven and liberation; they go to whatever other desired state is appropriate for them.
O best of sages, those creatures created by Brahmā were established in the system of the four castes; they possessed perfect faith and were devoted to right conduct.
Delighting in the dwelling of their own desires, free from all afflictions, pure in their inner faculties, purified, and stainless through the performance of their duties; ||| ViP_1,6.12 |||
And when their minds are purified and Hari is established within them,
they perceive pure knowledge called Bilva, by which that supreme state is attained.
Then, that which is the soul of time is said to be a portion of Hari;
it causes even a terrible sin to fall away, becoming exceedingly diminished in its potency.
O Maitreya, among those creatures, the seed of unrighteousness arose— born of darkness and greed— which, consisting of passion and other such qualities, was ineffective for achieving their goals.
Then, that innate perfection (sahajā siddhi) does not arise excessively for them;
rather, there are the other eight perfections, such as the exhilaration of rasa (rasollāsa) and so forth.
When those [virtues] have been entirely exhausted and sin is increasing,
the people then become afflicted by the suffering of being overwhelmed by the pairs of opposites (dvandva).
Then they constructed fortresses— namely, those in the desert, on mountains, and by water—
as well as artificial fortifications such as cities, market towns, and the like.
And for those cities and other settlements,
O Mahāmati, they established dwellings according to the rules in order to alleviate the afflictions of cold, heat, and so forth.
Having provided this remedy for cold and other afflictions,
those subjects then established the means of livelihood and manual crafts born of labor.
Rice, barley, wheat, chickpeas, sesame seeds, millet,
udāra grains, koradūṣa, and satīnaka beans.
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas, āḍhakīs, caṇakas, and śaṇas—these are recorded as the seventeen [types of pulses]. (ViP 1.6.22)
O Sage, these are the species of cultivated herbs;
there are fourteen types of herbs, both sacrificial and belonging to the village and the forest.
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, small grains, sesame seeds, and priyaṅgu as the seventh—these are they; and lentils are the eighth.
Furthermore, O Sage, śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka, as well as veṇuyava and markaṭaka are prescribed [as food].
These fourteen medicinal plants are indeed known as both cultivated and wild;
they exist for the accomplishment of sacrifice, and sacrifice is likewise their supreme cause.
These, along with sacrifice, are the supreme cause of all creatures;
therefore, the wise who know the higher and the lower should perform sacrifices.
O best of sages, the daily performance of sacrifices is beneficial for men;
when performed, it bestows prosperity and peace.
But those for whom that kinsman of evil, sent by Time, O great sage,
grew within their hearts, did not set their minds upon sacrifices.
Those who obstructed sacrifices censured all the declarations of the Vedas, as well as the Vedas themselves and whatever ritual acts such as sacrifice there might be.
They became destroyers of the path of worldly activity,
revilers of the Vedas, evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and crooked in their intentions.
Once the means of subsistence were fully established, Prajāpati, having created living beings,
ordained the boundaries of conduct according to their respective places and qualities.
O best of the upholders of dharma, [you shall describe] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life,
as well as the worlds of all the castes who correctly follow their respective dharmas.
The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brahmins who perform their duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battles.
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who follow their own dharma;
that of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who are devoted to service.
It is recorded that the abode of the eighty-eight thousand sages who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is the very same as that of those who dwell with their teacher.
The station of the Seven Sages is indeed remembered as that of the forest-dwellers;
that of the householder stage belongs to Prajāpati, while that of the renunciants is designated as Brahman.
The immortal state belongs to the yogins who find contentment within their own selves.
But for those who are single-mindedly devoted, who always meditate upon Brahman, and who are yogis—
for them there is that supreme abode which the wise behold.
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again;
yet those who contemplate the twelve-syllable mantra do not return even to this day.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the terrible Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci.
This place is declared to be for those who revile the Veda, those who obstruct sacrifices, and those who abandon their own dharma.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born to him.
From the limbs of that wise one, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged together with those effects and instruments produced from his body.
All those whom I previously mentioned returned—
the gods and others down to the stationary beings— all remaining within the sphere of the three qualities (guṇas).
In this manner were created all beings, both moving and stationary.
When all those creatures of that wise one did not multiply,
he then created other mind-born sons who were like himself.
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras,
Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these were his mind-born sons.
"These are the nine Brahmās," so it is established in the Purāṇa.
Khyāti, Bhūti, Saṃbhūti, Kṣamā, Prīti, as well as Sannati, Urjā, and likewise Anasūyā.
Then, having created Prasūti, he gave her to those great-souled ones,
saying, "Be you their wives," and thus bestowed her upon them.
And those such as Sanandana and others who were previously created by the Creator did not become attached to the worlds, for they were indifferent toward progeny.
All those great-souled ones had attained knowledge, were free from passion, and devoid of envy; thus they remained indifferent toward the creation of the world.

O Sage, a great wrath arose in Brahmā, capable of consuming the three worlds. From that wrath, O Sage, the entire triple world then became intensely illuminated by garlands of flames that had burst forth from him.
Then, from his forehead, which was furrowed with a frown and inflamed by anger,
Rudra emerged, possessing a radiance equal to the midday sun.
Then Brahmā, having said to that Pracaṇḍa— who possessed a body half-female and half-male and was exceedingly large-bodied— "Divide yourself," disappeared from that place.
Thus addressed, he divided his female nature and male nature in two ways; he further divided his male nature tenfold and then again into a single unit.
Then that Lord divided his womanhood into many forms— gentle and fierce, peaceful and unpeaceful— into dark and light manifestations, O gods.
Then, O twice-born one, the Lord Brahmā, who was born of himself, first created Manu Svāyambhuva as his very self for the protection of creatures.
And the lord Svāyambhuva Manu took that woman Śatarūpā, whose impurities had been washed away by austerity, as his wife.
From that Puruṣa, however, the goddess Śatarūpā was born;
she gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, known as Prasūti and Ākūti.
O knower of dharma, in ancient times he gave two daughters, Prasūti and Ākūti, both endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, to Dakṣa and Ruci respectively.
Prajāpati took hold of them; from those two was born his son Dakṣiṇa at the sacrifice, O fortunate one, and from that couple a pair of twins was produced.
From the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the sacrifice, twelve sons were born;
they are known as the Yāma gods among the deities in the period of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
And likewise, O Dakṣa, at her birth, he begot twenty-four daughters; hear from me their names correctly.
Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Intelligence, Nourishment, as well as Action, Wisdom, Modesty, Form, Peace, Success, and Fame as the thirteenth.
The lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives;
from among them, eleven younger sisters remained, all of whom were beautiful-eyed.
Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Pīti, Kṣamā,
as well as Santati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā.
Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, as well as the sage Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu, the best among sages; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.7.26.
O best of sages, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs, in due order, took Khyāti and the other daughters as wives.
Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; Dhṛti, who was born of the Self, gave birth to Darpam and Niyama; Tuṣṭi gave birth to Saṃtoṣa; and Puṣṭi gave birth to Lobha.
Intelligence, sacred learning, ritual action, punishment, policy, and discipline as well.
Buddhi gave birth to Bodha, as well as Lajjā, Vinaya, Vapus, Ātmaja, Vyavasāya, Kṣema, and Śānti begat Prasāda.
Sukha, Siddhi, Yaśas, and Kīrti—these were the sons of Dharma;
from Kāma, Rati gave birth to a son, Harṣa, who was the grandson of Dharma.
Violence was the wife of Adharma; from them were born Untruth and the daughter Nikṛti, and from those two were born Illusion and Pain.
Māyā and Vedanā indeed formed a pair;
from those two, Māyā gave birth to Mṛtyu, the destroyer of living beings.
Then from Raurava, Vedanā gave birth to Duḥkha (Suffering),
and from Mṛtyu (Death) were born Vyādhi (Disease), Jarā (Old Age), Śoka (Grief), Tṛṣṇā (Thirst), and Krodha (Anger).
For all these are remembered as being characterized by suffering and marked by unrighteousness;
they have neither sons nor wives, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
O son of the best of sages, these forms of Viṣṇu are indeed fierce;
they truly become the cause of the constant dissolution of this world.
O highly fortunate one, Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Bhṛgu, and the other lords of progeny are the causes of the eternal creation in this world.
The Manus, the sons of Manu, and those kings who possess valor—
all those heroes devoted to the path of the righteous are the upholders of the world's stability.
The venerable Maitreya said:
O Brahmin, this eternal state has been described by you, as well as the eternal creation and their eternal non-existence; pray tell me their true nature.

Śrī Parāśara said: The Lord Madhusūdana, the all-pervading one whose nature is inconceivable, performs the creation, maintenance, and destruction [of the world] through various forms, remaining unimpeded.
O twice-born one, this dissolution of all beings is fourfold: occasional, elemental, ultimate, and eternal.
There, the Lord of the World shall bring about this occasional dissolution of Brahmā;
and the cosmic egg itself goes to dissolution within primordial nature.
Through knowledge, the ultimate [liberation] of the yogi in the Supreme Self is proclaimed;
for all beings, there is a constant destruction day and night.
That which is the manifestation of Prakṛti is known as the Prākṛta creation;
it is likewise called the daily creation, occurring after the intermediate dissolution (nāntarapralaya).
O best of sages, that place where beings are born every day is called the "eternal creation" (nityasarga) by those expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas.
In this way, the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the creator of beings, abiding within all bodies, performs their creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Maitreya, the powers of creation, maintenance, and destruction belonging to Viṣṇu revolve day and night within all embodied beings.
Indeed, that which consists of the three qualities is this Great One, the triple power;
he who transcends it truly goes to the Supreme and does not return again.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Śrī Parāśara said: O great sage, the Tāmasa creation of Brahmā has been described to you.
I shall proclaim the creation of Rudra; listen to me as I speak it.
Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord meditated upon a son equal to himself,
a blue-and-red youth appeared upon his lap.
Then he wept with a melodious voice and ran away, O best of the twice-born;
to him as he was weeping, Brahmā replied, "Why do you weep? 1.8.3.
Then Prajāpati replied to him, "Give me a name," and said, "By the name of the gods you are Rudra; you are Māra; maintain your fortitude.
Having been addressed thus, he wept seven times more.
Then the Lord gave him seven other names,
as well as the stations for these eight, their wives, and their sons.
Then, O twice-born one, that Grandfather spoke to Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, as well as Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva.
He established these names and assigned them their respective stations:
Sūrya, Jala, Mahī, Vāyu, Vahni, Ākāśa, Dīkṣita, Brahmaṇaspati, and Soma; these are his forms in due order.
Likewise Suvarcalā, Uṣā, Vikeśī, and the auspicious Aparā; then Svāhā, the Quarters (Diśas), Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī, in due order.
O best of the twice-born, O highly fortunate one, the wives of the Sun and the others are recorded along with the names of Rudra and the rest; now hear from me about their offspring.
By their births and progeny, this world was filled.
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava,
Skanda, Sarga, Santāna, and Budha were his sons in due order.
Rudra, being of such a nature, married Satī, the blameless daughter of the patriarch Dakṣa himself,
as his wife.
And due to Dakṣa’s wrath, Satī abandoned her own body;
O best of the twice-born, she was born as the daughter of Himavat from Menā.
Furthermore, the blessed Lord Hara married Umā, who was devoted to no other.
Khyāti bore to Bhṛgu two gods, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ,
as well as Śrī, who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa, the god of gods.
Śrī Maitreya said: It is heard that Śrī was born from the Ocean of Milk during the churning for nectar;
how is it that you say she was born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti?
Śrī Parāśara said:
O best of the twice-born, this Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu; as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is she.
Viṣṇu is wealth and this is speech; Hari is policy and this is conduct;
Viṣṇu is awakening and this is intellect; He is dharma and this is virtuous action.
Viṣṇu is the creator and this creation is Śrī; Bhūdhara is Hari, and the eternal Lakṣmī, O Maitreya, is the goddess Tuṣṭi, whose essence is contentment.
Desire is Śrī, the Blessed One is Kāma, he is the sacrifice, and she is the sacrificial fee;
this goddess is the oblation of clarified butter, and Janārdana is the sacrificial cake.

O Sage, Lakṣmī is the wife’s chamber (patnīśālā), and Madhusūdana is the eastern hall (prāgvaṃśa); Cit is Lakṣmī, Hari is the sacrificial post (yūpa), Śrī is the fuel (idhmā), and the Blessed One is the kuśa grass.
The Lord is the essence of the Sāman chants; Udgīti is Kamalālayā;
Svāhā is Lakṣmī; and Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, is the consumer of oblations (Agni).
O best of the twice-born, Maitreya, the Lord Śaṅkara is Śauri, and Gaurī is Lakṣmī; Keśava is the Sun, and his radiance is the lotus-dwelling goddess.
Viṣṇu is the host of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa), Padmā is the eternal bestower of nourishment (svadhā),
Dyauḥ is Śrī, and Viṣṇu, who is the soul of all, is the vast expanse of space.
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Kānti, and likewise Śrī who is never-failing;
Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Jagacceṣṭā, Vāyu, and the omnipresent Hari.
O great sage, the ocean was Dvija-Govinda, its shore was Śrī,
Lakṣmī was his essential form, Indrāṇī was Devendra, and Madhusūdana was the Lord of the Gods.
Yama was the wielder of the discus in person, and Dhūmorṇā was Kamalālayā;
Ṛddhi was Śrī, and the god Dhaneśvara was Śrīdhara himself.
Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and the highly blessed Mahābhāgā; Keśava himself, Varuṇa, Śrī, Devasenā, O best of Brahmins, and Hari, the commander of the divine army.
O best of the twice-born, Avaṣṭambha is Gadāpāṇi; Śakti is Lakṣmī;
Kāṣṭhā is Lakṣmī; he is Nimeṣa, he is Muhūrta, and she is Kalā.
The moonlight is Lakṣmī, and that lamp is Hari, the Lord of all;
Śrī, the mother of the world, has become the creeper, while Viṣṇu is designated as the tree.
The night was Śrī, and the day was Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus and mace;
he is the boon-granting suitor, and she is the bride who dwells within the lotus grove.
The Blessed One has the form of the Nanda [elephant], while Śrī is established in the form of the river;
the banner is the lotus-eyed one (Puṇḍarīkākṣa), and the flag is she whose abode is the lotus (Kamalālayā).
Thirst is Lakṣmī, O Maitreya, and the Lord of the World is the supreme Nārāyaṇa; passion is Rati, and Govinda is indeed Lakṣmī.
Moreover, what is the use of saying too much? This is stated in brief:
Among gods, animals, humans, and others, the Blessed Lord Hari is to be known by masculine names, and Śrī by feminine names; beyond these two, nothing else exists.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"And hear this, O Maitreya, which I have been asked by you here."
Even Māyā heard this glorious account of the lineage from Marīci.
Durvāsas, an emanation of Śaṅkara, was wandering this earth;
that seer beheld a divine garland in the hand of a Vidyādharī.
O Brahmin, that entire forest of the forest-dwellers became exceedingly pleasant to frequent because it was perfumed by the fragrance of the *saṃtānaka* trees.
Then a brahmin observing the vow of a madman, seeing that beautiful garland,
requested it from that lovely-limbed wife of a Vidyādhara.
Requested by him, that slender-limbed, large-eyed Vidyādhara woman respectfully prostrated before him and gave him the garland.
Taking that garland and placing it upon his own head, O Maitreya, that brahmin, assuming the appearance of a madman, wandered the earth.
He beheld that lord of the three worlds, the god Śacīpati, approaching together with the deities, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata who appeared like one mad.
Taking that garland from his own head, which was swarming with intoxicated bees,
the sage cast it toward the king of the gods like one who has lost his mind.
Having taken it, the king of the gods placed the garland upon the head of Airāvata;
it shone like the Gaṅgā upon the peak of Kailāsa.
With his eyes blinded by intoxication, that elephant, drawn by the fragrance,
sniffed the garland with his trunk and flung it onto the surface of the earth.
Thereupon the blessed Durvāsas, the best of sages, became enraged;
and being angry, O Maitreya, he spoke thus to the king of the gods.
Durvāsas said:
"O Vāsava, your soul is corrupted by the intoxication of power;
you are exceedingly arrogant, since you do not welcome the garland given by me, which is the very abode of prosperity."
You did not say "I am pleased" preceded by a prostration, nor was it accepted with a head bowed and cheeks blooming with joy. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9.13)
"Since you do not hold in high regard this garland given by me,
O fool, the splendor of the three worlds shall therefore meet its destruction."
"You surely consider me to be like those other twice-born ones who are superior to Śakra;
therefore, you, being arrogant, have shown us contempt."
"O Madatta, because you have cast this garland upon the ground,
the three worlds shall become bereft of prosperity for you."
When I am provoked to anger, all that moves and is stationary trembles with fear;
yet you, out of excessive pride, treat me, the King of the Gods, with contempt.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having descended from the shoulder of his elephant, Mahendra, filled with haste,
sought to propitiate the sinless sage Durvāsas.
Then, being propitiated with prostrations, Durvāsas, the best of sages, spoke thus to the thousand-eyed one: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9.19.
Durvāsas said:
"I am not compassionate of heart, nor does forbearance dwell within me;
those others are sages, O Śakra, but know me to be Durvāsas."
"You have been vainly made to feel pride by Gautama and others;
know me to be Durvāsas, whose entire essence consists of impatience."
"By whom you have been so filled with pride that you now even despise me, while Vasiṣṭha and others, whose essence is compassion, are loudly offering hymns of praise?"
Having beheld my face, with its mass of flaming matted locks and distorted by a frown, who in the three worlds has not fallen into fear?
O Śatakratu, why say more? I will not forgive this further mockery you offer in the form of conciliation.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, the sage departed; and the king of the gods, having mounted Airāvata, likewise returned once more to Amarāvatī.
From that time forth, O Maitreya, the three worlds, including Śakra, became bereft of splendor, utterly ruined, and stripped of their medicinal herbs and creepers.
Sacrifices were not performed, ascetics did not practice austerities,
and at that time, people set their minds upon neither the duty of giving nor other such virtues.
O best of the twice-born, all people became devoid of strength, their senses afflicted by greed and other passions; for even at the slightest thing, they were filled with longing.
Where there is courage, there is prosperity; and courage follows from well-being.
For those devoid of prosperity, whence can there be courage? And without that, whence can there be virtues?
Moreover, the absence of strength and valor in men occurs when they are devoid of virtues;
Lavaṇa was entirely bereft of both strength and valor.
Thus, when the three worlds are utterly bereft of splendor and devoid of living beings, even a renowned man becomes humiliated and his intellect is ruined.
The Daityas and Dānavas made preparations for military force against the gods.
Overcome by greed, devoid of splendor, and lacking in courage, the Daityas then waged war against the gods, who were likewise bereft of fortune and destitute of strength.
Defeated by the Daityas, Indra and the other gods, led by Agni, sought refuge with the illustrious Grandfather.
When Brahmā had been addressed by the gods as he truly was, he then said to the deities:
"Seek refuge in the Lord of the high and the low, the destroyer of the Asuras."
He is the Lord who is the causeless cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
the Lord of Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, the infinite and unconquered.
May that Viṣṇu, the cause of the unmanifest Pradhāna and Puruṣa who have become effects, and the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, bestow welfare upon you.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having thus addressed all the gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk accompanied by them.
Having gone there, the Grandfather, joined by all the gods,
praised Hari, the Lord of the high and the low, with pleasing words.
Brahmā said:
I bow to the All, the Lord of all, the infinite, unborn, and imperishable;
the abode of the worlds, the support of the earth, the unmanifest, and the indivisible.
He is smaller than the smallest of all minute things, Nārāyaṇa;
and he is the greatest among all the great things, such as the earth and the rest.
In whom all is contained, from whom all has arisen with me as its precursor, who is the god of all beings, and who is even higher than the highest; ||| ViP_1,9.42 |||
He who is higher than the highest person, who bears the nature of the Supreme Self,
and who is meditated upon by yogis seeking liberation for the sake of attaining release.
May that primordial Person, who is pure and superior to all that is pure, be gracious— he in whom the primal qualities such as *sattva* and the rest do not exist.
May that Viṣṇu be gracious to us— he whose power does not fall within the range of the thread of time consisting of kalās, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, and so forth, for he is pure.
May that Viṣṇu, who is the Supreme Lord— though pure, yet spoken of as such through figurative designation— and who is the Self of all embodied beings, be gracious toward us.
May that Hari be gracious to us— he who is both cause and effect, as well as the cause of the cause and the effect of the effect.
We bow down to him who is himself the effect of that which is the effect of an effect,
and who is the one produced by the effect of that very effect.
We bow down to that Supreme Lord, the cause even of the cause, the cause of the cause of that [cause], the ultimate source of all those causes.
To him who is both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the creator and the created,
whose nature is that of both the effect and the agent— to that supreme state, we bow.
That which is like pure awakening, eternal, unborn, inexhaustible, immutable,
unmanifest, and changeless— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
That which is neither gross nor subtle, and which is not within the range of any qualification— that supreme, eternally pure state of Viṣṇu, we bow down to forever.
We bow to that imperishable one, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, in a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of whom this power of the universe resides.
That supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is to be contemplated within the *praṇava*, is perceived by yogins who are ever-diligent in bringing about the destruction of both merit and sin.
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, which neither the gods, nor the sages, nor I, nor even Śaṅkara know— // ViP_1.9.55 //
That supreme state of Viṣṇu belongs to that God, who was never before born, whose powers consist of the natures of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Lord of all, O Soul of all beings, O All, O Acyuta who is the refuge of all! Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, and come within the range of our vision.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard these words spoken by Brahmā, the gods then bowed and said, "Be gracious; come within the range of our vision."
O Lord, that supreme state which you, the Brahman, know—
that abode of the world, O All-pervading One, O Imperishable One— we bow before you.
At the conclusion of these words of those gods and of Brahmā,
all the celestial sages, led by Bṛhaspati, spoke.
We bow to that one who is the primordial sacrifice, the man to be worshiped, and the first-born of the ancients—
the indefinable creator of the creator of the world.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, imperishable one who bears the form of sacrifice, be gracious; grant Your vision to all of us who have bowed before You.
This three-eyed one is Brahmā along with us and the Rudras;
Pūṣan is together with all the Ādityas, and this Pāvaka is with the Agnis.
The two Aśvins, these Vasus, and all these hosts of Maruts,
the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and this lord Indra, the king of gods.
O Lord, bowed down in prostration and defeated by the armies of the Daityas,
all the hosts of deities have come to you for refuge.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus being praised, O Maitreya, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One who bears the conch and the discus, appeared before their very eyes.
Then, having seen him bearing the conch, discus, and mace, with an unprecedented form and appearance, a formidable mass of splendors, those gods—
Having prostrated themselves, all of them, bowed down with eyes fixed in stillness despite their agitation,
praised the lotus-eyed one, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The gods said:
"Salutations, salutations! You are the Supreme; you are Brahman; you are the wielder of the Pināka bow.
You are Indra, Agni, Pavana, Varuṇa, Savitṛ, and Yama."
The Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas—
the host of deities who stand here before you, O God, in your presence—
are indeed you alone, for you are the creator of the universe and you are omnipresent.
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are Prajāpati;
O Soul of All, you are knowledge and the object of knowledge, and the entire universe consists of you alone.
"O Viṣṇu, we have come to you for refuge, afflicted and defeated by the Daityas;
be gracious, O Soul of All, and invigorate us with your splendor."
So long does suffering, longing, delusion,
and distress persist as one does not go for refuge to you, the destroyer of all sins without exception.
O you of serene soul, grant your grace to us who have sought refuge;
O Lord of all splendors, nourish us by your own power.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus being praised by the immortals who were prostrate before him, the blessed Lord Hari,
the creator of the universe, spoke these words with a gracious glance.
"O gods, I shall provide an augmentation of your splendor;
O deities, listen to what I say and let this be done by you."
Having brought together all the medicinal herbs from the Ocean of Milk along with the Daityas,
and having cast them into the vessel for the sake of the nectar, all the Daityas and Dānavas made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope.
"O gods, let the nectar be churned while I stand as your helper."
And you Daityas, having been addressed with conciliation regarding the act of assistance there, shall be declared as sharers in the common fruit.
And when the ocean is being churned there, whatever nectar shall arise,
by drinking that you will become strong and immortal.
And so I shall act for you in such a way that the gods, the enemies of the thirty [gods], shall not obtain the nectar, but shall experience only affliction.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, all the deities then entered into an alliance with the Asuras and exerted themselves for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Having gathered various medicinal herbs, the gods, Daityas,
and Dānavas cast them into the waters of the Ocean of Milk, which possessed a luster as pure as a cloudless autumnal moon.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
O Maitreya, they then began to churn for the nectar of immortality with great force.
All the gods were stationed together where the tail was,
while the Daityas were placed by Kṛṣṇa on the front part of Vāsuki’s body.
With their splendor struck down by the heat of the fire from his breath,
all those asuras, though possessed of immeasurable power, became devoid of luster.
At that time, the gods were nourished by the clouds formed from the very breath of his mouth, which rained down upon the region of his tail.
O great sage, in the midst of the milk ocean, the Blessed Lord Hari himself, in the form of a tortoise,
became the support for the churning mountain as it revolved.
In another form, the wielder of the discus and mace dragged the king of the Nāgas from among the gods, and in yet another form, he did so from among the Daityas.
O Maitreya, Keśava, assuming a massive form, stepped upon the mountain; it was such that it could not be seen by the gods or the asuras.
Although the Nāgaras already knew him by his own splendor, Hari, the Lord, further nourished them with that splendor;
moreover, he strengthened the gods with another splendor.
Then, as that ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and the dānavas,
Surabhi, the worshipful one of the gods, first emerged as the sacrificial vessel.
Then, O great sage, the gods and the Dānavas experienced joy;
yet their minds became distracted, and they stood with fixed gazes.
Then, as the Siddhas in heaven were wondering, "What is this?",
the goddess Vāruṇī appeared, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
Then, from that churned Ocean of Milk,
which perfumed the world with its fragrance, there arose the Pārijāta tree, the delight of the celestial women.
O Maitreya, a most wonderful host of Apsarases, endowed with the quality of magnificent beauty, was likewise produced from the Ocean of Milk.
Then the Moon (Śītāṃśu) appeared, which Maheśvara took hold of;
and the Nāgas took up the poison that had arisen from the Ocean of Milk.
Then the god Dhanvantari himself arose, wearing white garments and carrying a water-pot filled with nectar.
Then, O Maitreya, all those Daityas and Dānavas, together with the sages, became joyful and composed in mind.
Then, from that water, the goddess Śrī emerged, radiant with shimmering splendor, seated upon a blooming lotus and holding a lotus in her hand.
Filled with joy, the great seers praised her with the Śrīsūkta.
The Gandharvas, headed by Viśvāvasu, sang before her,
while the hosts of Apsarases, led by Ghṛtācī, danced there.
The rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, approached with their waters for the purpose of bathing; and the elephants of the quarters, taking pure water held in golden vessels,
caused the Goddess, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, to be bathed.
The Ocean of Milk, assuming a physical form, gave her a garland of unfading lotuses;
and Viśvakarman fashioned ornaments for her body.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, protected and adorned with ornaments,
she went to the chest of Hari while all the gods were looking on.
O Maitreya, when the gods were gazed upon by Lakṣmī as she rested upon the chest of Hari, they suddenly attained supreme bliss.
O highly fortunate one, the Daityas, who had turned their backs on Viṣṇu, fell into the utmost agitation; they were abandoned by Lakṣmī and became dejected in heart.
Then those Daityas of great prowess seized the water-pot held in the hand of Dhanvantari, wherein the supreme nectar resided.
Having deluded them with illusion, Viṣṇu, the Lord, assuming the form of a woman,
took that [amṛta] from the Dānavas and gave it to the gods.
Then Śakra and the other gods, possessing divine qualities, drank that respective nectar;
meanwhile, the Daityas, with their weapons and swords raised, rushed toward them.
Then, while the nectar was being drunk by the powerful gods, the army of the Daityas,
being slaughtered, fled in all directions and entered the netherworld (pātāla).
Then the gods, filled with joy, prostrated before the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
and as before, they blessed that celestial realm.
Then, O best of sages, the sun, its radiance restored, proceeded upon its own path, and the luminaries likewise moved according to their respective courses.
The blessed Lord Vibhāvasu blazed forth with intense and beautiful radiance,
and at that time, the minds of all beings were turned toward righteousness (dharma).
And the three worlds became endowed with prosperity, O best of the twice-born;
and Śakra, the foremost of the thirty gods, was once again possessed of glory.
Having regained the third heaven and seated upon his throne, Śakra,
established in the sovereignty of the gods, then praised the Goddess who holds a lotus in her hand.
Indra said:
I pay homage to the lotus-born mother of all the worlds,
Śrī, whose eyes are like blooming lotuses, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
I bow to the goddess Padmasukhī, whose abode is the lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, whose eyes resemble lotus petals,
and who is the beloved of Padmanābha.
You are accomplishment, you are *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and nectar; you are the purifier of the worlds, the twilight, the night, radiance, prosperity, intelligence, faith, and Sarasvatī.
O beautiful goddess, you are the science of sacrifice, the great science, the secret science, and the science of the self; you are the bestower of the fruit of liberation.
O Goddess, you alone are Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti;
this entire world has been filled by you through forms both fierce and gentle.
O Goddess, who else but you could occupy the body of the God of gods, the wielder of the mace, which consists of all sacrifices and is conceivable only by yogis?
O Goddess, through you the entire triple world was abandoned and had become almost utterly destroyed; now, by you, it has been fully restored.
O highly fortunate lady, wives, sons, home, friends, grain, wealth, and so forth— these are always like blades of grass to those who behold you.
O Goddess, physical health, sovereign power, the destruction of the enemy faction, and happiness are not difficult to obtain for those men who have been beheld by your glance.
You are the mother of all worlds, and Hari, the god of gods, is the father;
by you and by Viṣṇu, O Mother, this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.
