O purifier of all, do not abandon our treasury, nor our cow-pen, nor our home, nor our belongings, nor our bodies, nor our wives.
O you who dwell upon the chest of me, the god Viṣṇu, do not abandon my sons, nor my friends, nor my kinsmen, nor my cattle, nor my ornaments.
Those men who have abandoned you, O Āyāmala, are instantly forsaken by goodness, truth, purity, as well as by virtues such as moral conduct.
Beheld by you, even men devoid of merit are immediately endowed with all virtues such as good character, as well as noble lineage and sovereignty.
O Goddess, he whom you have looked upon is praiseworthy, virtuous, blessed, well-born, wise, heroic, and valiant.
All virtues, such as moral conduct and the rest, immediately fall into disarray for one from whom you,
O beloved of Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world, have turned your face away.
Even the Creator himself would not be able to describe your virtues;
be gracious, O lotus-eyed Goddess, and never forsake us.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus properly praised, O twice-born one, the goddess Śrī, who dwells within all beings, spoke to Śatakratu in the hearing of all the gods.
Śrī said: "O Lord of gods, O Hari, I am well-pleased with this hymn of yours.
Choose a boon that is desired; I have come to you as a giver of boons."
Indra said:
"O Goddess, if you are a giver of boons to me, or if I am indeed worthy of a boon, then the three worlds must not be abandoned by you; let this be my supreme boon."
"O you who are born from the ocean, he who shall praise you with this hymn must not be abandoned by you; let this be my second boon."
Śrī said: "O Vāsava, best of the gods, I shall not abandon the three worlds;
for a boon has been granted by me to you, being pleased by your hymn of praise and worship."
And whatever man shall praise me with this hymn both in the evening and in the morning, I shall not turn my face away from him.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus, O Maitreya, in ancient times the illustrious and highly fortunate Goddess Śrī, gratified by his hymn of praise and worship, granted this boon to the king of the gods.
Śrī was first born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti, and later she was produced from the ocean through the efforts of the gods and demons during the churning for nectar.
Thus, whenever Janārdana, the Lord of the world and God of gods,
takes an incarnation, Śrī likewise becomes his companion.
Furthermore, when Hari was born from a lotus and became the Sun,
this earth then became Bhārgava Rāma.
She was Sītā when he was Rāghava and Rukmiṇī at the birth of Kṛṣṇa; she is the inseparable companion of Viṣṇu in all his other incarnations as well.
In the state of divinity she possesses a divine body, and in the state of humanity she is human;
indeed, she fashions her own form in accordance with the body of Viṣṇu.
The man who hears this account of Lakṣmī’s birth, or who recites it,
shall experience no loss of fortune in his home for as long as three generations.
O Sage, in those houses where this hymn of praise to Śrī is recited,
misfortune— the source of strife— never dwells.
O Brahmin, I have thus related to you that which you asked me:
how Śrī was formerly born from the Ocean of Milk, having previously been the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Thus, this hymn to Lakṣmī, which issues from the mouth of Indra and is the cause for attaining all prosperity,
is recited here daily by those men with whom misfortune never dwells at any time.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said: O Sage, you have told me everything about which I questioned you.
"Tell me again of this creation, beginning from the progeny of Bhṛgu."
Śrī Parāśara said: Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, was born to Bhṛgu by Khyāti;
likewise, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were born as two sons to Bhṛgu by Khyāti.
Āyati and Niyati were the two daughters of the high-souled Meru;
they became the wives of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and from them both sons were born.
Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍu; from Mṛkaṇḍu came Mārkaṇḍeya, and from him was born Vedaśiras. Now hear also of the son of Prāṇa.
Prāṇa’s son was Dyutimat, and from him Rājavat was born;
from him, O illustrious one, the lineage of Bhārgava attained great expansion.
Marīci’s wife was Saṃbhūti; she gave birth to Paurṇamāsa.
Virajas and Parvata were the sons of that high-souled one.
O twice-born one, I shall next recount his sons in the proclamation of the lineage.
Smṛti, the wife of Aṅgiras, likewise gave birth to daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumatī.
In the same way, Anasūyā bore to Atri sons free from all blemish:
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
From Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, Dattoli was born as their son;
he is remembered as Agastya in his previous birth during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Kardama, Ārvarīvat, and Sahiṣṇu were the three sons;
Kṣamā, however, gave birth [to them] as the wife of the progenitor Pulaha.
And Kratu’s wife Saṃtati gave birth to the Vālakhilyas—
sixty thousand sages who were perpetual celibates,
each the size of a thumb-joint, and possessing the blazing splendor of the sun.
In Ūrjā, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha.
Raja, Gotra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukra— these are all the stainless Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
O twice-born one, he who was the presiding deity of fire was the first-born son of Brahmā;
from him, Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor.
He is Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and also Jalāśin.
In their lineage, forty-five other fires are said to have arisen, as well as these three pairs of father and son.
Thus, forty-nine fires have been proclaimed.
O twice-born one, those ancestors created by Brahmā whom I have described to you are the Āgniṣvāttas,
the Barhiṣads, and those who are without fire as well as those who possess fire.
From them, Svadhā gave birth to Menā and Dhārīṇī;
both of them, O twice-born one, were exponents of the Veda and both were practitioners of yoga.
Endowed with supreme knowledge and all exalted virtues.
Thus has been told this true lineage of Dakṣa’s daughters;
one who possesses faith and remembers this shall not remain childless.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: "Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu."
Two sons of great heroism, both knowers of dharma, have been described to you.
Of those two, O Brahmin, Uttānapāda had a son named Uttama by his beloved wife Suruci; he was exceedingly dear to his father.
O twice-born one, the king had a queen named Sunīti;
he was not particularly fond of her, whose son was Dhruva.
Seeing Uttama seated on his father’s lap upon the royal throne while his brother Dhruva was not, Dhruva formed the desire to ascend it himself.
The king did not welcome Suruci’s son with joy when he approached affectionately, eager to climb onto his lap, even though it was before his very eyes.
Seeing her co-wife’s son eager to climb onto his lap,
and her own son already seated there, Suruci spoke these words:
"O child, why do you act in vain? This is a great desire, for it cannot be fulfilled by one born from the womb of another woman without being conceived in my own womb."
"Indeed, you, lacking discrimination, desire that which is the highest of the high and unattainable;
it is true that you are his son, but you were not held by me."
"This entire royal throne, the banner of refuge for all sovereigns, is worthy of my son alone; why do you weary yourself?"
Why do you vainly steal the high aspirations of my son as if they were your own? Do you not realize that your own birth was from Sunīti?
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard those words spoken by his mother, the boy,
becoming angry, abandoned his father and went to the house of his own mother, O twice-born one.
Seeing her son thus enraged, with his lower lip slightly quivering, Sunīti placed him on her lap and spoke these words to Maitreya: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.12.
"My child, what is the cause of your anger, and who does not greet you with joy? Who, my child, would fail to recognize his father—he who has offended you?"
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, he related everything to his mother exactly as Suruci had spoken in the presence of the king, free from pride.
When her son had spoken thus with a deep sigh, the dejected Sunīti, her eyes red from weeping, spoke these words in distress.
Sunīti said: "Suruci has spoken the truth, my unfortunate little son;
for indeed, O child, those who possess merit are never released from their rivals."
"O dear one, you should not be distressed; for what has been done by you in the past, no one is able to take away, and what has not been done by you, who can give? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.17)
Therefore, you should not experience any sorrow arising from his words in this matter.
"The royal throne, the royal parasol, and the choice elephants—these belong to him whose merits they are; knowing this, my son, be at peace."
Through merits performed in other births, King Suruci is called "Suruci" (the Well-Looked-at) because of his wife; whereas another woman like me, devoid of merit, is called [Duryaśas].
Her son was likewise supreme, endowed with a great accumulation of merit;
my son, however, has been born as Dhruva, possessing very little merit.
Nevertheless, my dear son, you ought not to cause yourself grief;
for whatever a man possesses, he should be content with that very thing.
If your suffering has become excessive because of Suruci’s words,
then, O bestower of all fruits, exert yourself in the accumulation of merit.
Be virtuous, righteous in soul, friendly, and devoted to the welfare of living beings;
for just as water flows downward, so do riches come to one who is inclined toward them.
Dhruva said:
"O Mother, these words which you have spoken to me for the sake of calming me do not remain within my heart, which has been pierced by harsh speech."
Therefore, I shall strive in such a way that I may attain the most supreme of all states,
which is honored by the undecaying worlds.
"Suruci was the beloved wife of that king, and I was not born from her womb;
O mother, behold my power, even though I am old, within your womb."
"He who was carried by her in her womb is my most excellent brother;
let him obtain the royal throne granted by his father—so be it."
"O Mother, I do not desire any station bestowed by another; through my own karma, I wish for that station which my father attained."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having thus spoken to his mother, Dhruva departed from his mother’s house;
then, having emerged from the city, he went to the grove situated outside it.
There Dhruva saw seven sages who had arrived previously,
seated upon seats covered with cushions of kusha grass and deerskins.
That prince, bowing down with humility and having first offered a proper salutation, addressed them all.
Dhruva said:
"O best of beings, know me to be the son of Uttānapāda, born of Sunīti;
out of world-weariness, I have come into your presence."
The sages said:
"O son of Tṛpa, you are but a child, born only four or five years ago; even now, no cause for world-weariness has arisen within you."
"Nothing concerning you need be thought of; your father, the king, will not be distressed. Nor do we see any separation from what is desired for you, my child. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.35)
No disease is observed in your body by us;
if there is a cause for your despondency, let it be told.

Oh, how supreme is the warrior-spirit of this child, that even though he is but a boy,
the indignation at what his stepmother said does not depart from his heart!
"O scion of the Kṣatriyas! Since you have now resolved to act out of world-weariness, tell us what it is that you intend to do, if it pleases you."
And whatever task must be done by us for you, O one of immeasurable luster, let it be told; we perceive that you desire to speak.
Dhruva said:
"O best of the twice-born, I do not desire wealth nor do I desire a kingdom;
I desire only that place which has never before been enjoyed by another."
O best of sages, let this be properly performed for me; let it be told how that supreme state, higher than all other states, may be attained.
Marīci said:
"O Prince, this supreme station is certainly not attained by men who have failed to worship Govinda; therefore, worship Acyuta."
Atri said:
"He with whom Janārdana is pleased—that Supreme Person among all supreme beings—attains the imperishable state; this which I have spoken is the truth."
Aṅgiras said:
"Worship Govinda, within whom all this exists— the Imperishable One of immutable nature— if you desire that foremost station."
Pulastya said: Having propitiated Hari, who is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and that which is the highest Brahman, one attains even liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Pulaha said:
"O you of noble vows, propitiate that Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe and the Lord of sacrifice, by worshipping whom Indra attained his supreme station as Indra."
Kratu said:
"He who is the Lord of Sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, the Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Person—Janārdana; when he is satisfied, what is there that remains unattainable?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
When Viṣṇu is propitiated, one obtains with the mind whatever one desires, even a station within the three worlds; how much more so, my child, the most excellent of all?
Dhruva said:
"The deity to be propitiated has been described by you to me as I bow before you;
please tell me that which is to be chanted by me for his gratification."
And how I am to perform the propitiation of that Great-souled One—
may the great seers, with faces bright with favor, tell me that.
The sages said:
"O prince, you ought to hear from us duly how the propitiation of Viṣṇu is to be performed by men who are intent upon his worship."
First, a person should cause the mind to abandon all external objects;
thereafter, one should make it immovable within that very abode of the world.
In this way, O joy of the Pārthivas, that which must be recited should be chanted with a one-pointed mind, absorbed in that [deity], and with self-restraint, for the sake of awakening. ViP_1,11.54.
Obeisance to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge, who takes the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and the Manifested. ViP_1.11.55.
The blessed Svāyambhuva Manu, your grandfather, formerly recited this mantra to be recited; Janārdana was pleased with him.
Just as [the sage] was granted the accomplishment difficult to attain even in the three worlds according to his desire,
so too may you, by constantly reciting this, satisfy Govinda.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard this in its entirety, O Maitreya, the son of the king—
Having prostrated before those sages, he departed from that forest.
O twice-born one, considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose,
he then went to the highly meritorious bank of the Yamunā known as Madhu.
Furthermore, because it was presided over by the Daitya named Madhu,
it became renowned on this earth by the name Madhuvana.
And having slain the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu,
Śatrughna indeed founded the city named Mathurā.
In that very place, the Tapaḥ-tīrtha which removes all sins and where the presence of the god of gods, Hari-medhas, resides, he performed his penance.
Just as it had been instructed by the sages headed by Marīci, so it came to pass;
he perceived Viṣṇu, the Lord of all gods, residing within his own self.
O Brahmin, as he meditated with a mind focused on no other, Lord Hari,
who dwells within all beings, became present to him in every way.
O Maitreya, while that Viṣṇu remained thus absorbed in the mind of the yogi,
the Earth, the supporter of all beings, was unable to bear her burden.
While he stood upon his left foot, half of the earth bent down;
and while he stood upon his right foot, a second half of the earth likewise bent down.
As he stood pressing down upon the earth with the tips of his toes,
the entire earth, together with its mountains, trembled.
The rivers, streams, and oceans reached a state of supreme agitation;
because of that agitation, O great sage, the immortals likewise fell into the highest distress.
Then, O Maitreya, the gods known as the Yāmas, being extremely distressed,
consulted with Indra and proceeded to disrupt his meditative absorption.
O great sage, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, in various forms, became intensely distressed and began to strive to break Mahendra’s meditative absorption.
His mother, named Sunīti, stood before him with her weapons; then, composed of illusion, she spoke these piteous words: "O son! *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 1.12.14.
"O son, turn back from this [act] which is as terrible as the destruction of the body;
you were obtained by me through many longings and through persistent effort."
O child, you ought not to abandon me alone, helpless and distressed, merely because of the words of a co-wife; for when there is no one else to turn to, you are my refuge.
Where are you, a mere five-year-old child, and where is this harsh asceticism?
Let your mind turn away from this painful persistence that is devoid of fruit.
Time is for your playthings; after that, it is for your study.
After that, it is intended for all enjoyments, and at the end of that, austerity is prescribed.
O dear son, that which was the time for your play as a child— why do you now desire to practice asceticism during that very period, intent on your own destruction?
My pleasure is the supreme dharma; follow the sequence of actions according to your stage of life. Do not, out of delusion, turn away from this which is dharma.
"O dear child, if you do not undertake this penance,
then I shall surely give up my life here while you are looking on."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Although he was looking at her, who was thus lamenting with eyes clouded by tears,
his mind was concentrated on Viṣṇu, and so he did not truly see her.
"My child, my child! These most terrible Rākṣasas are approaching in this fearsome forest with their weapons raised; depart from here."
Having spoken thus, she then departed; immediately thereafter, the Rākṣasas appeared, brandishing fierce weapons with mouths wreathed in garlands of flames.
Then, before the prince,
those night-stalkers, brandishing their blazing weapons, released extremely fierce roars.
And hundreds of jackals, with mouths emitting flames,
howled in order to terrify that boy who was ever absorbed in yoga.
"Let him be killed! Let him be killed! Let him be cut asunder! Let him be cut asunder!
Let him be devoured! Let him be devoured!"—thus those night-stalkers cried out.
Then those night-stalkers, with faces like lions, camels, and sea-monsters, roared out various kinds of cries and food-words to terrify the prince.
Those rākṣasas became mere sounds to him, and those weapons became jackals;
for one whose mind was fixed on Govinda, they did not come within the range of his senses.
With a mind constantly one-pointed, the son of the lord of the earth saw none other whatsoever than Viṣṇu, who is the refuge of the self.
Then, when all those illusions had dissolved, the gods again fell into a state of supreme agitation, fearing his defeat.
Having come together and being tormented by his ascetic power, they sought refuge with Hari, the source of the universe, who is without beginning or end and the worthy protector.
The gods said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, Supreme Lord, Puruṣottama!
We, scorched by the ascetic penance of Dhruva, have come to you for refuge.
O Lord, just as the moon is filled day by day by its minute portions,
so does he attain prosperity through his asceticism night and day.
O Janārdana, having performed such penance, we have now become afraid; we have come to you for refuge—please cause that penance to cease.
We do not know whether he desires the status of Śakra, or the status of Sūrya; or perhaps he has a longing for the positions of the Lord of Wealth, Varuṇa, or Soma.
Therefore, O Lord, be gracious to us; extract this thorn from our hearts and cause the son of Uttānapāda to desist from his ascetic penance.
The Blessed One said: "O gods, he does not seek the status of Indra, nor that of the Sun, nor even the lordship over water or wealth;
whatever desire he seeks, I shall fulfill it all."
"O gods, go to your own abodes as you desire, free from all anxiety;
I shall bring back the boy whose mind is intent upon asceticism."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, the deities, led by Śatakratu, then bowed down and departed for their respective abodes.
The Blessed One, the Self of All, being gratified by his absorption in that [devotion], assumed a four-armed form and, having gone to Dhruva, spoke this: *Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.12.41*
The Blessed Lord said:
"O son of Uttānapāda, may it be well with you; I have been gratified by your austerity and have arrived as a giver of boons. Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
"Since your mind has been fixed upon me, independent of any external object, I am pleased with you for that; therefore, choose a supreme boon."
Parāśara said:
Having thus heard the speech of that God of gods, the boy opened his eyes and beheld Hari, whom he had previously perceived through meditation, standing before him.
Beholding Acyuta, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the excellent sword,
and who wears a diadem, he touched the earth with his head.
With his limbs bristling with horripilation and suddenly overcome by supreme awe,
Dhruva set his mind upon praising the God of gods.
"What shall I say in his praise? By whom has he been described so that I might offer him hymns?"—with such a troubled mind, he went to that very God for refuge.
Dhruva said:
"O Blessed One, if you have attained supreme satisfaction with my austerity, then I wish to offer praise; grant this boon to me."

O God, how can I, a mere child, praise You, whose origin is known as Brahma and others by those who know the Vedas, yet whose ultimate course remains unknown? O Supreme Lord, my mind is indeed inclined toward devotion to You.
"Grant me wisdom as I proceed to praise Your feet.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Govinda touched him, who stood with palms joined in reverence, with the edge of His conch.
O best of the twice-born, the Lord of the World [beheld] the son of Uttānapāda.
Then, with a serene countenance, that prince immediately bowed down and offered praise to the imperishable Sustainer of all beings.
Dhruva said: "I bow to Him whose form is earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
the source of the elements (ahaṃkāra), and primordial nature (prakṛti)."
Pure, subtle, and all-pervading, the Person (Puruṣa) is beyond Pradhāna;
salutations to that Puruṣa, whose form consists of the Guṇas.

He is the eternal one who transcends all the elements beginning with earth, as well as the objects of sense beginning with smell, and who is beyond the intellect and the rest, as well as primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
O Supreme Lord, I take refuge in that pure form of yours, which is the Self become Brahman and the Lord of the entire universe.
Salutations to You, the Self of all, whose form is designated as Brahman because of its vastness and its capacity for expansion; You who are inconceivable to yogis and immutable.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
pervading the entire universe, he transcends the earth by the measure of ten fingers.
O Supreme Person, whatever has been and whatever is yet to be, all that is You;
from You comes the Virāj, the Svarāj, and the Samrāj, and from You also comes the Adhipūruṣa.
It extended far beyond the earth, both across and upwards;
from you this entire universe was born, and from you it shall be in the past and the future.
This entire world of all beings exists within you, who assume their forms;
from you comes the sacrifice in which everything is offered, as well as the speckled butter and the two kinds of sacrificial animals.
From you the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born; from you the meters (chandas) arose;
from you the Yajus-formulas were produced; and from you came horses with teeth in only one jaw.
Cows were produced from you; from you came goats, sheep, and wild beasts.
From your mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born, and from your arms the Kṣatriya was born.
From Your broad chest the Vaiśyas were born, and from Your feet the Śūdras emerged;
from Your eyes arose the Sun, from Your breath the Wind, and from Your mind the Moon.
From his internal cavity the vital breath was born; from his mouth fire was produced;
from his navel the atmosphere arose, and from his head the heavens were formed.
The quarters of space arose from your ears and the earth from your feet; thus everything came into being from you.
Just as a very great banyan tree is contained within a tiny seed,
so too is the entire universe contained within you, who have become the seed of all, through self-restraint.
Just as the nyagrodha tree arises from the production of a sprout from a seed and attains vast expansion, so too does the world arise from you in the act of creation.

For just as no other substance is seen apart from the bark and leaves of the plantain tree, so too, O Lord, you are not seen as something other than the universe, nor does the universe appear as something other than you.
Bliss, existence, and consciousness—these three exist as one in You when all things are established;
however, pleasure, pain, and their mixture do not exist in You, who are devoid of the material qualities (guṇas).
Salutations to you who have become distinct and who have become one;
salutations to you, the being of beings, the self of all beings, and the source of all that has come into existence.
Manifest as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Virāj, Samrāj, and likewise Svarāj— you,
the imperishable one, are meditated upon within the inner organ of all persons.
You are all beings in everything; you are everything, assuming every form.
Everything originates from you, and therefore you are everything. Homage be to you, the Soul of All!
Since you are the soul of all, O Lord of All, and abide within all beings, what then shall I tell you? You know everything that dwells within the heart.
O Soul of all, Lord of all beings, source of all living creatures;
you, who are all beings, know the desire of every sentient being.
O Lord, that desire of mine has been made fruitful by you;
and my ascetic penance has borne fruit, since you, O Lord of the World, have been seen by me.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Dhruva, that you have seen me is the fruit of your ascetic penance;
for the sight of me, O Prince, never goes in vain."
Therefore, choose a boon according to your own desire;
everything is accomplished for men once I have come within the range of their vision.
Dhruva said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, you reside in the heart of all.
O Brahman, what is unknown to you that has been perceived by my mind?"
Nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, I shall tell you that which is being prayed for by me with a most ill-behaved heart— something exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Or rather, O Creator of the entire world, what is difficult to obtain when you are pleased?
Even Indra enjoys the three worlds as the fruit of your grace.
"This royal throne is not fit for one who has not been born from my womb"—
thus did my co-wife's mother speak to me loudly out of pride.
O Lord, by your grace, I pray for that imperishable state which is the supreme of all supremes and the foundational support of the entire world.
The Blessed One said:
"O child, that station which you pray for, you shall indeed attain it;
for I was gratified by you in a previous birth."
Formerly, you were always one whose mind was fixed with single-minded devotion on Brahman;
you were a servant to your mother and father, and a follower of your own dharma.
As time passed, a prince became your friend;
he was endowed with all the riches of youth and possessed a handsome and radiant form.
Having observed that prosperity of his, so difficult to attain even by the gods, which resulted from that association, you formed the desire: "May I become a prince."
Thus, you have obtained that state of being a prince as you desired;
O Dhruva, you were born in the house of Uttānapāda, which is so difficult to attain.
That station within the lineage of Svāyambhuva which is difficult for others to attain.
This is another [reason] why I am pleased with this fool:
by propitiating me, a man attains liberation without delay.
O child, for one whose mind is offered unto me, what need is there even for such states as heaven?
O Bhānu, by my grace, there shall be no doubt that he will dwell in a station superior to the three worlds, serving as the refuge for all the stars and planets.
From the Sun,
from the Moon, from Mars, from Mercury, from Jupiter, from Venus and Saturn, and likewise from all the constellations, Dhruva is the fixed point.
O Dhruva, a station above all the seven Ṛṣis and those gods who dwell in celestial chariots has been granted to you by me.
Some gods shall remain for the duration of four yugas, and some for an entire manvantara;
indeed, I have granted you the stability of a kalpa.
Your mother Sunīti as well, being exceedingly pure and remaining close to you,
shall dwell for that same duration of time having become a star in a celestial chariot.
And those men who, being well-composed, shall recite [this] to you in the morning and in the evening,
for them there will be great merit.
Śrī Parāśara said: O high-minded one, having thus previously obtained a boon from Janārdana, the Lord of the World and God of gods, Dhruva occupies that station.
This was due to his own righteous service to his mother and father,
as well as through the majesty of the twelve-syllable mantra and the power of his ascetic penance.
Indeed, having observed his arrogance, supernatural power, and majesty, Uśanas, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, sang this verse here: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.12.98.
Great indeed is the power of this asceticism, great is the fruit of this asceticism,
that the Seven Sages stand with Dhruva placed before them.
And this mother of Dhruva is named Sunīti, who is Sūnṛtā;
and who on earth is capable of describing her greatness?
She extends that supreme abode which has attained the status of being the refuge of the three worlds;
she who, having reached that supreme state, remains firmly within the cavity of her womb.
And whoever shall constantly recite this account of Dhruva’s ascent to heaven,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Svarga.
He does not suffer loss of his position, whether in heaven or on earth;
endowed with all auspicious things, he lives for a long time.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: From Dhruva were born Śiṣṭi and Bhavya; from Bhavya, Śambhu was born.
Succhāyā, the wife of Śiṣṭa, bore five sinless sons.
Bṛhatī bore to Ripu a son named Ripuñjaya, and to Vipra she bore Vṛkala, who possessed the splendor of a wolf; and to Ripu she bore Cākṣuṣa, who possessed all-encompassing energy.
Cākṣuṣa begot Manu upon Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of the high-souled Vīraṇa and the wife of Varuṇa.
O best of those who practice austerity, ten sons of great majesty were born to Naḍvalā, the daughter of the patriarch Vairāja, by Manoratha.
Kuru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavat, Śuci, Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these nine of great power,
along with Abhimanyu as the tenth, were born of Naḍvalā.
Āgneyī bore to Kuru six sons of great splendor:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Khyāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Śibi.
From the body of Aṅga, Sunīthā gave birth to a single son, Vena;
for the sake of progeny, the sages churned his right hand.
O great sage, when Vena’s hand was churned,
there arose a protector of the earth named Vainya, who is celebrated as Pṛthu.
By whom the earth was milked in former times for the sake of the welfare of all creatures.
Maitreya said: For what purpose was Vena’s hand churned by the supreme ṛṣis,
from which that highly powerful Pṛthu was born, O best of sages?
Śrī Parāśara said:
The maiden named Sunīthā, who was first born to Kṛtyā, was given as the wife of Aṅga; in her Vena was begotten.
O Maitreya, by virtue of that defect of his maternal grandfather, this son of Mṛtyu’s daughter was born wicked by nature.
When that Vena was consecrated in the kingdom by the supreme ṛṣis, he,
as the lord of the earth, then caused a proclamation to be made throughout the world.
One should not sacrifice, one should not give, and one should by no means offer oblations;
for who else is the enjoyer of the sacrifice? I am indeed the Lord, the Master of Sacrifice.
Then, O Maitreya, having first honored that lord of the earth who was present before them, the sages spoke these words in a conciliatory tone.
The sages said:
"O King, O lord of the earth, listen to what we say:
sovereignty is for the benefit of the body and for the supreme welfare of the subjects."
"O Lord of Gods, we shall worship Hari, the Lord of all sacrifices, with a long-duration sacrifice; may prosperity be yours, for a portion of that [merit] shall belong to you."
O King, when Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, has been fully gratified by us through this sacrifice,
he will grant you all your desires.
O King, in whose kingdom Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, is worshipped with sacrifices,
He grants those rulers the attainment of all their desires.
Vena said:
"Who is there superior to me? Who else is to be worshipped by me?
Who is this one known as Hari, whom you consider the lord of sacrifice?"
Brahmā, Janārdana, Śambhu, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Ravi, Hutabhuj, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, Bhūmi, and Niśākara; 1.13.21.
These and other gods who bestow curses and favors reside within the body of the king; thus, the king is composed of all the gods.
"Knowing this, O twice-born ones, act exactly as I have commanded: no gifts are to be given, no sacrifices performed, and no oblations offered."
O twice-born ones, just as service to the husband is considered the supreme duty for women,
so too is the observance of my command your duty.
The sages said:
"Grant us permission, O Great King; let not dharma go to destruction.
This entire world is the transformation of sacrificial oblations."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Although he was thus being addressed by the supreme sages, Vena gave no consent, even though he was told again and again.
Then all those sages, filled with anger and resentment, said to one another, "Let the sinner be slain! Let him be slain! (ViP 1.13.27).
He who, being of base conduct, reviles Viṣṇu— the Lord, the Person of Sacrifice, without beginning or end— is not fit to be the lord of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the hosts of sages struck the king with those kusha grasses purified by mantras,
for he had previously struck [them] down with insults and the like, O Blessed One.
Then, O twice-born one, the sages saw dust rising on all sides;
they asked the people nearby, "What is this? at that time.
And it was reported by the people to them that, in a kingless realm, the inhabitants had become like thieves and had begun to seize the property of others out of greed.
O best of sages, a very great cloud of dust was seen rising from those thieves who were rushing with impetuous speed to seize the wealth of others.
Then, having deliberated together, all those wise ministers diligently churned the thigh of that childless king for the sake of obtaining a son.
As he was being churned, a man indeed rose up from his thigh;
he resembled a burnt pillar, with a bald face and an extremely short stature.
"What shall I do? that clever man said to all those brahmins.
They told him, "Sit down" (niṣīda); because of that, he became a Niṣāda.
From that, O tiger among sages, there were born the Niṣādas who dwell on the Vindhya mountains, characterized by their evil deeds.
Through that opening, the sin of that king emerged;
from it were born those Niṣādas who destroyed the impurity of Vena.
Then those twice-born ones churned his very right hand.
And as it was being churned there, the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, appeared,
blazing with his own body like a manifest fire.
Then the first bow, named Ājagava, fell from the sky;
and divine arrows and armor also fell from the heavens.
When he was born, all living beings were filled with joy on every side.
By the mere birth of a virtuous son, even Vena went to the third heaven,
having been rescued from the hell named Put by his high-souled son.
The oceans and the rivers, bringing all kinds of jewels and their waters for the purpose of the consecration, all presented themselves before him.
And the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā), together with the gods and the descendants of Aṅgiras,
as well as all beings, both stationary and moving,
having assembled, then consecrated the son of Vena as the lord of men.
But seeing the discus in his right hand, the Grandfather (Brahmā),
considering him to be a portion of Viṣṇu, attained supreme satisfaction.
The mark of Viṣṇu’s discus appears on the hand of all universal emperors,
whose power remains unimpeded even by the gods.
The powerful and highly resplendent Pṛthu, son of Vena, was duly consecrated with the great sovereignty of a king by those learned in the Dharma.
His subjects were conquered by his father, but they were won over by him;
because of that affection, the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him.
As he was about to set out for the ocean, the waters solidified for him;
the mountains yielded the way, and his banner suffered no breakage.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed; food was prepared by mere thought;
cows milked all desires; and in every leaf-cup there was honey.
Indeed, as soon as he was born at the auspicious sacrifice of his grandfather,
that high-minded Sūta was produced during the Sautya pressing on the day of the Soma extraction.
Then, at that very great sacrifice, a wise Māgadha was born;
at that time, both the Sūta and the Māgadha were addressed by the best of sages.
"Praise this powerful King Pṛthu, the son of Vena;
this deed is worthy of you both, and he is another fit recipient for your hymn."
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the two of them said to all the brahmins:
"Today the ritual for this newborn lord of the earth is to be performed."
His virtues are not known, nor is his fame celebrated;
tell us, upon what basis should a hymn of praise for him be composed by us?
The farmers said:
"Whatever deeds this mighty universal monarch shall perform,
and whatever qualities he shall possess— by means of these, let this king be praised."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, having heard that, the king attained supreme satisfaction;
for one attains praise through good qualities, therefore my qualities are praiseworthy.
Therefore, whatever description of their qualities these two shall perform today with their hymn of praise,
that very thing I too shall perform with a concentrated mind.
The king formed this resolve: "Whatever these two may say here that is to be avoided, I shall avoid that."
Then the Sūta and Māgadha, singing with beautiful voices, properly performed a hymn of praise for the wise Pṛthu, the son of Vena, based on his future deeds.
This lord of men is truthful in speech, generous by nature, and faithful to his word;
he is modest, friendly, patient by disposition, valiant, and a subduer of the wicked.
He was a knower of dharma, grateful, compassionate, and pleasant of speech;
he honored those worthy of honor, performed sacrifices, was devoted to Brahman, and was esteemed by the virtuous.
The king should be impartial toward both enemy and friend when established in judicial proceedings.
Having thus heard the qualities described by the charioteer and by the Magadhan king,
he took them to heart and performed such deeds accordingly.
Thereafter, that protector of the earth, while ruling this world,
performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Afflicted by hunger at that time when the earth was without a king and the medicinal herbs had perished, the subjects approached that lord of the earth.
Bowed down, they were asked the reason for their coming and spoke to him.
The subjects said:
"O best of kings, O lord of subjects, in a kingless state all the medicinal herbs on the earth were devoured; consequently, all the subjects went to their destruction."
"You have been appointed by the Creator as our provider of livelihood and protector of the subjects;
grant us, your subjects who are overwhelmed by hunger, the medicinal herbs that sustain life."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then the king, enraged, took up the divine bow Jāgava and celestial arrows, and pursued the Earth.
Then the Earth, having become a cow, quickly vanished;
out of terror, she departed for the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā.
Wherever that goddess, the supporter of beings, went at that time,
there she beheld the son of Vena with his weapons raised.
Then the Earth, trembling and intent on protecting herself from his arrow, spoke to Pṛthu, who possessed the prowess of a king.
The Earth said:
"O lord of men, do you not see the great sin in the killing of a woman,
that you exert such effort, O King, to slay me?"
Pṛthu said:
"When the death of a single evildoer brings security to many, his killing bestows merit."
Pṛthu said:
"If you will kill me for the benefit of the subjects,
O best of kings, who will then be the support of those subjects?"
Pṛthu said:
"O Earth, having slain you with my arrows for turning away from my command,
I shall sustain these subjects by the power of my own yoga."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then the Earth, her limbs trembling and having fallen into a state of extreme trepidation, spoke once more to that king.
The Earth said:
"All undertakings succeed when commenced with the proper means;
therefore, I shall tell you the means—perform it, if you so desire."
"O Lord of Men, all those great medicinal herbs that I have consumed,
if you so desire, I shall give them back to you, transformed into milk."
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, for the sake of the welfare of all creatures, make him your calf, so that I, being affectionate toward my calf, may flow with milk.
"And make it level everywhere, so that the milk—
which is the seed consisting of excellent medicinal herbs— may nourish seeds on all sides."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then the son of Vena (Prthu) pushed aside mountains by the hundreds of thousands with the tip of his bow and with his foot; by that means, the mountains were leveled.
Indeed, in the previous dissolution, when the surface of the earth was uneven,
there existed no prior division of cities or villages before their creation.
O Maitreya, neither crops, nor cattle-rearing, nor agriculture, nor trade routes existed before the time of Vainya; it was from him that the origin of all these arose.
O best of the twice-born, wherever the ground was level for him,
there all the subjects chose to make their dwelling.
At that time, food for living beings consisted of fruits and roots;
even those became difficult to obtain when medicinal herbs had indeed perished due to great hardship.
Having appointed the lord Svāyambhuva Manu as his calf, Pṛthu,
the ruler of the earth, milked the earth with his own hand out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures, [obtaining] all kinds of grain-crops.
By that food, O dear one, all creatures still subsist perpetually even today.
Because that Pṛthu was the giver of life to the earth, which had been terrified,
she therefore obtained the name "Pṛthivī," the supporter of all.
And then [he was honored] by the gods, sages, Daityas, Rākṣasas, mountains,
Gandharvas, Uragas, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, and likewise by the trees.
O Sage, having taken up each respective vessel, the milk of each respective cow became their source; and the specific calves who had been milked were born from those [cows].
This very earth is the supporter, the ordainer, the sustainer, and likewise the nourisher;
it is the foundation of everything, having arisen from the sole of Viṣṇu’s foot.
Such was the power of that heroic Pṛthu, the son of Vainya;
he was born as the first lord of the earth and became a king because he delighted the people.
Whatever man should recite this account of the birth of Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
no evil deed whatsoever shall bear fruit for him.
For those who hear this supreme account of Pṛthu’s birth and power, it constantly brings about the pacification of evil dreams for men.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
The two sons of Pṛthu, who were knowers of dharma, were born as Antardhi and Vādin.
Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna and Antardhāna.
From Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā bore six sons: Āgneyī, Jayat, Suta, Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, and Gaya; and Kṛṣṇa begot Vṛjinī.
O highly fortunate one, the venerable Pracīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati, by whom all creatures were nourished from the Havirdhāna fire-chamber.
O Sage, because his *kuśa* grass was spread on the earth with its tips pointing eastward,
he became renowned on earth as the mighty Prācīnabarhis.
O high-minded one, having taken Savarṇā as his wife, the lord of the earth dwelt on the far shore of the great darkness within the daughter of the ocean.
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis of the same lineage;
all were named Prācetasas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great penance for ten thousand years while lying within the waters of the ocean.
The illustrious Maitreya said: O great sage, you ought to relate this for what purpose those high-souled ones, the sons of Pracetas, performed penance in the waters of the ocean.
Śrī Parāśara said: The Pracetasas were addressed by their father, who was of immeasurable soul and had been appointed as a Prajāpati, with great respect for the sake of creating progeny.
Prācīnabarhis said:
"O sons, I have been commanded by Brahmā, the God of gods: 'The subjects must be increased by you. And I replied to him, 'So be it.'"
Therefore, for my pleasure, O sons, you who are worthy of honor, diligently bring about the increase of progeny; this is the proper command of Prajāpati.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, O Sage, having heard those words of their father, those sons of the king replied,
"So be it," and questioned their father further.
The Pracetasas said:
"O father, you ought to explain to us in its entirety that action by which we may become capable of increasing our progeny."
The father said:
"By propitiating Viṣṇu, the granter of boons, a mortal undoubtedly attains his desired object; it cannot be otherwise. What more shall I tell you?"
Therefore, for the sake of increasing your progeny, worship Hari, the Lord of all beings,
Govinda, if you desire success.
For those who always seek righteousness, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
the Blessed One, the primordial Supreme Person, is to be propitiated.
Having propitiated that Acyuta, in whom Prajāpati performed creation at the beginning, there shall be an increase of your progeny.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by their father, those ten sons of Pracetas plunged into the waters of the ocean and performed austerities with concentrated minds.
O best of sages, for ten thousand years they fixed their minds upon Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, the supreme refuge of all the worlds.
Remaining right there with one-pointed minds, they praised Lord Hari,
who, when praised, bestows upon his worshiper the desired objects of their longing.
The illustrious Maitreya said:
O best of sages, you ought to relate to me that most meritorious hymn which the Pracetasas offered to Viṣṇu while they were situated within the waters of the ocean.
Śrī Parāśara said: Listen, Maitreya, to how the Pracetasas, having become absorbed in Him and lying within the waters of the ocean, praised Govinda as they did in former times.
The Pracetasas said:
We bow to that supreme Lord of the entire universe, who is without beginning or end, and in whom the eternal foundation of all speech is established.
He is light and the like, incomparable, minute, infinite, and boundless;
he is the source of all that is stationary and moving.
Salutation to Him, the soul of time, whose first form is day, as well as night and the twilight of the Supreme Lord.
He who consists of nectar is daily consumed by the gods and the ancestors;
he is the seed of everything—salutations to him in his lunar form.
Salutation to that one whose essence is the Sun, who consumes the darkness, who illuminates the sky with his rays, and whose source is both hot and cold water.

Salutation to that essence of the earth, who possesses solidity, who supports this entire world without exception, who is the substratum of sound and the other sense objects, and who is all-pervading.
We bow to that form of water belonging to the Lord Harimedhas, which is the womb of the world and the seed of all embodied beings.
Salutation to that Viṣṇu, whose nature is fire, who is the mouth of all the gods, as well as the consumer of sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya) for the ancestors.
Salutation to that Lord whose nature is wind, who has space as his source and who, abiding in five ways within the body, performs its activities incessantly.
Salutation to Him whose self is space, the awakened one who possesses infinite forms and provides room for all beings without exception.
Salutation to Kṛṣṇa, the creator, who is the eternal and supreme abode of the entire creation of the senses, and whose form consists of sound and the other objects of perception.
Salutations to that Harimedhas, the root of all knowledge, who— being both the imperishable and the perishable— is the self of the senses and constantly perceives the objects of the senses.
Salutation to that Universal Self, who, in the form of the internal organ, bestows upon the self the objects apprehended by the senses.
Salutation to Him whose nature is primordial matter (prakṛti), in whom the entire universe resides, from whom it has likewise emerged, and who is its place of dissolution— He who is infinite.
O Lord, we bow to that Supreme Person, whose nature is the Self; though devoid of qualities, he is perceived through delusion as if possessed of qualities because of his purity.
We bow to that supreme Brahman, which is unchanging, unborn, pure, devoid of qualities, and stainless— that which is the highest state of Viṣṇu.
Neither long nor short, neither gross nor subtle, neither dark nor red; without oiliness, without shadow, without mass, unattached, and bodiless.
That which is without space, without touch, without smell, and without taste;
which is without eyes, ears, motion, speech, hands, or feet.
It is beyond the scope of names and speech, consisting of bliss, consciousness, and splendor, and is without cause;
it is fearless, free from delusion, and without sleep, old age, or death.
That which is free from dust, soundless, immortal, unflooded, and unenclosed,
wherein there is neither before nor after— that indeed is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
We bow to that state of Viṣṇu, which possesses the quality of supreme lordship over all beings without doubt,
and which is not within the range of the tongue or the sight.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus, praising Viṣṇu with their minds absorbed in Him,
the Pracetasas performed austerities in the great ocean for ten thousand years.
Then the blessed Lord Hari, appearing with the luster of the petals of a blooming blue lotus, granted them a vision of himself while they were within the water.
Beholding him mounted upon the king of birds,
the sons of Pracetas prostrated themselves before him with their heads bowed down by the weight of devotion.
Then the Blessed One said to them, "Let the desired boon be requested;
I am well-disposed toward you and have appeared as a granter of boons."
Then, having prostrated before that giver of boons, the Pracetasas spoke to him concerning the cause for the increase of progeny as it had been commanded by their father.
And that god, having granted him the boon as desired, quickly vanished; and they emerged from the water.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Pracetasas," in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: While the Pracetasas were performing austerities over the earth, trees [arose].
When she was left unprotected, they covered her; thereafter, there occurred a destruction of the population.
The wind was unable to blow, for the sky was covered by trees;
for ten thousand years, living beings were unable to move.
Seeing them, all the Pracetasas emerged from the water and, filled with rage and their anger kindled,
they emitted wind and fire from their mouths.
Then, having uprooted those trees, the wind withered them;
thereafter, a terrible fire consumed them, and thus occurred the destruction of the forest.
Then, seeing that the trees were being exhausted and only a few branches remained,
King Soma approached those Prajāpatis and said to them:
"Restrain your anger, O kings, and listen to my words:
I shall effect a reconciliation between you and the trees."
This maiden Vārkṣeyī, of excellent complexion, is like a jewel;
knowing this would happen in the future, she was previously raised by me with cows.
This woman, created by name as Māriṣā among trees, let her be your wife, O fortunate ones; she shall surely increase your lineage.
"By half of your splendor and half of my own splendor,
a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her."
Endowed with a portion of myself and with your own fiery splendor,
he shall indeed increase the progeny once more, possessing a brilliance equal to fire.
Formerly, there was a sage named Kaṇḍu, the best among the knowers of the Vedas;
he performed supreme austerity on the beautiful bank of the Gomatī.
To disturb him, the Lord of the Gods dispatched a choice celestial nymph named Pramlocā;
that woman of pure smiles then sought to agitate the sage.
Agitated by her, he remained for more than a hundred years in the valley of Mount Mandara, his mind attached to the objects of the senses.
She said to him, "O illustrious one, I desire to go to heaven;
O Brahmin, being well-disposed toward me with favor, you should grant me permission."
Thus addressed by her, that sage, his mind attached to her, said:
"O blessed lady, please stay for a few days."
Having been addressed thus by him, that slender woman again enjoyed sensual pleasures together with that great-souled one for more than a hundred years.
"Grant me permission, O Blessed One; I am going to the abode of the thirty gods.
Being told "So be it," he replied, "Wait a moment."
When another hundred years had passed, that lady of auspicious countenance said,
"I am going to heaven, O Brahmin," with a beautiful smile of affection.
Having been addressed thus by her, that sage embraced her for a long moment and said:
"O fair-browed one, stay here for a moment; you shall depart after a long time."
Sporting with that rishi once more, that woman of beautiful hips remained for two hundred years, slightly less than that.
"O illustrious one, go to the abode of the king of the gods," she said repeatedly;
but addressed thus by that slender lady, he replied, "Stay."
Terrified by the fear of his curse, yet guided by courtesy and aware that the breach of affection would cause him pain, Dakṣiṇā did not abandon the sage.
And as that supreme ṛṣi took delight with her day and night, his mind possessed by the god of love, his pleasure became ever new.
Once, however, the sage emerged from his hut in a hurry;
as he was departing, that auspicious woman asked, "Where are you going?"
Thus addressed by her, he said: "O auspicious lady, the day has turned; I shall perform the twilight worship, otherwise there would be a lapse in my ritual duties."
Then, smiling brightly, she said to that great sage:
"O knower of all dharmas, why has your day turned into night today?"
O Brahmin, many years have passed by; tell me, who would not be filled with wonder that this has come to pass? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.15.27)
The sage said:
"O blessed lady, you arrived this morning at this auspicious riverbank;
O slender-limbed one, you were seen by me as you entered my hermitage."
This twilight has arrived as the day has come to its end;
for what purpose is this mockery? Let my true intention be told to me.
Pramloca said:
"O Brahmin, it is true that I arrived at dawn; this is not false.
Yet, of that very time, hundreds of years have passed for you."
Soma said:
Then, filled with trepidation, that brahmin asked the large-eyed woman,
"Tell me, O timid one, how much time has passed while I have been sporting with you?"
Pramlocā said:
"Seven hundred and seven years have passed for you,
as well as six months and another three days."
The sage said:
"O timid one, you speak this truth, or perhaps it is a jest, O auspicious lady; I believe that I have spent even a single day here together with you."
Prāmloca said: "O Brahmin, how could I speak an untruth here in your presence,
especially since I have been questioned today by you who follow the path of righteousness?"
Having heard those truthful words, O princes, that sage,
saying "Fie, fie upon me! reproached himself most bitterly.
The sage said:
"My ascetic merits have perished; the wealth of those who know Brahman has been destroyed; my discrimination has been slain by someone who fashioned women for the purpose of delusion."
"Brahman is to be known by me as transcending the six waves through self-conquest; fie on that great-grasping desire by which this mind of mine has been carried away! (ViP 1.15.37)
All my vows, which were the means for attaining the knowledge of the Vedas,
have been carried away by attachment, which leads along the path to the village of hell.
Thus reproaching himself by himself, that knower of dharma spoke these words to the Apsaras who was seated there: ||| ViP_1,15.39 |||
"Go, O wicked one, as you desire! You have accomplished your purpose by agitating the king of the gods with your amorous gestures."
I shall not reduce you to ashes with the fierce fire of my wrath;
for friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together. Thus have I spoken with you.
Or rather, what fault is there in you, or why should I be angry with you?
The fault is entirely my own, since I have failed to conquer my senses.
"Fie on you, that most loathsome basket of great delusion, by whom— desiring to please Śakra— the expenditure of my ascetic merit was caused!"
Soma said:
While that brahmin-sage was thus speaking to her in private,
she became covered in perspiring drops and seized by a violent trembling.
To her, who was trembling constantly with her vine-like limbs exhausted, that best of sages spoke angrily: "Go! Go! (ViP 1.15.45)
Rebuked by him, she departed from that hermitage and,
traveling through the sky, wiped away her sweat with the tender leaves of trees.
Wiping her limbs which were dripping with sweat,
Balā went from tree to tree, [using] their tips of reddish young shoots.
The embryo that had then been placed within her body by the sage emerged from her limbs in the form of horripilation and perspiration.
The trees received him as their embryo, and the Wind-god formed him into a single mass;
nourished by me with rays of light, he then grew gradually.
"A beautiful-faced woman named Māriṣā, born from the interior of the treetops, shall give herself to you; let this anger be appeased."
Thus she was the offspring of Kaṇḍu; she emerged from the trees, and likewise she was the offspring of Vāyu and the daughter of Pramlocā.
And that blessed Kaṇḍu, O best of beings, when his ascetic penance was exhausted,
went, O Maitreya, to the abode of Viṣṇu known as Puruṣottama.
There, O sons of the king, having become single-minded, that great yogi stood with his arms raised and performed the worship of Hari, reciting the *Brahmapāra* with a concentrated mind.
The Pracetasas said:
"O Sage, we wish to hear the supreme hymn that reaches the further shore of the Veda,
by which the god Keśava was propitiated while Kaṇḍu was chanting."
Soma said:

Viṣṇu is the further shore, the shore of the shoreless, higher than the high; he who has the form of the charioteer of the world, whose shore is Brahman, who has become the shore beyond all shores, and who is the shore of even the highest shores.
He is the cause from the perspective of causality, and even beyond that, he is the cause of that [cause] as well;
and thus, within effects, together with all forms of actions and agents, he enters into everything here without exception.
Brahmā is the Lord, Brahmā is he who has become all beings; that infallible one is the Lord of creatures.
He is Viṣṇu, the imperishable, eternal, and unborn Brahmā, unattached to all things such as decay and the like.
Just as this Supreme Person is the unborn, eternal syllable of Brahman,
so may my defects, such as passion and the rest, come to complete pacification.
Soma said:
By chanting this supreme hymn known as the *Parā*,
and by propitiating Keśava, he attained the highest perfection.
Whoever constantly recites or even hears this hymn shall be liberated from the unwholesome desires of passion and attain their wish.
And this Mārīṣā was formerly she whom I shall describe to you;
due to the importance of the matter, speaking of her will be fruitful for you.
O best of men, previously, when her husband had died, this highly fortunate wife of Bhīṣmaka, being childless, propitiated Viṣṇu with devotion.
Viṣṇu, being propitiated by her, appeared before her in person and said, "Choose a boon, O auspicious lady. She then spoke of her own desire.
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, I am such a woman whose birth is in vain due to widowhood in childhood; I have arisen with little fortune and am fruitless."
"By your grace, may I have praiseworthy husbands in birth after birth; likewise, O son, may I have a son equal to Prajāpati."
Noble lineage, virtuous conduct, youth, truthfulness, courtesy, promptness of action, reliability, courage, service to elders, and gratitude; // ViP_1,15.65 //
"Endowed with perfect beauty, pleasing to the sight of all,
and not born from a womb, may I be so born through your grace, O Lord of the Adityas."
Thus addressed by her, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of gods,
the supreme sovereign and giver of boons, raised her up as she was bowing low in prostration and spoke to her.
The god said:
"In a single birth alone, there shall be ten husbands for you, men of great heroism, whose noble fame will be renowned throughout the world."
And you, O beautiful one, shall obtain a son of great heroism, endowed with great strength and prowess, and possessed of the qualities of Prajāpati.
He shall be the founder of lineages in this world;
his progeny shall fill the entirety of the three worlds.
And you too, O virtuous lady, shall be born not from a womb, endowed with beauty, nobility, and excellent qualities;
by my grace, you shall be one who brings delight to the minds of men.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished before that large-eyed woman;
and she, O princes, has been born as this Māriṣā, your wife.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas withdrew their anger from the trees and accepted Mārīṣā as their wife according to the law of matrimony.
From the ten Pracetas, however, the illustrious Prajāpati Dakṣa was born of Mārīṣā— he who had previously been born from Brahmā.
But that highly fortunate Dakṣa, O great-minded one,
begot sons for the purpose of creation, for the sake of his own progeny.
Carrying out the command of Brahmā for the purpose of creation, he brought forth both inferior and superior beings, whether two-footed or four-footed.
Having first created by means of his mind, the skillful Dakṣa subsequently created women;
he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven, who are engaged in the guidance of time, to the Moon.
From them were born the gods, as well as the Daityas, Nāgas, cows, birds,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Dānavas, and others.
From that time forth, O Maitreya, progeny were born from sexual union;
whereas previously, the offspring of those ancient beings arose through mere intention, sight, or touch—
beings who were perfected by their specific austerities and were then supreme ascetics.
The illustrious Maitreya said:
"I have previously heard from you that Dakṣa was born from the right thumb;
how then, O great sage, was he born again as the son of Pracetas?"
O Brahman, this very great doubt dwells within my heart:
how it is that one who was the son-in-law of Soma has again become his father-in-law.
Śrī Rāśara said: "Arising and cessation are eternal among all beings at all times;
even the sages and others who possess divine vision do not understand this."
O best of sages, these beings, beginning with Dakṣa, come into existence in age after age, and likewise they are dissolved again; the wise man is not deluded by this.
O best of the twice-born, neither the state of being the youngest nor that of being the eldest existed among them previously;
austerity alone was weightier, and spiritual power was the sole cause [of their status].
Maitreya said: O Brahmin, proclaim to me here in detail the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.
Śrī Parāśara said: O great sage, listen to how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to "create progeny," created all beings.
In the beginning, Dakṣa then created from his mind alone the beings:
the gods, the ṛṣis, along with the gandharvas, as well as the asuras and the pannagas.
When those creatures being created by him did not increase in number,
the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) then reflected again for the sake of further creation.

Desiring to create various offspring through the very law of sexual union, he took as his wife Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa, who was endowed with great ascetic merit and was a mighty sustainer of the world.
Then, for the sake of creation, the powerful Prajāpati begot five thousand sons upon Vairuṇī and Asiknī.
O Brahmin, seeing them desiring to multiply their progeny, the celestial sage Nārada, who speaks with pleasing words, approached them and said this: ||| ViP_1,15.91 |||
"O Haryaśvas of great prowess, you shall create progeny;
such effort as this is seen in you, so listen to this."
"Alas, you are indeed childish; you do not know the interior, the heights, and the depths of this earth. How then will you create progeny?"
When your movement is unimpeded upwards, across, and downwards,
why then, O fools, do you all not see the end of the earth?
Having heard those words of his, they departed in every direction;
even today they do not return, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
Then, when the Haryashvas had perished,
the lord Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, again begot a thousand sons upon Vairuṇī.
O Brahmin, desiring once again to increase their progeny, those Śabalāśvas were urged by Nārada with the very words previously mentioned.
They all said to one another, "The great sage has spoken correctly;
the path of our brothers must indeed be followed, there is no doubt about this."
Having ascertained the measure of the earth, we shall then create living beings.
They too set out upon that very same path leading in every direction,
and even today they have not returned, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
From that time forth, O twice-born one, brother has indeed been engaged in the search for his brother.
Just as that which has set forth perishes, so too should that not be undertaken by one who possesses discernment.
And perceiving that his sons were lost, the illustrious Prajāpati Dakṣa became enraged and cursed Nārada.
Then, O Maitreya, that wise Prajāpati, desiring to create, fashioned sixty daughters from Vairuṇī; so we have heard.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were born to Bahuputra, two likewise to Aṅgiras, and two to the learned Kṛśāśva; hear their names from me.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmi, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—
these ten are the wives of Dharma; hear from me the offspring born of them.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas;
from Marutvatī came the Maruts, and the Vasus are said to have been born from Vasu.
The rays of the Sun were the sons of Muhūrtā, born at each muhūrta.
And from Laṅkā came Ghoṣa, while Nāgavīthī was born as Jāmitā.
Everything pertaining to the domain of the earth was born from Arundhatī;
but from Saṃkalpā was born Saṃkalpa himself, the soul of all.
Those who are known as the eight Vasus, preceded by Jyotis and consisting of many riches, vital breaths, and deities— I shall now describe them in detail.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dharma, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are remembered as the Vasus by name.
Āpa’s sons were Vaitaṇḍa, Śrama, Śānta, and likewise Adhvanī;
and the lordly Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, was the son of Dhruva.
The venerable Soma is the splendor by which one becomes resplendent.
The sons of Dharma were Draviṇa and Hutahavyavaha; likewise, from Manoharā were born Śiśira, Prāṇa, and Ravaṇa.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Manojava;
Avijñātagati was also [his son]; thus Anila had two sons.
Kumāra, the son of Agni, was born in a clump of reeds;
Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya were his younger brothers.
The offspring of the Kṛttikās is known as Kārttikeya.
They know Pratyūṣa’s son to be the sage named Devala;
Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise.
The sister of Bṛhaspati was an excellent woman who observed celibacy;
perfected in yoga, she wanders through the entire world unattached.
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
From her was born the highly fortunate Prajāpati Viśvakarman,
the creator of thousands of arts and the architect of the gods.
He was the creator of all ornaments and the best among artisans;
he indeed fashioned the celestial chariots for all the deities,
and human beings subsist upon the craftsmanship of that great-souled one.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra;
and also the son born of Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvarūpa, who possessed great ascetic power.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and Raivata are remembered [as his forms].
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kapālī— O great sage,
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
One hundred [sons] of immeasurable splendor are declared to be the Rudras.
Now hear from me the names of those who were the wives of Kaśyapa:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, and Khasā.
O knower of dharma, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni— listen to me as I describe their offspring.
When the period of the highly illustrious Manu Cākṣuṣa had arrived,
they all came together and assembled with one another.
"Come quickly, O gods, and indeed enter into Aditi;
we shall procreate during the Manvantara, for that will be for our welfare."
Having spoken thus, they were all born during the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, and Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa.
There, Viṣṇu and Śakra were indeed born once again,
as were Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aṃśu, and Bhaga of exceeding splendor— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
In the previous interval of Cākṣuṣa, there were the Tuṣita gods;
indeed, in the Vaivasvata interval, they are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
The twenty-seven wives of Soma who were mentioned, being of virtuous vows,
are all known as the Yoginīs of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), and they are remembered by their respective names.
Their offspring were radiant and possessed immeasurable splendor.
The offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi here [numbered] sixteen.
Four types of lightning are recorded for the learned Bahuputra.
The verses born of Pratyāṅgirasa were the most excellent, honored by the Brahman-sages.
The divine weapons are said to belong to the celestial sage Kṛśāśva.
At the end of a thousand yugas, O dear one, all these thirty-three classes of gods born of Chanda are indeed born again;
for them also, there is said to be constant cessation and origination in this world.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun occur here, O Maitreya,
so do those hosts of gods come into being age after age.
We have heard that Diti gave birth to two sons from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyakaśipu and the invincible Hiraṇyākṣa.
And Siṃhikā became the daughter who was the wife of Vipracitti.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of renowned prowess:
Anuhlāda, Hlāda, the wise Prahlāda, and Saṃhlāda;
they were of great heroism and increased the lineage of the Daityas.
Among them, O fortunate one, Prahlāda, who looked upon all things with an equal eye,
spoke of supreme devotion toward Janārdana.
O twice-born one, the fire kindled by the lord of the Daityas, though it enveloped all his limbs,
did not burn him, O Brahmin, because Vāsudeva was stationed in his heart.
While he, the wise one, remained within the waters at the edge of the great ocean, the earth shook as he moved,
bound by his own noose.
The body of him whose mind was never wavering from Acyuta remained unbroken by the various weapons hurled by the lord of the Daityas, for it was as hard as a mountain.
The lords of serpents, though possessed of great splendor and urged on by the Daityas, with mouths blazing like poisonous fire, were unable to bring about his end.
Even though his body was crushed by mountains, he who remembered Puruṣottama did not give up his life-breaths, being armored by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Approaching that high-minded one as he was falling from the sky toward the earth,
the Lord of the Daityas, who dwells in heaven, seized him.
The drying wind that had been unleashed upon his body by the lord of the Daityas was instantly brought to destruction, since Madhusūdana resided within his heart.
The intoxicated elephants of the quarters, transformed by the Lord of the Daityas, suffered the breaking of their tusks and the loss of their pride upon reaching his chest.
And the *kṛtyā* that had been produced by the priests of the Daitya king in former times did not lead to the end of him whose mind was fixed on Govinda.
And the thousand illusions of Śambara, the master of great magic,
were rendered futile by the discus of Kṛṣṇa when they were employed against him.
The wise and unenvious one digested the Hālāhala poison, brought by the cook of the lord of the Daityas, without undergoing any transformation.
He whose mind is equanimous toward all beings in this world, who possesses the supreme quality of friendliness and treats others just as he treats himself; ViP_1,15.155 //
He was a righteous soul, a supreme mine of virtues such as truthfulness and heroism,
who always served as the standard of comparison for all virtuous men.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said: "The lineage of the high-souled descendants of Manu has been recounted by you."
And the eternal Viṣṇu alone is the cause of this world.
As for that which the Blessed One said concerning Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas:
"The fire did not burn him, nor did he give up his life when struck by missiles."
The earth shook where he stood upon the waters of the ocean;
as he moved while bound by the noose, it was struck by his tossing limbs.
He whose body was once crushed by mountains yet did not die,
and of whom you have described the exceedingly great majesty— that wise one.
O Sage, I desire to hear of the incomparable power of that devoted Bhakta Viṣṇu, whose life-story is this and whose splendor is radiant.
For what reason was he struck with weapons by the son of Diti, O sage?
And for what purpose was he cast into the waters of the ocean, he who was devoted to righteousness?
Why was he overwhelmed by mountains, and why bitten by great serpents?
Why was he hurled from a mountain peak, or cast into a mass of fire?
And why was he appointed to the region of the tusks of the elephants of the quarters?
And why was the wind Śoṣaka employed against him by the great Asuras?
O sage, did the preceptors of the Daityas employ a *kṛtyā* there,
and did Śambara also deploy a thousand illusions?
Alas, why was the Hālāhala poison given for his destruction by the slayers of the Daityas to that great-souled and wise one, since it was digested by him?
O illustrious one, I desire to hear all this account of the high-souled Prahlāda, which indicates his great majesty.
Indeed, there was no cause for wonder in that, for he had already been slain by the Daityas;
for who would be capable of striking down Viṣṇu when his mind is focused on nothing else?
While he was thus constantly devoted to dharma and intent upon the worship of Keśava,
the Daityas born of his own lineage harbored a most difficult-to-overcome hatred toward him.
O illustrious one, why was the Daityas struck at one who is the very self of Dharma, devoted to Viṣṇu, and free from envy? You ought to explain that to me.
Even great-souled adversaries do not strike one such as this;
how much less so one who is born of their own side, when he is a virtuous person endowed with excellent qualities?
Therefore, O bull among sages, let all this be told in detail;
I wish to hear the life-story of the lord of the Daityas in its entirety.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: "O Maitreya, listen well to the life-story of that wise one."
Of the high-souled Prahlāda, whose conduct was ever noble.
In ancient times, the son of Diti, Hiraṇyakaśipu, who possessed great heroism and was arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, brought the three worlds under his control.
That Daitya made himself Indra, and he himself became the Sun;
the great Asura also became Vāyu, Agni, the Lord of Waters, and Soma.
He became the lord of riches; he himself was Yama;
and that asura personally consumed all the sacrificial portions without exception.
O best of sages, having abandoned heaven out of fear of him, all the gods wandered upon the earth,
assuming human bodies.
Having conquered the entire three worlds and being intoxicated by the sovereignty over the triple universe,
he enjoyed his beloved sensory objects while being celebrated in song by the Gandharvas.
Then all the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas waited upon the high-souled Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was devoted to drinking.
Others played instruments and sang, while still others raised shouts of victory;
filled with joy, the Siddhas performed these acts before the king of the Daityas.
There, in that most enchanting palace made of crystal, where celestial nymphs were dancing, the asura drank his drink with great joy.
His son, a highly fortunate one named Prahlāda by name, went to his teacher’s house and, as a young boy, recited the lessons intended for children.
Once, however, that righteous-souled one went with his preceptor into the presence of his father, the lord of the Daityas, who was then addicted to drink.
Raising up his son Prahlāda, who was of immeasurable splendor and prostrate at his feet in salutation, his father Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Recite, my child, that essential and well-spoken word which you have learned through such long time by being constantly diligent."
Prahlāda said:
"Listen, dear father; at your command I shall speak that which is the very essence, which dwells within my mind, with your attention fully composed."
I bow to Him who is without beginning, middle, or end; unborn, without increase, decay, or fall; the ultimate limit of limits, the cause of all causes.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard this, the lord of the Daityas, his eyes red with anger,
