looked at his preceptor and spoke, his sprout-like lips quivering.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O wretched Brahmin, why have you, having disregarded me, caused this foolish boy to be instructed in this worthless thing consisting of praise for my enemy, O evil-minded one?"
The Guru said:
"O Lord of Daityas, you ought not to fall under the sway of anger;
this son of yours does not speak [thus] because of my instruction."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"My child, tell me, by whom have you been instructed in such a way?
This teacher of yours does not say, 'This was taught by me. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.17.19)
Prahlāda said:
"O dear one, apart from that Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, who is the teacher of the entire world and resides within the heart, who could be taught by whom?"
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Who is this Viṣṇu, O evil-minded one, of whom you speak again and again so boldly in the presence of me, the lord of the worlds?"
Prahlāda said: He whose supreme state is beyond the range of sound and is the object of meditation for yogis;
from whom it arises, who he is, and who is himself the universe—he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O wise one, while I am present, who else can be designated as the Supreme Lord?
Nevertheless, desiring death, you speak thus again and again."
Prahlāda said:
"O father, that Viṣṇu is not only the creator of my progeny, but also of yours;
he is the sustainer, the ordainer, and the supreme lord. Why then do you display such anger?"
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Who has entered the heart of this evil-minded one, this perpetrator of great sins,
by whom his mind is so possessed that he speaks such wicked things?"
Prahlāda said:
O father, that Viṣṇu has not only pervaded my heart, but having entered all the worlds, he remains there;
omnipresent, he joins me, you, and all others to every activity.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Let this wicked man be cast out and let him be punished for staying in the teacher's house;
by whom was this evil-minded one employed to praise the domain of our enemy?"
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by the Daityas, he was then led back again to the teacher’s house;
there, intent on serving his preceptor, he mastered the sciences without ceasing.
When the great Kālotītā had finished, Prahlāda, the lord of the asuras,
summoned him and said, "O son, let some song be sung now."
Prahlāda said:
May that Viṣṇu, from whom Pradhāna and Puruṣa arise, and from whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings proceeds— the cause of all this— be gracious to us.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Let this evil-souled one be slain; there is no purpose in him living, for he has become a coal to his own lineage by causing the destruction of his own side."
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus commanded by him, hundreds of thousands of Daityas, seizing their great weapons, rose up for his destruction.
Prahlāda said:
"Viṣṇu is established in your weapons, in me, and in him; by that truth, O sons of Diti, let no weapons overcome me."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, although struck by those hundreds of Daityas with volleys of weapons,
he did not utter even a slight cry of pain and became as if newly born once again.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O evil-minded one, desist! Your enemy's side has been struck down.
I grant you safety; do not be so utterly deluded in mind."
Prahlāda said:
O remover of all fears, while You, the Infinite, abide within my mind, where can fear remain?
For when You are remembered, dear father, all fears such as birth, old age, and death depart.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O serpents, bring this man of evil conduct and extreme wickedness to his immediate destruction with your fangs, which are filled with the flames of poison!"
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, those serpents— Kuhaka, Takṣaka, and the others—
whose venom was exceedingly fierce, bit him on all his limbs.
But he, his mind entirely attached to Kṛṣṇa, though being bitten by great serpents,
did not perceive his own body, as he remained well-established in the bliss of remembering Him.
The serpents said:
"Our fangs are shattered, our jewels burst upon our hoods, there is burning in our hearts and trembling;
not even the slightest part of his skin is pierced here. O Lord of Daityas, accomplish some other task."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O elephants of the quarters, you whose tusks are formidable, slay this one who has betrayed our faction of enemies!
For those born from him lead to his own destruction, just as the blazing fire arises from the friction-sticks."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then that boy was cast down upon the surface of the earth by the elephants of the quarters, who resembled the peaks of mountains, and was tormented by their tusks.
As he was remembering Govinda, thousands of the elephant's tusks shattered upon striking his chest; thereupon, he spoke to his father.
That the tusks of the elephants—hard as the tip of a thunderbolt—were shattered by this [arrow] is due to my own strength;
yet, that it destroyed the torment of this great calamity is the power of recollecting Janārdana.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Asuras, let the fire be kindled; O elephants of the quarters, withdraw!
O Vāyu, fan the fire; let this evildoer be consumed!"
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, having kindled a fire upon a great heap of wood, the Dānavas, commanded by their lord, cremated that son of the Asura king.
Prahlāda said:
"O father, although this fire is fanned by the wind, it does not burn me here on all sides;
I see all the quarters of the sky as cool and covered with carpets of lotuses."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then the sons of Bhārgava, the high-souled and eloquent priests, praised the lord of the Daityas with conciliatory words and spoke to him.
The family priests said: "O King, let your anger be restrained even toward your own young son,
for your wrath would bring misfortune upon those hosts of gods."
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu was addressed by his own family priests:
"O King, we shall discipline this boy in such a way that he will become submissive for the sake of destroying your enemies."
Since childhood is the abode of all faults and the very foundation of the Daitya king,
you ought not to direct excessive anger toward this child.
"If he does not abandon the side of Hari at our word,
then we shall create an irresistible magical spell (kṛtyā) for his destruction."
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus entreated by those priests and the Daityas,
the king of the Daityas caused his son to be removed from the mass of fire.
Then, while living in the house of his preceptor, that boy repeatedly taught the young sons of the Dānavas during the intervals between his own lessons from the guru.
Prahlāda said:
"Listen to my ultimate truth, O sons of Diti, offspring of the Daityas;
this must not be considered otherwise, nor is there any cause such as greed or the like in this matter."
After birth, every living being attains childhood and then youth;
thereafter, old age proceeds day by day without obstruction.
And from that, O sons of the lord of the Daityas, a living being goes toward death;
this is seen directly by us as well as by you.
Furthermore, the rebirth of one who has died occurs, and this is not otherwise;
such is the traditional teaching (āgama), and likewise that there is no arising without a material cause (upādāna).
From dwelling in the womb until the production of rebirth, let it be understood that all those eight stages are nothing but suffering.

Likewise, due to their childish intellect, they consider the alleviation of hunger and thirst, as well as the relief from cold and other such things, to be happiness; yet that is in fact nothing but suffering.
For those whose limbs are utterly exhausted by exertion while seeking pleasure,
and whose eyes are shrouded by delusive cognition, suffering itself appears as happiness.
Where is the body— a vast accumulation of phlegm and other such substances—
and where are qualities such as luster, splendor, beauty, and charm?
If a fool feels delight in this body— a mere collection of flesh, blood, pus, feces, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones— he will surely find delight even in hell.
Fire produces pleasure through cold, water through thirst, and food through hunger; conversely, these same things produce the opposite effect when encountered by their opposites.
Whatever degree of attachment the daughter of the Daitya creates,
to that same degree she inflicts suffering upon his mind.
As many dear relationships as a living being forms with the mind,
so many spikes of sorrow are driven deep into his heart.
Whatever was in his house remained in his mind wherever he stayed;
the implements for its destruction and burning remained right there with them.
In this birth there is great suffering, as is that of one who is dying;
likewise, there is fierce agony in the hells of Yama and during the transitions through the womb.
If even a trace of pleasure is inferred by you within the womb,
then let it be explained how this entire world is thus composed of nothing but suffering.
Thus, in this ocean of existence which is the abode of such extreme sufferings,
it is told to you as a truth that Viṣṇu alone is the supreme refuge.
"Do not think that we are fools; the embodied soul is eternal within bodies.
Old age, youth, birth, and so forth are attributes of the body, not of the self."
"As long as I am a child, I will strive for my welfare according to my desire; or, when I am young, I will do so; and once old age has arrived, I shall accomplish what is beneficial for myself."
"I am old; all my duties are beyond my reach.
What shall I, a dull-witted man, do that which was not accomplished by one who was capable?"
Thus, a man whose mind is cast down by evil desires always moves away from what is beneficial; he never turns toward it when he is parched with thirst.
Attached to playthings in childhood and intent on sense-objects in youth, the ignorant pass their time until old age has arrived, rendered powerless.
Therefore, while still a child, one whose self is discerning should always strive for the highest good,
remaining unattached to the states of the body such as childhood, youth, and old age.
This which has been recounted by me to you— if you know it to be no falsehood—
then for our pleasure, let Viṣṇu, the giver of liberation from bondage, be remembered.
What effort is required for his remembrance? When remembered, he bestows auspiciousness;
and for those who remember him day and night, there occurs the destruction of their sins.
"May your minds, day and night, be established in loving-kindness toward Him who dwells within all beings;
by doing so, you shall abandon all afflictions."
When this entire world is afflicted by the threefold suffering,
what wise person would harbor hatred toward beings who are themselves objects of pity?
Moreover, even when other beings are prosperous while I am of inferior power, I should still feel joy; for loss is the fruit of hatred.
If beings who harbor enmity feel hatred toward one another, then they are truly pitiable, being overwhelmed by extreme delusion; such is the view of the wise.
These conceptual constructions of those with divergent views have been described by me;
having accepted that, now hear from me a summary.
This entire world is the expansion of Viṣṇu, who is the self of all beings;
therefore, it should be viewed by the wise as non-different from the Self.
Therefore, having cast off our asuric nature, we shall strive in such a manner that we may attain liberation, just as you have done.
She who cannot be [overpowered] by fire, nor by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by the wind;
nor by Pajanya or Varuna, nor by the Siddhas, nor by the Saksas.
Neither by Yakṣas, nor by lords of Daityas, nor by Uragas, nor by Kiṃnaras;
neither by humans, nor by animals, nor by defects arising from oneself.
Likewise, they go to ruin through fever, eye diseases, dysentery, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and the like;
or through the fires of hatred, envy, and malice, as well as passion, greed, and other such passions.
It is not led by anyone else; it is eternal and absolutely pure. A man attains that stainless heart of Keśava through another who is himself stainless.
"Do not yield to satisfaction amidst the revolutions of this essence-less saṃsāra; I speak to you with urgency.
O Daityas, attain equanimity toward all things, for equanimity is the means of propitiating Acyuta."
When he is pleased, what is there in this world that is unattainable? Dharma, artha, and kāma are of little account;
one who has taken refuge in the infinite banyan tree of Brahman undoubtedly obtains a truly great fruit.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Deeds of Prahlāda," in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having observed these actions of his, the Dānavas, out of fear of the lord of the Daityas, [acted accordingly].
They reported it, and he, having quickly summoned the cooks, spoke.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O cooks, this wicked-minded son of mine,
who is a corrupt teacher of evil paths even to others, must be killed without delay."
"Let the Hālāhala poison be given to him among all the foods;
let that wicked man be killed while it remains unknown—do not hesitate."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then they did exactly as they were commanded by his father— that is, they administered poison to the high-souled Prahlāda.
O Maitreya, having consecrated the terrible hālāhala poison with the recitation of the mantra of Ananta, he then consumed it along with his food.
Having consumed that poison without any change in his state, Prahlāda, with a composed mind,
digested that venom through his infinite renown and power.
Then the cooks, terrified with fear upon seeing the great poison had been digested,
approached the lord of the Daityas, prostrated themselves, and spoke as follows:
The cooks said:
"O King of the Daityas, the most terrifying poison was administered by us;
it was digested along with the food by your son Prahlāda."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Hurry, hurry, O priests of the Daityas!
Create a magical spell (kṛtyā) for his immediate destruction; do not delay!"
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then the family priests, having approached Prahlāda,
spoke with humility and conciliatory words to him who was full of discipline.
The family priests said:
"O long-lived one, you were born in the lineage of Brahmā, renowned throughout the three worlds;
you are the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the king of the Daityas."
What need have you for the gods, what for Ananta, or for anyone else? Your father is the refuge of all the worlds, and you likewise shall become so.
Therefore, abandon this hostile collection of verses;
your father is praiseworthy, the supreme preceptor among all gurus.
Prahlāda said:
"O highly fortunate ones, it is even so; this great lineage is praiseworthy.
Within this entire triple world, no one else than Marīci could speak otherwise."
And my father is the one whose deeds are most excellent in this entire world;
I understand this also to be true, for there is no falsehood in this matter.
Of all gurus, the father is the supreme guru;
for even a slight error in what he says does not exist. (ViP 1.18.16)
"The father is undoubtedly a guru; he must be honored with every effort.
Furthermore, it was established in his mind that 'I shall never offend him.'"
As for this which you have said—"What is this [world] that is infinite?"—who says it according to what is right? However, this statement is not meaningful.
Having spoken thus, he became silent, constrained by their respect;
yet, smiling again, he said: "What is the use of this endless talk? It is well."
"Excellent, O venerable ones! What need is there for me to speak at length? Listen, O teachers, to that which I shall say at length, if you will not grow weary."
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are declared to be the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha).
Since these four constitute the whole, what is the meaning of this statement?
Likewise, Dharma was attained by Dakṣa and others accompanied by Marīci, as well as by others in infinite numbers; and similarly, Artha was attained by some, and Kāma by others.
Having become knowers of that reality through knowledge, meditation, and concentration,
other persons attained liberation, their bonds destroyed.
The worship of Hari is the sole root from which may be obtained the perfection of wealth, sovereignty, majesty, knowledge, spiritual lineage, ritual action, and liberation.
"Since the fruits known as dharma, artha, kāma, and even liberation (mukti) [are obtained from it], O twice-born ones—what then is the use of that which is infinite? Thus it is asked."
Moreover, what is the use of speaking at length, O venerable ones, my teachers? Speak well what is right or wrong; our own discernment is but slight.
What need is there for much speaking here? He alone is the Lord of the universe;
he is the creator, the transformer, and the destroyer, residing within the heart.
He is the enjoyer and likewise the object of enjoyment; he alone is the Lord of the Universe.
Whatever has been said by me out of childishness, that must be forgiven by you.
The family priests said:
"O child, though you were being consumed by us with fire, you were protected;
thinking that you would never speak again, we did not realize you were lacking in intelligence."
O evil-minded one, when you do not abandon this deluded obsession because of our words, we shall then release a magical spirit (kṛtyā) for your destruction.
Prahlāda said:
By what is a living being slain, and by what is a living being protected?
Indeed, it is the self that slays and protects itself by practicing both evil and good.
Everything is born of karma; karma alone is the means for attaining a state of existence.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform virtuous action.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those enraged priests of the Daitya king produced a *kṛtyā* whose form blazed with garlands of flames.
Approaching with great ferocity, she who mangled the earth with her footsteps,
being thoroughly enraged, swiftly struck him in the chest with her trident.
Having reached the heart of that boy, the blazing trident shattered upon the ground, splitting there as well into a hundred pieces.
Wherever the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, dwells unfailingly within the heart, even a diamond may break; what then need be said of a mere spear?
In that place devoid of sin, she was cast down by the sinful Daityas who were acting as officiating priests;
she quickly slew those very ones and then herself met her destruction.
Seeing them being consumed by the magical spell (kṛtyā), that highly intelligent one rushed forward, crying out, "Save us, O Kṛṣṇa! Save us, O Ananta!"
Prahlāda said:
O all-pervading one, whose form is the universe, creator of the world, Janārdana!
Protect these brahmins from this unbearable fire of mantras.
Just as Viṣṇu alone is the all-pervading teacher of the world among all beings, so may all these priests live.
"Just as I regard Viṣṇu as omnipresent and never-failing, so do I think even of those on the side of my enemies: may these priests live."

Those who came to kill me, those who gave poison, those who kindled the fire, those world-elephants by whom I was crushed, and even those serpents by whom I was bitten—[to all of them I offer salutations].* *Note: This verse functions as a formal salutation (namaskāra) to the various agents of the speaker's past misfortunes.*
"Among them, I am equal through my friendly disposition; I have never been sinful toward anyone.
By that truth, may the sacrificers for the Asuras live today!"* *Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.18.43*
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus by him, all those twice-born ones, touched by his hand, rose up free from affliction and spoke to him with great humility.
The family priests said:
"O child, may you be long-lived, unassailable, and endowed with strength and valor; may you be pre-eminent, possessed of sons, grandsons, wealth, and horses."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having spoken thus to him, O great sage, the priests then went and related everything exactly as it had happened to the king of the Daityas.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter (18), titled "The Deeds of Prahlāda," in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard that the magical spell had been rendered futile, Hiraṇyakaśipu—
Having summoned his son, he asked him the cause of this power.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Prahlāda, you possess great power; what is this performance of yours?
Is it produced by mantras and the like, or is it innate to you?"
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus questioned by his father at that time, Prahlāda, the son of the asuras,
prostrated at his father’s feet and spoke these words.
"O dear one, this power of mine is neither produced by mantras and the like, nor is it innate;
rather, it is common to whomever Acyuta dwells within the heart."
O dear one, for him who does not contemplate the misdeeds of others as he would his own,
the arrival of evil does not exist, because of the absence of its cause.
Whoever inflicts suffering through action, mind, or speech,
that seed bears for him abundant and inauspicious fruit in his next birth.
Thus, reflecting upon Keśava, who dwells within all beings and within myself as well, I do not desire evil, nor do I commit it, nor do I speak it.
How could physical, mental, divine, or elemental suffering ever arise for me, whose mind is everywhere auspicious?
Thus, having realized that Hari consists of all beings, the wise should practice unwavering devotion toward all living creatures.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard this, the lord of the Daityas, standing upon the roof-peak of his palace,
his face darkened by rage, spoke to the servants of the Daityas.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Let this evil-souled one be hurled from this palace a hundred yojanas away;
let him fall upon the mountain peak with his mass of limbs shattered by rocks."
Then all the Daityas and Dānavas hurled that child;
though thus thrown down, he fell while bearing Hari within his heart.
As he was falling toward Keśava, the sustainer of the world, the Earth,
filled with devotion, approached and supported him.
Then, having observed that he was unharmed and his skeletal frame intact, Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke to Śambara, the best among magicians: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19.14.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "This foolish boy cannot be slain by us;
you, however, know the art of illusion (māyā), therefore destroy him with that very illusion."
Śambara said:
"O Lord of Daityas, I shall indeed destroy you; behold my power of illusion!
Behold here a thousand illusions, and likewise hundreds of millions."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then the evil-minded asura Śambara, desiring his destruction, created an illusion against Prahlāda, who perceives with equanimity toward all things.
Having become composed in mind and free from envy even toward Śambara,
O Maitreya, that Prahlāda also called to mind Madhusūdana.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, commanded by the Blessed One for the sake of his protection, the supreme Sudarśana discus, garlanded with flames, arrived.
By means of that swift-moving [missile], Māyāvatī created a thousand illusions for Śambara,
while he protected the body of the child, clearing away each one as it appeared.
Then the lord of the Daityas spoke thus to the wind that withers all:
"By my command, let this evil-souled one be swiftly led to his destruction."
Having said "So be it," the wind also swiftly entered him—
cold, excessively harsh, and unbearable, for the purpose of withering his body.
Then that child-like Buddha, perceiving himself to be possessed by him,
held the Great-Souled Sustainer of the Earth within his heart.
Then Janārdana, enraged, drank up that most terrifying wind situated within his heart; that wind went to its destruction.
When all his illusions had vanished and the wind had subsided,
that highly intelligent one also went to the palace of Kuru.
Day after day, the preceptor taught that boy the policy for securing the fruits of sovereignty, as composed by Uśanas for kings.
When the preceptor perceived that he had mastered the science of polity and was well-disciplined,
he then informed his father that he had been instructed.
The teacher said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, your son Prahlāda has been made a student of the science of polity;
he knows in truth that which was uttered by the descendant of Bhṛgu."

Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O Prahlāda, how should a king behave toward his friends, how toward the ranks of his enemies, and how should he conduct himself toward those who are neutral among the three worlds?"
How [should he act] toward his ministers and counselors, both those from outside and those from within, toward his spies and the body of citizens, whether they are suspected or otherwise?
O Prahlāda, tell us correctly the rules for what ought and ought not to be done, the means of subduing forts and forest tribes, and likewise the purification of thorns.
"Tell me all this and whatever else you have studied, exactly as it is; I wish to know what is in your mind."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then Prahlāda, adorned with humility, having prostrated at his father’s feet,
spoke to the lord of the Daityas with his palms joined in reverence.
Prahlāda said:
"Everything has been taught to me by my preceptor; there is no doubt about this.
However, it has been accepted by me, yet in truth, this doctrine is not my own conviction."
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment— these four means have been described for the accomplishment of objectives concerning friends and others.
O dear one, do not be angry with Govinda, the Supreme Self, nor with your friends and others;
O mighty-armed one, in the absence of that which is to be accomplished (the goal), what is the use of the means?

"O dear one, since Govinda is the self of all beings, the lord of the world, and identical with the world— the Supreme Self— do not be angry with your friends and others, my son. O mighty-armed one, in the absence of an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), what is the use of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)?"
O dear one, when Govinda— the Supreme Self, the Lord of the world, who consists of the world and whose essence is all beings—
is present, whence can there be any talk of friend or foe?
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides in you, and he resides in me and elsewhere as well;
therefore, the notion that "this one is my friend" and "that one is my enemy" arises only from a sense of duality.
Therefore, enough with these excessively wicked and elaborate discourses;
O dear Śobhana, you should instead apply yourself to that which lies within the sphere of ignorance.
O Lord of Asuras, from ignorance arises the notion of knowledge; does a child not mistake a firefly for fire because of his lack of discernment? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19.40)
That action which does not lead to bondage is ignorance; that which leads to liberation is knowledge.
One kind of action leads to weariness, while the other kind of knowledge is skill in the arts.
Having understood this, O illustrious one, I prostrate before you and speak; listen as I declare the supreme essence, which is devoid of all that is insubstantial.
No one thinks, "Who will have the kingdom? nor does anyone fail to desire wealth;
nevertheless, both of these are obtained by men only as they are destined to be.
O highly fortunate one, all beings indeed exert themselves toward greatness;
nevertheless, for men, it is their fortunes, not their efforts, that are the cause of prosperity.
O Lord, even for those who are dull-witted, lacking in discernment, and unheroic—
even for those devoid of statesmanship— kingdoms exist as things to be enjoyed through sheer fortune.
Therefore, he who desires great prosperity should strive for meritorious deeds; and by one who desires even Nirvana, equanimity must be practiced.
Gods, humans, animals, birds, trees, and reptiles—
this form of the infinite Viṣṇu stands as if it were distinct.
One who understands this should regard the entire world, both stationary and moving,
as equal to the Self, for this Viṣṇu assumes the form of the universe.
When he is known thus, that Blessed One, the beginningless Supreme Lord, Acyuta, becomes gracious; when he is gracious, there is the destruction of the afflictions.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard this, Hiraṇyakaśipu rose up from his excellent throne in a fit of rage and struck his son on the chest with his foot.
And he spoke with fury, as if burning with indignation,
crushing his fist with his hand as if wishing to destroy the world.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Vipracitti, O Rāhu, O Bala! Let this one be bound with firm serpent-nooses in the great ocean; let there be no delay!"
Otherwise, all the worlds, as well as the Daityas and Dānavas,
will follow the opinion of this foolish and evil-minded man.
"Though we have repeatedly offered water to him, this enemy still offers praise; for wicked men, only their execution is a true service."
Parāśara said:
Then those Daityas, acting with haste and honoring their lord’s command, bound him with serpent-nooses and cast him into the ocean.
Then, by the movement of the trembling Prahlāda, the great ocean shook;
having reached a state of extreme agitation, it overflowed its shores on all sides.
Having seen the entire Bhūrloka being submerged by the great waters, Hiraṇyakaśipu said this to the Daityas, O dull-witted one: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19.57.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Daityas, let this evil-minded one be covered right here in the abode of Varuṇa by all the mountains, entirely without gaps on every side."
Fire does not burn him, nor is he cut by weapons,
nor is he brought to destruction by serpents, by wind, by poison, or by magical spells.
"He has not been struck down by illusions, nor by a thunderbolt, nor by the elephants of the quarters;
this boy is of an exceedingly wicked mind, and there is no purpose in his remaining alive."
Thus, having been overwhelmed by mountains in the midst of the waters, let that evil-minded one remain there until the end of a thousand years; then he shall give up his life.
Then the Daityas and Dānavas, having covered him with mountains in the great ocean,
performed a sacrificial piling for thousands of yojanas.
That high-minded one, having been placed within the ocean by the mountains,
praised Acyuta with one-pointed mind at the time of his daily ritual.
Prahlāda said:
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O Supreme Person;
salutations to you, the soul of all worlds; salutations to you, the wielder of the sharp discus.
Salutations to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to him who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins;
salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, who acts for the benefit of the world.
Salutations to you, the triple-formed one, who as Brahmā creates the universe, who again protects it in its maintenance, and who takes the form of Rudra at the end of the aeon.
Gods, yakṣas, asuras, siddhas, nāgas, gandharvas, kinnaras,
piśācas, rākṣasas, humans, and likewise animals.
Birds and stationary beings, ants and reptiles; earth, water, fire, ether, and wind; as well as sound, touch, and taste.
Form, smell, mind, intellect, the self, time, as well as the qualities— O Acyuta, you are all these and their ultimate reality.
You are indeed knowledge and ignorance, truth and falsehood, poison and nectar;
you are the action enjoined by the Veda, both that which leads to worldly engagement and that which leads to its cessation.
O Viṣṇu, you alone are the enjoyer of all actions, as well as all the instruments of action and whatever fruit results from all those actions.
O Lord, your pervasiveness alone— manifesting the quality of sovereignty— extends throughout me, others, all beings, and all worlds.
Yogis meditate upon you, and sacrificers worship you;
you alone consume the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, assuming the forms of both the deities and the manes.
O Lord, this entire universe, both gross and subtle, is situated here within Your form;
I behold all the various elements of beings, and within them, that which is called the inner self, which is exceedingly subtle.

And beyond that, which is the form of the Supreme Self, beyond the range of specific attributes such as subtlety and the like, there exists some inconceivable form of yours; homage to You, O Supreme Person!
O Lord of the Gods, salutations to that eternal, inferior power of yours which resides in all beings as their universal soul and is the substratum of the qualities (guṇas).
I bow to that supreme Sovereign Lady, who transcends the range of words and is beyond the reach of the mind; she is to be discerned only by the knowledge of the wise.
Oṃ, salutation always to that Blessed One Vāsudeva,
for whom nothing exists as separate, and who is the one who transcends everything.
Salutations to him, salutations to him, salutations to that Great Soul,
whose single name and form are not perceived as existing in duality.
Salutations to that Great Soul, whose manifested forms the denizens of heaven worship while failing to perceive his supreme form.
Abiding within the heart, the Lord perceives both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
I bow to that Supreme Lord, the witness of all and the universe itself.
Homage be to that Viṣṇu from whom this world is differentiated;
may He, the primordial source of the worlds, the imperishable, be gracious unto me.
May that Hari, in whom this entire universe is woven like warp and woof, who is imperishable and immutable, and who is the support of all— may he be gracious to me.
Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu; salutations to him again and again—he in whom all is, from whom all is, who is all, and the refuge of all.
Because the Infinite One is omnipresent, he alone abides as I;
from me everything comes, I am everything, and everything exists within me, the Eternal One.
I alone am the imperishable, eternal Supreme Self, the refuge of the individual soul;
I alone am known as Brahman in the beginning, and likewise at the end, the Supreme Person.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, thus reflecting upon Viṣṇu as non-different from himself, he—
Having attained identity with that supreme [reality], he considered himself to be the infallible Acyuta.
He thus forgot his own self and knew nothing else;
he thought, "I alone am the imperishable, infinite Supreme Self."
Through the practice of that meditation, his sins were gradually exhausted; then, when his inner organ was purified, the infallible Viṣṇu, who consists of knowledge, took up residence within him.
O Maitreya, when Prahlāda had become one with Viṣṇu through the power of yoga,
those serpent-bonds slipped away from him in an instant.
The great ocean, its course obstructed by the grasping of delusion, was tossed with waves;
and the entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Then that highly intelligent one, having lifted up that mass of rocks placed upon him by the Daityas, emerged from those waters.
And having seen the world once more, characterized by the sky and other elements,
he remembered himself within his own self, thinking, "I am Prahlāda."
And with one-pointed mind, undisturbed, his speech, body, and mind restrained, he again praised the Supreme Person, the beginningless Abode.
Prahlāda said: Om, salutation to the Supreme Reality, who is both gross and subtle,
perishable and imperishable, manifest and unmanifest, beyond all parts, the Lord of all, and free from all taint.
O you who are the collyrium of qualities, the substratum of qualities, whose self is beyond qualities yet abides within them;
O you of manifest and unmanifest form, of great form, of subtle form, both distinct and indistinct!

O Acyuta, whose nature consists of both terrible and gentle forms; O you who are composed of both knowledge and ignorance; O true being whose form is both existent and non-existent; O you who bring about the manifestation of both existence and non-existence.

O You whose self transcends the manifold of the eternal and the non-eternal, who are free from conceptual proliferation and rely upon the stainless; O One and Many, Vāsudeva, the primordial cause—salutations to You!

Salutations to that Supreme Person, who is both gross and subtle, manifest and luminous; who is all beings and yet not all beings; and from whom this universe proceeds, though he is not the cause of the universe.
Parāśara said:
As he was thus offering praise with that mind,
the Lord Hari, the Blessed One, wearing yellow garments, manifested himself before him.
Beholding him with agitation, the twice-born rose up and, with faltering words, repeatedly uttered: "Obeisance to Viṣṇu!"
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, O Keśava, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, grant me your grace;
O Acyuta, purify me once again by bestowing upon me your glance.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am pleased with you for your unwavering devotion;
O Prahlāda, choose from me whatever boon you desire."
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, in whichever of the thousands of wombs I may enter, may my devotion to You, O Acyuta, remain forever unswerving toward You, the Imperishable.
May that pleasure which the undiscriminating feel toward sense objects never depart from my heart as I remember you.
The Blessed Lord said: "You already possess devotion toward me; it shall remain so even further.
O Prahlāda, choose from me whatever boon you desire."
Prahlāda said:
"O Lord, because of my praise, an attachment to hatred arose in you toward my father when he was prepared for battle; may the sin committed by him against you be wiped away."
Weapons were hurled at my body, and I was cast into a mass of fire;
I was bitten by serpents, and poison was administered to me in my food.
That I was bound and cast into the ocean, that I was covered with heaps of rocks, and whatever other wicked deeds were done to me by my father; ||| ViP_1,20.23 |||
O Lord, by your grace, may my father be instantly liberated from that sin arising from hatred toward one who is devoted to you, and from whatever [suffering] is born thereof.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Prahlāda, all this shall come to pass for you through my grace;
furthermore, O son of an Asura, choose another boon from me."
Prahlāda said:
"O Blessed One, I have accomplished my purpose by this boon that you have granted me:
that through your grace, there shall be in me unwavering devotion to you."
What need has he for dharma, artha, and kāma? Liberation stands in his very hand, he whose devotion to You is firm at the root of all the worlds.
The Blessed Lord said: "Since your mind is thus unwavering and endowed with devotion toward me, you shall,
by my grace, attain supreme liberation."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O Maitreya, Viṣṇu vanished while he was looking on;
and he, having returned once more, prostrated at the feet of his father.
His father, having smelled his head and embraced him while he was still distressed, said with eyes moistened by tears, "O child, do you live? Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.20.30.
The great asura became full of joy and free from remorse;
he likewise performed service toward his teachers and parents in accordance with righteousness.
O Maitreya, after his father had been brought to his end by Viṣṇu in the form of Narasiṃha, he then became the lord of the Daityas.
Then, O twice-born one, having obtained the splendor of sovereignty which purifies one's karma,
and having acquired many sons, grandsons, and even great power, [he attained liberation].
When his office had expired and he was freed from both merit and sin,
he then attained supreme nirvāṇa through meditation on the Blessed One.
Such was the power of that high-minded Daitya Prahlāda, O Maitreya,
who was a devotee of the Blessed One, about whom you have questioned me.
Whoever hears this life-story of the high-souled Prahlāda, his sins immediately go to complete destruction.
O Maitreya, by hearing and reciting the life-story of Prahlāda, a person undoubtedly dispels the sin committed during a day and a night.
O twice-born one, by reciting this on the full moon, the new moon, the eighth day,
or the twelfth day, one then obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
Just as Hari protected Prahlāda in all his calamities,
so does He protect whoever constantly listens to his life story.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Prahlāda’s sons were Āyuṣmat, Śibi, and Bāṣkala; Virocana was the son of Prahlāda, and from Virocana, Bali was born.
O great sage, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest;
and all the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were likewise possessed of great strength.
Jharjhara, Śakuni, and likewise Bhūtasantāpana;
Mahānābha, Mahābāhu, and another, Kālanābha.
And Abhava, Anupūrva, Dvimūrdhan, Śambara,
Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Kapila, and likewise Śaṅkara.
Ekacakra, the long-armed Tāraka of great strength,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the mighty Puloman.
These are known as the sons of Danu, along with the powerful Vipracitti.
Svarbhānu’s daughter was Prabhā, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan; Upadānavī and Hayaśiras were also renowned as excellent daughters.
Both Vaiśvānarasū and Pulomā, as well as Kālakā—
these two highly fortunate daughters were the wives of Mārīci.
From those two were born sixty thousand sons, the best of the Dānavas,
known as the Paulomas and the Kālakeyas, the offspring of Mārīca.
Then others, who were of great heroism, cruel, and exceedingly pitiless,
were likewise born as sons of Vipracitti from Siṃhikā.
Tryaṃśa, the powerful Śalya, and the exceedingly mighty Nabhas;
Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, and likewise Khasṛma.
Āndhaka, Naraka, and likewise Kālanābha;
and Svarbhānu, the great hero, that mighty asura who fought with his mouth.
These indeed were the foremost Dānavas, the increasers of Danu’s lineage;
their sons and grandsons numbered by the hundreds and thousands.
In the lineage of the Daitya Prahlāda, the Nivātakavacas were born,
their souls purified by great ascetic penance.
Six sons of great being are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrakā.
Śukī gave birth to parrots and to owls and female owls; Śyenī produced hawks, and Bhāsī produced Bhasas, while Gṛdhri produced vultures.
Sugrīvī gave birth to the two Śucis and the flocks of birds;
Tāmrā is celebrated as having given birth to horses, camels, and donkeys—this is known as the lineage of Tāmrā.
Vinatā had two sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa, who were both heroic;
Suparṇa was the best of winged creatures, formidable, and a devourer of serpents.
O Brahmin, in Surasā there were a thousand serpents of immeasurable power, many-headed, sky-faring, and high-souled.
O Brahmin, from Kādraveya were born a thousand powerful sons of immeasurable energy, who lived under the dominion of Suparṇa and possessed many heads.
Among them, the principal ones were Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka,
Śaṅkha, Śveta, Mahāpadma, as well as Kambala and Aśvatara.
Elāputra, as well as the nāgas Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya—
these and many other venomous serpents with fierce poison [reside there].
Know that her host is Krodhavaśa; all its members are fanged creatures—terrible flesh-eaters dwelling on land, in the air, and in the water.
Out of anger, he gave birth to the Piśācas of great strength;
and from Surabhi, he produced cows, as well as female buffaloes,
and all kinds of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and grasses.
Svasā gave birth to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni likewise gave birth to the Apsarases;
Ārīṣṭā, however, gave birth to the Gandharvas of great being.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been proclaimed;
their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
O Brahmin, this creation is recorded as having occurred during the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
When the great sacrifice to Vaivasvata had been performed and the rite to Varuṇa was fully extended, the creation of progeny by Brahmā while he was offering oblations is here described.

O best of beings, it was previously there that the Grandfather himself designated the seven mind-born [sons], who had arisen as the Seven Sages, to be the sons of the Gandharvas, the Bhogins, the gods, and the Dānavas.
Diti, whose sons had indeed been destroyed, propitiated Kaśyapa;
and Kaśyapa, the supreme among those who practice austerities, was duly honored by her.
He invited her to choose a boon, and she then chose this boon:
a son of immeasurable splendor, capable of slaying Indra.
And that best of sages granted a boon to his wife;
having bestowed that most formidable boon, Kaśyapa spoke to her.
"Your son shall be the slayer of Śakra, provided that you,
being composed, exceedingly diligent, and pure, carry the fetus for a hundred autumns."
Having spoken thus to the goddess, the sage Kaśyapa united with her;
and she, endowed with perfect luster, conceived that embryo.
Knowing that the embryo was intended for his own destruction, Maghavan,
the lord of the immortals, nevertheless approached her with humility, desiring to serve her.
Seeking a vulnerability in her, the subduer of Pāka remained waiting;
when less than a hundred years had passed, he perceived a weakness within himself.
Without having performed the purification of her feet, Diti went to bed and fell asleep;
he entered her womb.
Then Vajrapāṇi cut Mahāgarbha into seven pieces;
being crushed by the thunderbolt, he wailed most piteously.
"Do not weep," Śakra said to him again and again;
yet that embryo became divided into seven parts, and Indra, becoming enraged, struck it once more.
With his thunderbolt that rends enemies, he split each one of them into seven parts;
they became the gods known as the Maruts, who were exceedingly swift.
As was indeed stated by the Blessed One, from that very [seed] the Maruts became the forty-nine gods who are the companions of Vajrapāṇi.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When Pṛthu had previously been consecrated in the kingdom by the great sages, [he performed his duties].
Thereafter, the Grandfather of the World gradually bestowed the kingdoms [upon them].
He established Soma in the sovereignty over the stars, the planets, the Brahmins, and all plants without exception, as well as over the Vedas, sacrifices, and ascetic penances.
He appointed Vaiśravaṇa as the king of kings, Varuṇa likewise over the waters,
Viṣṇu as the lord of the Ādityas, and Pāvaka (Fire) over the Vasus.
He appointed Dakṣa as the lord of the Prajāpatis, Vāsava of the Maruts,
and Prahlāda as the sovereign of the Daityas and Dānavas.
He consecrated Yama, the King of Dharma, in the sovereignty over the ancestors,
and gave Airāvata, the trumpeting lord of the non-fading elephants, to him.
Among winged creatures he is Garuḍa; among gods, Vāsava;
among horses, Uccaiḥśravas; and among cattle, the bull.
The Lord appointed the lion as the king over all wild beasts, while the imperishable one made the serpent the lord of the remaining creatures.
Himālaya is the lord of stationary things; Kapila is the sage of sages;
and the tiger is the sovereign of clawed and tusked beasts.
He consecrated the Plakṣa tree as the king of the lords of the forest; in this very same manner, he appointed the leaders of other species according to their preeminence.
Having thus divided the kingdoms, Brahmā, the Lord of the Progenitors, immediately thereafter established the Guardians of the Quarters everywhere.
In the eastern direction, he consecrated Sudhanvan, the son of Vairāja Prajāpati, as the king and guardian of that quarter.
In the southern direction,
he consecrated as king the son of the Prajāpati Kardama, named Śaṅkhapada.
In the western direction,
he consecrated the high-souled King Ketumān, the son of Rajas, who is steadfast and unshakable.
Likewise, he consecrated Hiraṇyaroman as the invincible king over the northern quarter of Parjanya Prajāpati.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities—
is even today protected according to their respective regions and in accordance with righteousness.
O best of sages, all these kings and others are manifestations of the power of the high-souled Viṣṇu while he is engaged in the maintenance of the world.
O twice-born one, those who will be and those who have been— all these lords of beings—
are portions of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, O best of the twice-born.
Those who are the lords of the gods, as well as the lords of the Daityas, those who are the protectors of the Dānavas, and those who are the protectors of the flesh-eaters; ||| ViP_1,22.18 |||
Those who are the lords of beasts, and those who are the lords of birds;
those who are the masters of humans, of serpents, and of the Nāgas.
Those who are the lords of trees, of mountains, and even of the planets—
those who have passed away, those who exist now, and those others who will be in the future—
all of them have arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings.
For indeed, O highly wise one, apart from Hari, the Lord of All, no other whatsoever exists who is capable of maintaining the stability of the world.
This eternal one creates the world during its creation, protects it during its maintenance,
and destroys it by means of his nature as the Ender, relying upon the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
Divided into four parts during the process of creation, Janārdana remains established in a fourfold manner during its maintenance;
and at the end, he brings about dissolution through his fourfold division.
With one portion he becomes Brahmā, possessing an unmanifest form;
with another portion, he becomes the lords of creatures, accompanied by Marīci and the others.
Time is its third part, and all beings are its other part;
thus, this quality of passion (rajas) exists in a fourfold combination.
Viṣṇu, established in one part, performs the work of preservation;
in another form as Manu and others, and in yet another as Time itself.
And established elsewhere among all beings,
the Supreme Person brings about stability for the world by relying upon the quality of *sattva*.
Furthermore, at the time of the end, having resorted to the function of Tamas,
the unborn Lord becomes Rudra in one of his portions.
He exists through another portion in the form of Agni, Antaka, and others;
one portion is the nature of Time, and the other is all living beings.
O Brahmin, as that great-souled one undergoes destruction in this fourfold manner, the eternal conceptualization of his divisions is thus described.
Brahmā, Dakṣa and the others, Time, and likewise all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Hari, the causes of the creation of the world.
O twice-born one, Viṣṇu, Manu and the others, time, and all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world's maintenance.
Rudra, Kāla, Antaka, and all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Janārdana for the sake of the fourfold dissolution.
O twice-born one, in the beginning, middle, and until the dissolution of the world, the creation is performed by the Creator,
by Marīci and the others, and likewise by living beings.
At the beginning of time, Brahmā creates; thereafter, Marīci and the others produce offspring, and living beings do so at every moment.
O twice-born one, without Kāla, neither Brahmā nor all the Prajāpatis, nor indeed all living beings, are capable of accomplishing creation.
In this very same way, O Maitreya, this fourfold division of that deity is taught even regarding his continued existence, as well as during the dissolution of the world.
O twice-born one, whatever being is created by whatever [cause],
all that which has come into existence as a creation is indeed the body of Hari.
O Maitreya, whatever living being he slays, whether stationary or moving, that is the fierce word of Janārdana which brings about the end.
Thus, this Lord Janārdana is the creator of the world, the protector of the world, as well as the devourer of the world; he is the god of all.
Thus, at the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he proceeds in these three ways through the activity of the qualities; yet his supreme state is great and devoid of qualities.
And that nature of the Supreme Self consists of knowledge, is all-pervading, self-cognizable, incomparable, and is likewise fourfold in its manifestation.
The venerable Maitreya said: O Sage, explain to me according to the proper method the fourfold nature of that which has become Brahman, which is called the supreme state.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, the cause has been declared, as well as the means for accomplishing all things,
and the desired object that one intends to achieve for oneself.
For the yogin desiring liberation, there is the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other means, as well as the supreme Brahman to be realized; because of this, one does not return again.
O Sage, that knowledge which is the support for the means of liberation for yogins— that indeed is the first differentiation of Him who has become Brahman.
O Great Sage, that consciousness which has as its object the Brahman to be realized by the yogi who applies himself for the sake of liberation from afflictions is the second part.
That cognition which consists of non-duality, arising from the inseparability of both the means and the end, has been described by me as another part.
O great sage, that specific distinction of those three types of knowledge is like the true nature of the Self revealed through the means of their negation.
It is devoid of activity, inexpressible, mere pervasion, incomparable,
the object of self-realization, pure existence, and without defining characteristics.
"Tranquil, fearless, pure, difficult to conceive, and without support—
that knowledge of Viṣṇu, who consists of knowledge, is said to be designated as Brahman."
In that regard, O twice-born ones, those yogins who attain dissolution through the cessation of cognition reach a state of seedlessness when the sowing of the plow of saṃsāra is performed.
Thus, the supreme state called Viṣṇu is of such a nature: stainless, eternal, all-pervading, imperishable, and free from everything that is to be abandoned.
That is the supreme Brahman, from which the yogi does not return again;
he takes refuge in it when merit has ceased, the afflictions are exhausted, and he is utterly pure.
That Brahman has two forms, both manifest and unmanifest;
these two, consisting of the perishable and the imperishable, abide within all beings.
That which is imperishable is the Supreme Brahman; this entire world is perishable.
Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this entire universe the power of the Supreme Brahman.
Even there, O Maitreya, a distinction in the moonlight exists according to its power, consisting of abundance or scarcity due to proximity or distance.
O Brahmin, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the primary powers of Brahman;
and from them, O Maitreya, the gods are inferior, and from those, Dakṣa and the others.
Then there were humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, and reptiles;
and likewise trees, shrubs, and so forth, each progressively lower and more inferior than the last.
O best of sages, this imperishable world is eternal,
yet it is characterized by the conceptualizations of manifestation and disappearance, as well as birth and destruction.
Viṣṇu, who consists of all powers, is the supreme form of Brahman;
he is the embodied one who was formerly meditated upon by yogis at the commencement of their yoga practices.
O Sage, for those who practice correctly with an unimpeded mind, the great yoga with an object and with seed arises, wherein one is firmly established.
He is beyond the supreme powers, immediately following Brahman;
O fortunate one, Hari is the embodied Brahman, consisting of all that is Brahman.
O Sage, that in which this entire world is woven like warp and woof, from that [source] the world arises, and within this world, he is the whole world.
Lord Viṣṇu, consisting of both the perishable and the imperishable, sustains the entire universe—
composed of the Person (Puruṣa) and the Undifferentiated (Avyākṛta)— in the form of his ornaments and weapons.
The illustrious Maitreya said: O Blessed One, you ought to explain to me how Viṣṇu sustains this entire universe, which exists in the form of his ornaments and weapons.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having paid homage to the immeasurable Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord,
I shall relate to you that which was told to me by Vasiṣṭha.
The Blessed Lord Hari bears as his own self the soul of this world— untainted, stainless, and devoid of qualities— in the form of the Kaustubha gem.
O Mādhava, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, Pradhāna and even Buddhi abide within you in the form of a cow, resting upon your infinite self.
The Lord sustains the two-fold ego— the one consisting of the elements and the other consisting of the senses—
abiding in the form of the conch and the form of the Śārṅga bow.
The mind, whose nature is to move and which surpasses the wind in speed,
takes on the form of a wheel as it rests in the hand of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, that Vaijayantī garland of the wielder of the mace, which consists of five forms, is indeed a collection of the causes of all beings; thus it is called the Bhūtamālā.
Janārdana indeed sustains all the senses without exception, which consist of both intellect and action, as well as all the forms of bodies without exception.
And that sword-jewel which Acyuta bears is utterly stainless;
it consists of knowledge, yet it resides within the sheath of ignorance.
In this manner, O Maitreya, both the individual soul (puruṣa) and primordial matter (pradhāna), as well as the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṅkāra),
the elements, the mind, all the sense organs, knowledge and ignorance— all this is fully supported by Hṛṣīkeśa.
Devoid of material form, Hari, assuming an illusory form, bears the appearance of weapons, ornaments, and physical stature for the welfare of living beings.

The Supreme Lord, whose eyes are like the lotus flower, sustains the primordial matter (pradhāna) along with its transformations, as well as the individual soul (puruṣa) and the entire universe. Thus it is.
Whatever is knowledge and whatever is ignorance, whatever is existent and whatever is non-existent and imperishable—
all that, O Maitreya, resides in Madhusūdana, the Lord of all beings.
The Lord Hari, the sinless and imperishable, is the very nature of time, consisting of the divisions of *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *nimeṣa*, and so forth, as well as days, seasons, solstices, and years.
O best of sages, Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka,
Maharloka, Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka— these are the seven worlds of the all-pervading Lord.
The embodiment of the self of the worlds, the first-born even of all the ancestors,
Hari himself stands as the foundation of all branches of knowledge.
Abiding in many forms such as gods, humans, and animals,
he is therefore the Lord of All, the infinite one who possesses both embodied and formless manifestations.
The Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, Sāma-veda, and likewise the Atharva-veda, as well as the Itihāsas, the Upavedas, and the declarations found within the Vedāntas; ViP_1.22.83.

All the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*), those proclaimed by Manu and others, all the treatises (*śāstra*) without exception, and whatever narratives (*ākhyāna*) and recitations (*anuvāka*) exist anywhere; [all these were produced from his mouth].
Whatever poetic compositions there may be, and all the Vedas as well—
these are the body of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound.
Whatever classes of entities exist— whether they be embodied or formless, whether here or elsewhere— they are all indeed his very body.
"I am Hari; all this is Janārdana; there is no other collection of causes and effects apart from him.
For one whose mind is thus disposed, the diseases of dualities arising from worldly existence do not occur again.
O twice-born one, this is the first section of this ancient [Purāṇa] which has been duly narrated to you; by holding it in mind, one is liberated from sins.
O Maitreya, by hearing this entire [account], a human being obtains that same fruit which is gained by bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika over a period of twelve years.
O Sage, as a man hears of the origin of the gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, and others, the gods and the rest become bestowers of boons upon him.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus concludes the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, composed by the sage Śrī Parāśara, which determines the supremacy of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Now begins the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as Viṣṇucittīya and Ātmaprakāśa by Śrīdhara.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, all of this has been correctly explained to me by you."
O Teacher, that which you have been asked by me regarding the creation of the world;
O best of sages, regarding that portion concerning the creation of the world which has been described by you, I wish to hear it once again.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Svāyambhuva;
of those two, you have mentioned that Dhruva was the son of Uttānapāda.
"O twice-born one, you have not yet mentioned the progeny of Priyavrata;
I desire to hear about that, so please, being gracious, deign to speak."
Śrī Parāśara said: Prayivrata married the daughter of Kardama;
his two daughters were Samrāṭ and Kukṣi, and he had ten other sons.
They were possessed of great wisdom and great vigor, disciplined and beloved by their father;
they were the renowned sons of Priyavrata—listen to their names from me.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vapuṣmat, and Dyutimat, as well as Medhā, Medhātithi, Bhavya, Savana, and Putra.
Jyotiṣmat was the tenth among them, and his son was Satyanāman;
these sons of Priyavrata were renowned for their strength and heroism.
Medhāgni, Bāhu, and Putra—these three, devoted to yoga, possessed the memory of their former births and were highly fortunate; they did not set their minds upon sovereignty.
O Sage, being pure at all times regarding all matters,
they indeed performed their duties according to the rule, for they were free from desire for rewards.
O best of sages, O Maitreya, Priyavrata divided the seven continents among those seven high-souled sons and gave them to them.
O fortunate one, the father gave Jambūdvīpa to Agnīdhra,
and likewise he bestowed Plakṣadvīpa upon Medhātithi.
And on Śālmala, the Lord consecrated Vapuṣmat as the lord of men;
he established Jyotiṣmat as the king in Kuśadvīpa.
And Priyavrata appointed Dyutimat as the king in Krauñcadvīpa,
and he also made Bhavya the lord of Śākadvīpa.
That lord also made Savana the ruler of Puṣkara;
and he who was Āgnīdhra, O best of sages, became the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa.
He had nine sons who were equal to Prajāpatis: Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, and Ilāvṛta; [and further] Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, and Ketumāla.
Ramya, Hiraṇvān as the sixth, Kurubhadra, Āśva, and another, Ketumāla, who was a king of virtuous conduct, were likewise born.
O Brahmin, learn from me now the divisions of Jambūdvīpa;
the region called Himavat was given by his father to Nābhi as his southern portion.
He gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kiṃpuruṣa,
and he gave the third region, Naiṣadha, to Harivarṣa.
The father gave Ilāvṛta to him where Meru stands as the center;
he gave the region situated by the Nīla mountain to Ramya.
That which was white and superior was given by his father to Hiraṇvat.
He gave the region north of Śṛṅgavat to Kuru,
and the region to the east of Meru he bestowed upon Bhadrāśva.
He gave the region of Gandhamādana to Ketumāla;
thus did that lord of men bestow these lands upon his sons.
O Maitreya, after consecrating those sons in these realms, that lord of the earth went to the highly meritorious Sālāgrāma to perform austerities.
O great sage, these are the eight regions, beginning with Kimpuruṣa;
their natural accomplishment consists primarily of happiness and is attained without effort.
For them there is no perversion, nor is there the fear of old age and death;
neither merit nor demerit exists for them, nor are there high, low, or middling states.

In those eight regions, the condition of the Yuga never existed at any time. However, in the region called Himavat, belonging to the high-souled Nābhi, there was no such state; for his son, the immensely radiant Ṛṣabha, was born of Merudevī.
From Ṛṣabha was born Bharata, the eldest of his hundred sons;
having ruled the kingdom according to his own dharma and having likewise performed various sacrifices.
Having consecrated his heroic son Bharata as lord of the earth,
that illustrious sovereign departed for the hermitage of Pulaha to practice asceticism.
Having made a firm resolve even there according to the rules for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*),
that lord of the earth performed austerities and offered sacrifices in accordance with the prescribed law.
Exhausted by his austerities, exceedingly emaciated and covered with visible veins,
naked and with a pebble held in his mouth, he then set out upon the path of heroes.
And for this reason, this region is celebrated among the worlds as Bhāratavarṣa,
because it was given to Bharata by his father when he departed for the forest.
Sumati was the son of Bharata, a man of supreme righteousness;
having performed sacrifices properly, his father bestowed the beloved kingdom upon him.
O Sage, that lord of the earth, Bharata, having transferred his royal splendor to his son and being devoted to the practice of yoga, cast off his life-breaths at Sālagrāma.
And that brahmin was born into a family preeminent among yogis;
O Maitreya, I shall relate his life story to you again.
From that Mumata was born Tejas, from whom Indradyumna was born; from him came Parameṣṭhin, and from him Pratihāra, who was his descendant.
His son was born as the one renowned as Pratiharta;
from him came Bhava, and from him Udgītha; his son was the powerful Prastāvin.
From him was born Pṛthu; from him, Nakta; Nakta’s son was Gaya;
Nara was the son of Gaya; his son was Virāj.
From him was born a wise son of great heroism;
his son was Mahānta, and Manasyu was his offspring.
Tvaṣṭṛ was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, and his son was Viraja;
O Sage, Śatajit was born as the son of that Viraja.
Those [sages] who are preeminent in universal light and by whom these subjects were nourished have adorned this land of Bhārata with its nine divisions.
And by those born of their lineage, this land of Bhārata was enjoyed in former times for seventy-one cycles of the ages, through the creation of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other yugas.
This is the Svāyambhuva creation by which this world was filled;
O Sage, he was the lord of the previous Manvantara during the Vārāha Kalpa.
Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said:
"O Brahman, you have described to me the creation and the period of Svāyambhuva Manu."
I desire to hear from you the entire mandala of the earth.
O Sage, you ought to explain correctly what the measure of all this is, what its support is, what its nature is, and what its configuration is.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this as I speak it in brief;
for its full detail could not be told even in a hundred years.
O twice-born one, the islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and another called Śālmali,
as well as Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven seas,
equal [in number], consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
It enters sixteen thousand yojanas below and extends thirty-two thousand at its summit;
its circumference at the base is sixteen thousand yojanas on all sides.
This mountain stands in the form of a pericarp for this earth-lotus.
To its south are the Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha;
and to its north are the Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin—the mountain ranges that demarcate the regions.
Two of them are one hundred thousand yojanas in measure, two are half that size, and the others are ten times less;
they are each two thousand yojanas in height and as many in breadth.
O twice-born one, Bhārata is the first region, followed by Kimpuruṣa;
likewise, Harivarṣa is another [region] to the south of Meru.
To the north is the region of Ramyaka, and following that is Hiraṇmaya;
and the Uttarakurus are just as [the other regions] are, like Bhārata itself.
O best of the twice-born, each of these [continents] is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent;
and in their midst is Ilāvṛta, where the golden Meru rises up.
O illustrious one, that region of Ilāvṛta, extending nine thousand yojanas in each of the four directions from Meru,
contains four mountains.
These mountains of Keśava, supported by the Viṣkaṃbha range and rising ten thousand yojanas high,
stand equal in all directions along with the nine lakes.
Mandara is known to be in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vipula on the western side, and Supārśva in the north.
Among them are the Kadamba, Jambu, Pippala, and Vaṭa trees;
these eleven hundred-foot-tall trees serve as the banners of the mountains.
O Great Sage, that Jambū tree is the cause of the name of Jambūdvīpa;
its fruits, indeed as large as great elephants,
fall and shatter everywhere upon the back of the mountain.
From their juice, the river known as Jāmbūnadī indeed flows there; it is also drunk by the inhabitants of that region.
Neither perspiration nor foul odor, neither old age nor the decay of the senses arises there for those people whose minds are pure from drinking that [water].
Having reached the moisture of the earth on its banks and being dried by pleasant breezes,
it becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
To the east of Meru is Bhadrāśva, and to the west is Ketumāla;
O best of sages, between these two regions lies Ilāvṛta.
Caitraratha is known to be in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vaibhrāja likewise in the west, and Nandana in the north.
Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Asitoda, and Samānasa—
these four lakes are always enjoyed by the gods.
Śītāmbhas, Kumuda, Kurarī, and Mālyavat— these and others,
headed by Vaikaṅka, are the Kesara mountains to the east of Meru.
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, and Rucaka, as well as Niṣadha and others, are to its south; [and there is] the Kesara mountain.
Śikhivāsa, Savaiḍūrya, Kapila, Gandhamādana,
and likewise Jārudhi and the others are the Kesara mountains in the west.
Situated on the intermediate ridges of Meru, beginning with Jaṭhara,
are Śaṅkukūṭa, Ṛṣabha, Haṃsa, Nāga, and another; likewise, Kālañjana and others are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) on the north.
O Maitreya, the great city of Brahmā, renowned in heaven, is situated above Mount Meru at a height of fourteen thousand yojanas.
On all sides of it— in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions—
there are the renowned and preeminent cities of the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Issuing from the foot of Viṣṇu and having bathed the lunar orb,
the Gaṅgā indeed falls from heaven into the city of Brahmā on all sides.
Having fallen there, it proceeds in four directions as the Sītā,
the Alakanandā, the Cakṣus, and the Bhadrā, respectively.
Flowing from the mountain in the east, the Śītā travels through the sky to the mountain;
thence, by means of the eastern region of Bhadrāśva, it reaches the ocean.
In the same way, O great sage, the Alakanandā also flows southward toward Bhārata and enters the ocean after dividing into seven streams.
And the Cakṣu river, having passed beyond all the western mountains,
then goes to the western region called Ketumāla and enters the ocean.
O Great Sage, having passed beyond Bhadrāśva, the Northern Mountains, and likewise the Uttarakurus, it flows into the northern ocean.
The Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains;
situated between them stands Mount Meru, shaped like the pericarp of a lotus.
The Bhāratas, the Ketumālas, the Bhadrāśvas,
and the Kurus are the petals of the world-lotus, situated outside the boundary mountains.
Jaṭhara and Hemakūṭa are both boundary mountains;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha.
Gandhamādana and Kailāsa are both as long as before; eighty yojanas in extent, they are situated reaching to the edge of the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are both boundary mountains situated on the western side of Meru,
just as they are on the eastern side.
Triśṛṅga and Jārudhi are the two northern mountain ranges;
these extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
Thus, these boundary mountains beginning with Jaṭhara, which were described by the best of sages, stand around Meru, two by two in each of the four directions.
O Sage, those Kesara mountains beginning with Śītānta, which have been described as being in the four directions of Meru, are exceedingly delightful;
in the valleys between these mountains dwell the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
O best of sages, there are likewise delightful forests and cities upon those [continents],
containing excellent abodes of the gods such as Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Sūrya, frequented by the finest kinnaras.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as daityas and dānavas,
sport day and night in those delightful mountain valleys.
O Sage, these are remembered as terrestrial heavens, the abodes of the righteous;
those who perform evil deeds do not go there even in hundreds of births.
O twice-born one, the Lord Viṣṇu dwells in Bhadrāśva with a horse's head;
in Ketumāla he is Varāha, and in Bhārata he assumes the form of a tortoise.
Govinda, Janārdana, exists among the Kurus in the form of a fish;
Hari, the All-pervading One, is everywhere as the Universal Form, being all things in all places.
O Maitreya, he exists as the support of all, being the soul of everything.
O great sage, in those eight regions beginning with Kimpuruṣa,
there is no sorrow, no exertion, no agitation, nor hunger, fear, and the like.
The subjects will be healthy, free from fear, and devoid of all suffering;
they will have a stable lifespan of ten or twelve thousand years.
The god does not rain upon them; indeed, there are no terrestrial waters in those places.
The divisions of time such as the Kṛta, Tretā, and others do not exist in those regions.
O best of the twice-born, in all these regions there are seven mountain ranges for each, and from them flow hundreds of rivers.
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: That region which lies north of the ocean and south of the Himavat mountains [is known as Bhārata-varṣa].
That region is named Bhārata, where the lineage of Bharata resides.
O Great Sage, its extent is nine thousand yojanas;
this is the land of action for those who go to heaven and liberation.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these are the seven principal mountain ranges here.
Therefore, O Sage, from this [conduct] heaven is attained; indeed, from this they go to liberation; and from this, men also go to the state of animals or to hell. (ViP 2.3.4)
From here, heaven, liberation, the intermediate state, and the end are reached;
indeed, for mortals, nothing else is ordained except on this land of action.
Learn from me the nine divisions of this land of Bhārata:
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmraparṇa, and Gabhastimān; 2.3.6.
Likewise, Nāgadvīpa, Sāmya, Gandharva, and Cāruṇa;
this, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean.
This island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north;
the Kirātas dwell at its eastern edge, while the Yavanas are situated in the west.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective portions,
subsisting through the performance of sacrifices, the use of weapons, trade, and other such occupations.
O Sage, the Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, and others flow from the foot that produces snow; while the Vedasmṛti, Mukhā, and others arise from the Pāriyātra mountain.
The Narmadā, Murasā, and other rivers flow from the Vindhya mountains;
the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Prasū, and others originate from the Ṛkṣa mountains.
Likewise, the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and others—
these rivers originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountains— are remembered as the removers of the fear of sin.

The Kṛtamālā, Tāmraparṇī, and others originating from the Malaya mountains are known as those arising from Mahendra; likewise, the Trisāmā, Carṣikulyā, and others are remembered as originating from Mahendra.
The Ṛṣikulyā, Kumārī, and others originate from the foot of Śuktimat;
there are thousands of other rivers besides these that serve as their tributaries.
In those [cities] dwell these people: the Kurus, Pañcālas, and others from the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), as well as those from the Eastern regions and so forth, and the inhabitants of Kāmarūpa.
The Puṇḍras, Kaliṅgas, Magadhas, and all those from the south,
as well as the Aparāntas, Saurāṣṭras, Śūras, Ābhīras, and Arbudas.
The Kārūṣas and Mālavas, the inhabitants of the Pāriyātra mountains, the Sauvīras, Saindhavas, Hūṇas, Sālvas, and the dwellers of Kosala; ViṣṇuP_2.3.17 //
The Mādrārāmas, Ambaṣṭhas, Pārasīkas, and others likewise always dwell together, drinking the water of these rivers;
O illustrious one, they are crowded with people who are joyful and well-nourished in their vicinity.
O great sage, in this land of Bhārata alone do the four ages—the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—exist; they are not found anywhere else.
In this place, sages perform austerities and sacrificers offer oblations;
here, gifts are bestowed with devotion for the sake of the world beyond.
In Jambūdvīpa, the Lord of Sacrifice, Viṣṇu, who consists of sacrifice, is worshipped by men with sacrifices; in other dvīpas, he is worshipped in other ways.
Even here, O great sage, Bhārata is the most excellent within Jambūdvīpa;
for this is the land of action (karmabhūmi), whereas all others are lands of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi).
In this regard, O best of beings, even after thousands upon thousands of births,
a living being may sometimes obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit.
"O Bhārata, the gods indeed sing songs, saying:
'Blessed are those men on the land that serves as the path to the abodes of heaven and liberation; for they shall become men once again after their time as gods.'"
Having renounced their actions along with the desire for their fruits unto Viṣṇu, who has become the Supreme Self,
those stainless ones attain that sovereignty over action and proceed to dissolution within Him, the Infinite.
We do not know where we shall obtain a bodily bond once the merit that grants heaven has dissolved; indeed, blessed are those men in Bhārata who are not deprived of their senses.
O Maitreya, I have thus briefly described to you this Jambūdvīpa, which is nine thousand yojanas in extent and one hundred thousand yojanas in width.
O Maitreya, surrounding Jambūdvīpa and extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, the salt ocean stands outside in the form of a ring.
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Just as the island named Jambū is surrounded by the salt ocean, so too is it encompassed.
Plakṣadvīpa is situated thus, encircling the salt-water ocean.
The extent of Jambūdvīpa is measured at one hundred thousand [yojanas];
O Brahmin, Plakṣadvīpa is said to be twice that size.
Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, indeed had seven sons:
the eldest was named Śāntahaya, and after him came Śiśira.
Sukhoda, Tathānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka,
