and Dhruva as the seventh— these indeed were the lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
Formerly, there were the years Śāntahaya, Varṣa, Śiśira, and likewise Sukha;
as well as Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva.
There are boundary-forming mountains for them, as well as other mountain ranges that serve as the limits of the regions;
hear their seven names, O best of sages.
Gomada, Candra, Nārada, Dundubhi,
Somaka, Sumanas, and Vaibhrāja as the seventh.
O sinless ones, in these delightful mountain ranges of the Varṣas,
the inhabitants dwell constantly together with gods and Gandharvas.
In those regions the districts are meritorious, and people die only after a long time;
there are neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases, for that place is pleasant at all times.
There are exactly seven rivers that flow from those regions into the ocean;
I shall name them, for by hearing their names, one's sins are removed.
The Anutaptā, the Śikhī, the Vipāśā, the Tridivā,
the Aklamā, the Amṛtā, and the Sukṛtā— these seven are the rivers there.
These mountains and principal rivers have thus been described to you;
there are also thousands of minor mountains and rivers there,
which the inhabitants of those regions always drink from with great joy.
O twice-born one, for them there is indeed neither a period of decline (apasarpiṇī) nor a period of increase (utsarpiṇī);
nor does the state of the Yugas exist in those seven regions.
O high-minded one, O Brahmin, in Plakṣadvīpa and the other continents up to Śākadvīpa, time is always equal to that of the Tretā Yuga.
People lived for five thousand years, free from disease;
and during those five periods, Dharma existed according to the divisions of the social classes and stages of life.
And there were four castes therein; learn of them as I describe them to you.
O best of sages, the Āryakas, Kurāras, Vidiśyas, and Bhāvinas— these shall be the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
In its center, O best of the twice-born, there is a very great tree, equal in size to the Jambū tree; it is a Plakṣa tree, and from its name this continent is called Plakṣadvīpa.
There, the Blessed Lord Hari— the creator of the world in the form of Sīma, the All, and the Lord of All— is worshipped by those castes beginning with the Āryakas.
Plakṣadvīpa is surrounded by a sea equal in extent to Plakṣadvīpa itself, namely the sea of Ikṣurasa,
which resembles a surrounding rim.
Thus, O Maitreya, has Plakṣadvīpa been described by me to you in brief; now listen further to my account of Śālmala.
The lord of Śālmaladvīpa was the heroic Vapuṣmat; hear now of his sons, for those seven regions are indeed named after them.
O great sage, they were Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha.
This ocean of sugarcane juice is surrounded on all sides by the continent of Śālmaladvīpa, which is twice its extent in width.
Therein also, seven mountain ranges are to be known as the sources of jewels,
which likewise manifest the [seven] regions, as well as seven rivers.
Kumuda, Nata, and the third, Balāhaka;
where the Droṇa mountain is, there are great medicinal herbs, and that is the fourth mountain.
Kaṅka was the fifth, Mahiṣa the sixth, and likewise Kakudmān, the best of mountains, was the seventh; now hear from me the names of the rivers.
Yonitoyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Muktā, Vimocanī, and Nivṛtti is known as the seventh among them; these are remembered as bestowing the pacification of sins.
Śveta, Harita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa,
Jīmūta, Rohita, and the beautiful Suprabha—
these seven regions are indeed endowed with the four social orders (cāturvarṇya).
O great sage, as for the castes who dwell there on Śālmala,
they are— separately— the Kapilas, the Āruṇas, the Pītas, and the Kṛṣṇas.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras likewise worship that Blessed One,
the imperishable Self of all, Viṣṇu,
who has become the wind, the foundation of sacrifice, through the most excellent sacrifices.
In this exceedingly beautiful place, there is the constant presence of the gods;
there stands a very great śālmali tree, which by its name brings about tranquility.
This island is surrounded on all sides by the Suroda ocean,
which is equal in extent to the Śālmala island itself.
Surrounded on all sides by Kuśadvīpa, the Surodaka ocean is twice the extent of Śālmala [dvīpa] in every direction.
Hear now of those seven sons of Jyotiṣmān in Kuśadvīpa.
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Veratha, Lambana, Dhṛti,
Prabhākara, and Kapila— the sequence of these regions bears their names.
In that place dwell humans together with the Daityas and Dānavas,
as well as gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others.
O great sage, there too were four castes, devoted to their own respective duties:
the Damins, the Śuṣmins, the Snehas, and the Mandehas.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are declared in their proper sequence.
Because they are the performers of their own respective duties,
they exhaust their fierce authority— which yields its fruit— right there in Kuśadvīpa by worshipping Janārdana in the form of Brahmā for the sake of the cessation of that very authority.
Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān,
Kuśaśaya, Hari, and the seventh, Mandarācala.
O great sage, these seven Varṣa-mountains are located there on that continent;
listen now to the names of the seven rivers in their proper order.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, as well as Sammatis,
Vidyudambhā, and Mahī— these others are the removers of all sins.
There are thousands of other small rivers and mountains there;
because of a clump of *kuśa* grass, that island is known by the name Kuśadvīpa.
That island is surrounded by the Ghṛtoda ocean, which is of the same extent as it;
and the Ghṛtoda ocean is indeed surrounded by Krauñcadvīpa.
O highly fortunate one, hear now of another great island, Krauñcadvīpa,
whose extent is twice that of Kuśadvīpa.
In Krauñcadvīpa, the sons of that high-souled Dyutimat were born;
the lord of the earth named the regions after them.
Kuśala, Mallaga, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, Andhakāraka,
Muni, and Dundubhi— these seven, O Sage, were his sons.
Even there, O Great Sage, are the mountain ranges of the rain-clouds, frequented by gods and Gandharvas and exceedingly beautiful; hear their names from me.
Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third, Andhakāraka;
the fourth was Ratnaśaila, and Svāhinī was like a horse.
In this regard, Divāvṛt is the fifth, and another is Puṇḍarīkavat;
then there is Dundubhi and Mahāśaila. These are each double the size of one another.
Just as the continents are, so too are the mountains within those continents.
In these delightful regions as well as upon the excellent mountains,
the subjects dwell free from fear together with hosts of gods.
O great sage, the Puṣkaras, Puṣkalas, Dhanyas, and Titikhyas are declared to be,
respectively, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Listen, Maitreya, to those rivers which they drink there:
seven are principal, and there are hundreds of other minor streams.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojavā,
Kṣānti, and Puṇḍarīkā— these seven are the rivers that flow through the [seven] regions.
There too, the Lord Viṣṇu, the agitator of men, is worshipped by means of Puṣkara and other rites;
and Rudra, in his own form, is worshipped in the vicinity of the sacrifice.
Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of curd-cream water, which is equal in measurement to Krauñcadvīpa itself.
And the ocean of curd-cream water is surrounded by Śākadvīpa,
O great sage, which is twice the extent of Krauñcadvīpa.
To the noble and great-souled Bhavya, the lord of Śākadvīpa,
he gave seven sons and assigned those seven regions to them.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Marīcaka,
Kusumoda, Maudāki, and the seventh, Mahādruma.
There too, there are seven regions in succession with those very same names;
there also are seven mountains that serve to demarcate the regions.
There, O twice-born one, is the eastern Udayagiri, and likewise the western Jalādhāra;
similarly Raivataka, Śyāma, and Astagiri;
as well as the delightful Āmbikeya and Kesara, the best of mountains.
There stands a great śāka tree frequented by siddhas and gandharvas,
from the touch of whose breeze supreme delight arises.
There, the regions are meritorious and inhabited by the four social orders;
and there are rivers of great merit that remove all sins and fear.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and Dhenukā; Ikṣu, Veṇukā, and Gabhastī was the seventh.
And there, O great sage, there are hundreds of other small rivers,
as well as mountains by the hundreds and thousands.
Those inhabitants of the regions who dwell in places such as Jalada drink them with joy;
having descended from heaven to the earth, they become those very people.
In those seven regions, there was no decline of dharma, no mutual strife, nor any transgression of the bounds of propriety.
The Vaṅgas, the Māgadhas, the Mānasas, and likewise the Mandagas; among them,
the Vaṅgas were mostly Brāhmaṇas, the Māgadhas were Kṣatriyas,
the Mānasas were Vaiśyas, and the Mandagas were their Śūdras.
O Sage, in Śākadvīpa, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of the Sun,
is duly worshipped by those self-controlled ones with the rituals as prescribed.
But Śākadvīpa, O Maitreya, is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk,
encircling it like a bracelet according to the measurement of Śākadvīpa itself.
O Brahmin, the Ocean of Milk is surrounded on all sides by the continent named Puṣkara,
which is twice the size of Śākadvīpa in every direction.
From Puṣkara, Savana also had a son named Mahāvīra;
and Dhātuki was the other—those two regions there were marked by their names: one was Mahāvīra and the other was known as Dhātukī-khaṇḍa.
O highly fortunate one, there is a single famous mountain range there called Mānasaottara, which forms a circular ring around the center.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas upward,
and it is just as wide, being perfectly circular on all sides.
Standing as if dividing the circular Puṣkara-dvīpa through its center, he caused that land to be split into two regions by him.
Each of those two regions is ring-shaped, and likewise is the mountain.
There, human beings live for ten thousand years;
they are free from disease and sorrow, and devoid of passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.
O twice-born one, among them there was neither low nor high status, nor were there the slain and the slayer;
there was no envy, malice, fear, hatred, fault, or greed and the like.
Outside the Great Yellow [continent] is Dhātakīkhaṇḍa at the edge;
it is frequented by gods, Daityas, and others, and lies beyond the Mānasottara mountain range.
Truth and falsehood both exist there on that island known as Puṣkara;
on that island, which comprises two regions, there are neither rivers nor mountains.
But there, the gods and humans are of equal status and possess a uniform appearance.
O Maitreya, for two years this terrestrial realm is like the highest heaven;
it is a time that grants the happiness of all seasons and is free from old age, disease, and the like,
in the regions known as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and Mahāvīra, O Sage.
In Puṣkaradvīpa there is a Nyagrodha tree, the supreme abode of Brahmā;
therein dwells Brahmā, being worshipped by the gods and the asuras.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water; its circumference is equal to its own extent.
Thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each successive continent and ocean is twice the size of the one preceding it.
The waters in all the oceans are indeed always equal;
never does any deficiency or excess arise among them.
O best of sages, just as water in a pot overflows due to contact with fire, so too does the water in the ocean swell during the waxing of the moon.
Neither decreasing nor increasing, the waters swell and diminish during the rising and setting of the moon in its bright and dark fortnights.
O great sage, the increase and decrease of the waters of the oceans is observed to be exactly five hundred and ten finger-breadths.
O Brahmin, in Puṣkaradvīpa, food endowed with the six flavors is always spontaneously present there for all the subjects to eat.
Surrounding the sweet-water ocean is seen the arrangement of the world:
a golden land twice its size, devoid of all living beings.
Beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in width;
for that mountain is likewise [ten] thousand [yojanas] in height.
Then darkness enveloped that Śauṇḍa standing on all sides,
and he was surrounded on every side by a shell of dense gloom.
O great sage, this earth, together with its shell, its islands, oceans, and mountains, extends to five hundred million leagues.
O Maitreya, she is the sustainer and the creator, superior to all beings in her qualities; she is the foundation of all the worlds.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: This detailed account of the earth has been narrated by me to you.
The height of the mountain, O twice-born one, is also said to be seventy thousand [yojanas].
O best of sages, each individual netherworld (pātāla) extends for ten thousand [yojanas]:
A-tala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat,
the one called Mahātala, Sutala, and Pātāla as the seventh.
O Maitreya, there the grounds are white, black, reddish, yellow, sandy, stony, and golden, adorned with the pleasure-groves of others.
In them, O great sage, dwell by the hundreds Dānavas, Daityas, and Yakṣas, as well as great Nāgas and Jātayas.
"Nārada, having arrived from Pātāla in the heavens, declared in the midst of the dwellers of heaven: 'The netherworlds are even more delightful than the world of the gods.'"
Where the brilliant, white, and radiant jewels that serve as ornaments for the Nagas provide such delight, who could compare Patala to anything else?
In Pātāla, which is adorned here and there by the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas,
who would not feel delight, even one who is liberated?
There, the rays of the sun during the day spread forth radiance but not heat; and the moonbeam at night does not lead to cold, but serves solely for illumination.
There, even by the Danujas and other beings who enjoy themselves with various foods, edibles, and great drinks, time is not perceived, even as it passes away.
Forests, rivers, delightful lakes, lotus-pools, the songs of male cuckoos, and beautiful garments; ||| ViP_2,5.10 |||
There were exceedingly bright ornaments and fragrant unguents rich with scent,
and the air was filled with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums.
These and other vast objects of enjoyment are enjoyed by the Daityas and Uragas, who range within the depths of Pātāla.
Beneath the netherworlds (pātāla) resides that tamasic form of Viṣṇu known as Śeṣa,
whose qualities even the Daityas and Dānavas are unable to describe.
This divine [form], worshipped by the celestial sages, is recited internally by the perfected ones;
it has a thousand heads and is adorned with manifest svastikas and pure ornaments.
He who, illuminating all directions with a thousand crest-jewels,
renders all the asuras powerless for the welfare of the world.
With eyes rolling from intoxication, always wearing a single earring,
a diadem, and a garland, he shines like the white mountain Sumeru accompanied by fire.
Clad in blue garments, intoxicated with pride, and adorned with white necklaces,
he was like another Mount Kailāsa with the flow of the Gaṅgā amidst its clouds.
With the tip of his hand grasping a plow and bearing an excellent mace,
he is himself worshipped by the goddess Vāruṇī through her own radiant form.
At the end of the kalpa, from whose mouths emerges Rudra in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, blazing with the flames of poisonous fire, and devours the three worlds.
Bearing upon his head as a crest the entire circle of the earth,
Śeṣa, who is worshipped by all the gods, remains stationed at the base of the netherworld (pātāla).
His valor, his power, his essential nature, and even his form— indeed,
these cannot be described or even known by the gods themselves.
Who can describe the prowess of him for whom this entire earth rests like a garland of flowers, reddened by the tips of the jewels upon his hoods?
When Ananta yawns, his eyes rolling with intoxication,
then this earth, together with its ocean waters and its forests, trembles.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas do not reach the end of his qualities; therefore, he is the infinite and imperishable one.
The yellow sandalwood paste, hanging from the hands of the Naga maidens,
is repeatedly brushed away by their breath and becomes like a fragrant powder for the quarters of the sky.
By propitiating whom the ancient seer Garga came to know the celestial bodies in their true nature, as well as the entire fruit indicated by omens.
Therefore, this earth, supported on his head by that best of Nāgas,
bears the garland of the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
And then, O Brahmin, the hells are situated below the earth and beneath the waters.
O great sage, hear now those [hells] into which sinners are cast.
Raurava, Sūkara, Rodha, Tāla, as well as Viśasana, Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, and Vilohita; ViP_2.6.2 //
Rudhirāmbhas, Vaitaraṇī, Kṛmisa, Kṛmibhojana,
Asipatravana, Kṛṣṇa, and the dreadful Lālābhakṣa.
Likewise, there are Pūyavaha, the sinful Vahnijvāla, Adhaḥśiras, Saṃdaṃśa, Kālasūtra, Tamas, and Avīci.
Śvabhojana, Apratiṣṭha, and likewise Apraci—
these and other such hells are exceedingly terrible.
In the realm of Yama, those men who delight in evil deeds fall into terrible places that inflict the fear of weapons and fire.
A false witness, as well as one who speaks unjustly through partiality,
and he who speaks any other untruth— that man goes to Raurava.
O best of sages, the killer of an embryo, the destroyer of a city, the slayer of a cow,
and he who obstructs the breath— all these go to the Rodha hell.
The drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the stealer of gold go to the Sūkara hell,
as does indeed anyone who enters into association with them.
The slayer of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed, one who has sexual intercourse with his sister,
and he who kills the king’s soldiers— [these go] to the Taptakuṇḍa hell.
The seller of a virtuous woman, the keeper of a slaughterhouse, the seller of lions,
and he who abandons his dependents— these fall into the Taptaloha hell.
Having approached his daughter-in-law or even his own daughter, he is cast into Mahājvāla; so too is that lowest of men who treats his elders with contempt or who reviles them.
O twice-born one, he who reviles the Vedas, he who sells the Vedas,
and he who approaches a woman who should not be approached— these go to the Lavaṇa hell.
A thief falls into a pit of longing, and likewise one who violates the bounds of propriety.
He who hates the gods, the twice-born, and the ancestors, and he who shows hostility toward jewels,
as well as one who performs improper sacrifices, goes indeed to the Kṛmibhakṣa and Kṛmiśa hells.
That lowest of men who eats while neglecting his ancestors, gods, and guests, goes to the Ugra hell;
and the maker of arrows goes to the Vedhaka hell, where one must consume saliva.
The man who makes earrings and the man who fashions swords and such weapons go to the Viśasana hell, which is intensely crimson.
But she who accepts gifts from the unworthy goes to the downward-facing hell;
likewise does one who officiates at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, as well as one who indicates the auspiciousness of constellations for hire.
One who eats impure food becomes a carrier of pus, while one who eats consecrated food becomes a swift-moving wind.
O twice-born one, the Brahmin who sells lac, meat, liquor, sesame seeds, and salt goes to that very same hell.
O best of the twice-born, one who rears cats, chickens, goats, dogs, pigs, and birds goes to that very same hell.

One who lives by painting, a fisherman, one who eats the food of a prostitute, a poisoner, a tailor, a buffalo-breeder, and that twice-born man who performs rituals on forbidden festival days; // ViP_2,6.22 //
An arsonist, a betrayer of friends, a fowler, a village priest, and those who sell Soma—all these fall into the Rudhirāndha hell. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.6.23)
The man who destroys sacrifices and the destroyer of villages goes to the Vaitaraṇī river.
For those who spill semen and the like, those who violate established boundaries,
those who are impure, and those who live by deceit— all such go to the realm of Kṛṣṇa.
He who cuts down a forest goes to the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) in vain;
the sheep-slaughterer and the deer-hunter indeed fall into the Blazing Fire (Vahnijvāla).
O twice-born one, those who set fire to uncooked food go to that very same place.
Both he who violates his vows and he who has fallen away from his own stage of life fall into the midst of the Sandaṃśa (tongs) hell.
Those men who, though practicing celibacy, discharge semen during the day or while sleeping,
and those who are taught by their own sons, fall into the Śvabhojana hell.
These and other hells exist by the hundreds and thousands,
wherein those who have performed evil deeds are cooked, having undergone their torments.
Just as these sins are, so too are others by the thousands experienced by men who range within the various hells.
Those men who perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—
whether by deed, thought, or speech— fall into the hells.
The gods in heaven are seen by the denizens of hell with their heads downward;
likewise, the gods see all the hell-beings below them with their faces turned downwards.
Immobile beings, worms, those born from eggs, birds, animals, humans,
the righteous, the gods, and those who have attained liberation follow one another in this sequence.
The first is a thousandth part [of the second], and so on in sequence;
indeed, all these are highly fortunate, up to those who have taken refuge in liberation.
As many beings as there are in heaven, so many are the inhabitants of hell;
the evildoer who turns his back on expiation goes to hell.
The supreme sages, having reflected upon them accordingly, have prescribed penances that correspond precisely to each of the various sins.
O Maitreya, those who know the truth— the Svāyambhuva Manu and others— have declared that for great sins there are great expiations, and for minor sins, minor ones.
Of all the various penances consisting of ascetic practices and ritual acts,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme among them all.
For that man in whom remorse indeed arises after a sin has been committed,
the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
By recollecting Nārāyaṇa at dawn, at night, at twilight, at midday, and so forth, a person immediately attains the destruction of all sins;
through the remembrance of Viṣṇu, the entire accumulation of afflictions is exhausted.
He attains liberation; for him, the attainment of heaven is considered a mere obstacle.
O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during the practices of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
even the status of Indra or other such rewards are considered obstacles.
Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven, which is characterized by return?
Where is the recitation of "Vāsudeva," the unsurpassed seed of liberation?
Therefore, O sage, a mortal man who remembers Viṣṇu day and night,
having all his sins completely destroyed, does not go to hell.
Heaven is that which brings delight to the mind; hell is the opposite of that.
O best of the twice-born, merit and demerit are indeed what are designated as heaven and hell.
Since a single object leads to suffering, to pleasure,
to the arrival of envy, and to anger, how can an object possess an inherent nature of its own?
That very same thing which once became a source of joy later arises as suffering; that which once gave rise to anger later gives rise to serenity.
Therefore, nothing exists that is essentially suffering, nor anything that is essentially happiness;
this is merely a transformation of the mind characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; yet knowledge is also considered the cause of bondage.
This entire universe consists of knowledge, and nothing exists beyond knowledge.
O Maitreya, understand that what are called "knowledge" and "ignorance" are in fact nothing other than wisdom itself.
Thus have I described to you this mandala of the earth,
as well as all the subterranean realms (pātālas) and likewise the hells, O twice-born one.
The oceans, the mountains, the islands, the regions, and the rivers—everything has been briefly described. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Brahmin, you have described this entire surface of the earth."
O Sage, I desire to hear about the worlds, beginning with Bhuvarloka.
In the same way, O highly fortunate one, explain to me, who am questioning you, the configuration of the planets and their respective dimensions exactly as they are.
Śrī Parāśara said: As far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon— including its oceans, rivers, and mountains— that much is traditionally held to be the extent of the earth.
O twice-born one, as great as the earth is in its extent and circumference,
so great indeed is the sky in its breadth and circumference.
O Maitreya, one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth is the solar orb; and one hundred thousand yojanas from the sun, the orb of the moon is situated.
At a full hundred thousand yojanas above the moon,
the entire circle of constellations shines forth.
O Brahmin, two hundred thousand yojanas above the circle of the constellations is Mercury;
and at a distance equal to that same measure, Venus is situated above Mercury.
Aṅgāraka is situated at that same distance from Śukra,
while the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) is situated at twice a hundred thousand [yojanas] from Bhauma.
O best of the twice-born, the circle of the Seven Sages is situated two hundred thousand yojanas above Saturn and Jupiter, and one hundred thousand yojanas from that [circle of the Seven Sages].
Situated more than a hundred thousand yojanas above the ṛṣis,
Dhruva stands as the central pivot for the entire wheel of luminaries.
O great sage, this triple world has been described according to its height;
it is the ground for the fruit of sacrifice, and sacrifice is established herein.
Above Dhruva is Maharloka, where those who dwell for a kalpa reside;
it extends for one koṭi of yojanas, where those who dwell for a kalpa reside.
But there are two crores of beings in that world where those sons of Brahmā dwell—
Sanandana and others who are renowned, O Maitreya, and possessed of stainless minds.
Fourfold higher than Janaloka stands Tapoloka,
where those Vairāja gods reside, free from the affliction of burning.
Satyaloka shines forth, sixfold in extent beyond the Tapoloka;
it is indeed remembered as the world of Brahmā, where there is no further death.
Whatever object made of earth exists that can be traversed on foot is designated as the Bhūrloka; its extent has been described by me in detail.
O best of sages, that which lies between the earth and the sun, frequented by the Siddhas and other sages, is called the second world, Bhuvarloka.
That which lies between Dhruva and the Sun, measuring fourteen hundred thousand [yojanas],
is declared by those who contemplate the structure of the worlds to be the Svarloka.
O Maitreya, this triple world is taught to be uncreated;
the three realms of Jana, Tapa, and Satya likewise constitute the triad of the uncreated.
Between the created and the uncreated, it is known as Maharloka;
it becomes empty at the end of a kalpa, yet it is never utterly destroyed.
O Maitreya, these seven worlds have been described by me to you;
likewise, there are exactly seven nether regions (pātālas). This is the extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
This [egg] is entirely enclosed on all sides by the shell and the inner membrane, like the seed of a wood-apple fruit, extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
And that egg of Maitreya is surrounded by ten times as much water;
this entire shell of water is, in turn, enveloped on the outside by fire.
And fire is enveloped by wind, O Maitreya, and the wind is covered by space;
space is surrounded by the source of the elements (the ego-principle), and that too is encircled by the Great Principle (mahat).
All these seven, O Maitreya, increase tenfold at each successive stage.
Enveloping the Great One (mahat), Pradhāna stands established;
it has no end, nor is its number known.
Since it is indeed infinite and its measure is incalculable,
O Sage, that supreme Prakṛti is the cause of everything without exception.
There were thousands of thousands of eggs, tens of thousands,
and likewise hundreds of millions upon millions of such [eggs] there.
Just as fire exists in flax-seed and oil in sesame, so too does the pervasive Spirit (puruṣa),
whose nature is consciousness and who knows itself, abide within Pradhāna.
O one of great intelligence, both Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, having become the self of all beings, abide in a state of mutual dependence, enveloped by the power of Viṣṇu.
O Mahāmati, at the time of creation, that very [power] is the cause of their separation, the support for them both, and the cause of their agitation.
Just as the wind, clinging to water, supports hundreds of droplets,
so too is that power of Viṣṇu, which consists of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
And just as a tree, endowed with roots, trunk, branches, and so forth, arises from its original seed, and from it indeed other seeds [are produced]; ||| ViP_2.7.32 |||
From them, O Sage, other trees arise endowed with radiance; they too follow the same characteristics, substances, and causes as those [original trees].

Thus, from the Unmanifest (avyākṛta), Mahat and the others arise first; from them, the specific evolutes (viśeṣa) up to the gross elements are produced; from those, the Asuras and other beings come into existence;
from them, their sons are born, and from those sons, yet other offspring are born.
Just as there is no depletion of a tree through the growth of sprouts from its seed,
so too there is no depletion of the primary elements through the creation of beings.
Just as space, time, and so forth are the causes of a tree due to their mere proximity,
even so is the Lord Hari the cause of the universe without undergoing any transformation.
Just as in a grain of rice there is the root, the stalk, the leaf,
and the sprout, so too are the stem, the husk, the flower, the milk, and the awns.
O best of sages, even husks and chaff, being existent, indeed manifest their own nature once they encounter the totality of causes for growth.
Likewise, within the manifold karmas, the gods and others,
having attained the power of Viṣṇu, indeed attain growth.
And that Viṣṇu is the Supreme Brahman, from whom this entire world arises, who is the world,
in whom this world exists, and into whom it shall go to its dissolution.

That is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, the highest state beyond both being and non-being; that from which this world of moving and unmoving things arises, and in which all exists as non-differentiation.
He alone is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and he is the world in its manifested form;
everything goes into dissolution within him alone, and in him it abides.
He is the agent of all actions, and he is the sacrifice; he alone is the fruit of that ritual act.
Even the entire collection of implements, such as the sacrificial ladle and so forth, is Hari himself; there is nothing whatsoever distinct from him.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O you of noble vows, this structure of the cosmic egg has been explained to you.
Next, hear from me regarding the dimensions and configurations of the sun and the other celestial bodies.
O best of sages, the chariot of the Sun consists of nine thousand yojanas,
and its pole is twice that length.
Its axle is indeed one and a half crores and seven additional niyutas of yojanas in length; upon it the wheel is established.
The entire wheel of time (kālacakra) is established within that which has three naves, five spokes, six rims, and consists of three parts— the year.
And their horses are seven-choked; hear from me their names:
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti—these are said to be the meters that serve as the Sun’s bay horses.
O Mahāmati, the second axle of Vivasvat’s chariot is forty thousand [yojanas] long, while the other five are each one thousand five hundred.
The axle is the measure for both of those [wheels], and it is equal to half the yoke;
the short axle, supported by the pole-star (dhruva), belongs indeed to the chariot.
But the second wheel is situated upon Mount Mānasa.
To the east of the Mānasottara mountain is the city of Vāsava;
to the south is that of Yama, to the west that of Varuṇa, and to the north that of Soma. Hear their names from me.
Vasvaukasārā is the city of Śakra; likewise, Saṃyamanī belongs to Yama; Sukhā is the city of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa); and Vibhāvarī is that of Soma.
O Maitreya, the Blessed Sun, accompanied by the wheel of luminaries, has reached its southern limit and glides along like an arrow shot [toward the south].
The Blessed Sun is the cause for the regulation of day and night;
he is the supreme path of the gods for yogins who have exhausted their afflictions.
O Maitreya, at midday in one part of the world, it stands at all times facing midnight in all other continents.
At both sunrise and sunset, indeed at all times,
he stands facing him from all the intermediate directions as well as the cardinal directions, O Brahmin.
Wherever the radiant sun is seen by people, that is considered his rising;
and wherever he becomes invisible, right there occurs the setting of the sun.
For the sun that exists eternally, there is neither setting nor rising;
what are called "rising" and "setting" are merely the visibility and invisibility of the sun.
Abiding in the city of Śakra and the others, he touches three cities;
standing in two intermediate corners, he touches three corners, and likewise two cities.
The sun, having risen, shines intensely until midday;
thereafter, as its rays diminish, it proceeds toward its setting.
By its rising and setting, the eastern and western directions are defined;
as far as it shines in front, so far does it shine behind and on both sides.
Except for the assembly hall of Brahmā atop Mount Meru, the king of mountains,
whatever rays of the sun proceed toward the assembly hall of Brahmā,
they are all cast back by its radiance and indeed return in the opposite direction.
Therefore, in the northern direction indeed, day and night always exist for all the continents and regions, because Mount Meru is situated to the north.
When the sun has set at night, the radiance of Vivasvat enters the fire;
therefore, the fire shines from afar during the night.
O twice-born one, just as the light of fire enters the sun during the days,
the sun shines exceedingly due to its intense conjunction with fire.
The two splendors— those of the sun and of fire— consisting of light and heat,
mutually nourish one another day and night through their mutual interpenetration.
When the sun rises halfway between the southern and northern regions,
day and night enter the waters like darkness and lightness enter a garment.
For the waters indeed become copper-colored from being entered by day and night; and when the sun has set, the water enters the day,
therefore the waters become white from the entry of the night into the day.
Thus, when the sun passes through the center of Puṣkara,
its velocity at that moment is such that it traverses a thirtieth part of the earth.
O twice-born one, as this sun revolves at the edge of the potter's wheel,
it creates day and night while traversing the earth.
At the beginning of the northern solstice, O twice-born one, the Sun enters Capricorn; from there he proceeds to Aquarius and Pisces, moving from one zodiac sign to another.
Then, when these three have been traversed,
the sun proceeds toward the equinoctial course (vaiṣuvatī gati), thereby making day and night equal.
Then the night comes to an end, and the day increases day by day.
And then, having reached the end of Gemini and attained the ultimate limit,
he enters the sign of Cancer and begins his southern course.
Just as the circumference of a potter’s wheel revolves very rapidly,
so does the sun move swiftly during its southern course.
Moving through time with extreme velocity by the power of the wind's speed,
he traverses a vast distance in a short period of time.
O twice-born one, during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana), the sun moves through thirteen and a half lunar mansions in a day with speed due to its twelve muhūrtas; at night,
it traverses that same number of mansions in eighteen muhūrtas.
Just as an object situated in the center of a potter's wheel moves slowly,
so too does the sun move with slow progress during its northern course (udagayana).
Therefore, after a long period of time, it reaches a small portion of the earth—
that which lasts for eighteen muhūrtas at the end of the northern course.
He becomes a day, and he moves about with slow gait.
During the day, the sun traverses thirteen and a half constellations;
at night, moving through twelve constellations, it covers the same number of muhūrtas.
Therefore, just as the wheel rotates more slowly at the nave,
so indeed does Dhruva, situated in the center like a lump of clay, revolve.
Just as the hub of a potter’s wheel remains in that very place,
so too, Maitreya, the fixed pole (dhruva) revolves in that very place.
As the sun revolves between the two poles,
its orbits are indeed slow by day and swift by night.
On whichever day its motion is slow, on that night it is swift;
and when its motion is swift at night, then its motion is slow during the day.
O twice-born one, this sun-god travels along a single path alone, traversing all the zodiacal signs in the course of a day and night.
He who consumes exactly six zodiac signs at night and the other six during the day; ||| ViP_2,8.44 ||
The quality of being long or short during the day is produced by the measure of the zodiacal signs;
likewise, during the night, the brevity or length [of the day] is determined by the measures of the signs.
The lengthening and shortening of the day and other periods occurs solely through the experience of that [motion].
At the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the motion is swift at night and slow during the day.
And during the southern solstice, the course of Vivasvat is indeed the reverse.
Uṣas is designated as night, and vyuṣṭi is said to be day;
likewise, that which lies between uṣas and vyuṣṭi is called saṃdhyā.
And when the terrible and most dreadful time of twilight has arrived,
the fierce Mandeha Rākṣasas desire to devour the sun.
O Maitreya, a curse was pronounced upon those Rākṣasas by Prajāpati:
that their bodies should be indestructible, yet they should undergo death day after day.
Then a most terrible battle takes place between the Sun and them;
thereafter, O great sage, the best of the twice-born withdraw the water.
Conjoined with the Brahman-syllable Oṃ and consecrated by the Gāyatrī,
those sins are consumed by that water which has become like a thunderbolt.
The first oblation that is offered with mantras in the Agnihotra sacrifice blazes forth as the thousand-rayed Sun, the Maker of Light.
The syllable Oṃ is the Lord Viṣṇu, the abode of the three worlds and the master of speech;
by its utterance, those Rākṣasas go to their destruction.
The supreme Vaiṣṇava portion is the Sun, which is the internal light that is undifferentiated;
the syllable Oṃ is its means of approach, and that [Sun] is the supreme impeller of it.
Then, impelled by him, that radiant light, through the syllable Om (oṃkāra),
indeed burns away all the sinful Rākṣasas known as Mandehas.
Therefore, one must not neglect the rite of twilight worship;
for he who does not perform the worship at twilight slays the sun.
Then the Blessed One, intent on the protection of the world, set forth, guarded by the Brāhmaṇas and the Vālakhilyas and others.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* one should count as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and by thirty of those, day and night are combined.
The decrease and increase of the portions of the day and the days occur respectively;
indeed, during these decreases and increases, the twilight is traditionally held to last for exactly one muhūrta.
Then, when the sun has risen as far as the horizon line and three muhūrtas have passed, that time is known as morning; it constitutes the fifth part of the day.
From that morning time, the period of three muhūrtas is the saṅgava;
and from that saṅgava time, the midday consists of three muhūrtas.
Therefore, the period following the midday hour is known as the afternoon;
it is recorded by the wise that this division of time consists of exactly three muhūrtas.
When the afternoon has passed, it is indeed the time of evening;
it consists of fifteen muhūrtas and exactly three muhūrtas [of the following day].
Indeed, fifteen muhūrtas are traditionally held to constitute the day at the equinox.
It increases and decreases during the northern and southern courses;
the day swallows the night, and the night swallows the day.
Between autumn and spring, the equinox is perceived;
when the sun has entered Libra and Aries, that is the time when day and night are equal.
When the sun is situated in Cancer, it is called the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana);
the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is likewise said to occur when the sun is in Capricorn.
O Brahmin, fifteen of those days and nights, each consisting of thirty muhūrtas as described by me, are designated as a *pakṣa* (fortnight).
A month is said to consist of two fortnights; two months, produced by the sun, constitute a season (ṛtu);
three seasons make an ayana, and two ayanas are designated as a year.
The five periods beginning with the year are divided into four-month units;
the determination of all time is designated as a *yuga*.
The first is Saṃvatsara, the second is Parivatsara,
the third is Idvatsara, the fourth is Anuvatsara,
and the fifth here is Vatsara; this period of time is designated as a Yuga.
The mountain that lies to the north of Śveta is renowned as Śṛṅgavān;
it is known as Śṛṅgavān because it possesses three peaks.

The sun reaches the southern, the northern, and likewise the central equinox (vaiṣuvata) between the autumns and the springs; O Maitreya, this equinox is traditionally taught to occur at the beginning of Aries and the beginning of Libra.
Then the dispeller of darkness makes day and night equal;
indeed, both are recorded as being fifteen muhūrtas each.
O Sage, when the sun is in the first quarter of Kṛttikā, then the moon undoubtedly stays in the fourth quarter of Viśākhā.
When the sun moves through the third division of Viśākhā,
one should know that the moon is situated at the head of Kṛttikā.
At that very time, this period called the equinox (viṣuva) is declared to be meritorious;
then, gifts and other offerings should be given to the gods by those of purified soul.
This mouth of mine is for the Brahmins and the ancestors; it is born of giving.
One who has given a gift at the equinox becomes one who has fulfilled his duty.
Day and night, the half-month, as well as the *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and *kṣaṇas* are likewise known; so too are the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*),
as well as *sinīvālī*, *kuhū*, and *anumati*.
Tapa and Tapasya, Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci—these constitute the northern course (ayana).
Nabha and Nabhasya, Iṣa and Ūrja, as well as Sahas and Sahasya—these constitute the southern course.
Regarding the mountain Loka and Aloka which I previously mentioned to you,
the four world-protectors (Lokapālas), firm in their vows, reside there.
O twice-born one, Sudhāmā and Śaṅkhapāda were the two sons of Kardama;
Hiraṇyaroman was another, and Kekumān was the fourth.
Free from enmity, free from pride, free from sloth, and free from possessiveness,
these guardians of the world (Lokapālas) indeed abide in the four directions throughout the worlds.
To the north of Agastya’s station and to the south of the Ajavīthī is the path of the ancestors; indeed, it lies outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There dwell the high-souled sages who maintain the sacred fire;
praising the Brahman as created through the initiation of beings, they stand ready as officiating priests.
That path which those who initiate worldly activities take is the Southern Path (dakṣiṇa).
Furthermore, O Brahmā, they establish what has fallen away in age after age through continuity, austerity, the observance of boundaries, and sacred revelation.
In this world, those born earlier are indeed born in the houses of those born later,
and those born later are likewise born in the dwellings of those born earlier.
Thus revolving, they remain fixed in their vows,
following the southern path of the sun where neither moon nor stars appear.
That which lies north of the Nāgāvīthī and south of the Seven Sages is known as the northern path of the sun, the path of the gods (devayāna).
There, those perfected ones (siddhas), free from impurity and living as celibates (brahmacārins) who dwell, loathe progeny; therefore, death has been conquered by them.
Eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital seed remain on the northern path of the Sun until the dissolution of all beings.

Through the avoidance of attachment to sensual pleasures and sexual intercourse, through the non-occurrence of desire and aversion, and through the avoidance of initiating violence against living beings; // ViP_2.8.93 //
Furthermore, due to their lack of attachment to desires and because they perceived defects in sound and the other sense objects,
by these causes they became pure and indeed attained immortality.
The state that endures until the dissolution of all beings is considered immortality;
this duration of the three worlds is called "no further death."

O twice-born one, the rule regarding the performer of sin and merit through the killing of a Brahmin and the horse-sacrifice respectively has been declared; their fruits last until the dissolution of all beings.
In whatever extent of space Maitreya remains established,
the earth will undergo destruction to that same extent until the dissolution of all beings.
Above and beyond the Ṛṣis, where Dhruva is established,
is this divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.
O Brahmin, that supreme state belongs to those ascetics who have shaken off the mud of defects, whose selves are restrained, and for whom merit and sin have been exhausted.
When merit and demerit have ceased and all causes for attainment are exhausted,
that supreme state of Viṣṇu, having gone to which they do not grieve, is the highest abode.
That place where Dhruva and the others, who are witnesses to the world, abide;
which is attained through the yoga-powers produced by equality with Him—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
That in which this entire universe— the past, the present, and the future, including all that is moving and unmoving— is woven like warp and woof, O Maitreya, is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Like an eye stretched across the sky, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is perceived by yogis whose selves are absorbed in it through the vision of discriminative knowledge.
O twice-born one, upon that [pole-star] Dhruva is established as its own central pillar;
and upon Dhruva rest all the luminaries, and within the luminaries, the clouds.
O great sage, rain is gathered within the clouds; from rain comes the creation [of crops], and from that creation comes the nourishment and the satiation of all beings, beginning with the gods.
Then, nourished by means of offerings of clarified butter (ājya), those consumers of oblations (havirbhuj) again become the cause of rain for the sustenance of all beings.
Thus is this third step of Viṣṇu, pure in nature,
which serves as the support for the three worlds and is the cause of rain.
From there, O Brahmin, flows the river Gaṅgā, the remover of all sins,
which is tawny with the unguents from the bodies of the celestial nymphs.
Which [the river] Dhruva bears day and night with devotion upon his head— she who has issued forth from the stream of the toenail of Viṣṇu’s left lotus-foot.
Beyond that is the river upon whose waters, drenched with garlands of waves, the Seven Sages remain intent on their breath-control, their matted locks floating along.
By her continuous torrents of water, the orb of the moon was so inundated that it now bears an even greater luster at the time of its waning.
Emerging from the lunar orb, she falls high upon the summit of Mount Meru and proceeds in the four directions for the sake of purifying the world.
The Sītā, the Alakanandā, the Cakṣu, and the Bhadrā are established as one and the same river, distinguished by four divisions according to their course through the different directions.
And her southern branch, known as the Alakanandā,
even Śarva bore upon his head with affection for more than a hundred years.
And from the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks emerged the skeletal fragments;
having flooded the heavens, they led the sinful sons of Sagara to their end.
O Maitreya, for one who has bathed in her waters, sin is instantly destroyed and the attainment of unprecedented merit arises immediately.
O Maitreya, the waters offered there by sons endowed with faith to their ancestors provide a hundredfold satisfaction that is otherwise difficult to attain.
Having sacrificed with great sacrifices to Him, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person,
twice-born men and kings attained supreme perfection both in heaven and here on earth.
Likewise, by bathing in its waters, ascetics whose sins were shaken off attained supreme liberation,
even though their minds remained attached to their hair.
Whether heard, longed for, seen, touched, drunk, or plunged into, she purifies all beings; and when recited day after day, she likewise purifies them.
Even for those who, while standing hundreds of *yojanas* away, utter the name "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," it destroys the sin accumulated over three lifetimes.
For she is capable of purifying even the three worlds;
yet that supreme third state of the Blessed One is the source from which she arose.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
The form of the Lord, the Supreme Master, consists of the stars and has the shape of a porpoise.
That which is the form of Hari in the heavens—Dhruva is situated at its tail.
This very [wind], as it revolves, causes the planets, such as the moon and the sun, to revolve;
and following its revolution, the constellations move like a wheel.
The sun and moon, the stars, and the constellations together with the planets,
are indeed bound to Dhruva by bonds consisting of the hosts of winds.
That form of the luminaries in the sky which is described as having the shape of a crocodile is Nārāyaṇa, the refuge of all abodes; he himself is its support within the heart.
But Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, having propitiated that Lord of the World,
became established in the tail of the stellar Śiśumāra constellation.
Janārdana, the overseer of all, is the support of the Śiśumāra;
the Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva, and upon Dhruva the sun is established.
Upon him rests this entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the manner by which that occurs:
Vivasvat, having taken up the waters consisting of essence over eight months, rains them down;
from that comes food, and from food, the entire world arises.
Vivasvat, having drawn up the essence of the world with his sharp rays, causes the moon to nourish it;
and the moon, through channels consisting of the wind, disperses it into the clouds in heaven via conduits composed of smoke, fire, and air.

Because the waters do not fall away from them, they are called clouds (*abhra*). O Maitreya, the pure waters, impelled by the wind and having attained a refinement produced by time, descend from their place in the clouds.
O Sage, the Blessed Sun-god draws up the four kinds of water: that from rivers, from the ocean, from the earth, and that which originates from living beings.
Likewise, the sun, having taken up the water of the celestial Gaṅgā,
immediately casts it down upon the earth from the cloudless sky by means of its rays.
O best of the twice-born, a mortal whose stain of sin has been shaken off by contact with that [water] does not go to hell; for that is remembered as a divine bath.
For that water which, having seen the sun, falls from the sky through the clouds without them, is the water of the celestial Gaṅgā; it is cast down by the rays of the sun.
That portion of the sky which falls upon the sun during the odd-numbered lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā should be known as the water of the Gaṅgā, released by the elephants of the quarters.
And whatever water falls from the sky during the twin constellations,
released by the sun, all of that is drawn up again by the solar rays and cast down once more.
O great sage, both the water of the celestial Gaṅgā and the divine bath are exceedingly meritorious for men and remove the fear of sin.
O twice-born one, the water released by the clouds nourishes all plants; for that is indeed the nectar of immortality for the sustenance of living beings.
By that [power], O twice-born one, the entire collection of medicinal herbs was brought to supreme growth; it becomes effective for living beings until the ripening of its fruit.
Therefore, men who possess the eye of the scriptures perform sacrifices daily according to the injunctions as they have been proclaimed, and thereby they nourish the gods.
In this same way, the sacrifices, the Vedas, and the social classes headed by the twice-born,
as well as all the hosts of gods and all the multitudes of living beings— ViP_2,9.21.
O best of sages, all this food is produced by rain; yet that rain itself is produced by the Sun.
O best of eminent sages, Dhruva is the support of Savitṛ;
Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva, and he, too, has Nārāyaṇa as his essence.
Within the heart of that Śiśumāra resides Nārāyaṇa,
the supporter of all beings, the primordial and eternal source.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
The interval between the two solstices consists of one hundred and eighty-three maṇḍalas.
The movement of the sun through its ascent and descent over the course of a year—
He was stationed upon his chariot by the gods, the Ādityas, the sages,
as well as by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
Dhātṛ and Kratusthalā, Pulastya and Vāsuki,
Rathabhṛt the grāmaṇī, Heti, and Tumburu as the seventh.
O Maitreya, these seven indeed always reside during the month of Caitra, the month of honey (madhu), serving as the presiding deities of the Sun’s chariot for seven months.
Āryamā, Pulaha, Rathaujas, Puñjikasthalā,
Praheti, Kacchavīra, and Nārada were in the chariot of Ravi.
These dwell in Mādhava; learn from me [their names] in the month known as Śuci.
Mitra, Trisṭakṣaka, the Rākṣasa Pauruṣeya, Menakā,
Hāhā, and Rathasvana— these, O Maitreya, indeed dwell there.
Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha, Rambhā, Sahajanyā, Huhū,
Ratha, and Rathacitra dwell in the constellation known as Āṣāḍhā, presided over by Śukra.
Indra, Viśvāvasu, Srotas, Elāputra, as well as Aṅgiras,
Pramlocā, Na-bhasya, and Saptya indeed dwell in Arka.
Vivasvān, Ugrasena, Bhṛgu, Āpūraṇa,
Anumlocā, Śaṅkhapāla, and Vyāghra likewise [reigned] in the month of Bhādrapada.
Pūṣan, Suruci, Vāta, Gautama, Dhanañjaya,
Suṣeṇa, and another, as well as Ghṛtācī, dwell when the sun is in Āśvayuja.
Viśvāvasu, Bharadvāja, Parjanya,
Āvata, as well as Viśvācī and Senajit, indeed dwell in Kārttika.
Aṃśa, Kāśyapa, Tārkṣya, Mahāpadma, Urvaśī, Citrasena, Vidyunmān, and Mārgaśīrṣa were the presiding deities.
Kratu, Bhaga, Urṇāyu, Sphūrja, Kārkoṭaka,
Ariṣṭanemi, and another, the excellent Apsaras Pūrvacitti.
In the month of Pauṣa, these excellent Brahmins, acting as officiants for the purpose of illuminating the world, dwell upon the stalk of the seven-sun lotus.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, Jamadagni, Kambala, Tilottamā,
Brahmopeta, Ṛtajit, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the seventh.
O Maitreya, these seven dwell in the sun during the month of Māgha;
now hear about those who reside in the sun during the month of Phālguna.
O great sage, [the sons were] Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Rambha, Sūryavarcas, Satyajit, Viśvāmitra, and likewise the Rākṣasa Yajñopeta.
O Maitreya, O Brahmin, during these months these seven dwell within the orb of the sun, empowered by the energy of Viṣṇu.
The sages praise the Sun; he is sung of before him by the Gandharvas;
the Apsarases dance, and the night-rangers follow after the Sun.
The serpents carry it, and the Yakṣas hold the reins.
Likewise, the Vālakhilyas sit surrounding him on all sides.
Thus, O best of sages, this group of seven within the solar disc becomes the cause of cold, heat, and the falling of rain, according to its own fixed time.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second part of the *Kṣīrārṇava-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Maitreya said:
"Regarding that which the Blessed One has stated—that the host of the Sun is sevenfold—"
I have heard from him the cause of the cold, heat, and so forth within the cosmic egg (maṇḍala).
O Preceptor, the activities of the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as those of the Vālakhilya sages and the Apsarases, have also been described.
O Sage, you have not yet described here the deeds of the Yakṣas in the chariot of the Sun, nor those of Viṣṇu whose soul is sustained by his power, nor whatever action belongs to Āditya himself.
If the seven classes [of clouds] rain water that is both cold and hot,
what is the role of the sun in this regard, by virtue of which it is said that "the rain comes from the sun"?
Why does the common folk say that Vivasvat rises in the middle and then sets,
if his activity were identical to that of the group of seven [sages]?
Parāśara said: O Maitreya, listen to this which you ask:
how it is that the Sun, though belonging to the group of seven, is preeminent as the one who excels them all.
The supreme power of Viṣṇu, known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—
this very Trayī is what burns away evil and destroys the suffering of the world.
This very Viṣṇu, intent on protecting the world, remains established in the act of preservation;
he dwells within the sun as the essence of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, O twice-born one.
Indeed, in each and every month, that supreme power of Viṣṇu, consisting of the three Vedas, establishes her presence wherever the sun may be.
In the forenoon they chant the Ṛg-verses; at midday, indeed, the Yajus-formulas;
and at the close of day, the Sāman-chants such as the Bṛhat and Rathantara, [they praise] the Sun.
O Viṣṇu, this triad known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma is your limb;
it, as the power of Viṣṇu, eternally abides within the sun.
That Vaiṣṇava power of the Sun is not only composed of the three Vedas;
for Brahmā, Puruṣa, and Rudra—these three are likewise composed of the three Vedas.
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā consists of the Ṛgveda; for the sake of preservation, Viṣṇu consists of the Yajurveda;
and Rudra consists of the Sāmaveda for the sake of dissolution. Therefore, his sound is impure.
Thus, that Vaiṣṇavī power of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī), which consists of the three Vedas,
presides over that radiant one who resides within the seven groups of the self.
Empowered by her, he too blazes forth with his own rays and brings about the destruction of all darkness throughout the entire world.
Sages praise him, Gandharvas sing before him,
Apsarases dance as they go, and night-stalkers follow after him.
The serpents carry it, the Yakṣas hold the reins,
and the Vālakhilyas sit surrounding it on all sides.
Bearing the form of power, Viṣṇu never rises nor ever sets;
he is distinct from Viṣṇu, and his attendants likewise constitute these sevenfold groups.

Just as a mirror situated on a pillar, when it comes into proximity with someone, attains a connection with the perception of that person's reflection, so too does he [the soul] attain such a connection for himself.
In this way, O twice-born one, that Vaiṣṇava power never departs from him;
month after month, she dwells within him as he remains established there, radiant with light.
O twice-born one, that Lord Savitṛ, perpetually nourishing the ancestors, gods, humans, and others,
revolves as the cause of day and night.
The moon, which consists of nectar, is nourished by the sun's rays through the *suṣumṇā* channel; it is then constantly drunk by the gods during the dark fortnight.
O twice-born one, at the end of the dark fortnight, those who subsist on rainwater drink that two-part Soma which has been drunk [by the sun]; likewise, their satisfaction comes from the sun.
The Sun, with his rays, takes up the moisture situated upon the earth;
he releases it for the nourishment of living beings and for the growth of crops.
By that, the Blessed Lord Sun gladdens all beings without exception;
in this way, he nourishes the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and others.
O Maitreya, the Sun bestows upon the gods satisfaction for a fortnight, upon the ancestors for a month, and eternal satisfaction upon mortals.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: The chariot of Soma has three wheels, and its horses have the luster of jasmine.
Joined by ten on the left and right, he moves about.
The constellations resting upon the celestial path are held by the swift Dhruva,
just as the rays of the sun undergo a process of waning and waxing.
For his horses, born from the womb of the waters, once yoked carry him for an entire kalpa, O best of sages, just like the horses of the Sun.
O Maitreya, the radiant sun replenishes with a single ray the moon, which has been diminished and drunk by the gods until it remains as a single digit.
By that same process through which the moon was drunk by the gods,
the sun, the stealer of water, daily replenishes it.
O Maitreya, the gods drink that nectar of immortality which is collected within the moon over the course of half a month; it is because they consume this nectar that they are immortal.
Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
and thirty-three gods drink from the maker of night.
But having entered the solar orb, distinguished by two digits, he dwells in the ray called Amā; therefore, it is known as Amāvāsyā.
During that day and night, the moon first enters the waters;
thereafter it dwells in the plants, and from there it proceeds to the sun in due order.
He who cuts down a plant or causes even a single leaf to fall when the moon is situated in a lunar mansion associated with plants incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
When fifteen parts of the moon remain, with but a small portion of a *kalā* still left,
during the afternoon, the hosts of Pitṛs wait upon the youngest.
O Sage, the ancestors drink that portion of the moon which consists of two digits; however, the remaining digit of his, which is composed of nectar and is meritorious, [remains for the living].
On the new moon day, that nectar of immortality flows forth from the rays;
having obtained supreme satisfaction for a month, the ancestors remain in a state of bliss.
They are of three kinds: the Saumyas, the Barhiṣadas, and the Agniṣvāttas.
In this manner, he nourishes the gods during the bright fortnight and likewise the ancestors during the dark fortnight,
as well as the plants, with cool water-molecules consisting of nectar.
Through the production of creepers and medicinal herbs, the cool-rayed moon nourishes humans, cattle, and insects, as well as by means of its illumination and delight.
The chariot of the son of the Moon is composed of the substances of wind and fire;
it is yoked to eight tawny horses that possess the speed of the wind.
The great chariot of Śukra was also equipped with a protective fender and a chassis, yoked with horses born of the earth, and provided with quivers and banners.
The great golden chariot of Bhauma was also magnificent, possessing eight horses;
it was yoked with steeds as red as rubies, born from fire.
Yoked with eight white horses, his chariot is made of gold;
Bṛhaspati stands upon it at the end of each year, moving from one zodiac sign to the next.
Mounting a chariot yoked with dappled horses born of the sky,
the slow-moving Śanaiścara proceeds slowly.
Svarbhānu’s eight horses, which have the luster of bees, are always yoked at once and carry his grey chariot without ceasing, O Maitreya.
Emerging from the sun, Rāhu goes toward the moon during the lunar nodes;
from the moon he returns to the sun again during the solar nodes.
Likewise, the eight horses of Keturatha also possess the speed of the wind;
they have the hue of the smoke from burning straw and are as ruddy as liquid lac.
O highly fortunate one, these nine chariots of the planets have been described by me to you; all of them are fastened to Dhruva by cords of wind.
O Maitreya, all the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and celestial abodes are bound to Dhruva and revolve according to their proper courses by means of the reins of the wind.
As many stars as there are, so many are the cords of wind;
all of them are fastened to Dhruva, and as they revolve, they cause him to revolve.
Just as oil-pressers cause a wheel to revolve by their own rotation,
so too do the luminaries revolve in every direction, impelled by the wind.
Because it carries the luminaries like whirling firebrands driven by a circle of winds, it is therefore known as the Pravaha wind.
As for that which is called Śiśumāra, it is where Dhruva resides;
O best of sages, hear now its configuration as well.
Whatever sin one commits during the day, one is released from it by seeing him at night;
and for as many stars as there are situated upon the Śiśumāra in the sky,
for that many years, plus more, does he live.
Uttānapāda is to be known as his lower jaw, and Yajña as the upper jaw; Dharma is to be known as having taken refuge in his head.
Nārāyaṇa dwells in his heart; the two Aśvins are in his forefeet;
and Varuṇa and Aryaman are in his two hind-thighs.
The year is his phallus; Mitra is situated in his downward breath (apāna).
Pucchaṅgi, Mahendra, Kaśyapa, and then Dhruva—
this quartet, including the star Śiśumāra, never sets.
Thus has this configuration of the earth, as well as that of the luminaries,
the islands, the oceans, and the mountains, been described.
The nature of the rain-clouds, the rivers, and those who indeed dwell within them has been described; now hear again this summary.
O Brahmin, from that water which was indeed the body of Viṣṇu,
the earth emerged in the form of a lotus, endowed with mountains, oceans, and other features.
The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the forests, the mountains, and the quarters are Viṣṇu;
the rivers and the oceans—he alone is everything that exists and that does not exist, O best of brahmins.
Since the Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness and possesses a form that is non-material rather than a substantial entity,
you should understand that the distinctions such as mountains, oceans, and the earth are merely the manifestations of consciousness.
But when all knowledge is pure, possessing its own innate form, free from defects through the exhaustion of karma,
then indeed the fruits of the tree of conceptual construction do not arise as distinctions between objects within things.
Does there exist anywhere that which is vast, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and eternally of a single form?
And as for that which undergoes further alteration, O twice-born one, it is not truly so; for how could there be reality in that?
The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, shards; from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, atoms.
This is perceived by people whose certainty regarding the self is stilled by their own karma. Tell me, what is the reality here?
Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that exists apart from consciousness;
consciousness alone is conceived as manifold by minds differentiated according to the distinctions of their own respective karmas.
Knowledge is pure, stainless, sorrowless, and free from all attachment to greed and other passions;
it is one, eternally one, and that supreme Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists.

Thus have I described to you the true nature of existence, and how knowledge leads to the truth, while everything else is otherwise. Furthermore, that which pertains to worldly convention has also been explained to you as it relates to the universe.
The sacrifice, the animal, the fire, all the officiating priests, the Soma, the gods, and the desire consisting of heaven—
these are seen as the paths based on ritual action (karma), and the enjoyments of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are their fruits.
Whatever has been described by me to you as existing within the world, one who is subject to karma indeed wanders everywhere therein;
knowing this, one should perform that which is certain, immovable, and eternally uniform, by means of which one enters Vāsudeva.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, you have indeed correctly explained all that I asked of you."
The configuration of the earth, the oceans, and the rivers, as well as the positions of the planets;
Just as these three worlds are established with Viṣṇu as their support,
so has the ultimate truth been declared to you according to knowledge, primarily from the perspective of Pradhāna.
Regarding that which the Blessed One has spoken concerning the lord of the earth, Bharata—I desire to hear his life story; you should relate it to me.
That protector of the earth, Bharata, it is said, dwelt at Sālagrāma,
ever absorbed in yoga, having fixed his mind upon Vāsudeva.
By the power of that meritorious place and by constantly meditating on Hari,
why was liberation not attained, such that he became a twice-born man once again?
O best of sages, you ought to relate all that was further performed by that great-souled Bharata during his state as a Brahmin.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, that illustrious lord of the earth dwelt for a long time at Sālagrāma, having fixed his mind upon the Blessed Lord.
The best among those possessed of virtues attained the highest perfection in all virtues, beginning with non-violence, as well as in the restraint of the mind.
O Lord of Sacrifice, O Acyuta, Govinda, Mādhava, Ananta, Keśava,
Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva— salutations be unto You!
Thus King Bharata spoke, O Maitreya; he uttered nothing other than the names of Hari, even during the intervals of his sleep. He thought of nothing else, apart from these words and their meaning.
The ascetic yogi, free from attachment, performed the gathering of fuel, flowers, and *kuśa* grass for the sake of divine rites; he performed no other actions.
Once, he went to the great river for the purpose of consecration;
he bathed there and then performed the rites that follow bathing.
Then, O Brahmin, a single thirsty doe from the forest came to that shore to drink water, for she was near the time of her delivery.
Then, when the water had thus been almost entirely drunk, there arose from that place a truly great roar of a lion, terrifying to all living beings.
Then, suddenly leaping from the riverbank out of fear, she fell;
due to that excessively high leap, her fetus indeed fell into the river.
The king seized that young deer, which had fallen from the womb, as it was being carried away with great speed and overwhelmed by a garland of waves.
O Maitreya, due to the fault of a miscarriage and because of her excessive exertion,
that doe fell down and died.
Then, seeing that doe fallen,
the ascetic Tr̥pa took the fawn and returned to his own hermitage.
O Sage, that king performed the nourishment of the young deer day after day; and being nurtured by him, it grew up.
He grazed on grass in the thickets at the edge of the hermitage;
and having gone toward the entrance, he would return again out of fear of tigers.
Having gone very far in the morning, she would return to the hermitage in the evening;
and again, Bharata appeared in the courtyard of the leaf-hut of the hermitage.
O twice-born one, as that deer moved about at a distance or nearby, his mind remained fixed upon it and did not go elsewhere.
Having renounced his kingdom and sons, and having abandoned all his kinsmen,
he felt a profound sense of possessiveness toward that young fawn.
"Has he been devoured by wolves or tigers? Has he been struck down by a lion?"—such was the thought in his mind as [the boy] went out and delayed for a long time.
This earth is mottled by the wounds from the tips of his hooves.
"Where is this young fawn of mine, born for my delight?
For he is intent on scratching my arm with the tips of his antlers;
having returned safely from the forest, he will surely bring me joy."
With their tufts of hair recently shorn by his teeth,
these kuśas and kāśas shine like young brahmin students chanting the Sāman hymns.
When he had thus departed for a long time, the sage, his face bright with joy, directed his mind toward him and remained with the deer standing by his side.
Because his mind was absorbed in that [truth], the king’s concentration was unbroken,
even though he had renounced his kingdom, enjoyments, prosperity, and kinsmen.
Although that fawn was restless, moving far away, and prone to wandering at great distances,
the mind of that king became as steady as it was toward the young deer.
Then, as time passed, that lord of the earth met his end,
gazed upon by his son with tears in his eyes, just as a young deer gazes upon its father.
O Maitreya, even as he was giving up his life-breaths, he saw only the deer; through being absorbed in that [deer], he thought of nothing else at all.
And then, having attained such a state of meditative cultivation formed at that time,
he was born as a deer with the memory of his former births in the great forest of Jambūmārga.
O best of the twice-born, being distressed by the cycle of existence due to his memory of past births,
he abandoned his mother and returned once more to Sālagrāma.
Sustaining himself with dry grass and leaves in that manner,
he attained the expiation for the karma that had caused his birth as a deer.
And there, having cast off his body, he was born as a twice-born man who remembered his former births,
into a pure and preeminent family of yogis who were devoted to virtuous conduct.
Endowed with all forms of knowledge and knowing the true reality of the meaning of all scriptures,
Maitreya beheld the Self as transcendent to primordial nature (prakṛti).
O great sage, having attained knowledge of the Self, he beheld all beings, beginning with the gods, as non-different from his own self.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, he did not recite the Veda as taught by his teacher;
he neither observed the ritual acts nor did he master the scriptures.
Although addressed many times, he spoke only a few words that were dull; even those lacked the quality of refinement and relied upon the speech patterns of the vulgar.
With his body disfigured, that twice-born man,
clad in soiled garments and with the spaces between his teeth dripping, was held in contempt by all the citizens.
Since the practice of yoga brings about a loss that is greater than any dishonor,
the yogi who is disregarded by people attains the perfection of yoga.
Therefore, the yogi should indeed practice the dharma of the virtuous without causing offense, so that people do not despise him and do not seek his company.
Reflecting thus upon the words of Hiraṇyagarbha,
the high-minded one revealed himself to the people in the form of a dull-witted madman.
Having eaten boiled pulse, potherbs such as vāṭyāla, wild fruits, or grains,
he eats whatever he obtains in great abundance, practicing self-restraint according to the time.
Then, upon the death of his father, he was made by his brothers, cousins,
and kinsmen to perform field labor and other such tasks, being nourished on food consisting of coarse grain.
With symmetrical and stout limbs, yet dull-witted in his actions,
he became a provider for all the world, his consciousness focused solely on food.
The steward prepared that man— who was thus unrefined and possessed the appearance and behavior of a brahmin— as a sacrificial animal for the queen of the Sauvīra king.
Having adorned him at night according to the ritual for slaughter,
Mahākālī likewise recognized that he was possessed by Yogeśvara.
Then, taking up a sharpened sword at night,
she likewise severed the neck of the steward of cruel deeds at its root;
accompanied by her own attendants, the goddess drank the copious blood.
Then, as the high-souled king of Sauvīra was departing,
the one who had performed the ritual service thought, "This man is indeed worthy of labor."
The steward of the Sauvīra king considered that great-souled one— who was like a fire covered by ashes— to be fit for manual labor.
O twice-born one, that king, having mounted his palanquin,
resolved to go to the excellent hermitage of the seer Kapila on the bank of the Ikṣumatī.
"What is the highest good for men in this cycle of existence, which is mostly suffering?"—
with these words he questioned that great sage named Kapila, who was a knower of the dharma of liberation.
Urged by the words of the steward (kṣattṛ), he carried the palanquin,
standing in the midst of other men who had been conscripted for forced labor.
The Brahmin, the sole vessel of all knowledge,
who remembered his former births and desired the destruction of his sins, carried her as he was seized by forced labor.
Then that dull-witted one went on, looking only for the deer;
the best among the intelligent, however, proceeded swiftly, leaving him behind.
Then, observing the uneven motion of the palanquin, the king said, "What is this? O bearers of the palanquin, proceed evenly."
Again, observing the palanquin to be uneven in that same manner, the king said: "What is this? You are traveling in a different way than before."
Having heard these words spoken many times by the king,
the bearers of the palanquin said, "He goes," without any haste.
The King said:
"Are you weary from this short distance, having carried my palanquin?
Are you not able to endure it, for you appear to be stout?"
The Brahmin said:
"I am not fat, nor has this palanquin been carried by me;
I am not weary, O Lord of the Earth, nor is there any fatigue to be endured."
The king said:
"You appear visibly fat even now, and the palanquin is upon you;
for embodied beings certainly experience fatigue from carrying a burden."
Brahmā said:
"O King, tell me what was seen by you directly;
the terms 'strong' and 'weak' are qualifiers that should be stated afterwards."
"The palanquin was carried by you, and it remains with you even now;
this is false. Listen here to my words."
The pair of feet rested upon the ground; the two shanks were situated on the two feet;
the two thighs were positioned upon the two shanks; and the belly was likewise supported by them.
