"The chest, the arms, and the shoulders are situated upon the belly;
this palanquin rests upon the shoulders—what burden has been placed here upon me?"
This body that you have observed standing in the palanquin—therein you are one thing, and I am another; yet here it is said to be otherwise.
"O King, you, I, and others as well are carried along by the elements;
this entire collection of elements also moves, fallen into the stream of the qualities."
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities, beginning with *sattva*, are subject to karma;
and that karma, accumulated through ignorance, exists in all living beings without exception.
The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature;
it neither increases nor decreases, being one and the same among all living beings.
O King, when there was neither increase nor decrease for him, by what logic did you say, "He was fat"? (ViP 2.13.72)
Just as this palanquin rests upon the feet, shanks, hips, thighs,
and belly, so too has the burden been equally borne by you.
Likewise, O King, the palanquin was carried not only by other living beings,
but also by mountains, trees, houses, and even the earth itself.
O King, when a man's state of separation from Prakṛti occurs through natural causes, how could that hardship possibly be endured by me, O Lord of Men? (ViP 2.13.75)
Of whatever substance this palanquin is made, of that same substance is the aggregate of beings;
yet for you, who are not free from delusion, it is augmented by the sense of "mine."
Śrī Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, having spoken thus, he became silent while carrying the palanquin;
the king also, descending to the ground, quickly grasped his feet.
The king said:
"O twice-born one, set down the palanquin and show me favor!
Tell me, who are you that stands here assuming the form of a commoner?"
O learned one, let all that be told by you to me, who am desirous of hearing it— whether it be your purpose, the cause for your presence, or the reason for your arrival.
Brahmā said:
"O King, it is impossible to say 'I am that';
moreover, the act of moving everywhere is for the sake of experience."

The experience of pleasure and pain, which give rise to the body and its like, originates from merit and demerit; it is in order to experience these that a living being undergoes the acquisition of a body and so forth.
For indeed, O protector of the earth, dharma and adharma are the cause for every living being in all circumstances; why then do you ask me about the cause?
The King said:
"There is no doubt that dharma and adharma are the cause in all actions;
and the transition from one body to another is for the purpose of experiencing [the fruits of those actions]."
As for that which was spoken by you, "I am this very self," it is impossible to express; yet, the desire to hear it arises within me.
O Brahmin, how can it be said that the expression "I am he who exists" is impossible? O twice-born one, the word "I" used with respect to the Self is not a fault.

The Brahmin said: "The notion 'I am sound' leads to error; it is not so with respect to the Self. To perceive the Self in what is not the Self—whether as a sound or otherwise—is characterized by delusion."
"O King, the tongue says 'I am,' as do the teeth, the lips, and the palate;
for it is by means of these that I exist, since they are all the causes for the production of speech."
"Why does she speak by means of such reasons, saying 'I am speech' herself?
Therefore, it is not appropriate to say of her, 'You are fat.'"
Since this body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the person,
O King, why then do I apply this notion of "I" to it?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else whatsoever superior to me,
then it would be appropriate to say that "this one is I" and "that one is another."
When the one Supreme Person is established within all bodies, then indeed such speech as "Who are you? or "Who am I? is meaningless.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, these are the bearers and the attendants before you, and this is your world; yet, O King, all this is said not to be real."
From a tree comes wood, and from that, this palanquin occupied by you;
O King, would it have the designation of "tree" or the designation of "wood"?
"This great king is mounted upon a tree," so says this person to you; nor does anyone say that you are seated in a palanquin made of wood.

O best of kings, let this collection of wooden beams that constitutes the palanquin, which remains stable through its particular arrangement, be examined by you; for when it is broken apart, the palanquin [is no longer found].
In this way, consider the separation of the ribs of an umbrella:
"Where has the umbrella gone? This same principle applies to you and to me.
"Man, woman, cow, goat, horse, elephant, bird,
and tree— this is to be understood as the worldly designation for bodies produced by the causes of karma."
The Self (puruṣa) is neither a god, nor a human, nor an animal, nor a plant;
O King, these distinctions of bodily form have their origin in karma.
Whatever in this world is called "the king," as well as that which consists of the king's soldiers and other such things—O King, all that is not real; it is composed of mental construction.
O King, what indeed is that entity which, even after the passage of time, does not assume another designation produced by transformation and the like? ViP 2.13.100.
You are the king of the entire world; you are the son of your father and the enemy of your foe;
you are the husband of your wife and the father of your son—what more can I say to you, O protector of the earth?
"O Lord of the Earth, what is this head? Is it you? What indeed is your neck, and likewise your belly? Are you the feet and so forth, or do these belong to you?"
O King, having become distinct from all your constituent parts, reflect skillfully upon this: "Who am I? (ViP 2.13.103)
Since reality is established in this way, O King, how could it be possible for me to speak of "I" as something to be produced by means of separation?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of his, which were endowed with the highest truth, [the king was filled with wonder].
Bowing down with humility, the king spoke to that twice-born man.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, as for these words consisting of the supreme truth which have been spoken by you,
upon hearing them, the functions of my mind seem to whirl."
This discriminative knowledge regarding all living beings,
which you have revealed, O Sage, is supreme and greater than primordial nature.
"I do not carry the palanquin, nor does the palanquin rest upon me;
the body is distinct from us, and by it this palanquin is supported."
"The activity of beings proceeds from the activity of the *guṇas*, impelled by karma;
for these *guṇas* indeed act [of their own accord]. What is it to me?"—this was spoken by you.
When these words concerning the ultimate truth reached my ears,
my mind became overwhelmed, having attained a longing for that supreme reality.
O twice-born one, previously I set out to go and question the highly fortunate sage Kapila regarding what is beneficial in this matter; tell me that.
And during that interval, because this very statement was uttered by you,
my mind runs toward you for the sake of the ultimate truth.
O twice-born one, the sage Kapila, a devotee of the Lord, was indeed a portion of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, who descended to the earth to destroy the delusion of the world.
Surely that very Blessed One, out of a desire for our welfare,
has become manifest here, since he speaks of this matter as it truly is.
O twice-born one, you who are an ocean whose waves are the waters of all-encompassing knowledge— tell me, who am bowed before you, that which is the supreme good.
The Brahmin said:
"O King, do you ask what is the highest good, or do you ask about the ultimate truth?
For there are many goods that are not the ultimate truth, O Lord of the Earth."
O King, he who, having performed the propitiation of the deities, desires wealth and prosperity, sons, and sovereignty— his very effort toward these goals leads to his ultimate welfare.
Action consisting of sacrifice is the highest good, having as its characteristic the attainment of that [state];
and when the fruit is not sought after, that very action is the primary excellence in the result.
O King, the Self should always be meditated upon by those engaged in yoga, as well as that which is beyond it;
for union with that very Supreme Self is the highest good.
"In this world there are thus many such superior states by the hundreds and thousands; however, these are not the ultimate truth—listen now to my words."
If the ultimate goal is indeed wealth, why is it being sacrificed for the sake of dharma,
and why is expenditure being made for the sake of attaining sensual desires?
O Lord of Men, if a son were the ultimate reality, he too would be the ultimate reality for someone else;
for that father is indeed the ultimate reality for him.
Thus, there is no ultimate reality in this world of moving and unmoving beings;
for the ultimate reality consists of the effects of causes in their entirety.

If the attainment of sovereignty and so forth mentioned here were [to exist] from the perspective of ultimate reality, then things would either truly exist in this world or truly not exist; yet such is not the case.
In your view, sacrificial rites are considered to be accomplished through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
even regarding those, hear from me as I speak of their ultimate reality.
O King, whatever effect is produced from clay as its material cause is known to be made of clay, because it follows the nature of that cause.
In this way, whatever action is accomplished by means of perishable substances such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and kuśa grass,
that action itself must be perishable.
The wise accept that the ultimate reality is indestructible;
however, that [universe] is destructible, without a doubt, as it is produced from a destructible substance.

Therefore, that very action which yields no fruit is considered by you to be the ultimate reality (paramārtha), because it serves as the means to liberation; yet the ultimate reality itself is not a means.
O King, meditation is indeed called the ultimate reality for oneself;
yet while it creates distinctions from others, the ultimate reality itself is devoid of distinction.
"The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
yet this is false, because one substance does not become the substance of another."
Therefore, O King, there is no doubt that all these human states are superior;
however, hear from me in brief the ultimate truth.
The Self is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), free from birth, growth, and so forth, omnipresent, and immutable.
O King, that all-pervading Lord, who consists of supreme knowledge, has never been joined with the wise through names, castes, and the like; He was not united with them, nor will He ever be.

That consciousness which is indeed one and the same within the bodies of oneself and others, even though they exist as distinct, is the ultimate reality; those who perceive duality are seers of the unreal.
Just as the distinction of the air pervading without differentiation is designated by names such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth according to the different holes of a flute, so it is with this Supreme Self.
And the distinction of a single nature arises from the veil of Brahma’s karma;
for when the distinctions of gods and so forth have been destroyed, that [distinction] certainly does not exist in the absence of obscuration.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Śrī Parāśara said:
When this had been said, that Brahmin then replied with a discourse concerning non-duality to the king, who remained silent and deep in thought.
The Brahmin said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to that which was sung by Ṛbhu in the past,
generating awakening in the high-souled Nidāgha."
O King, Rbhu was the son of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin;
he understood the true nature of reality by his very nature.
In former times, his disciple was Nidāgha, the son of Pulastya;
he bestowed upon him all branches of knowledge with supreme joy.
O Lord of Men, because his mastery over knowledge was not yet attained, he had no latent impression of non-duality; that Ribhu then reflected upon Nidagha.
On the bank of the Devikā is a city named Vīranagara, which is prosperous and exceedingly beautiful; it was established by Pulastya.
O best of kings,
in former times, a knower of yoga named Nidāgha, a disciple of Ṛbhu, lived on the edge of that delightful grove.
When a thousand divine years had passed,
that Ṛbhu went to his city to look for his disciple Nidāgha.
At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, as he stood within the range of vision at the doorway,
[the sage] was offered the guest-offering (arghya) by him and led into his own dwelling.
When he had washed his hands and feet and had accepted a seat,
that best of brahmins respectfully said to him, "Please eat."
R̥bhu said: "O best of Brahmins, please tell me what food is to be eaten in your house;
for I have no constant pleasure in coarse foods."
Nidāgha said:
"O best of the twice-born, in my house there are barley-meal, barley-gruel, vāṭya, and cakes; whatever pleases you, O most excellent of the twice-born, eat that according to your desire."
R̥bhu said:
"O twice-born one, give me food that is not coarse; give me delicious food such as *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, and the like, along with drops of molasses."
Nidāgha said:
"O virtuous lady, whatever is most excellent in my house—
whether it be food or condiments, however delicious— prepare his meal with that."
The Brahmin said:
Having been addressed thus by him, she, out of respect for her husband's words, prepared that delicious food which was intended for the twice-born.
When that great sage had finished eating the delicious food according to his desire,
O protector of the earth, he stood bowed with humility and spoke to him from below.
Nidāgha said:
"O twice-born one, has supreme satisfaction and contentment arisen within you? Is your mind at ease now that it has been provided with food?"
"O Brahmin, where is your residence, and where are you prepared to go? Furthermore, O twice-born one, tell us from where you have come."
Ṛmu said: "O Brāhmaṇa, for one who has hunger, satisfaction arises from eating food;
I have neither hunger nor lack of satisfaction—why do you question me?"
When the earth element has been consumed by fire, hunger arises;
and when the water element is exhausted, thirst likewise arises for human beings.
"Hunger and thirst, O twice-born one, are called the properties of the body; since these do not belong to me, I am always truly satisfied because of the absence of the occurrence of hunger."
O twice-born one, composure of mind and contentment are these two qualities of the intellect;
ask about that person whose mind possesses them, for such a man is not bound by these [worldly states].
When asked, "Where is your residence?", "Where are you going?",
and "From where have you come?", listen to my reply regarding these three matters.
Since this person is all-pervading and omnipresent like space, how could even such questions as "From where?", "Where?", or "Whither will you go? be meaningful?
Thus, I am neither a goer nor a comer, nor do I have a dwelling in any single place;
you and others are not you, nor are they others, and even I am not "I."
"Whether it was delicious or not, I have made this inquiry of you:
'What will you say? In that regard as well, O best of the twice-born, let it be heard."
"O best of the twice-born, what is there to enjoy in this food, whether it be unpalatable or delicious?
For even that which is delicious, once it has become as delicious [as this], causes only distress."
What is unrefined becomes refined, and people recoil from what is already refined;
what food is there that provides pleasure in its beginning, middle, and end?
Just as a house made of clay becomes stable when plastered with clay,
so too is this body composed of earth, formed from earthly atoms.
Barley, wheat, mung beans, and so forth; clarified butter, oil, milk, curd, molasses, fruits, and the like, as well as the atoms of the earth element—[all these were produced]. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15.30)
Therefore, having understood this, you should allow that mind—which discriminates between the pleasant and the unpleasant—to rest in equanimity; for equanimity leads to liberation.
The Brahmin said:
O King, having heard those words of his which were grounded in the supreme truth,
the illustrious Nidāgha prostrated himself and spoke these words.
Be gracious for the sake of my welfare; tell me why you have come.
O twice-born one, my delusion has vanished upon hearing these words of yours.
Ṛbhu said:
"O twice-born one, I am Ṛbhu, your teacher; I have come here for the sake of bestowing wisdom upon you. Having explained the supreme truth to you, I shall now depart."
In this way, know that this entire world is one and without division;
it is the very nature of the Supreme Self, who is designated as Vāsudeva.
The Brahmin said: Having been addressed with "So be it" by Nidāgha, who preceded his words with prostrations and worshipped him with supreme devotion, Ṛbhu departed according to his will.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O lord of men, when a thousand years had passed, Ṛbhu..."
He went to that very city in order to bestow the knowledge of Nidāgha.
Then, as the king was entering the city surrounded by a vast army, that sage beheld Nidāgha outside the city.
Standing at a distance, the illustrious one— avoiding the crush of the crowd,
his throat parched with hunger, and carrying sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass— was approaching from the forest.
Having seen Nidāgha, Ṛbhu approached him, saluted him, and said:
"O twice-born one, why are you standing in this secluded spot?"
Nidāgha said:
"O Brahmin, this great lord of men is about to enter the beautiful city amidst a throng of people; therefore, I am staying here."
Ṛbhu said: "O lord of men, who here is the one, and who is the other person?
Tell me, O best of the twice-born, for you are considered by me to be all-knowing."
Nidāgha said:
"This lord of men who has mounted this intoxicated lord of elephants, which is as towering as a mountain peak— this one is Parīlakṣa, and the other is likewise."
R̥bhu said:
"Indeed, these two kings of elephants were shown to me simultaneously by you; they could not be distinguished individually by their specific marks."
"O illustrious one, let the distinction between these two be told by you;
I wish to know which here is the elephant and which is the lord of men."
Nidāgha said: "O Brahmin, this elephant here, and that king upon it—
what twice-born man indeed does not know the relationship between the rider and the mount?"
Ṛbhu said: "I know this, O Brahman; therefore, instruct me accordingly.
For what indeed is denoted by the word 'below,' and what is designated as 'above'?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Thus addressed, Nidāgha immediately climbed up and spoke to that Ṛbhu:
"Listen, I shall tell you what you ask of me."
O Brahmin, I have shown this illustration to you for the sake of your awakening: as I am the king above, so you are the elephant below.
R̥bhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, you stand as a king, while I am like an elephant;
therefore, explain this to me: who are you, and likewise, who am I?"
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus, Nidāgha quickly grasped both of his feet and said,
"O Blessed One, you are certainly my preceptor, Ṛbhu."
No one else’s mind is so refined by the impressions of non-duality as that of the Teacher; therefore, I consider you to be my preceptor.
Ṛbhu said:
"O Nidāgha, out of affection for my guru and mindful of my former service to you, I, named Ṛbhu, have come here to give you instruction."
This very thing, O Mahāmati, has been taught to you in brief:
that which is non-duality in its entirety, the essence of the ultimate truth.
The Brahmin said:
Having spoken thus, the learned Ṛbhu, his preceptor, departed from Nidāgha;
and by that instruction, Nidāgha became devoted to non-duality.
He beheld all beings as non-different from his own self;
thus, devoted to Brahman, that twice-born man attained supreme liberation.
In the same way, O knower of dharma, O lord of the earth, knowing yourself to have entered this creation, become one whose self, enemies, and kinsmen are all equal.
Just as the single sky appears divided into white, blue, and other colors to those with distorted vision, so too the Self, though being one, appears as many distinct entities.
Whatever exists here as a whole is the one Acyuta; there is nothing else beyond him.
I am he, and you are he—this entire universe is the very nature of the Self. Abandon the delusion of duality.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus addressed by him, that best of kings, having attained the vision of the supreme truth, abandoned his sense of duality;
and he too, having gained awakening through the recollection of his former births, attained liberation in that very life.
Thus, whoever narrates or listens with devotion to this essential account of the deeds of Bharata, the lord of men,
becomes pure-minded, does not fall into self-delusion, and becomes fit for liberation amidst the cycles of worldly existence.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter (16) of the Śrī Viṣṇu-madhudviṭ-dṛṣ.
Thus the second part of the Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa is completed.
Now begins the third part of the Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as the Viṣṇucittīya and the Ātmaprakāśa-Śrīdharīya.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Maitreya said:
The arrangement of the earth, oceans, and other features has been correctly described by my teachers.
And the configuration of the sun and other luminaries is [described] in great detail.
In this manner, the creation of the gods and others, as well as that of the sages, has been described;
likewise, the origin of the fourfold caste system and of those belonging to the animal realm.
The life stories of Dhruva and Prahlāda have been recounted by you in detail;
now I wish to hear, in their proper sequence, all the Manvantaras without exception.
O Teacher, I desire to hear from you about these lords of the Manvantaras, headed by Śakra and the gods, as they have been described by you.
Śrī Parāśara said: I shall relate to you correctly and in due order all those Manvantaras that have passed and those yet to come in this world.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Para-Svārociṣa,
as well as Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
These six Manus have passed away; now, however, it is the seventh interval that is current, belonging to Vaivasvata, the son of Ravi.
I have thus described to you the Svāyambhuva period at the beginning of the Kalpa,
as well as the gods and the seven ṛṣis exactly as they were.
Hereafter, I shall correctly proclaim the lords of the Manvantara of Svārociṣa Manu, as well as the divine sages and their sons.
In the Svārociṣa interval, O Maitreya, the gods were the Pārāvatas along with the Tuṣitas; there, the mighty Vipaścit was the lord of the gods.
Ūrjastambha, Prāṇa, Vāta, Artha, Pṛṣabha,
Niraya, and Parīvan were the seven sages there.
Caitra, Kiṃpuruṣa, and others were the sons of Svārociṣa.
This second interval has been explained; now hear the excellent account of the next.
In the third interval as well, O Brahmin, there was a Manu named Uttama;
Maitreya, the lord of the gods was named Suśānti; now hear of his sons.
Sudhāmānas, Satyas, Japas, Pratardanas,
and Vaśavartins— these five groups are each recorded as consisting of twelve members.
These seven sons of Vasiṣṭha became the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), namely Aja, Paraśu, Dīpta, and the others; likewise, the sons of Uttama Manu were as follows.
Within the interval of Tāmasa were the gods Supārās and Haris, as well as the Satyas and Sudhiyas; these were the twenty-seven groups.
Śibi was likewise Indra, distinguished by the performance of a hundred sacrifices;
and there were the Seven Sages—listen to their names from me.
Jyotirdhāman, Pṛthu, Kātya, Caitra, Agni, Dhanaka,
and Pīvara— these seven sages were also there during that interval.
Nara, Khyāti, Ketu, Rūpa, Jānu, Jaṅgha, and others were the sons of Tāmasa; they were born of Ājānī and possessed great strength.
Or again, O Maitreya, in the fifth [Manvantara], there was a Manu named Raivata by name;
Vibhu was the Indra there, and hear now of the gods during that interval.
The Amitābhas, Bhūtarayas, Vaikuṇṭhas, and Susamedhas—
these are the fourteen groups of gods there, fourteen for each.
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedāśrin, Urdhvabāhu, as well as Avara,
Vedabāhu, Sudhāman, and the great sage Parjanya—
these, O Brahmin, were the seven ṛṣis during that Raivata Manvantara.
O best of sages, Balabandhu was honored, as were his sons Satyaka and others,
who became kings of great heroism.
Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa, and Raivata—
these four Manus are remembered as belonging to the lineage of Priyavrata.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu through ascetic penance, that royal sage Priyavrata obtained these lords of the Manvantaras, who were born from his own lineage.
In the sixth Manvantara, there was likewise a Manu named Cākṣuṣa;
Indrānuja (Manojava) was the Indra; now learn from me also about the gods.
The Āpyas, Prasūtas, Bhavyas, Pṛthukas, Divaukasas,
Mahānubhāvas, and Lakhās— these five groups each consist of eight classes.
Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Uttama, Madhu,
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu— these were the seven ṛṣis.
Ūru, Pūru, and others headed by Śatadyumna— these sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu, possessed of great strength, became lords of the earth.
O sage, the son of Vivasvat, the highly effulgent Manu Śrāddhadeva,
the wise one, is currently presiding over the seventh interval (manvantara).
O great sage Maitreya, the gods beginning with the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras are here, as is Purandara, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni along with Gautama,
Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja— these seven became the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti,
the renowned Nariṣyanta, and Nābhāga-Ariṣṭa as well.
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and the very great Sumahān, world-renowned—
these were the nine sons of Vaivasvata Manu, all of whom were highly righteous.
The incomparable power of Viṣṇu, abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva), is established in the state of maintenance;
throughout all the Manvantaras, she presides as the deity.
In the first interval, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, this deity Yajña was born as a mental son of Ākūti from a portion of him.
Then, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, that very god was born again in Tuṣitā together with the Tuṣitas as Ājiśat.
Furthermore, when Auttami passed away, that very Deva Tuṣita became Satya in the Satya-kalpa, together with the most excellent gods who were truthful.
And at the end of the Tāmasa Manvantara, he indeed appeared once again;
in the womb of Hariṇī, together with the Haris, he became Hari himself.
In the interval of Raivata as well, the god Hari, the best of deities, was born from the mind in Saṃbhūti;
that Hari was born together with the gods known as the Raivatikas.
And in the Cākṣuṣa interval, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person,
was born of Vikuṇṭhā together with the deities known as the Vaikuṇṭhas.
When this Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived, O twice-born one,
Viṣṇu was born as Vāmana from Kaśyapa and Aditi.
By that Great-Souled One, having conquered these worlds with three strides,
the three realms were given to Purandara, cleared of all thorns.
O Brahmin, these were indeed his seven bodies during the seven Manvantaras,
by which all living beings were nourished.
Because this entire universe is entered by the power of that Great Soul, he is called Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter."
All the gods, all human beings, the seven sages, and those who are the sons of Manu,
as well as this Indra who has become the lord of the thirty-three— these are but the manifestations of Viṣṇu’s power.
Thus ends the first chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"These seven Manvantaras have indeed been described by you."
O brahmin-sage, you ought to tell me even those things that are yet to come.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Sage, Saṃjñā, the daughter of Viśvakarman, was the wife of Sūrya; Manu, Yama, and Yamī were indeed their offspring.
Unable to endure her husband's splendor, she indeed cast off her shadow; she went to the forest herself for the sake of asceticism, while her shadow remained intent on serving her husband.
Then Arka begot three sons upon Chāyā— Śanaiścara, another named Manu, and also Tapatī— and she was known by that name.
When Chāyā, filled with anger, pronounced a curse upon Yama,
both Yama and Sūrya then thought, "This consciousness of hers is different from before."
Then Vivasvat, by means of his vision gained through meditative concentration, beheld that mare staying in the forest, as described by her [the goddess], established in ascetic penance.
Then, assuming the form of a horse, that Sun-god begat Revanta from her, while the two Aśvin deities were born at the conclusion of his seed.
And the Blessed Lord Ravi restored his consciousness and returned him to his own place;
furthermore, Viśvakarman performed the pacification of his fiery energy.
Having cast the sun into delusion, he performed the blinding of its splendor;
he shattered that imperishable [orb] into its eighth part.
O best of sages, that Vaiṣṇava splendor which had been severed by Viśvakarman fell blazing upon the earth.
With that same splendor, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the discus for Viṣṇu,
the trident for Śarva, and the palanquin for Dhanada.
Viśvakarman, by means of that splendor, strengthened the spear of Guha as well as whatever weapons belonged to the other gods.
He who was called the second Manu, the son of Chāyāsaṃjñā,
is known as Sāvarṇi because he is of the same lineage (savarṇa) as his elder brother.
Now, this eighth Manvantara belongs to Sāvarṇika;
listen to that, O highly fortunate one, as I tell you what is to come.
O Maitreya, that Manu who is to be known as Sāvarṇi will then have the Sutapas,
the Amitābhas, and the Mukhyas as his principal gods.
O best of sages, it is taught that each of those hosts of gods consists of twenty members; I shall now also describe the future seven ṛṣis.
Dīptimān, Gālava, Rāma, Kṛpa, and Droṇi as the next;
my son, Vyāsa, and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga as the seventh.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, that sinless one, who dwells within the subterranean realm of Pātāla,
Bali, the son of Virocana, shall become their Indra.
Viraja, Urvarīvan, Nirmoka, and others will likewise be the sons of Sāvarṇi Manu, who will become lords of men.
O Sage, the ninth Manu will be Dakṣasāvarṇi.
The Pāras, the Marīcigarbhas, and likewise the Sudharmas— these three types of gods shall each constitute a group of twelve.
O twice-born one, among them, Indra will become a being of great heroism and wonder.
Savana, Dyutimat, Bhavya, Vasu, Medhātithi, Jyotiṣmat as the seventh, and Satya— these were the great ṛṣis there.
Dhṛtaketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya,
Pṛthuśravas, and others were likewise the sons of Dakṣa Māriṣā.
O Sage, the tenth Manu will be Brahmasāvarṇi;
likewise, there will be one hundred gods who are pure and radiant.
Indra will be their lord, the very powerful one named Śānti;
and there will be seven Ṛṣis—listen now to who they are.
Haviṣmān, Sukṛta, Satya, another named Tapomūrti, Nābhāga of incomparable vigor, and likewise Satyaketu; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.2.27.
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, Bhūriṣeṇa, and the others— these ten sons of Brahmasāvarṇi will protect the earth.
And the eleventh Manu will be Dharmasāvarṇika.
The Vihaṅgamas, the Kāmāgamas, the Nirvāṇas, and likewise the Ṛṣis—
these shall then be the principal hosts of the future gods;
each of their hosts consists of thirty-three, and their Indra shall indeed be Pṛṣā.
Niḥsvara, Agnitejas, Vapuṣmat, Ghaṇi, Āruṇi,
Haviṣmat, and Anagha shall likewise be the seven ṛṣis.
Sarvatraga, Śuddhadharma, Devānīka, and others likewise shall be the sons of that Manu, sovereigns over the entire earth.
Rudraputra Sāvarṇi will be the twelfth Manu;
Ṛkudhāman will be the Indra there—now hear from me about the gods.
O twice-born one, the Haritas, Rohitas,
Devas, Mumanasas, Sukarmans, and Surāpas— these are indeed five groups of ten each.
Tapasvī, Sutapas, Tapomūrti, Taporati,
Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and another, the seventh, Tapodhana—
these are his seven ṛṣis; now learn from me also of his sons.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and others likewise—
these shall be the great kings of great prowess born of that Manu.
O Sage, the thirteenth will be named Ruci, and Mana will be his son.
The Sutramanas, Sukarmans, Sudharmans, and likewise the Amaras—
these are the thirty-three distinct classes where the hosts of gods reside.
The lord of the gods, Indra of great prowess, shall become their leader.
Nirmoha, Tattvadarśin, Niṣprakampya, Nirutsuka, Dhṛtimat, Avyaya, and the seventh, the sage Sutapas—
these are his seven Ṛṣis; now learn from me of his sons as well.
Citrasena, Vicitra, and others will become rulers of the earth.
O Maitreya, Bhauma will be the fourteenth Manu here;
Śuci will be the Indra, and there will be five groups of gods—listen to them.
The Cākṣuṣas, the Pavitras, the Kaniṣṭhas, the Bhrājikas, and the Vācavṛddhas were the gods; now hear from me also about the seven Ṛṣis.
Agnibāhu, Śuci, Śukra, Māgadha, Agnīdhra, Yukta, and likewise Jita—these were others; now hear of the sons of Manu.
Ūrugambhīrabuddhi and others were the sons of that Manu;
they are declared, O tiger among sages, to be the kings who shall protect the earth.
At the end of the four yugas, it is said that a confusion of the Vedas occurs;
then the seven sages descend from heaven to earth and cause them to be promulgated.
O Brahmin, at the completion of each completed age, Manu is born as the ordainer of memory;
and those gods who partake of the sacrifice remain for as long as that Manvantara lasts.
The earth is protected by those who are the sons of Manu throughout the duration of his manvantara,
as well as by those born of their lineage for that same period.
In each Manvantara, these— Manu, the seven sages, the gods, and the sons of Manu, as well as Śakra as the presiding authority— come into existence.
O twice-born one, when these fourteen Manvantaras have passed,
a Kalpa, consisting of a thousand Yugas, is said to be complete without remainder.
O best of beings, the night thereafter is of that same duration;
then, assuming the form of Brahmā, he rests upon Śeṣa amidst the flood of waters.
O Brahmin, having swallowed the entire triple world, the Lord Janārdana— the primordial creator and omnipresent one— remains established in his own māyā, being the soul of all beings.
Then the Blessed One, whose nature is imperishable, having awakened, creates the world anew in each kalpa just as before, being impelled by the quality of rajas.
O best of the twice-born, the Manus, the kings, the gods including Indra, and likewise the seven sages, are the sattvic portion that maintains the stability of the world.
O Maitreya, listen to how this very Viṣṇu, whose characteristic activity is maintenance, establishes the order of the four ages.
In the Kṛta age, the Self of all beings, who delights in the welfare of all beings, assumes the form of Kapila and others and bestows supreme knowledge.
In the Tretā age as well, that Lord, assuming the form of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
protects the three worlds by subduing the wicked.
Having divided the single Veda into four parts and further into hundreds of branches, the omnipresent Lord,
assuming the form of Vedavyāsa, repeatedly makes it manifold once again.
Having divided the Vedas during the Dvāpara age, the Lord Hari, at the end of the Kali age,
assumes the form of Kalki and establishes the wicked on the right path.
In this way, the infinite Self eternally protects and creates this entire world, and at the end, destroys it; there is nothing that exists apart from Him.
O Brahmin, the true nature of the past, the present, and the future— of all beings and of the Great Soul— has been described to you here and elsewhere.
All the Manvantaras have been recounted by me to you, as well as the lords of those Manvantaras; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the second chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"I have understood from you how this entire world [came to be]."
Viṣṇu is beyond Viṣṇu and beyond Viṣṇutva; nothing exists that is superior to him.
But I wish to hear this: how the Vedas were divided by that Great-Souled One in each age, through his form as Vedavyāsa.
O great sage, tell me who was the Vyāsa in each respective age,
and O Blessed One, explain to me the divisions of the Vedic branches.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, the branches of the tree of the Vedas are divided into thousands;
one is not able to describe them in detail, so hear them from me in brief.
In every Dvāpara age, O great sage, Viṣṇu,
in the form of Vyāsa and seeking the welfare of the world, divides the single Veda into many parts.
And observing that the energy, brilliance, and strength of human beings were diminished,
he divided the Vedas for the welfare of all living creatures.
That body by which the Lord, known by the name Vedavyāsa, divides the single Veda into many parts is indeed a manifestation of the Enemy of Madhu.
Learn from me, O Sage, who those Vyāsas were during each respective Manvantara,
and how the division of the Vedic branches was carried out by each Vyāsa.
Indeed, during that Vaivasvata Manvantara, in each of the Dvāpara ages, the Veda was divided twenty-eight times by the Ṛṣis, again and again.
O best of beings, twenty-eight Vedavyāsas have passed away,
by whom the Veda was divided into four parts again and again during the successive Dvāpara ages.
In the first Dvāpara age, the Veda was divided by the Self-born One himself;
and in the second Dvāpara age as well, Prajāpati was the Vedavyāsa.
In the third [age] Uśanas was the Vyāsa; in the fourth, Bṛhaspati;
Savitṛ was the Vyāsa in the fifth; and in the sixth, the Lord Mṛtyu is remembered as the Vyāsa.
In the seventh [Manvantara], Indra was likewise [Vasu]; in the eighth, Vasiṣṭha is remembered;
in the ninth, Sārasvata; and in the tenth, Tridhāman is remembered.
In the eleventh [Manvantara] was Triśikha, and after him Bharadvāja;
in the thirteenth was Antarikṣa, and Varṇin was in the fourteenth.
Trayyāruṇa was in the fifteenth [generation], Dhanañjaya in the sixteenth,
Kratuñjaya in the seventeenth, and after that, Jaya is remembered.
From him [Vyāsa] came Bharadvāja; from Bharadvāja, Gautama;
from Gautama, Uttara Vyāsa, who is called Haryātmā.
Then, after Haryātman, the sage Vājaśravas is remembered;
from him came Somaśuṣkāyaṇa, and from him Tṛṇabindu is recorded.
From him was born Ṛkṣa, from whom came Bhārgava, who is called Vālmīki;
from him was our father Śakti, from whom Vyāsa was born, and from him, O Sage, I am descended.
Jātukarṇa was born from me, and from him came Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana;
these are the twenty-eight ancient Vedavyāsas.
The single Veda was indeed divided into four by them during the Dvāpara and subsequent ages.
In the future Dvāpara age, O sage, the son of Droṇa will become Vyāsa after this son of mine, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, has passed away.
The single-syllable Brahman, established as "Om," is indeed eternal;
because of its vastness and its capacity for expansion, it is designated as "Brahman."

Salutation to that Brahman, who is eternally established in the Praṇava and from whom the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, as well as the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan Vedas, are proclaimed. ViP 3.3.23.
Salutation to that Subrahman, who is designated as the cause of the dissolution and origination of the universe, and who is the supreme secret beyond the Great Principle (mahat).
The world is unfathomable, boundless, and inexhaustible, a repository for the delusion of living beings;
its purpose is the fulfillment of the aims of man through both self-luminosity and active manifestation.

The ultimate goal and destination for those who possess knowledge of the enumerations and whose nature is tranquility and self-restraint is that which is unmanifest, immortal, active, and the eternal Brahman.
It is called Pradhāna, Ātmayoni, and that which resides in the cave (guhāsaṃstha);
likewise, it is indivisible, pure, imperishable, and manifold in nature.
Salutations again and again forever to that Supreme Brahman,
whose form is that of Vāsudeva, the embodiment of the Supreme Self.
This Brahman is threefold in its division, yet it is also non-dual;
that Lord is non-different amidst all differences, though he is perceived as divided by those with dualistic intellects.
He consists of the Ṛgveda, he consists of the Sāmaveda, he is the self of all; he consists of the Yajurveda.
He whose essence is the quintessence of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman—he alone is the Self of all embodied beings.
He, who consists of the Veda, divides his own Veda into many branches along with their sub-branches;
he is the Lord, free from attachment, whose very nature is the knowledge of all the branches, and who is the author of those branches.
Thus ends the third chapter in the third part of the Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
In the Kṛta age, the Veda was originally composed with four quarters and measured at one thousand [verses].
Then this entire sacrifice, consisting of ten parts, became the granter of all desires.
Then, during the twenty-eighth interval, my son Vyāsa,
the Lord, divided the single Veda consisting of four quarters into four parts.
And just as the Vedas were divided by that wise Vyāsa,
so too have they been divided by me— both collectively and individually— by all of them.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, understand that by this very means the various branches of the Vedas were recited throughout all the four ages.
Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
for who else on earth, O Maitreya, could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
Listen now, O Maitreya, exactly as it happened, how the Vedas were divided by my high-souled son during that Dvāpara age.
Urged by Brahmā, Vyāsa set about dividing the Vedas;
then he took four disciples who had mastered the Vedas.
That great sage took Paila as the reciter of the Ṛgveda,
and he accepted the one named Vaiśampāyana for the Yajurveda.
Jaimini was the knower of the Sāmaveda, and likewise Sumantu was the knower of the Atharvaveda;
he was the disciple of that wise Vedavyāsa.
The great sage took as his disciple, for the purpose of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the highly intelligent Sūta named Romaharṣaṇa.
The Yajurveda was originally one; he divided it into four parts.
From that arose the Cāturhotra ritual, and by means of it, he then performed the sacrifice.
The sage performed the duties of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, those of the Hotṛ with the Ṛks, those of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmans, and likewise the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans.
Then, having extracted the Ṛcas, the sage composed the Ṛgveda;
from the Yajus formulas he made the Yajurveda, and from the Sāmans, the Sāmaveda.
Furthermore, O Maitreya, the Lord caused all the rites for kings to be performed according to the Atharvaveda, and he likewise established the office of the Brahman priest according to tradition.
This single Veda-tree was divided by him into four parts; from that, the forest of Vedic trees was born.
O Brahmin, Paila first divided the tree of the Ṛgveda and gave the two Saṃhitās to Indrapramiti and Bāṣkala.
Then that great sage divided the Saṃhitā into four parts and gave them to Bāṣkala and others among his disciples.
O Sage, Bodhya and Āḍhakī were the sons of that [Yājñavalkya], and from them Yājñavalkya and Parāśara were born;
they, in turn, received those various sub-branches of that branch.
Then Indrapramiti taught one Saṃhitā to his own son,
the high-souled Māṇḍukeya, at that time, O Maitreya.
From him, it passed down through his disciples and grand-disciples, in the lineage of sons and pupils.
Vedamitra Śākalya, however, studied that Saṃhitā;
he composed five Saṃhitās and imparted them to his disciples.
Now hear from me the names of his five disciples:
Mudgala, Gomakha, Vātsya, Śālīya,
and the fifth was Śarīra, O Maitreya, who was possessed of great intelligence.
Śākapūrṇa and another likewise composed a triad of Saṃhitās;
O best of sages, he then made the Nirukta as the fourth.
Kraiñca was the bard (*vaitālika*), and likewise the great sage Balāka;
the fourth was Nirukta, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, from these primary branches there arose further sub-branches;
moreover, O twice-born one, Bāṣkala composed three other Saṃhitās,
which were transmitted by his disciples Kālāyani, Gārgya, and the third, Kathājapa.
These are declared to be the Bahvṛcas, by whom these Saṃhitās were promulgated.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: The great sage [Yājñavalkya] established twenty-seven branches of the Yajurveda.
The disciple of Vyāsa named Vaiśampāyana indeed composed it.
He gave them to his disciples, and they too received them in due order.
But there, O twice-born one, was Yājñavalkya, the son of Bāhyarāti;
he was a disciple who knew the supreme dharma and was always devoted to the service of his guru.
"If the sage does not come to the assembly on Mount Mahāmeru today,
he shall indeed incur the guilt of killing a Brahmin after seven nights."
O twice-born one, this was the agreement previously made by the hosts of sages;
at that time, however, Vaiśampāyana alone transgressed it.
Then he struck his sister's young son with his foot as he touched him.
He said to his disciples: "O disciples, all of you perform on my behalf this vow which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin; this must not be questioned."
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O Blessed One, what need have I for these twice-born ones, who are afflicted and of little luster? I shall observe this vow myself."
Then the enraged Guru said to the great sage Yājñavalkya:
"O Brahmin-insulter, let that which was studied by you from me be relinquished!"
"O bull among Brahmins, these others speak without luster;
therefore, I have no need for that disciple who violates my command."
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O twice-born one, this has been told to you by me out of devotion; enough of your learning from me—this which I have [taught] is it."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the sage vomited up those *yajus* mantras, which were identical in form to his own body and smeared with blood; he gave them to him and departed according to his own will.
Then, O twice-born one, the Yajus formulas released by Yājñavalkya were seized by [certain sages] who had become partridges; therefore, they are known as the Taittirīyas.

O best of sages, urged by their preceptor, they performed the vow for the expiation of the murder of a Brahmin; and because of that conduct, they became officiating priests (adhvaryus) of the Cākru lineage.
O Maitreya, Yājñavalkya as well, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
then praised the Sun with a composed mind, desiring to obtain the Yajus formulas.
Yājñavalkya said:
Salutations to Savitṛ, the gateway to liberation, who possesses immeasurable splendor;
salutations to you, who are the embodiment of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the abode of the triple Veda.
Salutation to the one who has become Agni and Soma, the causal self of the universe,
the Sun, who bears the supreme splendor and the radiance of the Suṣumṇa ray.
To Him whose nature is the self-knowledge of time— consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *nimeṣas*, and so forth—
to the one who is to be meditated upon, who is the form of Viṣṇu, and who is the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*).
Salutation to Him whose nature is satisfaction, who nourishes the hosts of gods by means of the moon with His own rays, and who satisfies the ancestors with the nectar of Svadhā.
Salutations to that Creator Sūrya, the Lord who is the maker and sustainer of snow, water, heat, and rain, and who possesses the form of the three times.
He who destroys the darkness of this world,
the Lord of the World— the God who bears his light— to that Vivasvat, homage be paid!
Salutations to that radiant God, without whose rising no person is fit for sacred rites and water itself is not a cause of purification.
When the world is touched by his rays, it indeed becomes fit for ritual action;
salutation to that Pure-Souled One, whose very nature is the cause of purification.
Salutations to Savitṛ, to Sūrya, to Bhāskara, to Vivasvat;
salutations again and again to Āditya, the primordial being of the gods and others.
I bow down to him whose golden chariot is drawn by horses that are immortal,
and who is the eye for beholding the worlds.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Being thus praised by him with these and other words, the Sun, assuming the form of a horse, said: "Let that which is desired be chosen."
Then Yājñavalkya, having prostrated before the Sun, said:
"Grant me those Yajus formulas which were not present with my teacher."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus addressed, the blessed Sun-god gave him the Yajus formulas known as *ayātayāma*,
which even his own preceptor did not know.
O best of the twice-born, those brahmins by whom the Yajus formulas have been studied are called Vājins, because even the Sun became a horse (aśva).
The branches of those Vājins are indeed fifteen;
the highly fortunate ones, beginning with Kāṇva and Yājñavalkya, are thus proclaimed.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Jaimini was a disciple of Vyāsa and [received] the branches of the Sāmaveda tree.
O Maitreya, listen to me as I describe that sequence by which [the dissolution occurs].
Susantushta had a son named Sūtvāna, and Sūtvāna’s son was Māhamati;
these two were both highly intelligent and each studied one Vedic Saṃhitā.
From him came Sukarman, his son, who made a division of the Saṃhitā into one thousand parts;
and two disciples of his, observers of great vows, received that [Saṃhitā].
O best of the twice-born, Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya and Pauṣpiñji were his disciples; five hundred Sāmavedic singers from the north are recorded as his pupils.
Those best of the twice-born by whom as many Saṃhitās were received from Hiraṇyanābha are also called by the learned "Eastern Sāma-singers" (Prācyasāmagāḥ).
Lokākṣi, Naidhami, Kakṣivān, Lāṅgali, and Pauṣpiji were his disciples; through their various divisions, the Saṃhitās were multiplied.
The great sage named Kṛta, a disciple of Hiraṇyanābha, taught twenty-four Saṃhitās to his own disciples.
And by them, that Sāmaveda was expanded into many branches.
Now I shall describe the collection of the Saṃhitās of the Atharvaṇas;
that sage Susaṃtu, of immeasurable luster, [compiled] the Atharvaveda.
He taught it to his disciple Kabandha; he, in turn, having divided it into two parts, gave them to Devadarśa and Pathya.
The disciples of Devadarśa were Medha, Brahmabali,
Śaulkāyani, Pippalāda, and another, O best of the twice-born.
O twice-born one, Pathya also had three disciples by whom the Saṃhitās were composed:
Jābāli, Kumuda and others, and the third was Śaunaka, O twice-born one.
Śaunaka, however, having divided [the text] into two parts, gave one to Babhru and bestowed the second Saṃhitā upon Saindhava, who was named Yaśasvin.
Mujikeśa [received] the Saindhava [branch], which was divided twofold and then again into three;
likewise, [he received] the Nakṣatrakalpa of the Vedas and their Saṃhitās.
The fourth would be the Āṅgirasa, and the fifth is the Śāntikalpa;
these, belonging to the Atharvans, are the most excellent variant recensions of the Saṃhitās.
Expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed a compendium of the Purāṇa through primary narratives, secondary episodes, verses, and accounts of the purification of the Kalpas.
The renowned Sūta Romaharṣaṇa became a disciple of Vyāsa;
to him, the high-minded Vyāsa gave the Purāṇasaṃhitā in former times.
Sumati, Agnivarcas, Mitrāyu, Śāṃsapāyana,
Akṛtavraṇa, and Sāvarṇi were his six disciples.
Kāśyapa, the compiler of the Saṃhitā, Sāvarṇi, and Śāṃsapāyana—
these, along with Romaharṣaṇi, are the three root-saṃhitās.
O Sage, this [account] of the Saṃhitās is divided into four parts.
The Brāhma Purāṇa is said to be the first among all Purāṇas;
those who know the Purāṇas declare that there are eighteen Purāṇas.
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śaiva, as well as the Bhāgavata,
and likewise another, the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh.
The eighth is indeed the Āgneya, and the ninth is remembered as the Bhaviṣya;
the tenth is the Brahmavaivarta, and the eleventh is remembered as the Laiṅga.
The twelfth is indeed the Vārāha, and the thirteenth here is the Skānda;
the fourteenth is the Vāmana, and likewise the fifteenth is the Kaurma;
then follow the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that the Brahmāṇḍa.
O great sage, these indeed are the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas.

Likewise, the ancient Purāṇas have been narrated by the sages; in all of them, the primary creation (sarga), the secondary creation (pratisarga), the genealogies (vaṃśa), the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita) are recounted.
O Maitreya, this ancient account which is being told by me to you is indeed known as the Vaiṣṇava, following immediately after the Pādma Purāṇa.

O best of men, in accounts of creation, secondary creation, genealogies, and the periods of the Manvantaras, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is described as if he were present in all of them without exception.
The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya,
the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—these three, along with Arthaśāstra as the fourth; these indeed are the eighteen branches of knowledge.
First, the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣis) are to be known; after them, the divine sages (devarṣis);
and after them, the royal sages (rājarṣis)—these are the three types of sages.
Thus have the branches been fully described, as well as their various divisions;
the authors of these branches and the cause of their differentiation have likewise been declared.
In this manner, it is traditionally held that the divisions of the branches are equal throughout all the Manvantaras.
O twice-born one, the Śruti concerning Prajāpati is eternal, whereas these alternatives are its variations.
All this that I was asked by you here has been told to you, O Maitreya, regarding the connection with the Vedas; what else shall I tell you?
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Guru, everything that you were asked by me has been related by you exactly as it is."
I desire to hear one thing; may your honor explain that to me.
O great sage, the seven continents, the subterranean realms,
and the worlds situated within this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) on all sides— these are the sevenfold divisions.
It is said that everything is pervaded by living beings—by those that are gross, as well as subtle, more subtle, and most subtle; indeed, by those that are even grosser than the gross.
O best of sages, there is not even an eighth part of a finger's breadth where living beings, bound by the fetters of karma, do not dwell.
"O Blessed One, it is said that all these come under the power of Yama;
at the end of their lifespan, they likewise go to the torments impelled by him."
"Having fallen from the states of torment, living beings revolve through births such as those of gods; this is the conclusion of the scriptures."
I desire to hear that by which men do not fall under the power of Yama; tell me that deed.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Sage, this very same question was asked by the high-souled Nakula; hear from me what the grandfather Bhīṣma replied.
Bhīṣma said: "O child, long ago a friend of mine, a twice-born man from Kaliṅga, came to me;
that sage, who remembered his former births, was questioned by me and spoke thus."
"Therefore, all this has been declared by him, and it shall happen exactly thus;
and so it came to pass, my dear child, just as it was spoken by that wise one."
And when that twice-born one was questioned by me again with faith,
whatever he said was never seen by me otherwise at any time.
Once, however, when I asked this very thing that you have mentioned,
the Brahmin from Kaliṅga spoke, recollecting the words of that sage.
I shall relate to you that supreme secret which was told to me by one who remembers his past lives— the conversation that took place between Yama and his servant.
Kaliṅga said:
Having observed his own servant with noose in hand, Yama indeed whispers into his ear:
"Avoid those who have sought refuge in Madhusūdana; I am the lord over other men who are not Vaiṣṇavas."
"I have been appointed as Yama by the Creator, who is honored by the foremost of the immortals, to oversee what is beneficial and harmful for the world;
yet I am subject to the will of Hari and my Guru, and I am not independent—for even Viṣṇu has power over my restraint."
Just as gold is considered one and undivided, despite the distinctions of bracelets, crowns, earrings, and so forth,
so too is Hari declared to be one, through all the conceptualizations of gods, animals, humans, and the like.
Just as the atoms of the earth's surface return once more to unity with the earth at the end of the wind,
so too do gods, animals, humans, and others [return] at the end to that eternal one, who is the essence of all qualities.
O Vraja, avoid and shun that mortal who bows down in truth to Hari, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the best of the immortals,
for he is freed from the bonds of all sins, like a fire drenched with clarified butter.
Having heard these words of Yama, the noose-bearing messenger of Yama spoke to that Lord of Dharma:
"Tell me, O All-pervading Lord, what kind of devotee indeed is this [servant] of Hari, who is the constituent of all beings?"
Yama said:

Know him to be a devotee of Viṣṇu who does not deviate from his own duty and nature, who is even-minded toward himself, friends, and enemies, who neither takes nor kills anything, and whose mind remains steadfastly elevated.
Know that man to be an exceedingly devoted worshipper of Hari, who, having taken Janārdana to heart, has not allowed his soul to be defiled by the impurities of the Kali age, O you of pure intellect.

Know that best of men to be a devotee of Viṣṇu who, having perceived even gold through his intellect as a secret, regards the property of another as a mere blade of grass, and whose mind is focused on no other than the Blessed Lord.

Where is Viṣṇu, who is as pure as a slab of crystal mountain, and where is the defect of envy and the like in the minds of men? Indeed, the scorching heat born of fire does not exist within a mass of rays from the moon made of frost.

One who is pure-minded, free from envy, tranquil, of holy conduct, a friend to all beings, whose speech is pleasant and beneficial, and from whom pride and deceit have vanished— in his heart Vāsudeva always dwells.

When that eternal one dwells within his heart, a man becomes gentle in appearance toward this world; even a young *sāla* tree proclaims the exquisite beauty of its own interior through its very loveliness, like the earth itself.

O soldier, keep at a great distance those men whose impurities have been shaken off by the observance of restraints and disciplines, whose minds are daily attached to Acyuta, and who are free from pride, arrogance, and envy.

If the Lord Hari, the beginningless Self, who bears the discus, conch, and mace, resides within the heart, then how can sin—which is destroyed by Him—remain? For when the sun is present, how can there be darkness?
In the heart of that man of impure mind and wicked intellect— who steals the wealth of others, kills living beings, and speaks lies and harsh words— there is no place for the Infinite One (Ananta).
The wicked one of defiled mind cannot endure the prosperity of others and utters insults;
he who neither practices discipline nor gives charity, and who does not honor the virtuous—Janārdana is not present in the mind of such a base person.

Know that man of base conduct to be unworthy of devotion who, being of deceitful mind, pursues the thirst for wealth even toward his dearest friends, kinsmen, wife, children, parents, and circle of servants.
One whose mind is impure, who is attached to improper conduct, who is constantly devoted to the company of ignoble and ill-behaved persons,
and who is bound by the sins committed day after day— such a harsh beast is certainly not a devotee of Vāsudeva.
"Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Lord, is that one alone; all this and I am He"—this unshakable conviction arose in Ananta as he departed, having left them far behind.
O lotus-eyed Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, upholder of the earth, Acyuta, wielder of the conch and discus—
those who truly come for refuge to you, O hero, abandon those sinless ones from afar.

He in whose mind dwells that immutable Self, the Best of Men—within his range of vision, neither you nor I have any power to move; for he, whose strength and valor are unassailable by the Wheel, is beyond the reach of other worlds.
Kāliṅga said:
"Thus the Lord Yama, the King of Dharma, spoke indeed for the purpose of commanding his own soldiers;
this was related to me by him, O best of the Kurus, and it has been correctly recounted by me to you as well."
Śrī Bhīṣma said: "O Nakula, this was previously told to me by that high-souled twice-born man, who, being pleased, came from the land of Kaliṅga."
"O child, I have also correctly explained this to you according to the proper method:
that there is no other refuge in the ocean of saṃsāra except for Viṣṇu."
Neither the servants, nor the nooses and staffs, nor Yama himself,
nor the torments are capable of overcoming him whose soul always takes refuge in Keśava.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Sage, this song which was sung by Vaivasvata has been fully related to you in accordance with your question; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, the Lord God is [worshipped] by those who seek to conquer the cycle of worldly existence."
O Lord of the World, explain how Viṣṇu is to be propitiated.
O great sage, I desire to hear about that fruit which is obtained by men devoted to his worship from Govinda once he has been propitiated.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Listen as I relate to you exactly what Aurva spoke when questioned in this same manner by the high-souled Sagara.
Having prostrated before him, Sagara questioned Aurva of the Bhṛgu lineage,
O best of sages, regarding the means for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
And hear from me in its entirety that fruit which arises for men when Viṣṇu is propitiated, and what he said when questioned with diligence; listen to all of that.
Aurva said: When Viṣṇu is propitiated, one attains the earthly desire, heaven, that delightful station in heaven, and even the highest liberation.
O Indra among kings, whatever fruit one desires and however great it may be, that very thing one obtains when Acyuta is propitiated, whether it be abundant or even small.
O protector of the earth, as for what you ask—how Hari is propitiated—I shall tell you all of that; listen to me.
By a person who observes the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction.
O King, he who performs sacrifices sacrifices Hari; he who mutters prayers mutters for him;
and even while striking down others, he strikes Hari, because Hari is present in every being.
Therefore, a person who possesses good conduct should propitiate Janārdana by performing the duties prescribed for his own social class.
O Lord of the Earth, whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one who is devoted to his own duty worships Viṣṇu; it is not otherwise.
He does not speak slander, calumny, or falsehood, nor anything that causes distress to others; by this, Keśava is pleased.
O King, that man who takes no delight in another's wife, another's wealth, or the harming of others— by him Keśava is pleased.
O Indra among men, that man who does not strike, does not kill, and is not harmful toward living beings— by him Keśava is pleased.
O lord of men, by that person who is ever intent upon serving the gods, the twice-born, and the gurus,
Govinda is propitiated.
Just as one desires the welfare of oneself, of one's son, and likewise of all beings, by that [attitude] Hari is always happily propitiated.
O King, he whose mind is not corrupted by defects such as passion and the like,
satisfies Viṣṇu at all times with his pure heart.
O best of sages, O king, by abiding in those duties prescribed for the castes and stages of life in the scriptures, a man attains Viṣṇu with an uncorrupted mind.
Sagara said:
"O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear those duties of the social classes in their entirety, as well as the duties of the stages of life; please explain them to me."
Aurva said:
"Listen with one-pointed mind, according to the order of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras, to the duties proclaimed by me."
A Brahmin should give gifts, sacrifice to the gods, be devoted to the study of his own Veda, remain constantly engaged in ritual bathing, and maintain the sacred fires.
For the sake of his livelihood, a twice-born man may officiate at sacrifices for others, likewise teach others,
and accept gifts from righteous persons in accordance with the law.
A twice-born man should act for the welfare of all beings and never for the harm of anyone;
friendliness toward all beings is the supreme wealth of a Brahmin.
O King, a twice-born man should maintain an equal mind toward both pressing-stones and the jewels of others;
he is praised for approaching his wife during her season.
A Kṣatriya or even a king may give gifts to the twice-born as he desires,
perform various sacrifices, and study the Vedas.
Living by the sword for the protection of the earth is his foremost means of livelihood;
even therein, the primary rule is the preservation of the earth.
By the mere protection of the earth, kings become ones who have fulfilled their duty,
since they are the portions of the sacrificer for rites such as sacrifices.
By punishing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, the king who maintains the social order of the castes attains the worlds he desires.
O lord of men, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bestowed upon the Vaiśya the means of livelihood consisting of cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture.
For him as well, study, sacrifice, giving, and dharma are praised,
as is the performance of obligatory and occasional rites and other actions.
The duty of one who has taken refuge with the twice-born consists of supporting him for that purpose,
whether by means of wealth acquired through buying and selling or through the labor of artisans.
For the Śūdra, [the duties are] humility, purity, service to the master without guile,
sacrifice without mantras, refraining from theft, association with them (the higher castes), and the protection of Brahmins.
Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices; indeed, by means of these, the Śūdra should perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors and so forth.
O Lord of the Earth, the acquisition of all things for the sake of maintaining servants and others, and approaching one's own wife during her fertile season; these are [the duties].
Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, absence of excessive pride, truthfulness, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, and pleasant speech; ViP_3,8.36 //
O Lord of Men, benevolence, lack of longing, as well as freedom from miserliness and absence of envy— these are said to be the common virtues of all the social classes.
These are the common characteristics of all the stages of life (āśramas). Now hear from me these qualities and duties of the Brahmins and the other [castes].
The duty of a Kṣatriya has been declared for a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise the duty of a Vaiśya;
the duty of a Vaiśya has been declared for a Rājanya, but the duty of a Śūdra is not prescribed for these two.
O King, when one has the capacity, both [father and son] should renounce that [duty];
however, in times of distress, that very same duty should be performed, but one must not cause a confusion of duties.
Thus, O King, these duties of the social classes have been described by me to you;
now listen as I correctly explain the duties of those belonging to the stages of life.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Aurva said:
"When he was a boy who had received the initiatory rite (upanayana), he became intent upon acquiring the Vedas."
O King, he should dwell in the house of his guru as a celibate student, composed in mind.
In that state, one must observe purity, proper conduct, and vows, as well as service to the guru;
and while practicing these vows, the Veda should be acquired by one whose intellect has been refined.
O King, being composed, he should worship both twilights facing the sun and likewise the fire; at that time, he should also perform the salutation to his guru.

O best of kings, when the teacher stands, the disciple should stand; when he walks, he should walk behind him; and when he sits, the disciple should sit lower; he should never act in opposition to his guru.
He was told by him: "Standing before [the teacher], one should recite the Veda with an undistracted mind;
then, having been permitted by the guru, one may eat food obtained as alms."
Having first been led into the water by his teacher, he should bathe; and every morning, the teacher should bring him fuel, water, and other such necessities.
Having mastered what is to be grasped and having received permission from his teacher,
the wise man, once he has fulfilled his obligations to the guru, should enter the state of a householder.
O King, having obtained a wife according to the prescribed rite and having acquired wealth through his own efforts, he should perform all the duties of a householder to the best of his ability.
He worshipped the ancestors with funeral offerings (nivāpa), the gods with sacrifices, as well as guests;
he honored the sages with food and Prajāpati with Vedic study and offspring.
Through offerings to the spirits and through affection for the entire world,
a person attains the worlds acquired by their own past actions.
And whatever wandering mendicants or celibate students there may be who subsist on alms, they too find their foundation in this very state; therefore, the householder’s life is indeed supreme.
O Lord, for the purpose of recovering the Vedas, for bathing at sacred fords,
and for seeing the earth, the Brahmins wander across the world.
For those who are homeless, who have no food, and who take shelter wherever evening falls—
the householder is the support and indeed the source for them all.
O King, one should speak sweet words of welcome and so forth to them;
and to those who have come to the house, one should provide a bed, a seat, and food.
When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that person and taking away their merit.
Contempt, egoism, and hypocrisy belong to one who dwells in a house;
likewise, causing distress, injury, and harshness are not praised.
But the householder who correctly performs this supreme rite is liberated from all bonds and attains the unsurpassed worlds.
O King, when a householder has reached the decline of age and accomplished his duties,
he should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, wearing his hair and beard in matted locks,
and sleeping upon the ground, the sage there, O King, should be a host to all.
O Lord of Men, he should make his lower garment and upper robe from leather, kāśa, or kuśa grass; likewise, bathing three times a day is prescribed for him.
O Lord of Men, the worship of the deities, the performance of fire-offerings (homa), the honoring of all guests, and the giving of alms and offerings to spirits are prescribed for him.
Anointing his limbs with forest oils is recommended for him, O Indra among kings; and his austerity consists in his endurance of cold, heat, and other such extremes.
But the sage who, as a forest-dweller, should practice this disciplined conduct,
burns away his defects like fire and conquers the eternal worlds.
O King, you ought to hear from me as I describe the true nature of that fourth stage of life for a mendicant, which is proclaimed by the wise.
O lord of men, having abandoned attachment to sons, wealth, and wife,
and having shaken off all envy, one should proceed to the state of the fourth stage of life.
O Lord of the Earth, one should abandon all undertakings pertaining to the three aims of life;
one should be friendly toward friends and others, and maintain equanimity toward all living beings.
One who is disciplined should not practice malice toward those born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth, through actions of speech, mind, or body; one should avoid all attachments.
One should stay for one night in a village and five nights in a town;
one should dwell in such a way that neither attachment nor aversion arises within him.

And for the sake of sustaining life, he should wander from house to house at the proper time for alms among those of commendable appearance, when the embers have been extinguished and the people have finished their meals.
Having completely abandoned desire, anger, as well as pride, delusion, greed, and all others like them, the wandering mendicant should become free from the sense of "mine."
For the sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings,
there is likewise no fear from any beings anywhere.
Having established the Agnihotra within his own body, the Brahmin offers the fire of the body into his own mouth with oblations consisting of alms;
thus he ascends to the worlds of those whose fires are kindled in the funeral pyre.

The twice-born who practices the stage of liberation as prescribed, being pure, happy, and endowed with a disciplined intellect, becomes tranquil like a flame without fuel and attains the world of Brahman.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Sagara said:
"The four stages of life and the duties of the four castes have been described."
O best of the twice-born, I desire to hear about the ritual activity of the Puruṣa.
O best of the Bhṛgus, please explain in their entirety the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites for men; for in my opinion, you are omniscient.
Aurva said:
"That which has been mentioned by you regarding the basis of the obligatory and occasional rites, I shall explain; listen to me with a one-pointed mind."
Upon the birth of a son, the father should perform the entire cycle of rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), as well as the *śrāddha* characterized by prosperity (*ābhyudayika*).
O Lord of Men, one should feed an even number of Brahmins facing the east;
one should ensure that the twice-born are satisfied in the rites for the gods and the ancestors.
O King, filled with joy, one should offer cakes mixed with curd and jujube fruits to the Nāndīmukha ancestors through the Daiva tīrtha.
Or, O King, one should perform every rite of service in a clockwise direction according to the Prajāpatya method; likewise, one should do so during all times of prosperity.
Then, on the tenth day, the father himself should indeed give him a name;
for it should be preceded by the word for "god" (deva), followed by a human designation, and joined with suffixes such as *śarman* or *varman*.
The suffix *śarman* is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while *varman* pertains to the Kṣatriya;
for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, a name consisting of *gupta* or *dāsa* is recommended.

One should give a name that is not devoid of meaning, nor inauspicious, nor containing incorrect words; it should not be inauspicious or loathsome, and it should consist of an even number of syllables.
One should choose a name that is neither too long nor too short, not composed of excessively heavy syllables, easy to pronounce, and containing the syllable *praṇava* (Om).
Then, having been refined by the immediate preparatory rites, he should undertake the acquisition of the Vidyā in the teacher’s house, relying upon the procedure as it has been described.
O King, having acquired knowledge and given the teacher’s fee to the guru,
one who desires the householder stage of life should take a wife.
Or he may pass his time in celibacy according to his resolve;
or he may perform service to his guru, or even to the guru’s son or other [disciples].
Or he may become a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), or a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) according to his will;
O lord of men, let him act in whatever manner was previously resolved.
A man of three times the [age] should marry a wife who is one-tenth his age;
she should not have too much hair nor be hairless, nor be too dark, nor tawny.
One should not marry a woman who is naturally deficient in limbs or even one with redundant limbs;
nor one who is impure, excessively hairy, of low birth, or afflicted by disease.

One should not marry a woman who is wicked, or one who speaks wickedly, or one who is physically deformed on account of her father or mother; nor one who has facial hair or other masculine characteristics, nor one who has the appearance of a man.

A wise man should not marry one with the voice of a house-lizard, nor one who is emaciated, nor one with a voice like a crow's; likewise, he should not marry one whose gaze is fixed or whose eyes are round.
One should not marry a woman whose shanks are hairy, whose ankles are prominent, or whose elbows protrude when she laughs.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose skin is excessively rough, whose toenails and fingernails are reddish-brown, or whose hands and feet are swollen.
A man should not marry one who is short, nor one who is excessively tall, nor one whose eyebrows meet; nor one with teeth that are too widely spaced, nor one with a hideous face.
O King, a householder should marry a maiden according to the proper rule and ritual, one who is within five generations on the mother's side and seven generations on the father's side.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura;
the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa are two others, and the Paiśāca is considered the eighth.
Among these, whichever dharma has been prescribed for each [class] by the great seers, one should take a wife according to that; one should avoid any other.
Having obtained a wife who practices the same dharma, he should maintain the life of a householder together with her;
he who bestows this properly hidden [duty] attains great fruit.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Sagara said:
