"O Sage, I desire to hear about the right conduct of a householder."
By abiding by which one does not fall away from this world or the next.
Aurva said:
"Listen, O protector of the earth, to the characteristics of right conduct (sadācāra);
by a man who possesses right conduct, both worlds are conquered."
The virtuous are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word "sat" denotes the virtuous. The conduct of those [virtuous ones] is what is called "sadācāra" (the conduct of the good).
Furthermore, O Lord of the Earth, the seven ṛṣis, the Manus,
and the lords of creatures are both the exponents and the practitioners of right conduct.
O King, having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, the wise man,
once awakened, should reflect in his mind upon dharma and upon wealth that is not in conflict with it.

One who views the three aims of life with equanimity should, without causing distress to either of them, consider the fulfillment of the desires of both, lest there be the destruction of their visible and invisible welfare.
O King, one should abandon wealth and pleasure if they cause harm to dharma;
and one should likewise abandon even dharma if it results in future suffering or is loathed by the world.
Then, having risen at dawn, O Lord of Men, one should void urine.
To the southwest,
having passed beyond the distance of an arrow-shot from the ground and further away from his dwelling, he should void urine and excrement.
One should not throw the water used for washing the feet or other remnants into the courtyard of the house.

A wise man should never urinate upon his own shadow, the shadow of a tree, nor upon cows, the sun, fire, or wind; likewise, he should never urinate upon his teacher, the twice-born, or others of that sort.
Not on ploughed land, nor in the midst of crops, nor in a cow-pen, nor in a gathering of people;
not on a path, nor at river-crossings and other such holy sites, O bull among men.
One should not perform the evacuation of feces or the discharge of urine in water, nor on the bank of a body of water, nor in a cremation ground. (ViP 3.11.13)
O King, a wise man should void urine facing north during the day, and facing the opposite direction at night; he should likewise discharge feces, except in times of distress.
Having strewn the earth with grass and covered his head with a cloth,
he should stand there for no very long time and should not utter anything at all.
One should not take earth from an anthill, from a mousehole, nor from within water, nor that which remains after cleansing, nor from one's own house, nor that which has been used for smearing.
O King, one should discard all these types of earth for the purpose of purification: that which contains living organisms, that which has been turned up by a plow, and that which is loose soil.
O King, there should be one application of earth on the penis, three on the anus, ten on the left hand, and seven on both hands; these are the applications of earth that effect purification.
With fragrant unguents and water free of bubbles,
he should sip water (ācamana) and then, being composed, apply clay once again.
Having completed the washing of his feet, he should sprinkle water over those feet again;
with that same water, he should drink three times and likewise rinse his mouth twice.
Then one should touch the apertures of the head, the crown of the head,
the arms, the navel, and the heart with water.
Having sipped water for purification, the man should then attend to his hair,
look into a mirror, apply collyrium, perform auspicious rites, and touch items such as *dūrvā* grass.
Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, being endowed with faith, he should acquire wealth for the sake of his livelihood according to the duties of his own caste, and he should perform sacrifices.
The Soma-sacrifices, the Havis-sacrifices, and the Pāka-sacrifices are established;
therefore, since men depend upon wealth, one should strive for the acquisition of wealth.
One should bathe for the sake of daily rites in rivers, streams, and lakes, in waters dug out by the gods, and in mountain springs.
One should perform one's bath with water drawn from wells, or on the ground;
or indeed with water drawn from houses, or on the ground if [water] is unavailable.

Having bathed and wearing clean garments, one should, with a well-concentrated mind, perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors using the specific *tīrtha* (parts of the hand) belonging to each of them.
One should offer water three times for the gratification of the gods,
and according to the rule, once each for the sages and for Prajāpati.
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of pleasing the ancestors,
one should likewise gratify the paternal grandfathers and the great-grandfathers with that water.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer [the water] to the maternal grandfather, his father, and his father, using the *paitṛka* tīrtha; now hear from me regarding other optional rites as well.
O King, one should likewise offer [respect] to one's mother, to one's own mother, to the mother of that person, to the wife of the guru,
to the gurus, to maternal uncles, to dear friends, and to the ruler of the earth.
And having performed the libation for the gods and others, O King, one should recite this [mantra] and offer water according to one's own desire for the benefit of all beings.
The gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas;
the piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, beasts, and birds.
Aquatic creatures, land-dwellers, those dwelling in the earth, and those born from moisture who subsist on air—
all of them quickly attain satisfaction through this water given by me.
"Established in all the hells and amidst their various torments,
this water is offered by me for their refreshment."
May those who were relatives, those who were not relatives, and those who were relatives in another birth— all of them,
as well as whoever desires [offerings] from us, attain complete satisfaction.
"May this water with sesame seeds, offered by me, serve as nourishment for those situated wherever they may be, whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst."
O King, I have thus described to you this ritual offering of water for the fulfillment of desires;
by giving this, a person gratifies the entire world and,
O sinless one, attains the merit arising from the nourishment of the universe.
Having duly offered the water for the desired purpose to these with devotion,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then offer a handful of water to the Sun.
Homage to Vivasvat, who shines with the splendor of Brahman, who possesses the luster of Viṣṇu,
the pure creator of the world, the progenitor, and the witness of all actions.
Then one should perform the worship of the house and the adoration of one's chosen deity,
with water ablutions, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
O King, he should first perform the *apūrva* Agnihotra sacrifice for the sake of the Brahmin.
One should reverently offer an oblation intended for Prajāpati; then, O descendant of Kaśya, one should offer to the domestic deities, and thereafter to Anumati in due order.
Then he should pour the remainder of that water into the water-jar for the sake of the Earth, Pṛthvī, and Janī;
at the door, he should offer it to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and in the middle, to Brahmā.
O tiger among men, hear from me also concerning the deities of the directions of the house.
A wise man should offer the bali consisting of the remnants of the oblation to Indra, Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, and likewise to Indu, in the eastern and other directions.
In the north-eastern direction, the wise man should offer the bali-oblation to Dhanvantari;
thereafter, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Vāyu in the northwestern direction, to all the quarters according to their respective directions,
and to Brahmā, the intermediate space, and the Sun.
O lord of men, one should offer the bali-oblation intended for the Viśvedevas, all beings, the eight Viśvapatī pitṛs, and the Yakṣas.
Then, having taken other food, the wise man, being well-composed, should offer it according to his own inclination upon a clean spot of ground to all beings without exception.
Gods, humans, animals, birds, Siddhas, along with hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas; Pretas, Piśācas, trees, and all others who desire food—may what is given here by me reach them.
May ants, insects, moths, and the like, who are hungry and bound by the fetters of karma, find satisfaction; this food has been offered by me to them—may they be happy.

May those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and for whom there is neither the preparation nor the availability of food—may they find satisfaction through this food given upon the earth; may they reach fulfillment and be joyful.
All beings, as well as this food and I myself, are Viṣṇu; there is nothing else besides this.
Therefore, I offer this food, which has become the very substance of the multitude of beings, for their sustenance.
This fourteenth class of spirits—whatever hosts of all beings reside therein—for their satisfaction this food has been released by me; may they be joyful in it.
Having uttered this, a man endowed with faith should give food for the benefit of all on earth, since the householder is the refuge of all.
O lord of men, one should give on the ground for dogs, Cāṇḍālas, and birds,
as well as for others who are outcasts, childless, and devoid of tranquility.
Then he should remain in the courtyard of his house for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow, for the purpose of receiving guests; after that, he may act according to his own will.
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies,
as well as by offering a seat and washing his feet.
A householder should generate affection by giving food with faith, by pleasant inquiries and replies, and by following those who are departing.
One should properly honor a guest who has arrived from another country and whose family name is unknown, but not one who resides in the same village.

Having eaten while failing to honor a guest who possesses nothing, has no relatives, and whose lineage and character are unknown— even if that guest is hungry and desires food— one goes to a state of downfall.
Without inquiring into his Vedic study, lineage, conduct, or family,
the householder should regard that guest with the thought that he is Hiraṇyagarbha himself.
O King, for the sake of the ancestors, he should also feed at least one other Brahmin who is a native of that region,
whose conduct and origins are well-known, and who performs the five great sacrifices.
O King, having set aside the first portion of the food prepared as alms (hantakāra),
one should present it to a Śrotriya as an offering for the ancestors.
And one should give three portions of alms to wandering mendicants and students;
and according to his desire, a wise man should give unreservedly when he has the means.
These lunar days have been declared, as well as those monks mentioned previously;
O King, by honoring these four, one is liberated from sin.
When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he transfers his own misdeeds to that person and departs taking away their merit.
O lord of men, Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Śakra, Vahni,
and the host of Vasus enter the guest and indeed consume the food.
Therefore, a man should always strive to honor his guests;
for he who eats without a guest consumes only sin.
Then, the householder should first feed his female dependents, the sorrowful, pregnant women, the elderly, and children with consecrated food, and only afterwards eat himself.
If he eats while these have not yet eaten, he consumes their misdeeds;
and having died, that man goes to hell and is born as one who feeds on phlegm.

One who eats before offering food to the gods and ancestors consumes impurity; one who does not recite prayers consumes pus and blood; one who eats unconsecrated food consumes urine; and one who eats before children and others consumes excrement. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.73)
And he who performs sacrifices for himself eats worms, and by eating without having given, he consumes poison.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, listen to how a householder should eat,
so that no bond of sin arises for the man who eats.
And here, O King, there arises abundant health, strength, and intelligence,
as well as the pacification of misfortunes and the subjugation of the faction of enemies.
Having bathed and likewise performed the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors,
the disciplined householder, holding auspicious gems in his hands, should eat.
When the recitation is completed and the oblation offered into the fire, O King, wearing clean garments,
having given [gifts] to guests, Brahmins, teachers, and dependents,
and wearing auspicious fragrant scents and garlands, O Lord of Men— (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.78)
O Lord of the Earth, one should eat wearing only a single garment, with hands and feet not wet,
with a pure face and a joyful mind, and not facing an intermediate direction.
Facing either east or north, with his mind focused on nothing else,
a man should eat food that is commendable, wholesome, and sprinkled with consecrated water.
A householder, having given food to his hungry disciples, should not give what has been brought with contempt, nor what has been prepared from objects of loathing.
A twice-born man, free from anger, should eat from a highly praised and pure vessel.

O Lord of Men, a man should not give [food] into a vessel that is not placed on a stand, nor in an improper place, nor at an improper time, nor in a place that is too crowded; and he should first offer a portion to the fire.
O King, food consecrated with mantras is recommended, provided it is not stale;
however, this does not apply to fruits and roots, nor likewise to dried branches and the like.
Likewise, O Lord of Men, one should never eat the pith extracted from dhārītakas or from sweetmeats made with jaggery.
O Lord of the World, a man possessed of discernment should not eat any leftovers, except for honey, water, the ocean, clarified butter, and barley meal.
Becoming absorbed in that [food], he should eat first the sweet flavor;
then the salty and sour in the middle; and thereafter those that are pungent, bitter, and so forth.
A person should eat liquid food first, solid food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end;
thus, one does not lose strength and health.
In this manner, one should eat blameless food while remaining silent and without disparaging it;
for taking five mouthfuls in great silence is indeed the nourishment of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the other life-forces.
Having eaten properly and sipped water for purification, facing either east or north,
he should again sip water according to rule after washing his hands from the base upwards.
Established in his own state, with a tranquil mind and having assumed his seat,
a man should perform the remembrance of his chosen deity.
May fire, impelled by the wind and granted space by ether, nourish my earthly element; may it digest my food, and may there be happiness for me.
"Food serves for the strength of my body, as do the earth, water, fire, and wind;
when these have been fully digested, there is unimpeded happiness for me."
May food be nourishing for my *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, as well as *udāna* and *vyāna*; and may there be unimpeded happiness for me as well.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest the food I have eaten without exception;
may they grant me the well-being arising from its digestion, and may there be freedom from disease in my body.
Viṣṇu is the soul of all senses and bodies; the Blessed One has never been in vain, being truly one.
By that truth, may this food, once consumed, lead to my complete well-being and its proper digestion.
"Viṣṇu is the eater, and likewise food is indeed subject to transformation;
by that truth, may this food eaten by me be thus digested."
Having recited this and rubbed his belly with his own hand, he should,
being untiring, perform those actions that bring about ease.

One should spend the day in the diversion of true scriptures and the like, which does not conflict with the path of the righteous; thereafter, one should perform the twilight worship with a concentrated mind.

O King, having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the wise man should worship the evening twilight with the Sun and the morning twilight joined with the stars, according to the prescribed rule.
A man who sleeps while the sun has risen over him, or while he is still abandoned by the sun,
must perform an expiation, except in the case of illness.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, having risen before the sun has appeared, a man should perform the morning twilight worship,
and likewise the evening twilight worship at the end of the day while still awake.
O King, those evil-minded ones who do not attend upon either the morning or the evening twilight go to the Tamisra hell.
Furthermore, O lord of the earth, having prepared the cooked food, one should offer the *bali* for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice together with one's wife, even in the evening.
Even there, one should likewise offer food to outcastes (śvapaca) and others.
A wise man should honor a guest who has arrived there according to his own ability;
honoring consists of washing his feet, offering a seat, bowing low, and greeting him with words of welcome,
followed, O King, by the gift of food and a place to sleep.

O King, whatever sin is incurred when a guest who has arrived by day departs unhonored, that very same sin is multiplied eightfold for a man when a guest who has arrived with the sun is sent away unhonored.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, a man should honor a guest who has arrived with the sun according to his own ability; when he is honored, all the deities are honored.
A man should honor him according to his own ability by the gift of food, vegetables, and water,
or else by the gift of a bed, a grass mat, or land.
O King, having washed his feet and other parts after eating in the evening, the householder should then go to a bed made of wood that is not cracked.
One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is bent, uneven, dirty, infested with insects, or uncovered.
O King, for a man who is always sleeping with his head toward the eastern direction or toward the southern direction, it is auspicious; however, the opposite position brings about disease.
O Lord of the Earth, approaching one's own wife during her fertile period is commended;
specifically, under an auspicious time when the moon is in a male asterism, during the nights following the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, and on even-numbered nights.
One should not approach a woman who is naked, nor one who is ill, nor one who is menstruating;
nor one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is terrified, nor one who is pregnant.

One should not approach a woman who has not given her consent, nor one who desires another, nor one who is unwilling, nor the wife of another; nor one who is emaciated by hunger, nor one who has overeaten; and he himself must be free from these same defects.
A man should engage in sexual intercourse when he is bathed, wearing garlands and perfumes, feeling joyful, neither overly full nor hungry, and being desirous and full of passion.
O King, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, and the full moon— these are the sacred festival days (parvan), as is the sun's transit into a new zodiac sign.
A man who indulges in sexual intercourse with his wife during the final three months of every season indeed goes,
upon death, to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana (Eating Excrement and Urine).
Therefore, on all these festival days, wise men who practice self-restraint should be devoted to the study of true scriptures, the worship of the gods, meditation, and the recitation of prayers.
He should not engage in sexual intercourse with one who is not of his own caste or who is not his wife, nor when he has consumed medicinal herbs,
nor with the twice-born, the gods, or his teacher, nor within a hermitage.
O Lord of the Earth, one should never [study] at the sites of shrines, at crossroads, on riverbanks, in cow-pens, at the junctions of four roads, nor in cremation grounds, groves, or in the waters.
O King, on all the aforementioned festival days, as well as during the two twilights,
one should not engage in sexual intercourse even in thought, nor when oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate.
O King, sexual union on the sacred festival days (parvan) is censurable; during the day it brings about sin;
and on the earth, near a reservoir of water, it is inauspicious and brings disease upon men.
One should not go to another's wife even in thought for a moment, much less in speech; for among those who engage in sexual union, there is not even the bond of bone [to hold them together].
Having died, one goes to hell, and even here one's lifespan is diminished;
for men, delighting in another’s wife brings fear both in this world and the next.

Thinking thus, a wise man should approach his own wives when they are in their fertile season, provided they are free from the aforementioned defects and are desirous; he may also do so even outside the season.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Aurva said:
One should worship the gods, cows, Brāhmaṇas, the Siddhas, the elders, and the teachers.
And he should perform the twilight devotions at the two junctions of the day, as well as tend to the sacred fires.
A self-restrained man should wear garments that are always unwashed, auspicious great medicinal herbs,
and gems belonging to Garuḍa.
A man should always wear hair that is well-oiled and free from dirt, be fragrant, dress elegantly, and carry pleasant white flowers that are agreeable to the heart.

One should not take even the slightest thing belonging to another; one should not speak even a small unkindness; one should not speak pleasant falsehoods, nor should one proclaim the faults of others.
O bull among men, one should not take pleasure in enmity toward another's wife;
one should not mount a defective vehicle, nor should one rely on the shade of a riverbank.
Nor with those who are hated, outcasts, insane, or those with many enemies;
nor with carpenters, prostitutes, their husbands, or those who speak mean and false words.
A wise man should not cultivate friendship with those who are excessively wasteful, those who delight in slander, or the deceitful; nor should he travel alone on a road.
O Lord, one should not plunge into the current of the worldly flood;
one should not enter a burning house, nor should one climb to the very top of a tree.
One should not grind one's teeth, nor should one scratch the nose;
one should not yawn with the mouth uncovered, and one should suppress sneezing and coughing.
A wise man should not laugh loudly, nor should he emit sound while passing wind;
he should not bite his nails, nor should he tear grass, nor should he scratch the earth.
A wise man should not bite his beard, nor should he crush a clod of earth;
O Lord, he should not gaze upon the celestial luminaries when they are defiled by impurity.

One should not utter the sound "huṃ" at a naked woman, another's wife, the sun at its rising or setting, a corpse, or a foul odor; for such a stench arises from the consumption of soma, O son of Soma.
One should always avoid crossroads, sacred trees, cemeteries, groves, and the company of wicked women, for they lead to one's destruction.
A wise man should not step over the shadow of those worthy of worship, such as deities, Brahmins, or luminaries;
he should not travel alone through a desolate forest, nor should he dwell in an empty house.
One should avoid from afar hair, bones, thorns, impurities, sacrificial offerings, ashes, chaff, as well as ground that is damp from bathing.
A wise man should not take refuge in ignoble persons, nor should he find pleasure in crookedness;
he should not approach a venomous serpent, nor should he remain standing for long.
O Lord of Men, a wise man should likewise avoid excessive wakefulness and sleep, as well as standing and sitting, and similarly avoid lying down and physical exertion.
A wise man should avoid from afar those with fangs and those with horns,
as well as frost, O King of kings, and likewise the east wind and the heat of the sun.
A wise man should not bathe, sleep, or perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) while naked;
he should not sip water with his hair loose, nor should he omit the worship of the gods and other deities.
In rites such as the fire sacrifice and the worship of deities,
as well as in the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and in washing the feet of the twice-born, one should not proceed wearing only a single garment.
One should never, under any circumstances, sit together with those of improper conduct;
for even half a moment’s association with the virtuous is praised.
A wise man should never enter into opposition with those who are superior nor with those who are inferior;
both marriage alliances and disputes are desired by kings only with those of equal character.
A wise man should not initiate a quarrel and should avoid dry enmity;
even a small loss should be endured, for one must not sacrifice future gain through hostility.

Having bathed, one should not rub one's limbs with the bathing cloth nor with the hands; one should not shake out the hair, nor should one sip water for ritual purification (ācamana) once one has stood up.
One should not step over another's foot, nor should one turn away from a venerable person;
one possessed of discipline should not occupy a high seat in the presence of a guru.

One should not pass by the left (keeping them to one's right) when approaching temples, crossroads, auspicious objects, and those worthy of worship; likewise, one should not keep such things to the right when departing.
A wise person should not spit, nor discharge feces or urine, while facing the moon, the sun, fire, water, the wind, or those worthy of worship.
Likewise, one should not urinate while standing, nor should one urinate on paths;
one must never step over phlegm, feces, urine, or blood.
The discharge of phlegm or nasal mucus is not recommended at the time of eating,
nor during the offering of oblations, auspicious rites, recitations, burnt offerings, or in the presence of a great assembly.
A wise man should neither despise women nor place absolute trust in them;
he should not be envious of them, nor should he ever hold them in contempt.
A wise man devoted to virtuous conduct should not depart from his home without first honoring auspicious objects, jewels, clarified butter, those worthy of worship, and the faces [of elders].
One should pay homage at crossroads, be devoted to the fire-oblation at the proper time,
uplift the distressed, and attend upon virtuous men who are deeply learned.
He who worships the celestial sages, who properly offers funeral cakes to the ancestors,
and who honors guests— he shall go to the highest worlds.
He who, having mastered his own self, speaks at the proper time words that are beneficial, measured, and pleasant,
goes to the imperishable worlds of kings, which are the cause of delight for all beings.
The wise man who possesses modesty, is endowed with patience, is a believer, and is possessed of discipline,
goes to the unsurpassed worlds of those who are advanced in learning and noble lineage.
A wise man should observe a suspension of study during unseasonable thunder and similar phenomena, on festival days, during periods of impurity, and likewise during eclipses and other such occasions.

He who leads those who are angry with equanimity, who is a kinsman to all and free from envy, and who provides comfort to the frightened— that virtuous man’s attainment of heaven is but a minor fruit.

In rain, heat, and similar conditions, one should always go with an umbrella and a staff; and when traveling through forests at night, one who desires protection for the body should always go wearing sandals.
A wise man should not wander about looking upward, downward, or into the distance;
rather, he should walk while looking at the ground, keeping his gaze within the span of a yoke.
For one who, having mastered his own self, casts out all causes of defect without exception,
not even the slightest loss of dharma, artha, or kāma occurs.
For the wise man who delights in virtuous conduct, who is trained in knowledge and humility,
who remains sinless even among the sinful and speaks kindly even to the harsh, and whose inner heart is moistened with loving-kindness— liberation stands within his grasp.
Those who have transcended the sphere of desire, anger, and greed,
and who abide in right conduct— it is by their spiritual power that the earth is sustained.
Therefore, a wise person should speak the truth when it causes pleasure to others;
but when truth leads to the suffering of others, one should then remain devoted to silence.
Thinking that what is pleasant has been said but is not beneficial, one should not speak it;
rather, in such a case, that which is beneficial should be spoken, even if it is extremely unpleasant.
For the benefit of living beings both in this world and the next,
a wise person should speak only that which is consistent with his actions, mind, and speech.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Aurva said:
"When a son is born, a bath with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father."
At that time, one should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman) as well as the śrāddha ceremony for auspicious occasions (abhyudaya).
With full attention and no other thought in mind, one should worship and feed pairs of deities and ancestors to the twice-born, proceeding correctly in a clockwise (savya) order.
O King, facing either eastward or northward, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with curd, unbroken rice, and jujube fruits, using either the *devatīrtha* or the *kāya-tīrtha*.
O King, by that śrāddha, the host of ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas is gratified;
therefore, it must be performed by men on all occasions of prosperity.
At the marriages of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house, at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and other such rites; ||| ViP_3.13.5 |||
At the parting of the hair ceremony, and likewise upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the disciplined householder should worship the Nāndīmukha group of ancestors.
The eternal procedure for the worship of the ancestors during rites of prosperity has been declared;
O protector of the earth, now hear the ritual rules for the performance of funeral rites for the deceased.
Having bathed the corpse with auspicious ablutions and adorned it with garlands,
and having cremated it outside the village, one should bathe with one's clothes on in a body of water.
Relatives, speaking thus, "To such-and-such a person, standing here or there," should offer handfuls of water while facing the south.
Having entered the village together with their cattle at the appearance of the stars,
they should then perform the rite of the mat, sleeping upon a layer of straw on the ground.
O King, bull among men, food should be given daily to the deceased on the earth,
and during the day one should eat a meal that is free of meat.
If those days are observed according to one's desire, the feeding of Brahmins should be performed;
thus the deceased attain satisfaction while their circle of kinsmen partakes of the meal.
On the first, third, seventh, and likewise the ninth day,
having performed the discarding of garments and bathing outside, one should offer water with sesame seeds.
O King, on the fourth day, the piling of his bones should be performed;
after that, even for the sapindas, the touching of the limbs [of the corpse] is permitted.
O King, they are indeed fit for all ritual acts, provided they possess a mind as pure as water, except for the enjoyment of ointments, flowers, and other such luxuries.
The use of beds and seats is permitted even for those who share the funeral cakes (sapindas) after the collection of ashes and bones; however, there is no sexual union with women.

In the case of an infant, one who is in a foreign land, an ascetic (muni), or one who has fallen [from his caste], purification is immediate; likewise, it is by choice in cases such as death by water, fire, or hanging.
For ten days after a relative has died, the food of that family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and the private recitation of the Vedas are suspended.
This twelve-day period of impurity for a Brahmin applies also to a Kṣatriya;
however, for a Vaiśya it lasts half a month, and for a Śūdra, one month, for the sake of purification.
On the following day, he may at his pleasure feed an odd number of twice-born men;
then, upon darbha grass near the remains of the food, he should offer a pinda for the deceased.
Water, weapons, a goad, and a staff may be touched by the [other] castes immediately after a meal given to a twice-born; through these, they are purified in that order.
Therefore, a man should practice all those duties that have been proclaimed by the Brahmins and others, and likewise live by means of the acquisition of his own specific dharma.
Thereafter, on the anniversary of the day of death, the ekoddiṣṭa rite must be performed;
it is that which is devoid of the invocation and other rites pertaining to the gods.
There, a single *ūrdhva* [blade of grass] and likewise a single *pavitraka* [purifier] should be offered;
the *piṇḍa* should be given to the deceased once the twice-born have finished eating.

There, the question and the delight of the sacrificers and the twice-born [should be expressed]; likewise, upon its conclusion, it should be said: "May this be inexhaustible for such-and-such a person."
O King of kings, the dharma consisting of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites is thus prescribed for one year; now listen to the rules regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at that time.
O King, that too should be performed according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite,
either after a year, or in the sixth month, or on the twelfth day.
There, four bowls were provided, filled with sesame seeds, perfumes, and water.
There should be one vessel for the deceased (preta) and likewise three vessels for the ancestors (pitṛ).
One should then pour the water from the preta-vessel into those three ancestral vessels.
Then, O lord of the earth, when that deceased person has attained the status of an ancestor (pitṛ),
one should worship his preceding ancestors in their entirety through the rites of the śrāddha.
O King, a son, a grandson, a great-grandson, or a brother, or the offspring of a brother,
or even the lineage of a sapinda, becomes eligible to perform the funeral rites.
In the absence of all those, the inheritance belongs to the lineage of the *samānodaka* relatives—
those who are connected to the maternal side either by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) or by the offering of water.
O King, when both families have become extinct, the rites must be performed by women,
as well as by the paternal and maternal sapindas and those who share the same water (samānodaka).

The funeral rites for the deceased should be performed by those included within his family group; or, if his kinsmen have perished, the king should cause them to be performed from the deceased's estate.
The preliminary rites, the intermediate ones, and likewise the concluding rites—all these rites are of three kinds; hear from me their classification.

Those rites which begin with the cremation and last for ten days, as well as those beginning and ending with the touching [of the body], are the preliminary ones; those performed month by month are known as the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
O King, those ancestral rites which are performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony once a deceased person has attained the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor) are called the "later" (*uttara*) rites.

But by the father’s or mother’s sapindas, as well as by those sharing the same water (samānodaka), or by those included within the [same] community, or even by the king who takes that wealth; ViP_3,13.38.
The preliminary rites must be performed by the sons and others, while the subsequent ones,
O best of kings, should be performed by the daughters' sons or likewise by their own sons.
O King, on the anniversary of the day of death, the subsequent rites for women also must be performed annually according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceremony.
Therefore, O King, listen to those rites associated with the Uttarā constellation, how they are to be performed, and by what procedure, O sinless one. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.13.41)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Aurva said:
[He created] Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Nāsatyas, Sūrya, Agni, the Vasus, and the Maruts.
The Viśvedevas, the hosts of ancestors, birds, humans, and animals.
By performing a śrāddha endowed with faith, one gratifies the entire world, including the reptiles, the hosts of ṛṣis, and whatever else is designated as a living being.
O Lord of Men, one should perform [the rites] on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight month after month, as well as during the Aṣṭakās; now hear from me the times for optional rites.

One should perform a *śrāddha* upon learning that sacrificial material fit for the rite has arrived, or that a distinguished twice-born guest has come, as well as during the *vyatīpāta* yoga or on the new moon day.
O protector of the earth, when the equinox has arrived, as well as during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, and whenever the sun enters any of the zodiacal signs; ViP_3.14.5 //
One should perform voluntary śrāddhas during afflictions caused by the stars and planets, upon seeing evil dreams, and likewise at the arrival of new grain.
When the new moon coincides with the conjunction of Anurādhā, Viśākhā,
or Svātī, the host of ancestors attains satisfaction for eight years through those who perform the ancestral rites.
When the new moon occurs under the asterisms of Puṣya, Ārdrā, or Punarvasu,
then the ancestors, when duly honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.

On the day of Vāsava (Dhanishthā), Ajaikapād (Pūrvabhādrapadā), or Ārdrā, as well as on the new moon day of the month of Varuṇa (Śravaṇa), for those desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, [the offering] is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
O Lord of the Earth, when the new moon falls on these nine asterisms, the śrāddha performed then indeed brings satisfaction to the ancestors; now hear another [set].
This was sung by the high-souled Sanatkumāra to Elāna,
who was devoted to his father and had approached him with humility and reverence.

Sanatkumāra said: The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), and the fifteenth day of Māgha— Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.14.12.
These four lunar days, which are the beginnings of the Yugas and possess infinite merit, have been described in the Purāṇas:
during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, on the three Aṣṭakās, and on both solstices.
A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors here;
by performing such a śrāddha, he satisfies them for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare.

O King, when the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha coincides with the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), that is the supreme time for the ancestors; indeed, it cannot be attained by those of meager merit.
O protector of the earth, if the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā should coincide with that time,
then water and food offered to the ancestors provides satisfaction for ten thousand years to the men born in that family.
If, at that very time, the Śrāddha for the ancestors is performed according to rule during the sequence of the Bhādrapada month,
the ancestors attain supreme satisfaction and sleep for a thousand Yugas because of it.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, Śatadrū, Yamunā, Vipāśā, Sarasvatī, or the Naimiṣa-Gomatī,
and having performed worship there with devotion, one destroys the sins of the ancestors.

And the ancestors sing this: "When, having attained further satisfaction through the waters of auspicious bathing-places offered by our sons and others at the end of the dark fortnight of Māgha, shall we, filled with joy, go to that state of full contentment? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.14.19)
When the mind and wealth of men are pure, when the time and the prescribed rite are declared auspicious,
when the recipient is as described, and when there is supreme devotion— these grant men their heart's desires.
In this regard, there are verses sung by the ancestors; listen to them, O King, and having heard them, you should remain attentive there with a disciplined mind.
Blessed indeed would be the wise man born in our lineage who,
without practicing stinginess regarding wealth, would offer us funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
"Whoever, while possessing wealth, shall give gems, garments, the Mahāyāna, and all kinds of enjoyments and riches to the Brahmins on our behalf," [he shall attain our world].
Or else, at this time, a man whose wealth is limited to that alone, with a mind bowed in devotion, shall feed the foremost of Brahmins according to his ability with food.
Being unable to give cooked food, he will, according to his capacity,
give raw grain to the foremost of the twice-born, or even a very small sacrificial fee.
Even there, O King, being devoid of capability, he will bow down and give to some eminent brahmin the sesame seeds held on the tips of his fingers.
Bowing with devotion, he will offer a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds upon the earth, dedicating it to us.
Having obtained it from anywhere whatsoever, or even from cows for his daily cow-milk offering,
he will, being endowed with faith, give it to us when [the milk] is lacking, thereby pleasing us.
If all else fails, he shall go to the forest, expose his armpits,
and cry out loudly this to the Sun and the other world-protectors:

"I possess neither wealth nor riches, nor anything else fit for an offering to the ancestors; I bow to my forefathers. May my ancestors be satisfied by this devotion of mine, as I have placed these two arms upon the path of the wind."
Aurva said:
"O King, he who acts according to this which was sung by the ancestors regarding the purpose of existence and non-existence has performed the Śrāddha; by him it is truly accomplished."
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa. Aurva said:
"Listen to me as I describe the qualities of those Brāhmaṇas whom one should feed at a śrāddha."
The officiating priest, a sister’s son, a daughter’s son, a son-in-law, and likewise a father-in-law;
a maternal uncle, one devoted to austerity, one intent upon the five fires,
as well as disciples, kinsmen, and one who is devoted to his mother and father.

O King, one should employ these previously mentioned Brahmins at the first śrāddha for the sake of pleasing the ancestors; in the case of secondary options, those listed immediately following them should be employed.

A betrayer of friends, one with deformed nails, a eunuch, a twice-born man with black teeth, a defiler of virgins, one who has abandoned the sacred fires and the Vedas, and a seller of Soma; ViP_3.15.5 //
Likewise, one who is falsely accused, a thief, a dog-keeper, a village priest, a teacher for hire, and one who has been taught by a teacher for hire; ||| ViP_3,15.6 |||
The husband of a woman who previously had another husband, one who abandons his mother or father, one who rears the offspring of a Śūdra woman, and the husband of a Śūdra woman himself; ViP 3.15.7.
Likewise, a temple-priest (devalaka) is not worthy of an invitation to a śrāddha feast.
On the first day, the wise man should invite those praised for their learning, such as those well-versed in the Vedas,
and likewise inform them of the duties pertaining to the ancestors and the deities.
Therefore, the patron of the sacrifice should not engage in anger, sexual intercourse, or other forms of exertion with those twice-born; therein lies a great fault.
One who, having been appointed to a *śrāddha*, engages in sexual intercourse after eating, or after feeding others, or after appointing others,
causes his ancestors to sink into a pit of semen.
Therefore, the invitation of the foremost of the twice-born is mentioned here first;
one should feed the ascetics (yatis) only after having thus invited the twice-born who have arrived.
One should honor the twice-born who have come to one's house by washing their feet and other such hospitable acts.
With the sacred grass in hand, he should seat the twice-born who have sipped water on their seats: an even number for the ancestors and an odd number for the gods, according to his desire.
One should assign [a portion] to each of the gods individually, and likewise to the ancestors.

Likewise, one endowed with devotion should perform the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva rite; or else, he may perform the Vaiśvadeva rite at that [maternal] occasion.
One should feed the Brahmins representing the gods facing east;
one should also feed those representing the fathers and grandfathers facing north.
"O King, some say that the performance of the *śrāddha* for those two should be separate;
others, the great seers, declare that it may be done in one place with a single cooking."
Having offered *kuśa* grass for a seat and having worshipped with the ritual offering (*arghya*) according to the rules,
the wise man should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the gods with their permission.
One who knows the ritual injunctions should offer arghya to the gods with barley-water,
and he should present them with garlands, perfumes, incense, and lamps according to the prescribed rule.
One should prepare all of that for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
then, having obtained permission and having offered darbha grass cut in two, one should proceed.

O King, the wise man should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by mantras; wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should offer the arghya and other oblations with water mixed with sesame seeds.
If at that time a guest arrives there, a traveler on the king's road desiring food,
he should, with the permission of the Brahmins, feed him as well according to his desire.
Yogins, who bring benefit to human beings through various forms,
wander this earth with their true nature remaining unrecognized.
Therefore, a wise man should honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a śrāddha;
for a guest who is not honored, O King, destroys the fruit of the performance of the śrāddha.
Then, O bull among men, being permitted by those twice-born ones, he should offer food into the fire three times, excluding condiments and salt.
First, the king's oblation is offered to Agni Kavyavāha with the words "Svadhā!
and immediately thereafter, it should be given to Soma Pitṛmat.
Then another [portion] is offered to Vaivasvata;
thereafter, one should place a small amount of food remaining from the oblation into the bowls of the Brahmins.
Then, having offered food that is fresh, delicious, highly desirable, and well-prepared, one should say these gentle words: "Please enjoy it as you wish."
And those [ascetics], with focused minds, observing silence, with pleasant countenances, and free from anger and agitation, should eat comfortably; and he too should give with devotion.
Having recited the mantras that destroy demons and having strewn the ground with sesame seeds,
those best of the twice-born should meditate upon their own ancestors.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding today within the bodies of the Brahmins, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
their forms nourished by this oblation, attain satisfaction today.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth.
"May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this which has been offered by me with devotion. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.15.35)
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, as well as his father and his father’s father;
may the Viśvedevas reach supreme satisfaction, and may the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) perish.
Lord Hari, the Master of Sacrifice, the consumer of all *havya* and *kavya* offerings, the imperishable Self and Sovereign, is present here;
by His proximity, may all demons and asuras instantly depart without exception.
When these brahmins are satisfied, one should scatter food upon the ground;
then, for the sake of their ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should give them water once each.
When they have been fully satisfied, he, being composed, should then duly offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) upon the ground with all the food mixed with sesame seeds, having received their permission.

In the same manner, one should offer water at the *paitṛka* tīrtha, as well as the handful of water (*salilāñjali*) for the maternal grandfathers; with that very same tīrtha, one should present the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*).
Upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, having honored it with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
he should first present the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his own father near the remains of the meal.
He should satisfy the grandfather with another [portion] and his father’s father with yet another;
he should gratify those who partake of the smearings at the base of the *darbha* grass by rubbing off the smears.
Having likewise honored the maternal grandfathers with rice-balls accompanied by perfumes, garlands,
and other offerings, he should then give water for sipping (ācamana) to the foremost of the twice-born.

O Lord of Men, with devotion and a focused mind, one should first offer to the ancestors an oblation accompanied by the blessing "Svadhā," and according to one's ability, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them, he should cause those representing the Viśvedevas to recite:
"May the Viśvedevas here be pleased by this. Thus he should utter.
When those brahmins have said "So be it," one should request blessings;
thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, one should dismiss first the gods and afterwards the ancestors.
The same sequence is prescribed for the maternal grandfathers along with the gods;
one should feed them according to one's capacity, and likewise in the giving of gifts and the ritual dismissal.
Before the washing of the feet, one should perform the rites for the gods and the twice-born;
however, the dismissal (visarjana) should first be performed for the paternal ancestors and then for the maternal ancestors.
Then, having honored those who were requested, he should dismiss them with words of affection;
permitted by them, he should return as far as the door and follow after them.
Then the wise man should perform the daily rite known as Vaiśvadeva,
and having honored [the deities], he should eat together with his servants and kinsmen.
In this manner, a wise man should perform the śrāddha for his paternal ancestors as well as for his maternal ancestors;
nourished by these śrāddhas, the grandfathers grant all desires.
In a śrāddha ceremony, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds;
likewise, talk of silver, its gift, and its recitation [are purifying].
O King of kings, for one performing a *śrāddha*, causing distress, anger, and rising up are three things that are not praised; this applies to the eater as well in this case.
O King, for those men who perform the śrāddha rite, the Viśvedevas, the ancestors, as well as the maternal grandfathers, and their entire lineage are nourished.
The host of ancestors has Soma as its support, and the Moon is the support of Yoga;
therefore, O protector of the earth, the application of Yoga during a Śrāddha ceremony is highly recommended.
O King, if even a single yogi stands before a thousand brahmins,
he delivers all those who eat as well as the patron of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Aurva said:
"With sacrificial offerings, the flesh of fish, the hare, and the mongoose..."
With the meat of the black antelope, the kalaiṇeya, the ruru deer, and the gavaya.
Likewise, the ancestors attain satisfaction through the flesh of sheep and cattle, increasing month by month;
they are always satisfied by the meat of the vārdhraṇasa bird.
O Lord of Men, in this rite, the meat of the rhinoceros, kālaśāka greens, and honey are highly recommended,
as they provide extreme satisfaction.
O Lord of the Earth, for him who approaches Gayā and performs a śrāddha,
that birth becomes fruitful, as it grants the desired satisfaction to his ancestors.
Praśāntikas, samīvāras, and two kinds of śyāmākas— these,
O bull among men, are the preeminent wild herbs suitable for ancestral rites.
Barley, millet, mung beans, wheat, rice, sesame,
flat beans, kovidāra, and mustard seeds are auspicious here.
O Lord of Men, one should also avoid all types of grain for which the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice has not been performed, as well as kidney beans,
millet, and lentils.
The bottle-gourd, the garlic, the onion, the radish, the gāndhāraka, the karaṃbā, and salts from saline soil; ||| ViP_3.16.8 |||
Resins that are reddish, visible salts,
these indeed should be avoided at a śrāddha, as well as whatever is not commended by word.

O King, water that is brought at night, water whose source is not interrupted, water where a cow does not find satisfaction, and water that is foul-smelling or frothy, is unfit for use in a Śrāddha ceremony.
One should avoid the milk of single-hoofed animals, as well as that of camels and sheep, and likewise the milk of goats and buffaloes, during the performance of a śrāddha ceremony.
[The path is obstructed] by eunuchs, outcasts, Cāṇḍālas, sinners, heretics, and the diseased;
by cocks, dogs, naked ascetics, monkeys, and village pigs.

O bull among men, when a śrāddha is looked upon by a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, those impure from childbirth, or those carrying the dead, the ancestors do not partake of the offerings.
Therefore, endowed with faith, one should perform the Śrāddha in an enclosed space;
and by scattering sesame seeds upon the ground, one should ward off the Yātudhānas.
O King, food that has come into contact with fingernails and the like, or with hair and insects,
as well as food mixed with fermented liquors or that which is stale, should not be offered.
Whatever is given to the ancestors by those endowed with faith, according to their names and lineages,
becomes the very food they consume, provided that such was the nature of the food they were born to.
Moreover, O lord of the earth, a verse sung by the ancestors of Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu, is heard even now in the Kalāpa grove from long ago:
"Will there even be those in our lineage who, being devoted to the path of the righteous,
will go to Gayā and offer us funeral cakes with devotion?"
"May he be born in our lineage who would offer us milk-rice with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."
Or he may marry a Gaurī maiden, or release a dark-colored bull,
or perform the horse sacrifice according to the rules with the proper sacrificial fees.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus spoke the venerable Aurva to the high-souled Sagara.
O Maitreya, [this] was formerly asked by you in detail concerning the conduct of the virtuous.
O twice-born one, I too have done this entirely for your sake;
yet no one attains prosperity by transgressing the conduct of the virtuous.
The venerable Maitreya said:

"O Blessed One, those headed by the eunuch (ṣaṇḍha) and the outcaste (apaviddha), as well as the menstruating woman (udakyā) and others, are known to me; now I wish to know correctly about the naked man."
"Who is naked, what is his conduct, and how does a man acquire the designation 'naked'?
O best among the upholders of dharma, I wish to hear the true nature of the naked as it has been described by you; for indeed, nothing is unknown to you."
Śrī Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, this triad known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma is the covering for the social classes; he who abandons it out of delusion is a naked sinner, O twice-born one.
Since the triple Veda is the protection of all castes and of the twice-born,
there is no doubt that one becomes naked when it is abandoned.
And hear this other matter which Vasiṣṭha, our grandfather and knower of dharma, related to the high-souled Bhīṣma.
O Maitreya, as that great-souled one was speaking, I too heard this account concerning Nagna, about which I have questioned you here.
In ancient times, there was a divine battle between the gods and the asuras lasting for a hundred years;
in that conflict, the gods were defeated by the Daityas led by Hrāda.
Having gone to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, they indeed performed austerities;
for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu, they then sang this hymn of praise.
The gods said:
"For the sake of propitiating the worlds, we shall speak those words of the Lord Viṣṇu; by them, may the Blessed Viṣṇu be pleased today."
Since all beings without exception have been produced from that Great Soul,
and into him they shall go to their dissolution— who here is capable of praising him?

Nevertheless, though our vigor has been destroyed by the annihilation of our enemies and we are seekers of safety, we shall praise you; for the true nature of your words is not within the range of our comprehension.
You are the earth, the water, fire, air, and space;
you are the entire internal organ (antahkarana), primordial matter (pradhāna), and the Puruṣa who transcends it.
O Soul of all beings, this single body of yours, composed of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
extends from Brahma down to a blade of grass, distinguished by its various locations and times.
Salutations to that Brahma-self of yours, which was your primordial form arising from the lotus of your navel for the benefit of the universe.
Salutation to that Divine Self, whose single essential nature appears divided into Śakra, Arka, Rudra, Vasu, Aśvin, Marut, Soma, and others.
O Govinda, salutations to that form of yours which consists primarily of hypocrisy, lacks true awakening, and is devoid of compassion; salutations to you in the form of a Daitya.

Salutations to you, the Self, in whom the channels do not carry excessive consciousness because your splendor is stilled, and who, though lusting for sound and other objects, remains within that state.
O Supreme Person, salutations to you, the night-stalker, who possesses that fierce, dark form consisting of cruelty and illusion.
O Janārdana, salutations to you, whose form is called Dharma, which provides the means for the fruits of both the righteous and the unrighteous who reside in heaven.

Salutation to that form of yours which is the essence of perfection, consisting primarily of joy, unattached, and moving through gait, movement, and the like— to that one whose nature is perfected (Siddhātman).

O Hari, salutations to that form of yours which is of the nature of a serpent—cruel because it does not endure transgression, yet capable of enduring [all] enjoyments, and possessing two tongues. ViP 3.17.23.
And salutation to you, who have realized that which is peaceful, faultless, and free from conceptual construction; to you, the one whose nature is the Rishi, yet who possesses all forms.
O Lotus-eyed One, salutations to You, the soul of Time, whose form is that which devours all beings at the end of the eon without restraint.
Salutation to that one whose nature is Rudra, who, having consumed all beings without distinction, including the gods and others, dances at the end.
O Janārdana, salutations to that form of yours which is the self of man, consisting of the instruments of action through the activity of *rajas*.
O Soul of All, salutations to You, the self-subdued one, whose tamasic form consists of twenty-eight varieties and who follows the path of error.

Salutation to that Supreme Self, who is the constituent part of sacrifice, who is the means for the maintenance of the world, and who is divided into six types through the distinctions of trees and other such forms.
Salutation to You, the Self of all, who are the form of everything— from animals, humans, and gods, to space, sound, and so forth— beginning with that which is first.

O Supreme Self, salutations to You, the cause of all causes, whose primordial form is other than and superior to this entire world composed of Pradhāna, Mahat, and the rest— a form that is peerless and non-dual.

We bow to that Blessed One for the sake of his form—that which is devoid of white, long, thick, and so forth; which is beyond the scope of all qualifiers; which is pure and supremely pure; and which is visible only to the supreme seers.
That which is unborn and undecaying within our own bodies, within the bodies of others, and within all things without exception—
that which exists as nothing other than that and distinct from it— to Him who is the very nature of Brahman, we bow.

We bow down to that stainless Lord Vāsudeva, whose form is this entire universe, who is unborn, eternal, and the self of the supreme state; he is the deathless one, the seed of all things, and the source of all.
Śrī Parāśara said: At the conclusion of their hymn of praise, the gods beheld Hari, the Supreme Lord, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, seated upon Garuḍa.
All the gods, preceded by prostration, said to him:
"Be gracious, O Lord; protect us from the Daityas, for we seek refuge in you."
O Supreme Lord, the shares of the sacrifice in the three worlds have been seized by the Daityas, led by Hlāda,
even in defiance of the command of Brahmā.
Although we and they are both born from portions of You, who are the entirety of all beings,
nevertheless, due to the diversity of ignorance, we perceive the world as divided.
Delighting in the duties of their own castes and following the path of the Vedas,
these enemies, shrouded by ascetic power, cannot be slain by us.
O Soul of All, it behooves you to grant us that means by which,
O Blessed One, we may become capable of slaying those Asuras.

Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, Lord Viṣṇu produced Māyāmoha from his body and gave him to them, and he spoke this to the best of the gods: Viṣṇu said: "O gods, go to the earth; there you will find the sons of Dharma, who are devoted to their own duties. They are performing a sacrifice for the sake of the gods, and they are intent on the destruction of the Daityas. Go there and, by means of this Māyāmoha, delude those sons of Dharma so that they may abandon the sacrifice and the penance. The gods said: "O Lord, we shall do as you have commanded; however, tell us how we are to proceed. Viṣṇu said: "Go to the earth and, having approached the sons of Dharma, speak these words: 'O sages, why do you strive in vain? We are the gods, and we are pleased with your penance. Choose whatever boon you desire. Then, when they have chosen the boons, you must grant them all their desires, except for the one thing they seek. The gods said: "We shall do exactly as you have instructed. Having spoken thus, the gods departed. Then, at the command of Viṣṇu, Māyāmoha went to the earth and stood near the sons of Dharma. He assumed the form of a sage and spoke to them: "O sages, why do you strive in vain? We are the gods, and we are pleased with your penance. Choose whatever boon you desire. Then the sons of Dharma, being deluded by Māyāmoha, spoke: "O gods, grant us the boon that we may never suffer from hunger, thirst, old age, or death. Māyāmoha said: "So be it. Then, having obtained those boons, the sons of Dharma abandoned the sacrifice and the penance. Thus, by the power of Viṣṇu, the gods were able to destroy the Daityas. ||| 3.17.41 ||||| 3.17.42 ||||| 3.17.43 ||||| 3.17.44 ||||| 3.17.45 ||||| 3.17.46 ||||| 3.17.47 ||||| 3.17.48 ||||| 3.17.49 ||||| 3.17.50 ||||| 3.17.51 ||||| 3.17.52 ||||| 3.17.53 ||||| 3.17.54 ||||| 3.17.55 ||||| 3.17.56 ||||| 3.17.57 ||||| 3.17.58 ||||| 3.17.59 ||||| 3.17.60 ||||| 3.17.61 ||||| 3.17.62 ||||| 3.17.63 ||||| 3.17.64 ||||| 3.17.65 ||||| 3.17.66 ||||| 3.17.67 ||||| 3.17.68 ||||| 3.17.69 ||||| 3.17.70 ||||| 3.17.71 ||||| 3.17.72 ||||| 3.17.73 ||||| 3.17.74 ||||| 3.17.75 ||||| 3.17.76 ||||| 3.17.77 ||||| 3.17.78 ||||| 3.17.79 ||||| 3.17.80 ||||| 3.17.81 ||||| 3.17.82 ||||| 3.17.83 ||||| 3.17.84 ||||| 3.17.85 ||||| 3.17.86 ||||| 3.17.87 ||||| 3.17.88 ||||| 3.17.89 ||||| 3.17.90 ||||| 3.17.
This Māyāmoha will delude all those Daityas;
consequently, having been cast outside the path of the Vedas, they shall become fit for slaughter.
While I am established in my station, those who stand as obstacles to me— whether gods, Daityas, or other celestial beings— are to be slain, for they oppose my office as Brahmā.
Therefore, go; you should have no fear, for this Māyāmoha is ahead of you.
O gods, as he goes today, he will become a benefactor to you.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the gods prostrated before him and departed as they had come;
Māyāmoha also went with them to where the great Asuras were.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then that Māyāmoha [approached] the great Asuras who were devoted to ascetic penance.
Maitreya, having gone there, saw those who were dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā.
Then, O twice-born one, Māyāmoha, naked, shaven-headed, and wearing a peacock feather, spoke these gentle words to the Asuras: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.18.2.
Māyāmoha said: "O lords of the Daityas, tell me for what purpose you perform this austerity;
do you desire the fruit of your penance to be for the sake of this world, or for the sake of the next?"
The Asuras said:
"O high-minded one, this practice of austerity has been undertaken by us for the sake of attaining rewards in the world beyond; what is it that you wish to say regarding this?"
Māyāmoha said:
"If you desire liberation, carry out my words;
all of you, who possess great strength, ought to practice this dharma."
This Dharma is worthy of liberation; there is no other superior to it.
Abiding firmly in this very [Dharma], you shall go either to heaven or to liberation.
And you all, being of great strength, must honor this Dharma.
Śrī Parāśara said:
By means of many such arguments, refined by the display of logic,
those Daityas were led away from the path of the Vedas through the delusion of Māyā.
"This is for dharma, this is for adharma; this is existent, this is non-existent";
"This is the ultimate truth, yet it is not the ultimate truth;
this is a duty, yet it is not a duty—this is not so, for this is indeed clear."
This is the dharma of those who go naked; this is the dharma of those who wear many garments.
Thus, O twice-born one, by that [Māyāmoha] who displayed the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) in many ways, the Daityas were made to abandon their own duty.
Because they were told by Māyāmoha, "Worship this great dharma," and because they resorted to that dharma, they became known as Arhatas.
Those Asuras, through illusion and delusion, were caused by you to abandon the dharma of the three Vedas;
for they became absorbed in that [unrighteousness], and others were likewise impelled by them.

By them others were defeated, and by those others still more; and by yet others, those [others] were likewise overcome. In a few days, the triple Veda was for the most part abandoned by those Daityas.
Furthermore, Māyāmoha, wearing red garments and having conquered his senses,
approached other Asuras and spoke with words that were few and sweet.
O Asuras, if you desire heaven or even the state of Nirvāṇa, then enough with these wicked practices such as the slaughter of animals; listen!
Understand that all this without exception consists of consciousness alone;
comprehend my words correctly, for thus has it been declared here by the wise.
This world, being without support and consisting essentially of the objects of deluded cognition,
is excessively corrupted by passion and other defilements, and thus wanders through the perils of existence.
"Awake thus! Wake up! Awake in this manner!"—uttering these words, that Māyāmoha led the sons of the Daityas away from their own dharma.
By means of various kinds of speech and logical arguments,
he acted in such a way that they gradually abandoned the dharma of the three Vedas.
Others likewise spoke thus to others, and by others yet others were addressed in the same way;
O Maitreya, they abandoned the supreme Dharma proclaimed in the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
O twice-born one, Māyāmoha, the original creator of delusion, also deluded other Daityas through many various forms of false doctrines.
Indeed, in a very short time, those Asuras were deluded by Māyāmoha and abandoned all discourse based on the path of the three Vedas.
O twice-born one, some [will] revile the Vedas, others the gods,
and likewise at the end [of the age], the assembly of sacrificial rites and the twice-born themselves.
This statement—that oblations consumed by fire lead to a fruit—is not consistent with reason, for it is asserted that violence constitutes dharma. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.18.26)
If Indra enjoys the status of a god attained through numerous sacrifices merely because it is wood such as the *śamyā*, then it would be better to be an animal that feeds on leaves.
If it is held that the attainment of heaven arises for the sacrificial animal once it has been slain,
then why is one's own father not likewise slain by the sacrificer?
If food eaten by one person were to produce satisfaction for another, then one might perform a *śrāddha* for the sake of mere labor; travelers would not carry provisions for their journeys.
Having understood that this matter is to be believed by the people, indifference toward it is for your own welfare; may the words spoken by me be pleasing to you.
O gods, authoritative words do not descend from the sky to the earth;
rather, speech that is endowed with reason must be accepted by me and by others like you.
Śrī Parāśara said: By my delusion, those Daityas were led astray in many ways so that not one among them took any pleasure in the three Vedas.
When those Daityas had thus gone astray, the immortals,
having made a supreme effort, stood ready for battle.
Then, O twice-born one, the war between the gods and the asuras broke out once again;
those asuras who were obstacles to the path of the righteous were slain by the gods.
O twice-born one, they possessed at first a coat of mail consisting of their own dharma;
by that they were protected previously, but when that was destroyed, they perished.
Then, O Maitreya, those people who followed that path became naked because they had abandoned the threefold covering;
and those asuras were made by the gods to be revilers of the various Vedas.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic;
the wandering mendicant is the fourth here, for a fifth does not exist.

O Maitreya, one who abandons the household stage of life for the forest-dwelling stage, or even for the wandering mendicant stage, without having first renounced worldly possessions, is a naked man and a doer of evil.
O Brahmin, he who neglects his daily obligatory rites day and night,
being capable yet failing to perform the prescribed action, falls on that very day.
O Maitreya, a man who neglects his daily obligatory rites for a fortnight attains purification through a great penance, provided he is not in a state of distress.
If a man suffers a lapse in his religious duties for a year,
virtuous people should always look upon the sun after first looking at him.
O Mahāmati, when [the body] is touched, bathing with one's clothes on is the cause of purification for a man;
however, no purification is declared for that person of evil deeds.
In the house of that Brahmin where the gods, sages, and ancestors depart unhonored and in fear, no one in this world commits evil because of him.
O twice-born one, for him who engages in conversation, inquiry, and even laughter with such a person, equality with that very person arises within a year.
One should not mix one's body, house, seat, or household furnishings with those of one whose body and home have been struck by the breath of gods and other such beings.
Furthermore, if he eats in his house, sits upon his seat,
or lies down on his bed, he becomes equal to him immediately.
He who eats without having first honored the deities, the ancestors, the spirits, and likewise the guests, eats sin; for him, no atonement is prescribed.
But those castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
who turn their faces away from their own duty and remain established in degraded actions, they indeed receive the designation "naked" (nagna).
Maitreya, wherever there is an extreme intermingling of the four castes,
it arises there for the sake of destroying the virtuous conduct of those who follow the righteous path.
He who eats without having first honored the sages, the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and guests— by conversing with him, men fall into hell.
Therefore, a wise man should always avoid these naked men, who are defiled by their abandonment of the three Vedas, in matters such as conversation and physical contact.
That śrāddha, even if performed with effort by those possessed of faith, does not gratify the gods, the fathers, or the grandfathers, if it is observed by these [unworthy persons].
And it is heard in an ancient narrative that there was once a king on earth named Śatadhanu,
and his wife was Śaivyā, who was exceedingly devoted to dharma.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, endowed with truthfulness, purity, and compassion,
she was possessed of all auspicious marks, as well as discipline and self-restraint.
That king, together with her, propitiated the omnipresent Janārdana, the god of gods, through supreme meditative concentration.
With devotion, day after day, with his mind fixed on Him and no other, he should worship through burnt offerings, recitations, gifts, fasts, and ritual honors.
Once, O twice-born one, that husband and wife, having fasted on the full moon day of Kārttika, bathed together in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī and emerged from it,
when they saw a heretic approaching toward them.
He was a friend of that high-souled king, who was the preceptor of archery;
therefore, out of respect for him, he then established a state of friendship with him.
But that goddess, his devoted wife, remained restrained in speech;
thinking "I have fasted," she looked at the sun when it was seen.
Having come together according to the rule and in accordance with the prescribed rites, O best of the twice-born, that couple performed all the worship of Viṣṇu and other ceremonies.
As time passed, that king, the conqueror of his enemies, died;
the queen ascended the funeral pyre after her husband, the lord of the earth.
But because of that transgression— namely, that he engaged in conversation with heretics while observing a fast— that lord of the earth was born as a dog.
Remembering her previous birth, that auspicious daughter of the King of Kāśī was born,
endowed with all branches of knowledge and honored for possessing every auspicious mark.
The father desired to give her away to a suitor, but was restrained by that very slender maiden;
thus the king desisted from the commencement of the marriage.
Then, having seen her own husband, the dog, with her divine vision,
she went to the city named Vidiśā and beheld him in that condition.
Upon seeing her husband who had become a dog, that auspicious woman,
devoted to showing hospitality, then gave him excellent food.
Eating the food given by her, which was most delicious and desirable,
he indeed performed many endearments, acting with the playful charm characteristic of his own species.
Deeply ashamed by him as he offered such flattery, Balā spoke these words with a bow to her beloved who was born of a low womb.
O Great King, let that graceful courtesy of yours be remembered,
by which you, though having entered the womb of a dog, have become a flatterer of mine.
"O Lord, having conversed with a heretic immediately after bathing at a sacred ford, you have entered a contemptible womb; do you not remember that?"

Śrī Parāśara said: When he had been thus reminded by her of that deed committed in a previous birth, he then reflected for a long time and attained an extreme detachment that is very difficult to find.
With a mind full of world-weariness, he then departed from the city;
having leaped down from the mountain peak, he entered the womb of a jackal.
When the second month arrived, she too, having perceived that jackal with her divine eye and recognized him, went to Mount Kolāhala to see him.
There too, having seen her husband who had entered the womb of a jackal, the daughter of the king, with her beautiful limbs, spoke to him.
Do you remember, O Indra among kings, that former deed of yours which was recounted by me while you were dwelling in the womb of a dog, and which was based on the discourse of heretics?
Furthermore, it is said that he, the best among the truthful, having realized the truth,
abandoned his own body in the forest while abstaining from food.
Then Būyas was born as a wolf; having gone to that solitary forest, the blameless woman reminded her husband of their former history.
"O illustrious one, you are not a wolf; you are King Śatadhanu.
Having first been a dog and then a jackal, you have now attained the state of a wolf."
When he was thus reminded and had clearly realized that his self had attained the state of a vulture, she, being free from sin, spoke to him again: "Bhā! (O, do not be angry!).
"Narendra, remember your true self; indeed, enough of this vulture-like behavior!
This fault that has caused you to become a vulture was born from the talk of heretics."
Then, having perceived through her own yogic power that he had attained the state of a crow in his immediately following birth, the slender lady spoke to her husband:
O Lord, you who formerly received tribute from all the kings without exception as those subject to your will, have now fallen into the state of a crow and have become a consumer of offerings.
In this very same way, even while in the state of a crane, the king was reminded of his former life;
he gave up his life and attained the state of a peacock.
Then that auspicious young woman indeed followed him in his state as a peacock,
providing him at every moment with food appropriate for his kind.
Then King Janaka performed the great horse sacrifice (vājimedha),
and at its concluding bath (avabhṛtha), he caused him to be sprinkled with water.
The slender-limbed woman bathed herself and also reminded him how that king had taken birth in the wombs of dogs, jackals, and other such creatures.
Then, remembering the sequence of his births, he abandoned that body of his own and was born as the son of the great-souled Janaka.
