Then that slender maiden urged her father to arrange her marriage; and he, the king, likewise caused a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice ceremony) to be held for her.
When the svayaṃvara had been performed, that beautiful woman chose him once again as her husband, having obtained her own lord with the status of a spouse.
And the prince enjoyed sensual pleasures together with her;
when his father had passed away, he ruled the kingdom among the Videhas.
He performed sacrifices, bestowed many gifts upon those who sought them,
begot sons, and fought with his enemies.
Having enjoyed the kingdom and protected the earth according to what is right,
that king, in accordance with dharma, gave up his dear life in battle.
Then that fair-eyed woman, filled with joy, once again ascended her husband who lay upon the funeral pyre according to the prescribed rite, just as she had done before.
Then that king, together with the princess,
attained those imperishable worlds, surpassing even the realms of Indra.
O best of the twice-born, having attained that purification, you have obtained the fruit of merit: incomparable and imperishable heaven, and a most rare conjugal union.
O twice-born one, I have thus declared to you the fault arising from conversing with heretics,
as well as the majesty of the purificatory bath at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice.
Therefore, one who has been initiated, especially at the time of ritual action or during sacrifices and the like, should avoid conversation and physical contact with sinful heretics.
If a cessation of ritual duties occurs in one's household for even a single month,
a wise man should look at the sun after beholding that person.
How much more so, O twice-born one, for those who have completely abandoned the three Vedas— those sinful men who eat with heretics and oppose the teachings of the Veda?
Conversation with them is social contact, and laughing with them is a great sin;
because of this, one should avoid those heretics of wicked conduct.
One should not honor, even with mere words, heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the "vow of the cat," rogues, rationalists, and those who act like herons.
One must avoid contact even at the doorway with those most sinful people—heretics and wicked kings; therefore, one should shun them from afar.
These naked ones have been described to you; they are seen to be destroyers of the merit of a śrāddha rite, by conversing with whom the religious merit of men perishes for a day.
These are sinful heretics; a wise man should not converse with them, for merit arising from that day is destroyed by speaking with them.
By even conversing with those men who wear matted hair merely out of pride, who eat in vain, who have cast aside all purity,
and who are excluded from the offering of water and funeral cakes for their ancestors, other men go to hell.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter (18) in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
The third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa is completed.
Thus ends the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as the Viṣṇucittīya and the Ātmaprakāśa of Śrīdhara.
Now begins the fourth book of the Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as Viṣṇucittīya and Ātmaprakāśa by Śrīdhara.
Homage to the venerable Rāmānuja.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, that which must be performed by men established in virtuous action—
namely, the rites consisting of the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*)— has been explained to me by my preceptor.
The duties of the armor and likewise those duties pertaining to the stages of life have been declared;
O Guru, I wish to hear the lineage of kings—tell that to me.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this lineage of Manu, beginning with Brahmā, which is adorned by many kings who were heroic, steadfast, and performers of sacrifices.
Therefore, O Maitreya, listen to this account of the successive order of his lineage, which serves to destroy the sins of the entire lineage.

Just as the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is the primordial, beginningless source of all the worlds, consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and other Vedas, so too in the past there existed the Blessed Lord Brahmā, who was Hiraṇyagarbha, the mortal form of that [Viṣṇu],
having become the cosmic egg.
From the right thumb of Brahmā was born Dakṣa Prajāpati; from Dakṣa came Aditi, from Aditi Vivasvat, and from Vivasvat, Manu.
Manu had ten sons named Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nābhāga, Diṣṭa, Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra.
And Manu, desiring a son, performed a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa.
In that regard, first, due to a transgression by the Hotṛ priest, there was born a daughter named Ilā.
And through the grace of Mitra and Varuṇa, O Maitreya, he became the son of Manu named Sudyumna.
Furthermore, due to the wrath of Īśvara, she, though remaining a virtuous woman, wandered near the hermitage of Soma’s son, Budha.
And because he was filled with passion for her, Budha begot upon her a son named Purūravas.

Even though he was born, the supreme rishis of immeasurable splendor performed a sacrifice for him; and by their grace, the Lord Yajñapuruṣa himself— consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan Vedas, consisting of all the Vedas, consisting of mind, consisting of knowledge, consisting of nothing else but food—
granted male virility to Sudyumna as desired, and through that favor, Ilā became Sudyumna once again.
To him also were born three sons: Utkala, Gaya, and Vinata.
But Sudyumna, because he had previously been a woman, did not obtain a share of the kingdom.

Freedom from attachment is the state of liberation for ascetics; from attachment, all defects arise.

And while being praised by those lords of serpents, who had recognized his Gandharva-like prowess, the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of all gods, remained there with his lotus-eyes—resembling white lotuses—unfolding and wide awake upon hearing that sound; he, who reclines upon the waters, having awakened at the end of his sleep, was saluted and addressed thus:
"O Blessed One, fear has arisen in us from these Gandharvas; how shall it be pacified?"

And the Blessed One, the Supreme Person without beginning or end, said: "Having entered into that son of Māndhātṛ, the descendant of Yuvanāśva named Purukutsa, I shall bring those wicked Gandharvas entirely to pacification."
Having heard that, the lords of the serpents offered salutations to the Blessed One who reclines upon the waters, returned to the world of the Nāgas, and urged Narmadā to bring Purukutsa.
And she led him down to Rasātala.
And having gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), his own vitality nourished by the splendor of the Blessed One, he slew all the Gandharvas.
And he returned once more to his own city.
And all the lords of the serpents granted a boon to Narmadā:
"Whoever shall utter her name accompanied by the recollection of this [boon], there shall be no fear for him from the poison of snakes."
And on this point, there is a verse: ViP_4,3.12.
Salutations to Narmadā in the morning; salutations to Narmadā at night. Homage be to you, O Narmadā; protect me from the venomous serpent.
Having recited this day and night, or upon entering the darkness, one is not bitten by snakes; nor does even the poison consumed by one who possesses the power of recollecting this lead to any harm.
The lords of the serpents granted this boon: "There shall be no severance of the lineage for Purukutsa."
Purukutsa begot Trasaddasyu upon Narmadā.
From Trasaddasyu was born Anaraṇya, whom Rāvaṇa slew during his conquest of the quarters.
Anaraṇya’s son was Pṛṣadaśva, and the son of Pṛṣadaśva was Haryaśva.
And his son was Hasta.
From him was born Sumanas; his son was Tridhanvan, and from Tridhanvan came Trayyāruṇi.
From Trayyāruṇi was born Satyavrata, who obtained the name Triśaṅku.
And he attained the state of a Caṇḍāla.

During a twelve-year drought, for the sake of supporting the wife and children of Viśvāmitra and in order to accept alms from a caṇḍāla, he hung deer meat daily upon a banyan tree on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
But he was raised bodily to heaven by Viśvāmitra, who was thoroughly pleased.
From Triśaṅku came Hariścandra; from him, Rohitāśva; from him, Harita; from Harita, Cañcu; from Cañcu, Vijaya and Vasudeva; from Vijaya, Ruruka; and from Ruruka, Vṛka.
Then there was the arm of Vṛka, who, having been defeated by the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, and others, entered the forest together with his pregnant queen.
And poison was administered by her co-wife to cause an obstruction of the fetus.
Because of that, his embryo remained within the womb for seven years.
And that arm, due to old age, died near the hermitage of Aurva.
His wife, having prepared a funeral pyre and placed him upon it, became resolved to follow him in death.
Then the Blessed One, the knower of the three times—past, future, and present—having emerged from his own hermitage, spoke these words to Aurva: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.3.31.

"Enough, enough with this false obsession! The Lord of the entire circle of the earth, possessed of extreme heroism and prowess, performer of many sacrifices, and destroyer of the faction of his enemies—the Universal Monarch dwells within your womb.
Thus addressed by him, she who had been so intent on such a rash resolve desisted from her insistence on following him in death.
And by that very Blessed One, she was brought to his own hermitage.
There, within a few days, a child of exceeding brilliance was born together with that very poison.
Having performed for him the birth rites and other ceremonies, Aurva gave him the name Sagara.
Once he had undergone the initiation ceremony, Aurva taught him the Vedic scriptures, as well as the fire-weapon known as Bhārgava.
And having conceived the thought [of renunciation], he spoke to his mother.
"Mother, tell us: where is our father?"—when they asked such questions as these, the mother told them everything.
And thereafter, incensed by the seizure of his father’s kingdom, he made a vow to slay the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, and others.
And he mostly slew the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas.
Being slaughtered, the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas went for refuge to Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor of their clans.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having rendered them as good as dead while they were still living, said to Sagara:
Enough of this dwelling with these who are dead while living and have followed in death.
And these very ones were made by me to abandon their own dharma and their association with the twice-born, solely for the sake of fulfilling your vow.
Saying "So be it," he welcomed those words of his guru and caused them to change their attire.

He made the Yavanas shave their heads entirely, the Śakas shave half their heads, the Pāradas grow long hair, and the Pahlavas grow beards; he deprived them of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, and he reduced these and other such people to the status of Kṣatriyas.
And because they abandoned their own dharma, these brahmins were cast out by others and fell into the state of barbarians.
Sagara also, having attained sovereign power, ruled this earth consisting of seven islands with unimpeded sovereignty.
Thus ends the third chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Sumati, the daughter of Kaśyapa, and Keśinī, the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, were the two wives of Sagara.
And Aurva, having been propitiated by those two with supreme meditative concentration for the sake of offspring, granted them a boon.

"One shall give birth to a single son who will perpetuate the lineage, while the other shall give birth to sixty thousand sons; whichever of these you desire, take it according to your wish. When this was said, Keśinī chose the one [son].
Sumati chose sixty thousand sons.
When he had said, "So be it," after a few days Keśinī gave birth to a single son named Asamañja, the perpetuator of the lineage.
To Sumati, the daughter of Kāśyapa, there were sixty thousand sons.
From that Asamañjasa was born a son named Aṃśumat.
But that foolish man was incoherent; due to his very folly, he became one of evil conduct.
And his father thought: "Now that he has passed beyond childhood, he will become very wise."
Then, when his youth had passed even there, his father abandoned him because of this conduct that was not true to his lineage.
Those sixty thousand sons also followed the very same conduct as Asamañjas.

Then, because the oceans had desecrated the sacrifices by imitating the improper conduct of Asuras, the gods, in this world, bowed down to Kapila— who was a portion of the Blessed Puruṣottama, who consists of all knowledge, and who is untouched by any defects— and spoke for his sake on the path of the righteous.
"O Blessed One, these sons of Sagara are following the conduct of Asamañja."
"How will the world fare with these who follow such improper conduct? ||| ViP_4,4.14 |||
Having heard that the Blessed One had assumed a body here for the sake of protecting the world which was exceedingly afflicted, the Blessed One said, "They shall perish in just a few days."
In the meantime, Sagara commenced a horse sacrifice.
And someone, having stolen the horse that was being tended by his sons, entered a hole in the earth.
Then his sons, by the persistent force of their horses' hooves, dug into the earth for a yojana each.
And in the netherworld (pātāla), those sons of the lord of the earth beheld that horse wandering about.

And not far away, they saw the Blessed One, the sage Kapila—the stealer of the horse—standing like the sun in the cloudless autumn season, with his head bowed and his splendors illuminating all directions below;

then those evil-minded men, raising their weapons, cried out, "This one who harms us and obstructs the sacrifice, the stealer of the horse, must be slain! He must be slain! and they rushed toward him.
Then, looked upon by that Blessed One with his eyes turned slightly, they perished, being consumed by a fire arising from his own body.

Sagara, having learned that the entire force of his sons following the horse had been consumed by the fiery energy of the supreme seer Kapila, then appointed Aṃśumat, the son of Aśmaka, to bring back the horse. He, however, having approached Kapila by the path excavated by Sagara’s sons, praised him with devotion, bowing low.
Then the Blessed One said to him: *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 4.4.25.
"Go, my son, and bring this horse to your grandfather; choose a boon, for your sons and grandsons shall bring the Gaṅgā from heaven to the earth."
Then Aṃśumān replied, "Grant us a boon that will cause our fathers—who have departed for heaven but were slain by the staff of Brahmā and are thus unworthy of heaven—to attain the celestial realm."
Having heard that, the Blessed One said to him: "I have already said this today: your grandson will bring the Gaṅgā from heaven to the earth."
And when their bones and ashes are touched by that water, they too shall ascend to heaven.
For such is the majesty of the water that has issued from the big toe of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.
"It is said that not only does [this water] assist in the enjoyment of baths and other rites when used intentionally, but even when unintentionally touched by the bones,

skin, sinews, hair, and so forth of a deceased being, or even when fallen from its body, it immediately leads the embodied soul to heaven. Having thus spoken, he bowed to Bhava (Śiva) and, taking the horse, returned to the sacrifice of Pitāmaha (Brahmā).
Having recovered the horse, Sagara completed that sacrifice.
And out of affection for his son, he adopted the ocean as his own son.
Dilīpa was the son of that Aṃśumat.
From Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, who, having brought the Gaṅgā here from heaven, gave her the name Bhāgīrathī.
From Bhagīratha came Suhotra; from Suhotra came Śruta; his son was Nābhāga; from him came Ambarīṣa; his son was Sindhudvīpa; and from Sindhudvīpa came Ayutāyus.
And his son was Ṛtuparṇa, who became Nala’s companion and was an expert in the science of horses.
Sarvakāma was the son of Ṛtuparṇa.
His son was Sudāsa.
From Sudāsa was born Saudāsa, whose name was Mitrasaha.
And while wandering through the forest for the sake of hunting, he saw two tigers.
Thinking that the forest had been cleared of deer by those two, he struck one of them with an arrow.
And as he was dying, he became a Rākṣasa of most terrifying form and an exceedingly hideous countenance.
The second one also, having said, "I shall perform a counter-action against you," vanished from sight.
As time passed, Saudāsa performed a sacrifice.

When the sacrifice was completed and the preceptor Vasiṣṭha had departed, that Rākṣasa assumed the form of Vasiṣṭha and said, "At the conclusion of the sacrifice, human flesh must be given as food; let it be prepared, and I shall return in a moment," and having spoken thus, he went out.
Furthermore, having assumed the guise of a cook by the king's command, he prepared human flesh and presented it to the king.
He too, taking meat in a golden vessel, remained waiting for Vasiṣṭha’s arrival.
He announced [the arrival] to Vasiṣṭha, who had come.
And he too thought: "Oh, what wickedness this king possesses, that he gives us this flesh! What kind of substance is this? and he became absorbed in meditation.
And he beheld that human flesh.
Therefore, his mind turbid with anger, he cast a curse upon the king.
"Since he gives this to me even though he knows it is unfit for ascetics like us to eat, therefore your own greed for it shall surely come to pass."
Immediately after he said, "I too was addressed by that very Blessed One," the Sage, wondering what he had been told, again entered into meditative absorption.
Understanding his state of mind through his concentration, he showed him favor by saying, "This food of yours shall last for twelve years, but it will not be permanent."

Having accepted the handful of water and being prepared to utter the sage’s curse, he was entreated by his wife Madayantī, who said, "O Blessed One, this is our preceptor; you ought not to curse him, for he is the guardian deity of our lineage. Thus appeased, and for the sake of protecting the crops and the waters, he did not cast that cursed water upon the earth nor into the sky, but instead sprinkled it upon his own feet.
And because his two feet were scorched by that wrathful fire, they became mottled; consequently, he acquired the name Kalmāṣapāda.
Furthermore, due to Vasiṣṭha’s curse, he would assume the nature of a Rākṣasa every sixth period; wandering through the forest, he devoured many human beings.
On one occasion, however, he saw a certain sage united with his wife during her season.
And seeing that most terrifying form of the Rākṣasa, the couple fled in terror, and he seized Brahmā.
Then that Brahmin woman entreated him many times.
Be gracious, O Great King, you who are the ornament of the Ikṣvāku dynasty; you are Priyavrata’s son, not a Rākṣasa.

While she was lamenting in many ways, saying, "It does not behove you, who know the happiness of a woman's duty, to kill our husband while I have yet to achieve my purpose," the tiger devoured that Brahmin— just as one might devour a desired animal in the forest—
and then the Brahmin woman, filled with extreme rage, cursed the king.
"Since you have devoured this husband of mine while I was thus unsatisfied, therefore you too, being engaged in the enjoyment of desire, shall meet your end."
And having uttered the curse, she entered the fire.
Then, at the end of twelve years, when he was freed from the curse and possessed a longing for women, Madayantī reminded him of that [past].
Thereafter, he renounced the enjoyment of women.
And Vasiṣṭha, being requested by the childless king for the sake of a son, performed the impregnation ceremony upon Madayantī.
And when she had been pregnant for seven years, that queen then struck the fetus with a stone.
And a son was born.
And his name became Āśmaka.
Aśmaka had a son named Mūlaka.
Since he was protected by naked women while this earth was being rendered devoid of Kshatriyas, they therefore call him Nārīkavaca (the one whose armor is women).
From Mūlaka came Daśaratha; from him, Ilavila; and from him, Viśvasaha.
And from him was born Khaṭvāṅga, who, being entreated by the gods in the battle between the gods and the asuras, slew the asuras.
And in heaven, urged by the gods who had done him favors to accept a boon, he spoke:
"If a boon must certainly be accepted, then let my lifespan be told."

Immediately after, they said, "A single moment is the measure of your lifespan. Having been told this, he descended to the mortal world in a celestial chariot with unerring movement, endowed with qualities such as levity (*laghimā*), and spoke as follows:

"Just as my own self is not dearer to me than the Brahmins, nor have I ever at any time committed a transgression of my own duty (*svadharma*), nor is there anything among all gods, humans, animals, birds, trees, and so forth that is distinct from Acyuta (the Imperishable)."

Such was my vision: "May I reach that very Blessed One, remembered by the sages, with unswerving gait. Thus he united his self with the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva—the Lord who is the teacher of all gods, whose form is indefinable, and whose essence is pure existence—and there alone he attained dissolution.
In this regard, a verse sung by the Seven Sages in former times is heard:
"There shall be no one else on earth equal to Khaṭvāṅga."
Having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment,
he indeed united the three worlds through his intellect and truthfulness.
From Khaṭvāṅga, a son named Dīrghabāhu was born.
From him, Raghu was born.
Therefore, for this reason also, he is unborn.
Daśaratha was born from Aja.

For him as well, the Lord whose navel is a lotus, for the sake of the world’s preservation, assumed the state of sonship in four ways through a portion of himself, in the forms of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna.
Rāma, too, while still a boy, went forth to protect Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice and slew Tāṭakā.
And during a sacrifice, he cast Mārīca, who had been struck by the wind of his arrow, into the ocean.
And he brought those headed by Subāhu to their destruction.
By his mere glance, he rendered Ahalyā free from sin.
And in the house of Janaka, he broke the bow of Maheśvara without any effort.
He obtained Sītā, who was not born from a womb, the daughter of King Janaka, for whom valor was the bride-price.
He caused Paraśurāma—the destroyer of all kṣatriyas and the comet of destruction for the entire Haihaya clan—to cast aside the arrogance born of his prowess and strength.
And, disregarding his desire for the kingdom at his father's word, he entered the forest accompanied by his brother and wife.
He slew Virādha, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and others, as well as Kabandha and Vālin.

Having bound the ocean and brought about the destruction of the entire race of Rākṣasas, he brought back to Ayodhyā the daughter of King Janaka—his wife who had been abducted by the Ten-faced one; she whose stain was removed by his slaying, who was purified by entering the fire, and whose virtue was praised by the hosts of all the gods.
Furthermore, Maitreya, the auspicious ceremony of his consecration cannot be described even in a hundred years; listen therefore to a brief account.

Dasaratha was attended by Lakshmana, Bharata, Shatrughna, Vibhishana, Sugriva, Angada, Jambavat, Hanuman, and others, whose faces were in full bloom and who carried parasols, chowries, and other regalia; he was likewise served by all the immortals, including Brahma, Indra, Agni, Yama, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera, Ishana, and the rest,
as well as by Vasishtha, Vamadeva, Valmiki, Markandeya, Vishvamitra, Bharadvaja, Agastya, and others.

Praised by the best of sages with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas; amidst all the auspicious musical instruments of the world, such as lutes, veṇus, mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, paṭahas, conchs, kāhalas, gomukhas, and others producing beautiful sounds;

and consecrated in the midst of all the world's warriors for the sake of protecting all people according to what was fitting—the son of Daśaratha, the lord of Kosala, the ornament of the Raghu clan, the beloved of Jānakī, and the beloved of his three brothers—sat upon the lion-throne for eleven thousand years.
He ruled the kingdom. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 4.4.99.
Bharata also, while proceeding to conquer the realm of the Gandharvas, slew thirty million Gandharvas in battle.
By Śatrughna as well, the impetuous Lavaṇa, son of Madhu, who possessed immeasurable strength and prowess, was slain, and Mathurā was resettled.

Thus, having accomplished the preservation of the entire world—which was being devoured by him as he sported with excessive power, prowess, and valor—Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna ascended once more to heaven;

and those inhabitants of the city and countryside of Kosala who were devoted to those portions of the Blessed One also attained residence in the same world (sālokya) as them, their minds fixed upon them.

Rāma, the destroyer of the exceedingly wicked, had two sons, Kuśa and Lava; Lakṣmaṇa had Aṅgada and Candraketu; Bharata had Takṣa and Puṣkala; and Śatrughna had Subāhu and Śūrasena. (ViP 4.4.104) The son of Kuśa was Atithi, and the son of Atithi was Niṣadha. (ViP 4.4.105)

From Niṣadha came Anala; from him, Nabha; from Nabha, Puṇḍarīka; his son was Kṣemadhanvan; his son was Devānīka; his son was Ahīnaka; from Ahīnaka came Ruru; his son was Pāriyātraka; from Pāriyātra came Devala;
from Devala, Vajrala; his son was Utka; from Utka came Vajranābha; from him, Śaṅkhaṇa; from him, Dyutimat; from him, Svastika.
And Viśvasaha was born.
From him, Hiraṇyanābha—the great yogi—attained yoga from Jaimini’s disciple, Yājñavalkya.

The son of Hiraṇyanābha was Puṣya; from him came Dhruvasandhi, from him Sudarśana, from him Agnivarman, and from him Śīghraga. From him also Maru was born as a son, who, having resorted to yoga, remains even today dwelling in the village of Kalāpa.
In a future age, he will be the one who revives the solar lineage and its sacred observances.
His son was Praśuśruka; his was Susaṃdhi; from him came Amarṣa; his son was Sahasvān; and from him came Viśvabhava.
His son, Bṛhadbala, was brought to his destruction in the Bhārata war by Abhimanyu, the son of Arjuna.
These kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty have been described by me according to their prominence;
by hearing their life stories, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
That Nimi, the son of Ikṣvāku, commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting for a thousand years.
And he chose Vasiṣṭhi as his Hotṛ priest.
Vasiṣṭha said to him, "I was first chosen by Indra for the purpose of performing sacrifices for five hundred years."
Immediately after that, when it was said, "The time for your protection has arrived; I shall also be your officiating priest," that lord of the earth said nothing at all.
Vasiṣṭha also performed a sacrifice for the Lord of the Asuras, as he had been requested by him.
At that very same time, he also performed a sacrifice along with others, such as Gautama and the rest.
And when the sacrifice of the Lord of the Apsarases was completed, Vasiṣṭha arrived in haste, saying, "I shall perform the sacrifice for Unmīya."

Seeing that Gautama was the performer of that very act while the king was asleep, he cursed him, saying: "Since you have rejected me and entrusted this task to Gautama instead, therefore he shall become bodiless (videha). Thus he gave the curse.
And having awakened, that lord of the earth also spoke.

Because that wicked preceptor had cast a curse upon me while I was sleeping and had not even spoken to me, doing so out of sheer ignorance, [Vasiṣṭha] gave him the curse, "Therefore his body too shall fall," and then abandoned his own body.
By that curse, Vasiṣṭha’s consciousness entered the vital energy (*tejas*) of Mitra and Varuṇa.
From those two, who had caused the fall of the seed through the sight of Ruśi, Vasiṣṭha obtained another body.
Even Nimi’s body, though being treated with highly fragrant oils and other substances, did not suffer any defect such as putrefaction; it remained as if he had only just died.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the officiating priests, having arrived to receive their shares, said to the gods:
"Let a boon be granted to the sacrificer."
And being entreated by the gods, that Nimi said:
The Blessed Ones are the destroyers of all the suffering inherent in saṃsāra.
For there is indeed no other suffering such as that which occurs upon the separation of the body and the self.

"Therefore, I wish to dwell within the eyes of all living beings, rather than undergoing the assumption of a physical body. When the gods had spoken thus, he was introduced into the eyes of all creatures without exception.
Thereupon, the beings performed the opening and closing of their eyes.
And the sages, fearing the state of having no king, churned the body of that childless monarch in the forest.
And there a prince was born.
And through his birth, he received the designation of "father."
His father was Abhūdvideha, from whom he was called Vaideha; and because of churning (mathana), he was called Mithi.
His son was Udāvasu.
From Udāvasu came Nadivardhana; from him, Suketu; from him, Devarāta; from him, Bṛhaduktha; his son was Mahāvīrya, and his son was Sudhṛti.
From him, Dhṛṣṭaketu was born.

From Dhṛṣṭaketu came Haryaśva; his son was Manu; from Manu came Patika; from him Kṛtaratha; his son was Devamīḍha; his son was Vibudha; from Vibudha came Mahādhṛti; from him Kṛtarāta; from him Mahāromā; his son was Svarṇaromā; the son of Hrasvaromā was Hrasvaromṇa; and from Hrasvaromṇa was born Sīradhvaja.
As he was plowing the sacrificial ground for the sake of obtaining a son, a daughter named Sītā was born from the furrow.
The brother of Sīradhvaja was named Kuśadhvaja, the lord of Saṃkāśya.
Sīradhvaja’s son was Bhānumat; from Bhānumat came Śatadyumna, and his son was Śuci. From him was born a son named Ūrja.

His son was Śatadhvaja; from him came Kṛti; from Kṛti, Añjana; his son was Kurujit; from him, Ariṣṭanemi; from him, Śrutāyus; from Śrutāyus, Supārśva; from him, Sṛñjaya; from him, Kṣemāvī; from Kṣemāvī, Anenā; from him, Bhaumaratha;
his son was Satyaratha; from him, Upagu; from Upagu, Upagupta; his son was Svāgata, and his son was Svānanda.
From him [Suhotra] came Suvarcas; from him Supārśva; from him also Subhāṣa; from Suśruta came Suśruta; from Suśruta came Jaya;
his son was Vijaya; from Vijaya came Ṛta; from Ṛta came Sunaya; from Sunaya came Vītahavya; from him came Dhṛti; from Dhṛti came Bahulāśva; his son was Kṛti.
Upon this [act] being performed, this lineage of Janaka is established.
Thus these were the Maithilas.
Generally, these kings are those who take refuge in the knowledge of the Self.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, you have described to me the descendants of Sūrya."
I also wish to hear about all the kings who were subject to Soma.
O Brahmin, you whose lineage still persists even today— you who possess enduring fame— please describe to me those whose faces were gracious with favor.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Listen, O tiger among sages, to the lineage of Soma, who possesses illustrious splendor,
in which the lords of the earth appeared in successive order.

For this lineage has been adorned by kings such as Nahuṣa, Yayāti, and Kārtavīryārjuna—who were endowed with extreme virtue and possessed of great lineage, strength, prowess, splendor, character, and conduct; I shall now relate its history, so listen.
From the lotus-navel of the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the entire world, was born Brahmā, and his son was Atri.
Soma was the son of Atri.
And the Blessed One, whose source is the lotus, consecrated him in the sovereignty over all medicinal herbs, birds, and constellations.
And he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Due to his power and his presiding over such supremely exalted sovereignty, pride entered into him.
And out of the arrogance of his pride, he abducted Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of all the gods.
And although he was repeatedly urged by the Lord Brahmā at the instigation of Bṛhaspati, and entreated by all the celestial sages, he did not release her.
Out of enmity toward that Candra and Bṛhaspati, Uśanas became their rear-guard ally.
And having acquired knowledge from Aṅgiras, the Blessed Lord Rudra rendered assistance to Bṛhaspati.
Where Uśanas was, there all the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, beginning with Jambha and Kumbha, made a great effort.
Even for Bṛhaspati, Śakra became an ally accompanied by the entire army of the gods.
And thus, between those two, there occurred an exceedingly fierce battle known as Tārānimitta or Tārakāmaya.
Then, all the weapons were released by the gods, led by Rudra, against the Asuras, and by the Dānavas against the gods without exception.
Thus, the entire world, its heart agitated by the turmoil of the battle between the gods and the asuras, went for refuge to Brahmā. // 18 //
Then the Lord Brahmā, having restrained Uśanas, Śaṅkara, the Asuras, and the Devas, caused Tārā to be restored to Bṛhaspati.
And seeing her with the fetus fully developed within, Bṛhaspati also said:
"This child is not to be held by you in my field; he belongs to another. Cast him out! Enough, enough of this excessive audacity!"
And she, being exceedingly devoted to her husband, having been thus addressed by him, immediately after her husband’s words, cast that embryo into a clump of *iṣīkā* reeds.
And as soon as it was released, by its extreme splendor, it overwhelmed the splendors of the gods.
Seeing both Bṛhaspati and Indu filled with longing for that boy due to his extreme beauty, the goddesses, their doubts aroused, questioned Tārā.
"Tell us the truth, O blessed lady: is this the son of Soma or of Bṛhaspati?"
Thus addressed by them, that Tārā said nothing at all out of shame.
When she did not disclose [the truth] to the gods despite being addressed many times, the prince, intent on cursing her, said:
"O wicked woman, why do you not tell me who my father is?"
This very day, I shall inflict such punishment upon you, who are possessed by the shame of your own falsehoods.
And so that you shall not remain with such exceedingly slow speech even until today.
Then the Blessed One, the Grandfather, having restrained that youth, himself questioned Tārā.
"O child, whose son is this—is he the son of Soma or of Bṛhaspati? Thus addressed, she, feeling ashamed, replied, "He is the son of Soma."

Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the Stars (the Moon), his stainless cheeks radiant with a shimmering upward glow, embraced the youth and said, "Excellent, excellent, my child! You are wise," and he gave him the name Budha.
This very account has been told; and he, in turn, begot a son named Purūravas upon Ilā.

Purūravas, who was exceedingly generous, a great sacrificer, and possessed of supreme splendor— truthful, of beautiful form, and high-minded— was seen by Urvaśī, who had resolved that she must dwell in the world of mortals due to the curse of Mitra and Varuṇa.
As soon as she saw him, she abandoned her pride entirely, cast off all longing for the pleasures of heaven, and with her mind fixed solely upon him, waited upon him.

And he too, beholding her who surpassed all women in the world in the qualities of beauty, delicacy, grace, gait, charm, laughter, and so forth, became one whose mental state was entirely dependent upon her.
Both of them became focused on that [object], their gaze fixed on nothing else, having abandoned all other purposes.
But the king, out of boldness, said to her:
"O fair-browed one, I am filled with desire for you; be gracious and return my love. Thus addressed, Urvaśī, her face broken by shame, spoke to him.
"Let it be so, provided that you fulfill my agreement," he said; when this was declared, he spoke to her once more.
"Tell me the rule," [he said]. (ViP 4.6.42)
Then, being questioned again, she spoke once more:
The pair of mongooses near my bed, who have become like sons to me, must not be removed.
And you, sir, must not be seen by me naked.
"And my food shall consist of nothing but ghee."
"So be it," the lord of the earth replied.

Together with her, that lord of the earth spent sixty-one years in Alakā, delighting in the Caitraratha and other groves, in clusters of pure lotuses, and in most enchanting lakes such as Mānasa, his joy increasing day by day.
And Urvashi, her passion increasing day by day through that enjoyment, felt no longing even for dwelling in the world of the immortals.
Without the celestial nymph Urvaśī, the world of the gods was no longer very delightful for the Apsarases, Siddhas, and Gandharvas.
Then, at night, Viśvāvasu, who was well-acquainted with the agreement between Urvaśī and Purūravas, joined by the Gandharvas, stole one of the rams from near their bed.
As he was being led away through the sky, Urvaśī heard his voice.
And thus she spoke: "By whom is my son being carried away? To whom shall I go for refuge?"
Having heard that, the king did not go, thinking, "The queen will look upon me."
Then, taking yet another ram, the Gandharvas departed.
Hearing the sound of that [jewel] being carried away through the sky, she again cried out in distress: "I am once more without a protector, without a husband, and dependent on a base man!"
The king also, under the sway of indignation, thinking "this is darkness," took up his sword and rushed forward, crying out, "Wicked one! Wicked one! You are slain!"
And at that moment, an exceedingly brilliant lightning flash was produced by the Gandharvas.
By that radiance, Urvaśī, seeing the king divested of his garments and her agreement having expired, departed from that very moment.
Having abandoned even those two rams, the Gandharvas departed for the world of the gods.
And the king, having taken those two rams with an exceedingly joyful mind, returned to his own bedchamber and did not see Urvaśī.
And not seeing her, he wandered about in a state of madness, his garments fallen away.
And at Kurukṣetra, in the lake of lotuses, he beheld Urvaśī joined by four other celestial nymphs.
Then, appearing like a madman, he spoke many kinds of wise words, saying: "O wife, stay! Stay in my mind, O fierce one! Stay in my speech, O deceitful one! and so forth.
Urvaśī said:
"O Great King, enough of this undiscriminating conduct!"
"I am pregnant; at the end of the year you must come here, for a son shall be born to you. And I shall dwell with you for one night. Having been told this, he went to his own city overjoyed.
And he related this to Urvaśī among those Apsarases.
"This is that most excellent of men, by whom I have lived for so long with my mind drawn by affection."
Thus addressed, those Apsarases replied:
"May we also always have the opportunity to dwell together with him, who is the very embodiment of goodness."
And when the year was complete, that king came there.
And Urvaśī gave him the long-lived Kumāra.
And having spent one night with that king, she conceived a child for the sake of producing five sons.
And he said to that king, "Out of affection for us, all the Gandharvas have become granters of boons to the great king; let a boon be chosen."
And the king said:

When he said, "I have conquered all enemies and my sensory faculties are unimpaired; I possess kinsmen, allies, and a great treasury; there is nothing else for us to attain except co-residence (*sālokya*) with Urvaśī; therefore, I desire to spend my time with this Urvaśī," the Gandharvas gave a fire-vessel (*agnisthālī*) to the king.

They said to him: "Becoming one who follows the Vedic injunctions, divide Agni into three parts and perform the sacrifice properly with the desire for the goal of attaining the same world [as the gods]. Then you will certainly obtain what you long for. Having been told this, he took that *agni-tālī* and departed.
In the middle of the forest, he reflected: "Alas, how great is my delusion! What have I done?"
"This is merely a fire-vessel brought by me; it is not Urvaśī."
Then, in that very forest, he abandoned the fire-vessel and went to his own city.
When midnight had passed, he woke from sleep and reflected:
For the sake of attaining the same world as Urvaśī, a fire-vessel was given to me by the Gandharvas; however, I abandoned it in the forest.
Thinking, "Therefore, I shall go there to fetch it," he rose and went to that place, but he did not see the fire-vessel there.
Seeing an Aśvattha tree growing from the heart of a Śamī tree at the site of the fire-vessel, he reflected:
I placed a fire-vessel here, and it became an aśvattha tree with a śamī tree at its core.
"Therefore, taking this very form of Agni, I shall go to my own city, prepare the fire-drills (araṇī), and perform the worship of the fire produced therefrom."
In this very manner, having returned to his own city, he prepared the fire-drill.
And while measuring that [distance] with his fingers, he recited the Gāyatrī.
And as he recited, the forest became [a space] measured in finger-breadths equal to the number of syllables.
There, having churned the fire and become one who follows the traditional injunctions, he offered oblations into the three sacred fires.
He had set his heart upon the fruit of attaining the same world as Urvaśī.
Having performed various sacrifices according to that very ritual of Agni, he attained the world of the Gandharvas and achieved non-separation from Urvaśī.
In the beginning there was only one fire, but in this present Manvantara it has been set forth in a threefold manner.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
He, too, had six sons known by the names Dhīmat, Āmāvasu, Vani, Śvāvasu, Śrutāyu, and Śayu, as well as Ayutāyu.
In that manner, Amāvasu had a son named Bhīma.
From Bhīma came Kāñcana; from Kāñcana came Suhotra, and his son was Jahnu.

When he beheld the entire sacrificial enclosure flooded by the waters of the Gaṅgā, his eyes became bloodshot with rage; having then established the Blessed Lord of Sacrifice within himself through supreme meditative absorption, he drank up the Gaṅgā in its entirety.
Then the celestial sages sought to appease him.
And they brought Gaṅgā to be his daughter.
And Jahnu had a son named Sumandu.
His son was Ajaka; from him came Balākāśva; from him, Kuśa; and he too had four sons: Kuśāmbu, Kuśanābha, Dhūrtarajas, and Vasu.
Among them, Kuśāmba, who was equal to Śakra, performed austerities with the thought, "May I become a protector."
Beholding him performing such fierce asceticism, Indra thought, "Let him not become equal to me in prowess," and so he himself became his son.
He became the son named Gādhi, a descendant of Kuśika.
And Gādhi begot a daughter, Satyavatī.
And Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, chose her as his bride.

Gādhi, however, being unwilling to give her to a Brahmin who was excessively irascible and very old, requested as the bride-price a thousand horses, each with one black ear, possessing the luster of the moon and the speed of the wind.
That rishi, having obtained it from Varuṇa, gave him a thousand such horses born at Aśvatīrtha.
Then Ṛcīka married that maiden.
And Ṛcīka prepared for her a sacrificial oblation intended to procure offspring.
And being propitiated by him, he performed the final rite for the sake of producing a son of the highest Kṣatriya lineage upon her alone.
"This is one sacrificial oblation; this other oblation must be properly prepared by you from your own portion," he said, and then departed for the forest.
At the time of her employment, her mother Satyavatī said to her:
"Daughter, everyone indeed desires their own son to possess supreme qualities; one does not, however, show such great regard for the qualities of one's daughter or brother."
"You ought not to consume my own sacrificial oblation as if it were your own."

"Indeed, my son must perform the protection of the entire circle of the earth; what need has a Brahmin for such abundance of strength and heroism? Having said this, she gave her own sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to her mother.
Then, having returned from the forest, the sage beheld Satyavatī.
And he said to her: "O most wicked woman, what is this improper act you have committed? Your body appears exceedingly terrible."
Having been entrusted by you to your mother, Nīla is endowed with a beautiful form; it is not fitting for this [to happen].

For I have bestowed upon that porridge the perfection of all sovereignty, heroism, valor, and strength; and upon your porridge, I have placed the entire collection of Brahmanic qualities, such as peace, knowledge, and forbearance.

Hearing that her son would follow the conduct of a Kṣatriya— intent on wielding and protecting most terrible weapons— if she were to act contrary to that, while his [other] son would follow the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa, delighting in tranquility,
she grasped his feet at the very moment she heard this.
And having prostrated before him, he said:

"O Blessed One, this was performed by me out of ignorance; please show me favor. Let my son not be such as this; let my grandson indeed be of such a nature. When he had spoken thus, the sage replied, "So be it."
And immediately thereafter, she gave birth to Jamadagni.
And his mother gave birth to Viśvāmitra.
Satyavatī also became a river named Kauśikī.
Jamadagni married Reṇukā, the daughter of Reṇu, who was born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
And in her, Jamadagni begot the one known as Paraśurāma, the destroyer of all Kṣatriyas, who was a portion (aṃśa) of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of all the worlds.
Śunaḥśepa, though the son of Viśvāmitra, was indeed a Bhārgava given by the gods; consequently, he became known by the name Devarāta.
And thereafter, there were other sons of Viśvāmitra named Madhu, Chanda, Dhanañjaya, Kṛtadeva, Aṣṭaka, Kacchapa, and Hari.
And among them, many lineages of the Kauśikas became intermarried with other ṛṣi families.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: The eldest son of Purūravas, named Āyu, married the daughter of Rāhu.
And upon her, he begot five sons.
Nahuṣa, Kṣatravṛddha, Raṃbha, Raji, and likewise Anenas was the fifth son.
From Kṣatravṛddha, a son named Suhotra was born.
Kāśyapa, Kāśa, and Gṛtsamada were his three sons.
Śaunaka was the son of Gṛtsamada, and he was the one who established the system of the four social orders.
Kāśeya was the son of Kāśya, the king of Kāśī; from him came Rāṣṭra, and Dīrghatapas was the son of Rāṣṭra.
Dhanvantari, however, was the son of Dīrghatapas.
For he was one whose purpose was fully accomplished; and by the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, the knower of all knowledge, a boon was granted to him in a former birth regarding all manifestations.
"Having descended into the lineage of the King of Kāśī, you shall properly divide the Ayurveda into eight parts and become a partaker of the sacrificial offerings."
The son of that Dhanvantari was Ketumān; the son of Ketumān was Bhīmaratha; his son was Divodāsa; and his son was Pratardana.
And because he destroyed the lineage of Bhadraśreṇya and conquered all his enemies, he became known as Śatrujit (the Conqueror of Enemies).
And because he was addressed as "Vatsavatsa" by his joyful father, he became known as Vatsa.
Through his devotion to truth, he obtained the name Ṛtadhvaja.
And from that he obtained a horse named Kuvalaya; consequently, he became renowned throughout this earth as Kuvalayāśva.

And that Vatsa had a son named Alarka, concerning whom this verse is sung even today: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.8.16: "O Alarka, do not set your mind upon unrighteousness; for the wheel of the kingdom turns with great speed."
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
no other youth besides Alarka enjoyed the earth.
To that Alarka also was born a son named Sannati.
From Sannati was born Sunītha; his son was Suketu, and from him Dharmaketu was born.

From him came Satyaketu; from him, Vibhu; from him, Tattvayajña; from him, Sukumāra; his son was Dṛṣṭaketu; from him, Vītihotra; from him, Bhārga; and the son of Bhārga was Bhārgabhūmi. From him arose the Cāturvarṇya dynasty;
these are declared to be the kings of the Kāśyapa lineage.
Now hear about the lineage of Raji.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth part of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"Rajas, moreover, had five hundred sons who were endowed with incomparable strength, prowess, and the essence of illusion."
And at the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras, both the gods and the asuras, desiring to slay one another, approached Brahmā and questioned him.
"O Blessed One, in this dispute between us, which side will be the victor?"
Then the Blessed One said:
"For whose sake will Raji himself, with weapons grasped, fight so that their side shall be victorious?"
Then, having been approached by the Daityas and requested to provide them with his assistance, Raji spoke:
Having heard this—"I shall fight for your sake, provided that through victory over the immortals I shall become your Indra"—they spoke as follows.
"We shall not speak otherwise nor act otherwise; Prahlāda is our Indra, and for that purpose alone is this effort," said the Asuras,
and when they had departed, the gods likewise spoke to that lord of the earth, and when he replied in the same manner, the gods desired that he should become their Indra.
Raji, assisted by the divine army, also destroyed that entire host of great asuras with numerous mighty weapons.
Then Devendra, having conquered the faction of his enemies, pressed his own pair of feet against his head and said:
"Because you provide protection from fear and give the gift of food, you are our father; you are the most supreme among all people, whose son I am, the lord of the three worlds."
And that king, laughing, said:
"So be it, so be it; this prostration, though filled with many kinds of flattering words, is not to be transgressed even by an enemy," having said this, he went to his own city.
Śatakratu also exercised the office of Indra.
When Raji had ascended to heaven, the sons of Raji, urged by the seer Nārada, requested the kingdom from Śatakratu, their own father’s son, according to established custom.
And by not giving [the sacrificial horse], they conquered Indra and, being exceedingly powerful themselves, assumed the status of Indra.
Then, after a long period of time had passed, Śatakratu, having seen Bṛhaspati in private and having been deprived of his sacrificial portion from the three worlds, said:
"Even a piece of sacrificial cake the size of a jujube fruit would suffice to satisfy me; please give it to me," he said, and Bṛhaspati replied:
"If you had urged me to this earlier, what would I not have done for your sake?

In just a few days, I would have caused you to attain your own station," he said; and having spoken thus, he offered oblations day after day for their sorcery and for the delusion of their intellects, as well as for the increase of Indra's splendor.
And they too, being overcome by that delusion of intellect, became haters of Brahman, abandoners of dharma, and turned their backs on the declarations of the Vedas.
Then Indra struck them down, for they had departed from the practice of dharma.
And Śakra, his splendor nourished by the domestic priest, ascended to heaven.
Having heard this account of Indra’s ascent from his fall from his own station, a person does not suffer the loss of their own position nor the corruption of their character.
Rambha, however, was childless.
The son of Kṣatravṛddha was Pratikṣatra.
His son was Saṃjaya; his son was Jaya; his son was Vijaya; and from him was born Kṛta.
His son was Haryadhana; Haryadhana’s son was Sahadeva; from him came Adīna; his son was Jayatsena; and from him came Saṃkṛti. His son was Kṣatradharmā—these were the descendants of Kṣatravṛddha.
Next, I shall proclaim the lineage of Nahuṣa.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Viyāti, and Kṛti—these were the six sons of Nahuṣa, endowed with great strength and prowess.
The ascetic did not desire the kingdom.
Yayāti, however, became a king.
And he married Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Uśanas, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan named Devayānī.

Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Druhyu, as well as Turvasu;
and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, bore Anu, Pūru, and [the others].
And due to the curse of a poet, Yayāti attained old age in the course of time alone.
And because of the words of Prasannaśukra, he spoke to his eldest son Yadu in order to transfer his own old age upon him.
"My child, due to the curse of your maternal grandfather, this old age has come upon me prematurely; by his grace, I shall transfer it to you."
For a thousand years I have remained unsatiated with sense-objects; through your youth, I desire to enjoy those objects.
When he was told, "You must not refuse this," Yadu did not wish to accept that old age.
And his father cursed him, saying: "Your offspring shall not be worthy of the kingdom."
And immediately thereafter, the lord of the earth requested Durvasu, Druhyu, and Anu to accept his old age in exchange for the gift of his own youth.
Being rejected by each of them in turn, he cursed them.
Then she spoke in the same manner to Puru, the youngest son of Śarmiṣṭhā.
With a mind deeply inclined toward it, he bowed with great reverence to his father, declared, "This is a great favor for us," and accepted old age.
And he gave his own youth to his father.
Having attained youth, he too enjoyed the objects of the senses according to his desire, at the appropriate time, with due energy, and without contravening righteousness.
And he protected his subjects correctly.
Thinking, "Having enjoyed pleasures together with Viśvācī and Devayānī, I shall reach the end of all desires," he became day by day single-mindedly intent upon that.
And day by day, through his enjoyment of them, he considered even the most delightful desires to be no more than that.
Then they sang this verse to him:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more. (ViP 4.10.22–23)
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon this earth are not sufficient for even one person; therefore, one should abandon craving.
When a man harbors no evil intent toward any living being,
then, possessing an even vision, all directions appear full of happiness to him.
The wise man should utterly abandon that craving which is so difficult for the foolish to give up and which does not age even as one ages; by doing so, he is filled with happiness.
The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth of an aging man decay;
but the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay, even as one ages.
For a full thousand years my mind has been attached to sense objects;
nevertheless, day after day, thirst for them continues to arise within me.
Therefore, having abandoned this [world] and fixed my mind upon Brahman,
I shall become free from dualities and free from the sense of "mine," and wander together with the deer.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having taken the old age from Puru and having given him his youth,
and having consecrated Puru upon the throne, he departed for the forest to practice asceticism.
He assigned Durvasu to the south-eastern quarter,
Druhyu to the western, and then Yadu to the southern.
And having likewise subdued the sovereign kings of the north,
he consecrated Puru as the lord of the entire earth and retired to the forest.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Hereafter, I shall narrate the lineage of Yadu, the first son of Yayāti.

Therein, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu— without beginning or end, whose majesty is immeasurable, and who is eternally praised by all the inhabitants of the world, including humans, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, guhyakas, kiṃpuruṣas, apsarases, uragas, birds, daityas, dānavas, ādityas, rudras, vasus, aśvins, maruts, and divine sages, as well as by those seeking liberation and those desiring virtue, wealth, pleasure, and release, for the sake of attaining their respective fruits— descended.
On this point, there is a verse: // ViP_4,11.3 //
When a person hears the lineage of Yadu, they are liberated from all sins;
therein descended the Supreme Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a human form.
Sahasrajit, Kroṣṭu, Nala, and Nahuṣa were the four sons of Yadu.
Sahasrajit’s son was Śatajit.
He had three sons: Haihaya, Haya, and Veṇuhaya.
The son of Haihaya was Dharma; his son was Dharmanetra, from whom came Kunti, and the son of Kunti was Sahajit.
His son was Mahiṣmān, who laid waste to the city of Māhiṣmatī.
From him came Bhadraśreṇya; from him, Durdama; and from him, Dhanaka. To Dhanaka were born four sons: Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, Kṛtadharma, and Kṛtaujas.
From Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna, who possessed a thousand arms and was the sovereign of the seven continents.
He, who was born in the lineage of Atri as a portion of the Blessed One, having propitiated the one named Dattātreya, obtained these boons: a thousand arms for the prevention of unrighteousness,

devotion to his own duty, victory over the earth in battle, protection according to dharma, invincibility against enemies, and death at the hands of a man renowned throughout the entire world— and he indeed received them.
By him, this earth, comprising all its continents, was perfectly protected.
He performed ten thousand sacrifices.
And a verse concerning him is sung even today: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.11.15: "O King, you have indeed performed a great deed; for you have slain the wicked son of Tāraka, who was invincible to all the gods."
Surely no other kings will ever attain the status of Kārtavīrya,
whether by means of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, humility, or sacred learning.
And in his kingdom, there was no loss of property.
And thus, for eighty-five thousand years, he ruled the kingdom with unimpeded health, prosperity, strength, and valor.
He was stationed in Māhiṣmatī after arriving there during his conquest of the quarters.
And he who was withdrawn at the conclusion of the period characterized by eighty-five thousand years by Paraśurāma, who was a portion of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa.
And he had five sons who were the foremost among his hundred sons, known by the names Śūra, Śūrasena, Vṛṣasena, Madhu, and Jayadhvaja.
From Jayadhvaja was born a son named Tālajaṅgha. // 22 //
Tālajaṅgha had a hundred sons known as the Tālajaṅghas.
Among these, the eldest was Vītihotra, and another was Bharata.
From Bharata came Vṛṣa.
Vaṣa’s son was Madhu.
He, too, had one hundred sons, the foremost of whom was Vṛṣṇi.
From him this lineage obtained the name of Vṛṣṇi.
And because of the cause known as Madhu, he became sweet.
And the Yādavas are so called because they are characterized by the name Yadu.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: The son of Kroṣṭu, the son of Yadu, was Dhvajinīvān.
From him came Svāti; from him, Ruśaṅku; and from Ruśaṅku, Citraratha.
His son was Śaśibindu, who became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and the lord of the fourteen great jewels.
And he had one hundred thousand wives by name.
And his sons numbered one million.
And they had six principal sons: Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthukarman, Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthujaya, and Pṛthudāna.
And the son of Pṛthuśravas was Pṛthutama.
Therefore, Uśanas was he who performed a hundred horse sacrifices.
And he had a son named Śitapu.
After him came Rukmakavaca, and after him Paravṛt.
His son was Parāvṛta; his five sons were Rukmeṣu, Pṛthu, Jyāmagha, Valita, and Harita by name.
Therefore, even today, the verse concerning Jyāmagha is sung:
Among all those who will exist or have existed as men subject to their wives,
King Jyāmagha, the husband of Śaivyā, was the most excellent.
His wife, named Śaivyā, was childless;
nevertheless, although he desired offspring, he did not take another wife out of fear.
Once, however, while fighting in a great and most terrible battle crowded with many chariots, horses, and elephants, he conquered the entire circle of his enemies.
And that sixfold circle [of his forces]—having abandoned its own capital and cast aside its sons, wives, kinsmen, troops, and treasury—fled in all directions.
And as he fled, he beheld that jewel of a princess, her pair of long eyes trembling with extreme terror, distressed by agitated lamentations such as, "Save me, save me, father! Mother! Brother!
Upon seeing her, the king’s inner soul was filled with passion for her, and he thought: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.12.17–18.18b.
"Excellent! To me, who am childless and the husband of a barren woman, Fate has now provided this jewel of a daughter as the very cause for obtaining offspring."
"Therefore, I shall carry this [burden]. (ViP 4.12.20)
Or else, having placed her upon a chariot, I shall lead her to my own abode.
"Permitted by that very goddess Śivā, I shall marry her."
Then, having placed her upon the chariot, he went to his own city.
And Śaivyā, accompanied by the entire assembly of citizens, servants, attendants, and ministers, came to the palace gate to see King Vijayin.
Having looked at the maiden standing on the king’s left side, her sprout-like lower lip quivering with a slight surge of indignation, she spoke to the king.
"Who is this woman with such an unagitated mind who has been placed upon this chariot? ||| ViP_4.12.26 |||
He too, out of extreme fear that his reply would not be well-considered, said to her, "She is my daughter-in-law."
Then Śaivya said to him:
I was not born of your son, nor did any other woman become your wife;
for with which of your sons, O Uṣas, do you have the relationship of a daughter-in-law?
Śrī Parāśara said:

Thus, his discrimination having been stolen away by words defiled with self-conceit, envy, and anger, the lord of the earth spoke this out of fear, in order to avoid the censure of the harsh words [already spoken].

Hearing it said, "This [daughter] has been designated as the wife for that son who shall be born to you, even though he is yet to come," she replied, "So be it," with a gentle smile arising on her face.
And he entered the city together with the king.

Immediately thereafter, Śaibyā—though she had reached the decline of her youth due to the merits of the birth of a son having been secured through the auspicious conjunctions of an exceedingly pure *lagna*, *horā*, *aṃśaka*, and other divisions—conceived a child within just a few days.
In due time, she gave birth to a boy.
And his father gave him the name Vidarbha.
And he married that daughter-in-law.
And upon her he begot two sons named Āsoka and Krathakaiśika.
And again, he begot a third son named Romapāda, who was destined to obtain knowledge from Nārada.
From Romapāda was born Babhru; from Babhru came Dhṛti; from Dhṛti came Kaiśika; and from Kaiśika was born Cedi as a son, in whose lineage the Caidya kings arose.
Kunti became the daughter-in-law of Kratha's son.

From Kunti was born Dhṛṣṭi; from Dhṛṣṭi came Nidhṛti; from Nidhṛti came Daśārha, and from him Vyoma; his son was Jīmūta, and from him Vikṛti; from him came Bhībharatha, from whom Navaratha was born; his son was Daśaratha, and from him Śakuni; his son was Karaṃbhi, and from Karaṃbhi Devarāta was born.
From him came Devakṣatra; his son was Madhu; from Madhu came Kumāravaṃśa; from Kumāravaṃśa came Anu; and from Anu came Purumitra, who became the lord of the earth.
And from him, Aṃśu was born of Satvata.
Because they possess the quality of goodness (sattva), they are called Sātvatas.
O Maitreya, having heard this lineage of Jyāmagha, a man who is endowed with perfect faith is liberated from his own sins.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Bhajana, Bhajamāna, Divya, Andhaka, Devāvṛdha, Mahābhoja, and Vṛṣṇi were the sons of Satvata.
To Bhajamāna were born Nimi, Kṛkaṇa, and Vṛṣmi; likewise, there were three others of different mothers known as Śatajit, Sahasrajit, and Ayutajit.
Babhru was also the son of Devāvṛdha.

And this verse is sung in three parts: ViP_4.13.4: "From the mind was born the first creation, consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest; from the Unmanifest arose the Manifest, and from the Manifest arose the Manifest again."
Just as we hear him from afar, so do we behold him from nearby;
he is the tawny one, the best among men, equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
Sixty-eight thousand and six men attained immortality through Babhru Devāvṛdha as well.
Mahābhoja, however, was exceedingly righteous; in his lineage were the Bhojas, who became known as the Mārtikāvatas because they resided in the city of Mṛttikāvatī.
To Vṛṣṇi were born two sons, Sumitra and Yudhājit.
From him was born Anamitra, and from Anamitra was born Nighna.
Nighna’s [sons] were Prasena and Satrājit.
And the blessed Āditya was a friend of that Satrājit.
Once, while staying on the shore of the ocean, Satrājit praised the Sun with single-minded devotion; and being thus extolled, the Radiant One stood before him.
Then, seeing the Sun with his form indistinct, Satrājit spoke to him.

"Just as I previously saw you in the sky like a mass of fire, even though you have now come before me, I do not perceive any specific mark bestowed upon you by the Blessed One. When this was said, the Blessed One Sūrya unfastened from his own neck the supreme great jewel named Syamantaka, brought it down, and placed it aside.
Then he beheld the Sun, whose body was copper-red and radiant, short of stature, and with eyes slightly tawny.
After Satrājit had performed prostrations, hymns of praise, and other such acts, the Blessed Lord Āditya, the thousand-rayed one, said to him: "Choose from me whatever boon you desire."
And he requested that very same jewel.
And he, the lord of rays, having given that to him, ascended his own celestial chariot in the sky.
Satrājit also, his neck adorned with that stainless jewel-gem, entered Dvārakā, illuminating the interiors of all directions with his splendors like the sun.

The people residing in Dvārakā, beholding the Blessed One—the primordial person, the Supreme Person—who had assumed a human form through a portion of himself for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, prostrated before him and said:
"O Blessed One, surely it is the sun that comes to see you. Thus addressed, the Blessed One replied.
"O Blessed One, this is not the sun; this is Satrājit, who approaches here bearing the great jewel-gem named Amataka, which was given to him by the Sun."
Having been told, "Therefore, look at this with confidence," they saw it exactly as described.
And he placed that Syamantaka jewel in his own residence.
Every day, that jewel-gem flows forth eight bhāras of gold.
And by his power, no fear arises for the entire kingdom from calamities such as drought, predatory beasts, fire, or famine.
Acyuta also desired that divine jewel, thinking, "This is suitable for King Ugrasena."
Out of fear of causing a division among the clans, he did not take it away, even though he was capable of doing so. // 28 //
Thinking, "Satrājit will surely ask me for this," and out of greed for the jewel, he gave that gem to his brother Prasena.

When worn by one who is pure, it produces an entire multitude of qualities, such as the flow of gold; otherwise, it destroys the very person wearing it. Unaware of this, Prasena, with the Syamantaka fastened around his neck, mounted his horse and went out into the forest for the hunt.
And there, he met his death at the hands of a lion.
Having slain him along with his horse, the lion was about to depart, seizing a pure jewel from its mouth with its jaws, when he was spotted and killed by Jāmbavān, the lord of the bears.
Jāmbavān also, taking a spotless jewel-gem, entered his own cave.
And for the boy known as Sukumāra, he fashioned a toy.

When Prasena did not return, Kṛṣṇa desired that jewel-gem; and since it had been found, all the Yadu people, having heard of the matter from one another, said to each other, "Surely this is his doing.
Having learned of this report of public scandal, the Blessed One, surrounded by the entire host of the Yadu army, followed the tracks of Prasena’s horse.
And he beheld Prasena, who had been slain by a lion, lying there together with his horse.
Having been cleared of suspicion by the sight of the lion’s tracks in the midst of all the people, he followed the lion’s tracks.
And having seen even a lion slain by the lord of bears within a small area of ground, he then followed the tracks of the bear out of respect for that jewel.
Having stationed that entire Yadu army on the mountain slope, he followed their tracks and entered the bear's cave.
And having entered within, he heard the voice of the nurse as she was fondling the delicate infant.
"The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep for Sukumāra, for this Syamantaka belongs to you."
Having heard this, he entered and saw the Syamantaka gem, which had been turned into a plaything by the prince and was held in the hand of the nurse, blazing with its own splendors.
Beholding that unprecedented man who had arrived with eyes longing for the Syamantaka, the nurse cried out, "Save me! Save me! (ViP 4.13.43–44).
Immediately after hearing that cry of distress, Jāmbavān, his heart filled with indignation, arrived there.
And between those two, who were both arrogant and filled with mutual wrath, the battle lasted for twenty-one days.
And those soldiers of the Yadus remained there for seven or eight days, waiting expectantly for his departure.
"If he does not escape, this enemy of Madhu will certainly meet his utter destruction here in this cave;
otherwise, while he is still alive, how could he have been so preoccupied with conquering his enemies for all these days?
Having thus resolved, they returned to Dvārakā and announced, "Kṛṣṇa has been killed."
And his kinsmen performed the entire range of subsequent funeral rites appropriate for that occasion.
And as he was fighting, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s strength and vital energy were nourished by the food, water, and other provisions provided in excellent vessels by those who offered with great faith.

For the other, who was being struck daily by a man of exceeding great strength, with all his limbs pained by the falling of excessively harsh blows, there occurred a loss of strength due to his lack of food.
And having been defeated by the Blessed One, Jāmbavān bowed down and spoke.

Even by all the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others, you cannot be conquered; how much less so by men of little prowess who range upon the earth, who are merely parts of a man, and who follow the path of animal births? How much more so then by one like me? Surely our lord Rāma is the Blessed One, an emanation of Nārāyaṇa, the ultimate refuge of the entire world.
When he was told, "You must be born," the Blessed One explained his descent to him for the purpose of removing the entire burden of the earth.
And by touching him with the palm of his hand, which was expressive of affection, he caused him to be free from the fatigue of battle.
And he, having prostrated himself and once again propitiated him, caused his daughter named Jāmbavatī to be offered as an *arghya* gift to her who had come to his house.
He also prostrated before him and presented the Syamantaka jewel.
Although it was ungraspable, Viṣṇu, despite being immovable, took that jewel from him who was deeply prostrate, for the sake of purifying himself.
Together with Jāmbavatī, he returned to Dvārakā.

At the mere sight of Kṛṣṇa, the inhabitants of Dvārakā, whose joy had reached its peak at the Lord’s arrival, appeared as if they had entered the prime of youth at that very moment, even though their ages were already far advanced. "By good fortune! By good fortune! cried all the Yādavas and the women, offering their congratulations.
The Blessed One, for his part, related everything exactly as it had been experienced, in its entirety and in due order, to the assembly of the Yādavas.
And having given the Syamantaka jewel to Satrājit, he attained purification from the false accusation.
And he settled Jāmbavatī in the inner apartments.
Satrājit, too, being seized with terror because I had falsely attributed the stain of sin to him, gave his daughter Satyabhāmā to the Blessed One as a wife.
And the Yādavas, headed by Akrūra, Kṛtavarman, and Śatadhanvan, had previously sought her hand in marriage.
Then, considering themselves insulted by that gift, they harbored a persistent enmity toward Satrājit.
And Akrūra, Kṛtavarman, and the others, headed by them, spoke to Śatadhanvan:
This Satrājit is exceedingly wicked, for even though he was sought after by us and by you, he disregarded both us and you and gave his daughter to Kṛṣṇa.
"Therefore, enough with this life; why do you not kill him and take that great jewel called Syamantaka?
We shall support you if Acyuta continues his pursuit of enmity against you. Being addressed thus, he replied, "So be it."

Although the Blessed One knew the ultimate truth regarding the sons of Pāṇḍu who had been burned in the house of lac, he went to Vāraṇāvata to cause Duryodhana’s efforts to slacken or to act in favor of the Pārthas; and when he had departed, Śatadhanvan killed Satrājit while he was asleep and took the jewel-gem.

Filled with indignation at the murder of her father, Satyabhāmā quickly mounted her chariot and went to Vāraṇāvata. She said to the Blessed One, "Our father was slain by the intolerant Śatadhanvan, who claimed, 'I have bestowed [you] upon the Blessed One'; he has also stolen that Syamantaka jewel, by whose radiance the three worlds shall be freed from darkness."
Having considered that derision of yours directed toward him, he said to Kṛṣṇa, "Let that which is appropriate in this matter be done."
Thus addressed by her, Kṛṣṇa, though his heart was deeply gratified, spoke to Satyabhāmā with eyes copper-red with indignation.
By truth, this mockery is directed at me alone; I shall not endure it from that evil-minded one.

"For birds that dwell in nests built upon another tree are not killed without first having bypassed that tree. Having said, "Enough of this elaborate speech of the son of Sukanyā before us," Vāsudeva went to Dvārakā and spoke to Baladeva in private.
While Prasenajit was out hunting in the forest, a lord of beasts killed him.
Now Satrājit, too, has been brought to his death by Śatadhanvan.
Because both of those will be destroyed, that jewel will become common property for us two.
"Therefore, rise up; mount the chariot and make an effort for the destruction of Śatadhanvan. Being thus addressed, he replied, "So be it," and prepared accordingly.
Perceiving that both of them were exerting themselves, Śatadhanvan approached Kṛtavarman and urged him to provide support for the sake of the task.
And Kṛtavarman said this to him:
Having been told, "I am not capable of opposing Baladeva and Vāsudeva," he urged Akrūra [to go].
He too said:

Indeed, no one was capable of fighting even against the foremost of the immortals, who are worshipped by the entire world— let alone against the Blessed One, the wielder of the discus (Cakrin), whose wheel is unimpeded by the hosts of powerful enemies, who caused the widowhood of the wives of the gods' enemies by shaking the three worlds with a kick of his foot; nor against the wielder of the plow (Sīrin), whose great strength and vast furrow-like arms stripped away the most formidable enemy elephants, and who destroys all the night-stalkers (demons) with a glance from eyes gladdened by intoxication.
"How much more so am I, who am other than him? Let another refuge be sought," he said; thus addressed, Śatadhanu replied:
"If you perceive yourself to be incapable of protecting us, then let this jewel be taken from us for now and preserved."
Being addressed thus, he also spoke:
"If you do not tell this to anyone even in the final stage [of life], then I shall accept it."
When he had said, "So be it," Akrūra took that precious jewel.
Śatadhanu, moreover, mounted the mare Vaḍavā—who possessed incomparable speed and could travel a hundred yojanas—and escaped.
Baladeva and Vāsudeva followed him as they sat upon a chariot yoked with the four horses Śaivya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka.
And that mare, having traversed a path measuring one hundred yojanas, while being driven further, gave up her life in the region of the Mithilā forest.
Śatadhanu, too, having abandoned her, fled on foot.
Kṛṣṇa also spoke to Balabhadra.

"You must remain here in this chariot while I, on foot, follow that man of vile conduct on foot until I have slain him; for in this region there are visible dangers and fears, so these horses of yours must not be allowed to cross over this stretch of ground."
Having said, "So be it," Baladeva remained right there upon the chariot.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having followed the ground for a distance of two krośas, hurled his discus from afar and severed the head of Śatadhanu.
Although he searched in many ways through his body, garments, and other belongings, he did not find the Syamantaka jewel; then, approaching Balabhadra, he said:

Hearing that Śatadhanu had been killed by us in vain, and that the great jewel named Syamantaka—the very essence of the world which is not made of stone—had not been obtained, Baladeva was filled with rage and said to Vāsudeva:
"Fie on you! You who desire wealth in this manner—this I have endured because of our brotherhood. Therefore, this is the path; go as you please.

I have no need for Dvārakā, nor for you, nor for all my kinsmen. Enough, enough with these false oaths before me! Having thus rebuked him, he did not remain, even though he was being entreated in some way to stay.
He entered the city of Videha.
King Janaka, having first offered him the arghya water, caused him to enter his palace.
And he remained right there.
Vāsudeva also returned to Dvārakā.
And for as long as Balabhadra remained in the palace of King Janaka, Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, received instruction in the art of the mace from him.

At the end of three years, the Yādavas, led by Babhru and Ugrasena, having concluded that Kṛṣṇa had not taken that jewel, went to the city of Videha; there they convinced Baladeva and brought him back to Dvārakā.
Akrūra, intent on meditation upon the Blessed One, incessantly performed sacrifices with gold produced from the finest jewels.

For he remained there, having entered the armor of initiation (dīkṣākavaca) in this manner: "Indeed, by slaying even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has gone to a Soma sacrifice, one does not become a Brahmin-slayer."
For exactly sixty-two years, by the power of that jewel, there was no occurrence of calamities, famine, pestilence, or death there.
Then, when Śatrughna had slain Akrūra’s great-grandson on behalf of the Bhojas who were partisans of Akrūra, Akrūra himself fled from Dvārakā along with those Bhojas.
From the day he departed, calamities such as portents, famine, predatory beasts, drought, pestilence, and other afflictions occurred there.
Then the Yādavas, assembled with Balabhadra and Ugrasena, held a consultation.
The Blessed One, whose banner bears the serpent-king, said, "What is this? Let this sudden arrival of so many calamities be considered. Thus addressed, the elder of the Yadus named Indhaka spoke.
