Wherever this Akrūra’s father, Śvaphalka, was present, there no famine, pestilence, drought, or similar calamities occurred.
In the territory of the King of Kāśī, however, Śvaphalka was led away due to a drought; and from that very moment, the god sent down rain.
And previously, there was a jewel of a daughter in the womb of the wife of the King of Kāśī.
And that maiden did not emerge at all, even when the time for birth was fully arrived.
And thus twelve years passed for that embryo while it remained within her womb.
And the King of Kāśī spoke to his daughter while she was still in the womb:
"Daughter, why do you not come forth? I wish to see your face, and why will you cause this mother of yours to suffer for so long? Having been addressed thus, while still within the womb she replied:
"Father, if you give one cow each day to a Brāhmaṇa, then after three more years I shall certainly emerge from this womb. Hearing these words, the king [began] giving [a cow] to a Brāhmaṇa every day.
He gave a cow.
She too was born after that same amount of time.
Thereupon, her father gave her the name Gāndinī.
And he gave that maiden Gāndinī as an offering of hospitality (arghya) to Śphalka, who had come to his house as a benefactor.
From him and Śvaphalkā was born this Akrūra.
From that very pair of qualities, his birth occurred.
Therefore, how will there be no calamities such as famine and pestilence here once he has departed?

"Therefore, let him be brought here; enough with searching for faults in one who possesses such great virtues. Having heard these words of the elder Andhaka, the Yadus—headed by Keśava, Ugrasena, and Balabhadra—desiring to forgive the offense committed, granted him safety, and the son of Śvaphalka was brought forth by them. Thus ends the thirteenth canto of the fourth book.
And as soon as he arrived there, by the power of that Syamantaka jewel, the calamities of drought, pestilence, famine, wild beasts, and so forth were all pacified.
Kṛṣṇa reflected.
This is a very minor cause: that this Akrūra was begotten by Śvaphalka upon Gāndinī.
And this power of his is exceedingly great, acting as a preventer of calamities such as drought, famine, and pestilence.
That great jewel named Syamantaka remains with that person who possesses the entire horde of cattle.
For indeed, such powers of his are heard of.
Moreover, immediately after one sacrifice he performs another rite, and immediately after that another sacrifice; thus he sacrifices incessantly and without interruption.

Having become certain that "without a doubt this excellent jewel remains here," and having resolved that it was there, Janārdana convened the entire assembly of the Yādavas at his own home under the pretext of some other purpose.
When all the Yadus were seated there, he first introduced the original matter; once that was concluded, and after engaging in casual conversation with Akrūra on another topic, Janārdana said to him:
"O Lord of Generosity, we already know how Śatadhanvan [stole] this Syamantaka, which is the very essence of the entire world."

"This jewel of yours, which benefits the entire kingdom, remains in your presence; let it remain there, for we all shall enjoy its power and fruit. However, this Balabhadra has become suspicious of us; therefore, show it to him for our sake. Having spoken thus, while the Blessed Vāsudeva remained silent, he [Balarāma] reflected upon the jewel.
"What should be done here? If I speak otherwise, these men, searching for a jewel, will see only the concealment of the sky.
Thinking that such extreme opposition would not be appropriate, Krūra spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the cause of the entire world.

"O Blessed One, this Syamantaka jewel was entrusted to me by Satadhanvan; and thinking that the Blessed One would request it today, tomorrow, or the day after, now that he has departed, I have held onto it for so long with great difficulty."
And by means of the power of that retention, my mind became unattached to all enjoyments, so that I did not perceive even a fraction of my own happiness.
Thinking that you might consider yourself unable to sustain even this much for the benefit of the entire kingdom, he did not urge you himself.
Therefore, let this Syamantaka jewel be taken; let it be handed over to whomever desires it.
Then he revealed a very small golden casket that had been hidden within the garment on his own belly.
Then, having departed, he released the Syamantaka jewel into that assembly of the Yadu clan.
And as soon as he was released, that entire assembly hall was illuminated by his exceeding splendor.
Then Akrūra said: "This is the very jewel that was entrusted to us by Śatadhanvan; let him who is its rightful owner take it."
Beholding him, the voices of all the Yādavas, their minds filled with wonder, were heard crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Beholding him, Balabhadra felt an intense longing, thinking, "This man is sought after by me as being equal to Acyuta himself."
Thinking, "This is my father's wealth," Satyabhāmā also desired it exceedingly.
By beholding his own power and truth, even Kṛṣṇa considered himself as if situated within the interior of a wheel of spokes.
In the presence of all the Yādavas, he spoke to Akrūra.
For this jewel was shown by me for the sake of purifying myself before these Yadus; it is the common paternal inheritance of both myself and Balabhadra, belonging to Satyabhāmā and no one else.

It must always be worn by one who is pure and endowed with virtues such as celibacy, for while being so worn, it benefits the entire kingdom; however, if worn by one who is impure, it destroys the very vessel that holds it.
Therefore, since I am unable to maintain this collection of sixteen thousand women, how can Satyavāmā accept this?
Ārbaḷabhadra, too, must renounce the drinking of wine and all other forms of sensual enjoyment.
Therefore, enough of this; O Lord of Generosity, we—the people of Yadu, Balabhadra, myself, and Satyā—all entreat you.
Therefore, you alone are capable of upholding it.

"Moreover, that which you hold is beneficial to this kingdom; therefore, for the sake of the entire realm, may your lordship continue to wear it as before. Nothing more need be said. Thus addressed, the Lord of Gifts replied, "So be it," and took up that great jewel.
From that time forward, Akrūra moved about with that exceedingly radiant necklace visibly hanging around his own neck, appearing like the sun encircled by its rays.

This is the cleansing of the Lord’s false accusation; whoever remembers this shall never suffer even the slightest false accusation, and with unimpeded conduct and senses, he attains liberation from all sins.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
The son of Anamitra was named Śini.
From that Satyaka was born Sātyaki, whose other name was Yuyudhāna.
From him also were born Saṃjaya, his son Kuṇi, and from Kuṇi, Yugandhara.
These were the descendants of Śini.
In the lineage of Anamitra was Vṛṣṇi; from him came Śvaphalka, whose power was such that he was born from a mere cough.
Śvaphalka had another younger brother named Citraka.
From Śvaphalka and Gāndinī, Akrūra was born.
Likewise was Upamadgu.
His sons were named Upamadgu, Mṛdu, Amṛdu, Viśvāri, Mejayagiri, Kṣatropa, Kṣatraśataghnāri, Mardana, Dharmadṛg, Dṛṣṭadharma, Gandha, Ojavāha, and Prativāha; his daughter was named Sutārā;
and Devavān and Upadeva were the two sons of Akrūra.
Citraka had many sons, of whom Pṛthu and Vivṛtha were the foremost.
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣ—these were the four sons of Andhaka.
From Kukura was born Dhṛṣṭa; from him came Kapotaroman; from him came Viloman; and from him was born one named Anu, who became a friend of Tumburu.
From Anurādhā comes Ārdrā, from that Abhijit, and from Abhijit Punarvasu.
His [sons] were Āhuka and his daughter Āhukī.
Āhuka had two sons, Devaka and Ugrasena.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Sahadeva, and Devarakṣita were the four sons of Devaka.
Their seven sisters were Vṛkā, Devā, Upadevā, Devarakṣitā, Śrīdevā, Śāntidevā, Sahadevā, and Devakī.
And Vasudeva married all of them.
Ugrasena also had sons named Kaṃsa, Nyagrodha, Sunāmānaka, Āhvaya, Śaṅku, Subhūmi, Rāṣṭrapāla, Yuddhatuṣṭi, Sutuṣṭi, and Matsya.
Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapālī, and Āhvayā were the daughters of Ugrasena.
And from Bhajamāna, a son named Vidūratha was born.
From Vidūratha came Śūra; from Śūra came Shamī; from Shamī came Pratikṣatra; from him came Svayaṃbhoja, and from him came Hṛdika.
He, too, had sons such as Kṛtavarman, Śatadhanu, Dvādaśārha, Devagarbha, and others.
Śūra was also the son of Devagarbha.
Mārīṣā was the name of Śūra’s wife as well, O noble one.
And upon her, he begot ten sons who were equal in splendor to Vasudeva.
As soon as Vasudeva was born, the gods, perceiving with unobstructed vision that an incarnation of a portion of the Blessed Lord had occurred in his house, sounded divine kettledrums.
And thereafter, he received the name Ānakadundubhi.
And he had nine brothers named Devabhāga, Devaśravas, Aṣṭaka, Kakutstha, Cakravat, Dhāraka, Sṛñjaya, Śyāma, and Śamika Gañjūṣa.
Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, Śrutakīrti, Śrutaśravā, and Rājādhidevī were the five sisters of Vasudeva and the others.
Śūra had a friend named Kunti.
And to him, who was childless, Śūra gave his own daughter Pṛthā according to the prescribed rites.
And Pāṇḍu married her.
And upon her, three sons named Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna were begotten by the winds of Dharma.
Even before she was married, a son named Karṇa, born of her maidenhood, was begotten by the illustrious Bhāsvat.
And she had a co-wife named Mādrī.
And upon her, Nakula and Sahadeva, the two sons of Pāṇḍu, were begotten by means of the two Aśvin deities.
Vṛddhadharmā, the king of the Kārūṣas, married Śrutadevā.
And from her was born a great asura named Dantavakra.
The King of Kekaya also married Śrutakīrti.
And in her were born five sons, the Kaikeyas, beginning with Santardana.
From Rājādhidevī were born the two Āvantyas, Vinda and Anuvinda.
The King of Cedi also married Śrutaśravas, whose name was Damaghoṣa.
And upon her, he begot Śiśupāla.
Indeed, he was formerly the first of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu, who possessed noble valor.
And he who was slain by the Blessed One, the teacher of all the worlds, in his Nārasiṃha [incarnation].
Furthermore, he became known as Daśānana, whose qualities of inexhaustible vigor, heroism, excellence, and prowess surpassed the sovereign power of all the lords of the three worlds.
He, who had long enjoyed the fruits of merit arising from the fall of his body obtained in the presence of the Blessed One, was likewise brought to his end by the Blessed One in the form of Rāghava.
Furthermore, there was a son of Damaghoṣa, the king of Cedi, named Śiśupāla.
Even while he was Śiśupāla, he maintained an exceedingly persistent enmity toward the lotus-eyed Lord, who had descended as a partial incarnation for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
And he was brought to his end by the Blessed One; there, through one-pointedness of mind, he attained union with that very Supreme Self.
If the Blessed One is pleased, he grants what is desired; likewise, even when slaying one who is not well-disposed, he bestows a divine and incomparable station.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"In his births as Hiraṇyakaśipu and as Rāvaṇa, [he was slain] by Viṣṇu."
Slain, he attained enjoyments that were unattainable even for the immortals.
How could he, who was slain by that very [Viṣṇu] and had not attained absorption (laya) therein,
again attain union (sāyujya) with the eternal Hari upon becoming Śiśupāla?
I desire to hear this, O best among all upholders of dharma;
being filled with curiosity, you should explain this to me as I have asked.
Śrī Parāśara said:
For the sake of slaying the lord of the Daityas, he who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds previously assumed a body and manifested the form of Nṛsiṃha.
And in that regard, it did not occur to Hiraṇyakaśipu's mind that this was Viṣṇu.
"This race of beings has arisen from a preeminent accumulation of merit."

With his one-pointed mind impelled by an excess of passion, through the practice of meditating upon that [form], he subsequently attained the unsurpassed abundance of enjoyments associated with the state of having ten faces—an achievement caused by the taking of life which brought about his dominion over the entire three worlds.
However, he did not attain absorption into that Blessed One, who is the Supreme Brahman without beginning or end and who provides no support for the mind.
Thus, even though he possessed ten faces, because his mind was dependent on the bodiless god of love and intent upon Jānakī, the Blessed One, assuming the form of the son of Daśaratha,
appeared to him merely in that form; for at the moment of his downfall, the thought "this is Acyuta" did not arise in his internal organ, but only the perception of him as a human being occurred.

Furthermore, he obtained as his fruit merely the avoidance of falling from his celestial state, birth in the royal family of Cedi—which is praised throughout the entire circle of the earth—and unimpeded sovereignty even during his existence as Śiśupāla.
In that regard, O Blessed One, he became the cause for the manifestation of all names indeed.

Consequently, with a mind whose continuity of hatred had been nurtured through many births, he incessantly uttered the names of Acyuta— names that had been used at that time for purposes such as reviling and threatening— in their entirety; and because of the deeply rooted influence of that enmity, his mind did not turn elsewhere from that form— which possessed eyes as pure as the petals of a full-blown lotus, wore exceedingly brilliant yellow garments, was adorned with a crown, armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments, and bore four noble arms holding the conch, discus, and mace— throughout all states of being, whether walking, eating, bathing, sitting, or lying down.

Then, while still uttering those very insults and holding him fast in his heart, he beheld the Blessed One— whose form was the nature of imperishable splendor, radiant with the garland of rays from the discus in his hand, who had become Brahman, free from defects such as hatred, and intent upon his own destruction.

And at that very moment, swiftly struck down by the discus of the Blessed One, with the entire accumulation of his sins burnt away by the remembrance of Him, he was brought to his end by the Blessed One and attained absorption into Him alone.
All this has been related by me to you.

For this Blessed One, when praised or even merely remembered—even through the persistence of hatred—bestows a fruit that is difficult to attain for all the gods and asuras; how much more so for one who possesses perfect devotion?
Vasudeva Ānakadundubhi had many wives, headed by Pauravī, Rohiṇī, Madirā, Bhadrā, Devakī, and others.
Ānakadundubhi begot upon Rohiṇī sons such as Balabhadra, Śaṭha, Sāraṇa, Durmada, and others.
Baladeva also begot two sons, Viśaṭha and Ulmuka, upon Revatī.
Sārṣṭi, Mārṣṭi, Śiśu, Satya, Satyadhṛti, and others were the sons of Sāraṇa.
Bhadrāśva, Bhadrabāhu, Durdama, Bhūta, and others were born into the lineage of Rohiṇī.
These sons of Madirā were produced by Nanda and Upananda through artificial means.
And from Bhadrā were born Upanidhi, Gadā, and others.
And in Vaiśālī, he begot only one son, Kauśika.
To Ānakadundubhi’s wife Devakī were born six sons, renowned as Kīrtimat, Suṣeṇa, Udāyu, Bhadrasena, Ṛjudāsa, and Bhadradeva.
And Kaṃsa slew them all.
And immediately thereafter, at midnight, the yogic sleep sent by the Blessed One drew the seventh embryo from the womb of Rohiṇī and carried it away.
And because of this drawing forth, he also obtained the name Saṃkarṣaṇa.

Then, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— who is the root of the great tree of the entire world, who is beyond the reach of the minds of all gods, asuras, and sages of the past, future, and present, and who was entreated by Brahmā and the other gods led by Agni to remove the burden of the earth— descended into the womb of Devakī, He who is without beginning, middle, or end.
And Yoganidrā, her vast majesty increasing through his grace, entered the womb of Yaśodā, the wife of the cowherd Nanda.
When that lotus-eyed one was being born, this entire world became free from unrighteousness, its mind composed, and devoid of fear from the sun, moon, planets, serpents, and other such dangers;
and by him, once born, this whole world was made to abide upon the path of truth.
When the Blessed One also descended here into the mortal world, he had sixteen thousand one hundred wives.
And among them, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Jāmbavatī, Cāruhāsinī, and others were the eight principal wives.
And upon them, the Lord, whose form is the entirety [of all things] and who is without beginning, begot eighty-eight thousand sons.
And among them, Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāmba, and others were the thirteen principal ones.
Pradyumna also married Rukmiṇī’s daughter, named Rukmavatī.
From her, Aniruddha was born.
Aniruddha also married Subhadrā by name, the granddaughter of Rukmin himself.
From her, his thunderbolt was born.
Sucāru was the younger brother of Vajra, and he too was very handsome.
Thus, even in hundreds of years, it is impossible to state the number of sons belonging to the Yādava clan, which consists of many hundreds of thousands.
For these two verses here have their purpose fulfilled by this.
There were thirty-eight million eight hundred thousand young princes who were skilled teachers and devoted to the practice of archery.
Who could possibly calculate the number of those high-souled Yādavas,
among whom Āhuka always dwells with tens of thousands upon tens of thousands?

Those Daityas of immense strength who were slain in the war between the gods and the asuras were reborn among humans; established in stature and power, all the Yādavas grew up remaining obedient to his command.
The man who always hears this account of the progeny of the Vṛṣṇis is liberated from all sins and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus has this lineage of Yadu been recounted to you in brief.
Now, learn the lineage of Durvāsas.
From Durvasas was born Vahni as his son; from Vahni came Bhārga; from Bhārga came Bhānu; from him came Trayīsānu; from him came Karandhama; and his son was Marutta.
He had a son named Patya.
And from him, she begot Duṣyanta as her son by Pūru.
Thus, due to the curse of Yayāti, his lineage came to rely solely upon the Paurava dynasty.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said: "The son of Druhyu was Babhru."
The bridge of Babhru.
His name was Ārabdha, the son of Setuputra.
The son of Ārabdha was Gāndhāra; from Gāndhāra came Dharma; from Dharma, Ghṛta; from Ghṛta, Durdama; and from him, Pracetās.
The son of Pracetas was Śatadharma; he exercised sovereignty over the numerous Mlecchas of the north.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fourth part of the Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: To Anu, the fourth son of Yayāti, there were three sons named Sabhānara, Cakṣu, and Parama.
Sabhānalaputra is Kālānala. // 2 //
From Kālānala was born Sṛñjaya.
From Sṛñjaya was born Purañjaya.
From Purañjaya was born Janamejaya.
Therefore, he was called Mahāśāla.
And from him was born Mahāmanas.
From him were born two sons, Uśīnara and Titikṣu.
Uśīnara also had five sons named Śibi, Nṛga, Navakṛmi, Varmaka, and Ākhyā.
Pṛṣadaśva, Suvīra, Kekaya, and Madra were the four sons of Śibi.
To Titikṣu also was born a son named Ruśadratha.
His son was Hema; Hema's son was Sutapas, and Sutapas' son was Bali.
In whose field the Vāleya Kṣatriyas were born, known as the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Suhyas, and Paiṇḍras.
And from that [union] there arose the five sense-objects, along with names, memory, and perception.
From Aṅga came Anapāna; from him, Diviratha; and from him, Dharmaratha.
From him was born Citraratha, also known as Romapāda.
He whose friend Daśaratha was born.
His son was Daśaratha, who, being childless, gave his daughter named Śāntā in adoption to him as a daughter.
From Romapāda came Caturaṅga, and from him was born Pṛthulākṣa.
And from him came Campa, who founded the city of Campā.
Caṃpa had a son named Haryaṅga.
From Haryaṅga was born Bhadraratha; from Bhadraratha, Bṛhadratha; from Bṛhadratha, Bṛhatkarman; from Bṛhatkarman, Bṛhadbhānu; from him, Bṛhanmanas; and from Bṛhanmanas was born Jayadratha.
Jayadratha begot a son named Vijaya upon his wife, who was born from the union of a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya.
And Vijaya obtained a son named Dhṛti.
He, too, had a son named Dhṛtavrata.
From Dhṛtavrata came Satyakarman.
From Satyakarman was born an Atiratha.
He who obtained as his son Karṇa, who had been cast away by Pṛthā and placed within a chest, from the Gaṅgā at its confluence with the Yamunā.
From Karṇa came Vṛṣasena; these were the last of the lineage of Aṅga.
Therefore, you ought to hear the lineage of Puru.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: From Pūru was born Janamejaya; his son was Pracinvān; from Pracinvān came Pravīra; from Pravīra came Manasyu; and from Manasyu came Abhayada.
His son was Sudyu; from Sudyu came Bahugata; his son was Saṃyāti; from Saṃyāti came Ahaṃyāti; and from him was born Raudrāśva.
Ṛteṣu, Kakṣeṣu, Sthaleṣu, Kṛteṣu, Jaleṣu, Dharmeṣu, Dhr̥teṣu, and Sannateṣu were the ten sons of Raudrāśva by name.
Antināra was the son of Riteyu.
Antināra obtained three sons: Sumati, Apratiratha, and Dhruva.
Apratiratha’s son was Kaṇva.
His son was Medhātithi.
From him were born the Kaṇvāyana brahmins.
The other son of Apratiratha was Ailīna.
Elīna had four sons, Duṣyanta and the others.
From Duṣyanta was born the universal monarch Bharata.

The gods sing this verse concerning the cause of his name: He who, having been born from the lotus, was first seen by the gods, and whose name is celebrated by them—by him, the lotus-born one, this world was created. (ViP 4.19.11)
"The mother is but a leather bellows; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very same as him by whom he was begotten.
Support your son, O Duṣyanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."
"O god among men, the son who has received the seed leads [the father] from the abode of Yama;
you are the progenitor of this child," Śakuntalā spoke the truth.
Bharata had nine sons by his three wives.
When they were told, "These are not suitable for me," their mothers killed their sons out of fear of being abandoned.

Then, when the birth of a son proved to be in vain for Dīrghatamas—who was desirous of a son and a performer of the Marutsoma sacrifice—a son named Bharadvāja was born to Mamatā, the wife of Utathya, through the seed of Bṛhaspati which had been cast aside by his heel; this son was granted by the Maruts.
For him as well, a verse explaining the etymology of his name is recited: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.19.17.
"O Bṛhaspati, support this Bharadvāja; O Mūḍha, support this Bharadvāja!"—having spoken thus to his parents, he then became known as Bharadvāja.
When the birth of his son had proved futile, Bharadvāja was given by the Maruts; therefore, he received the name Vitatha.
Vitatha’s son was Manyu.
Bṛhatkṣatra, Mahāvīrya, Nagara, and Garga were the sons of Manyu.
Nagarasya, Saṃkṛti, Saṃkṛti’s son Guruprīti, and Antideva.
From Garga came Śini, and from him were born the Gārgyas and Śainyas; these twice-born ones became endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
And from Mahāvīrya, a son named Durukṣaya was born.
His sons were Trayyāruṇi, Puṣkariṇa, and Kapi; [the latter] suffered the loss of his children.
And later, all three of those sons also attained the status of Brahmins.
Suhotra was the son of Bṛhatkṣatra.
Suhotra’s son was Hastī, who established this city of Hastinapura.
From Ajamīḍha and Dvijamīḍha, three [sons] were born.
From Ajamīḍha was born Kaṇva.
From Kaṇva, Medhātithi was born.
From whom the Kaṇvāyana twice-born [descended].
Another son of Ajamīḍha was Bṛhadiṣu.
From Bṛhadiṣu came Bṛhaddhanus; from Bṛhaddhanus came Bṛhatkarman; from him was born Jayadratha, and from him also Viśvajit.
And from him was born Senajit.
Rucirāśva, Kāśya, Dṛḍhahanu, Vatsa, and Anu were the sons of Senajit.
From Rucirāśva was born Pṛthusena, and from Pṛthusena came Pāra.
Pārānīla was his son.
He had one hundred sons.
Among them, the foremost was Samara, the lord of Kāmpilya.
Samaras also had three sons: Pāra, Supāra, and Sadāśva.
From Supāra came Pṛthu; from Pṛthu, the well-doer (Sukṛti), came Vibhrāja.
And from him was born Aṇuha.
He married Śukra’s daughter, named Kīrti.
From Aṇuha was born Brahmadaṭṭa.
And from him was born Viṣvaksena, and from him Udaksena.
And his son was Bhallābha.
The son of Dvijamīḍha was named Yavīnara.
From him [Vajranābha] came Dhṛtimān; from him, Satyadhṛti; from him, Dṛḍhanemi; from him, Supārśva; from him, Sumati; and from him, Sannatimān.
A son was born to Sannatimān.
Hiraṇyanābha taught this yoga to him.
He who composed the Saṃhitās of the twenty-four eastern Sāmavedic chanters.
From Kṛta was born Ugrāyudha.
By whom, through his abundance [of power], the destruction of the Nīpas was accomplished.
From Ugrāyudha came Kṣemya; from Kṣemya, Sudhīra; and from him, Ripuñjaya; and from him, Bahuratha—these were the Pauravas.
Ajamīḍha’s wife was named Nalinī; by her, a son named Nīla was born.
From him was born Śānti; from Śānti, Suśānti; from Suśānti, Purañjaya; and from him, Ṛkṣa.
And from him was born Haryaśva.
"Therefore, these sons of mine are capable of protecting the five regions known as Mudgala, Sṛñjaya, Bṛhadiṣu, Yavīnara, and Kāmpilya," said their father; thus were they called the Pāñcālas.
From Mudgala, moreover, there arose the Maudgalyas, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
From Mudgala came Haryaśva.
From Haryaśva, Divodāsa and Ahalyā were born as a pair.
And from Śaradvat, through Ahalyā, Śatānanda was born.
From Śatānanda was born Satyadhṛti, who reached the furthest limit of the science of archery.
Upon seeing the excellent Apsaras Urvaśī, Satyadhṛti’s semen was discharged and fell into a clump of reeds.
And that offspring, having come into being in two ways, became a son and a daughter.
And Śantanu, having gone out on a hunt, saw them and took them up out of compassion.
Then Kṛpī, the mother of Aśvatthāman, became the wife of the preceptor Droṇa.
Mitrāyu was the son of Divodāsa.
The son of Mitrāyu was the king named Cyavana.
From Cyavana came Sudāsa; from Sudāsa came Saudāsa; from Saudāsa came Sahadeva, and his son was Somaka.
From Somaka was born a being who became the eldest of a hundred sons.
The youngest among them was Pṛṣata; from Pṛṣata came Drupada, from him Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and from him Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Ajamīḍha had another son named Ṛkṣa. // 74 //
His son was Saṃvaraṇa.
He is called Sura because he covers [the world].
He who made this field of dharma, Kurukṣetra.
From Kuru were born Sudhanus, Jahnu, Parīkṣit, and others as their foremost.
The son of Sudhanu was Suhotra; from him came Cyavana, and from Cyavana, Kṛtaka.
And from him was born Vasu, known as Upāricara.
Seven sons were born to Vasu, namely Bṛhadratha, Pratyagra, Kuśāmba, Kucela, Mātsya, and others as their leaders.
From Bṛhadratha came Kuśāgra; from Kuśāgra, Vṛṣabha; from Vṛṣabha, Puṣpavān; from him, Satyahita; from him, Sudhanvan; and his son was Jatu.
And from Bṛhadratha there was another, born from two fragments and joined together by Jarā, who was named Jarāsaṃdha.
From him came Sahadeva; from Sahadeva, Somapa; and from him, Śrutiśravas.
Thus have these kings of Magadha been described by me.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Parīkṣit had four sons: Janamejaya, Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
Jahnu had a son named Suratha.
His son was Vidūratha.
From him [Sārvabhauma] came Sārvabhauma; from Sārvabhauma, Jayatsena; from him, Ārādhita; from him, Ayutāyu; and from Ayutāyu, Akrodhana.
Therefore, Deva was the guest.
And thereafter, he became another Ṛkṣa.
From Ṛkṣa came Bhīmasena, and from him, Dilīpa.
From Dilīpa was born Pratīpa.
He, too, had three sons known by the names Devāpi, Śantanu, and Bāhlīka.
Devāpi entered the forest while still a child.
But Śaṃtanu became the protector of the earth.
And this verse concerning him is sung upon the earth:
Whomever he touched with his two hands, that person attained youthfulness;
because of that deed, he was called Śāntanu.
And while Śāntanu was ruling the kingdom, the god did not send rain for twelve years.
Then, observing the destruction of his entire kingdom, that king questioned the brahmins: "Why does the god not send rain upon our kingdom? What is my transgression?"
And then the brahmins said to him:

"Since this earth, belonging to your elder brother, is being enjoyed by you, you are therefore a *parivetta* (one who marries before his elder brother). Having been addressed thus, the king questioned them again.
"What should be done by me in this matter? [he asked].
Then they spoke once more:
As long as Devāpi is not overcome by defects such as falling from his status, so long is this kingdom worthy of him.
When he said, "Enough of this; let it be given to him," the chief minister Aśmarāvin dispatched ascetics who spoke in opposition to the doctrines of the Vedas into that forest.
By them, the mind of that king’s son, who was exceedingly simple-minded, was led to follow a path contrary to the teachings of the Vedas.
And King Śantanu, his lamentation and grief aroused by the words of the twice-born, placed those brahmins at his head and went to the forest to give away his eldest son.
Having arrived at that hermitage, they approached Devāpi, the son of the king, as he stood bowed down.
Those brahmins spoke to him words connected with the declarations of the Vedas, meaningful in their assertion that the kingdom must be ruled by the eldest brother.
He, Devāpi, also spoke to them in many ways, employing arguments that contradicted the teachings of the Vedas.
Then those brahmins spoke to Śāntanu.
"Come, O King; enough of this excessive persistence here. This fault of drought has indeed been pacified by the utterance of the refutation of the Vedic words recited since time immemorial."

"Since your elder brother has fallen [from grace], you do not incur the status of a 'parivettṛ' (one who marries before his elder brother). Having been told this, Śantanu returned to his own city and ruled the kingdom.
And while that Devāpi remained tainted by his utterance of words contradicting the Vedic injunctions—even though he was the elder brother—the blessed Parjanya rained for the production of all crops.
From Bāhlīka, a son named Somadatta was born.
Somadatta also had three sons, known as Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
To Śantanu, moreover, was born a son named Bhīṣma of noble fame, who knew the meaning of all the scriptures, by the immortal river Jāhnavī.
And upon Satyavatī, Śaṃtanu begot two sons, Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya.
But Citrāṅgada, while still a child, was slain in battle by the Gandharva Citrāṅgada himself.
Vicitravīrya also married Ambā and Ambālikā, the two daughters of the King of Kāśī.
And from the extreme exhaustion caused by that enjoyment, he was seized by consumption and met his death.
And by the command of Satyavatī, my son Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, considering his mother’s word to be not to be transgressed, begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu upon the wives sent by her for Vicitravīrya’s field,
and he also begot Vidura upon a maidservant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra also begot a hundred sons upon Gāndhārī, of whom Duryodhana and Duḥśāsana were the foremost.

Furthermore, while Pāṇḍu was in the forest, his capacity for procreating offspring having been destroyed by the curse of a seer, five sons were begotten for him: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna by Dharma, Vāyu, and Śakra respectively in Kuntī; and Nakula and Sahadeva by the two Aśvins in Mādrī.
And to them, through Draupadī, five sons were born.
From Yudhiṣṭhira was born Prativindhya; from Bhīmasena, Śrutasena; from Arjuna, Śrutakīrti; from Nakula, Śrutānīka; and from Sahadeva, Śrutakarmā.
And Kāśī, from Bhīmasena alone, obtained a son named Sarvaga.
Yaudheyī bore a son, Devaka, to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Hiḍimbā obtained Ghaṭotkaca as a son from Bhīmasena.
And from Bhīmasena, Kāśī obtained a son named Sarvaga.
And from Sahadeva, Vijayin obtained a son named Kuhotra.
And Nakula also begot Niramitra upon Reṇumatī.
To Arjuna also, by the Naga maiden Ulūpī, a son named Irāvān was born.
Arjuna begot a son named Babhruvāhana upon the daughter of the lord of Maṇipura through the practice of the *putrikā* (appointed daughter) law.
And from Subhadrā was born Abhimanyu, who, even in his childhood, possessed exceeding strength and prowess, and was a conqueror of all the enemy's chariot-warriors.
When the Kurus had been destroyed and Abhimanyu’s embryo was reduced to ashes within Uttarā by the Brahmāstra weapon discharged by Aśvatthāman,
Parīkṣit was born after having regained life through the power of the Blessed One— whose pair of feet are worshipped by all gods and asuras— who, by his own will, assumed a non-human form.
He who now protects this circle of the earth with a dharma that is unbroken in its continuity.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the future kings.
Of this very Parīkṣit, who is now the lord of the earth, there will also be four sons: Janamejaya, Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
Janamejaya’s son will also be Śatānīka.

He who, having studied the Veda under Yājñavalkya and having obtained weapons from Kṛpa, with his mental faculties detached from the treacherous objects of the senses and becoming proficient in the knowledge of the Self through the instruction of Śaunaka, shall attain supreme liberation and become Aśvamedhadatta, the son of Śatānīka.
Therefore, he was also called Adhisīmakṛṣṇa.
They drove out the Kṛṣṇas beyond the boundary.
He who, when Hastinapura was carried away by the Gaṅgā, will dwell in Kauśāmbī.
His son, too, will be Uṣmaka.
From Uṣṇa was born Vicitraratha.
From him was born Śuciratha.
From him came Vṛṣṇimān; from him, Suṣeṇa; his son was Sunītha; from Sunītha came Nṛpacakṣus; from him, Sukhibala; his son was Pāriplava; from him, Sunaya; and his son was Medhāvī.
From Medhāvī came Ripuñjaya; from him, Avasta; from him, Tigma; from him, Bṛhadratha; and from Bṛhadratha came Vasudāsa.
After him was Śatanīka.
From him was born Codayana; from Udayana came Vihīnara; from him came Daṇḍapāṇi; and from him, Nimitta.
And from him was born Kṣemaka.
On this point, there is this verse: ViP 4.21.17.
Whosoever among the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas is without lineage, yet honored by divine sages,
shall reach their final end upon reaching King Kṣemaka during the Kali age.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: "Now, therefore, the future kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty shall be described."
Bṛhatkṣaṇa was the son of Bṛhadbala.
From him came Durukṣaya, from him Vatsavyūha, from him Prativyoma, and from him also Divāraka.

From him [Sudhanvan] was born Sahadeva; from Sahadeva, Bṛhadaśva; his son was Bhānuratha; his son was Pratītāśva; his son was Supratīka; from him came Marudeva; from him, Sunakṣatra; from him, Kinnara;
from Kinnara, Antarikṣa; from him, Suparṇa; and from him, Amitrajit.
And from him was born Bṛhadbhānu; his son was Dharmī, and the son of Dharmī was Kṛtañjaya.
From Kṛtañjaya was born Raṇañjaya.
From Raṇañjaya came Saṃjaya; from him, Śākya; from Śākya, Śuddhodana; from him, Rāhula; and from him, Prasenajit.
From him was born Kṣudraka, from him Kuṇḍaka, and from him Suratha.
And his son was Sumitra.
Thus these were the Ikṣvākus, the descendants of Bṛhadbala.
In this regard, there is a genealogical verse (anuvaṃśaśloka): [ViP 4.22.12]
This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall end with Sumitra;
for upon reaching that king, it will indeed come to its conclusion in the Kali age.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fourth part of the glorious Mahāviṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: I shall now relate the succession of the future Bārhadratha kings of Magadha.
For in this lineage there were those of great strength and prowess, headed by Jarāsandha.
Jarāsandha’s son was Sahadeva.
From Sahadeva came Somāpi; his son was Anuśrutaśravas, and his was Ayutāyu. From him came Niramitra, whose son was Sunetra, and from him Bṛhatkarman.
From him will come Senajit, from him Śrutañjaya, and from him a Brahmin whose son shall be named Śuci.
His son was Kṣemya; from him came Suvrata; from Suvrata came Dharma; and from him came Suśravas.
From him was born Dṛḍhasena.
From him was born Subala.
From Subala, Sunīta will be born.
From him was born Satyajit.
Therefore, he is called Viśvajit.
His son was Ripuñjaya.
Thus, these kings of the Bārhadratha dynasty will rule for one thousand years.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Of this last descendant of Bṛhadratha, named Ripuñjaya, there will be a minister named Munika.
And having slain his master, he will consecrate his own son, named Pradyota, as king.
He, too, will have a son named Balāka.
And from him was born Viśākhyūpa.
His son was Janaka.
And his [son] was Nandivardhana.
From him was born Nandin. 4.24.7.
Thus, these one hundred and thirty-five Pradyotas shall enjoy the earth.
And from him was born Śiśunābha.
His son will be Kākavarṇa.
And his son was Kṣemadharmā.
His vital energy was also diminished.
His son was Vidhisāra.
And from him was born Ajātaśatru.
Therefore, he is called Arbhaka.
And from him was born Codayana.
Therefore, he was named Nandivardhana.
From him was born Mahānandin.
Thus, these Śaiśunāga kings will exist for three hundred and sixty-two years.

Then, from that lineage of Nanda, there will arise one named Mahāpadma, born of a Śūdra womb, exceedingly greedy and very powerful; like Paraśurāma, he will be an enemy who brings about the end of all the Kṣatriyas.
From that time forward, the kings will be Śūdras.
And that Mahāpadma, whose command is not transgressed and under whose single umbrella he rules, shall enjoy the earth.
He too will have eight sons, beginning with Sumāli.
They shall enjoy the earth following that Mahāpadma.
The sons of Mahāpadma will be lords of the earth for one hundred years.
And then, the brahmin Kauṭilya will deliver these nine Nandas.
In their absence, the descendants of Mūri will enjoy the earth.
Kautilya himself shall consecrate Candragupta's son upon the throne.
His son, too, will be Bindusāra.
His son will be Aśokavardhana; from him, Suyaśas; from him, Daśaratha; from him, Saṃyuta; from him, Śaliśuka; from him, Somaśarman; and the son of that Somaśarman will be Śatadhanvan.
His successor will be named Anubṛhadratha.
Thus, these ten Maurya kings will rule for one hundred and thirty-seven years.
At the end of their reign, ten Śuṅgas shall rule the earth.
Puṣyamitra, the commander-in-chief, will kill his master and rule the kingdom; his son will be Agnimitra.
From him came Sujyotiṣṭha; from him, Vasumitra; from him, Udaṅka; from him, Pulindaka; from him, Ghoṣavasu; from him, Vajramitra; and from him, Bhagavanta.
Therefore, he was named Devabhūti.
Thus, these Śuṅgas shall enjoy the earth for one hundred and twelve years.
Then this great lineage shall go to Kaṇva.
But when King Śuṅga Devabhūti falls into misfortune, his own minister named Kaṇva, known as Vasudeva, will slay him and himself enjoy the earth.
His son was Bhūmitra, and his son was also Nārāyaṇa.
Suśarman was the son of Nārāyaṇa.
These four Kāṃvāyanas will be kings for forty-five years.
But a servant of his, an Andhra named Balipucchaka, having killed Suśarman the Kāṇva, will enjoy the earth.
And thereafter, his brother named Kṛṣṇa shall become the lord of the earth.
His son was Śāntakarṇi; his son was Pūrmotsaṅga; his son was Śatakarmi; from him came Lambodara; from him came Pilaka; from him Meghasvāti; and from him Paṭumān.
From him came Ariṣṭakarmā, and from him Hālāhala.
From Hālāhala came Palalaka; from him, Pulindasena; from him, Sunda; from him, Sātakarṇi; from him, Śivasvāti; and from him, Gomatiputra; his son was Alimān.
His son was Śāntakarṇi; from him came Śibiśrita, and from him Śivaskandha; from him came Yajñaśrī, from him Dvīpa, and from him Candraśrī.
Therefore, Pulomā also [gave birth]. ViP_4.24.49.
In this very manner, they shall enjoy the earth for three thousand four hundred and fifty-six years.
The Āndhrabhṛtyas, beginning with Taptabhīra and others, will become ten kings of the Gardhabhin dynasty.
After that, there will be sixteen kings.
Then there will be eight Yavanas, fourteen Turuṣkas, thirteen Muṇḍas, and eleven Maunas; these indeed shall be the lords of the earth and will enjoy the earth for nine hundred years.
And thereafter, eleven Mauna kings will enjoy the earth for three hundred years.
When they have been exterminated, the Kaiṅkilas will become Yavana kings who are not consecrated with the royal aspersion.
Their offspring will be Vindhyaśakti; from him, Puñrajaya; from him, Rāmacandra; from him, Arma-varman; from him, Vaṅga; from him, Nandana; from him, Sunandin;
his brother will be Nandīyaśas, Śukra, and Pravīra—these shall be kings for one hundred and six years.
From him were born thirteen sons, and three Bāhlikas.
Then there will be the Puṣpamitras, the Paṭumitras, the Yajñas, and the Atrēyas; and seven Andhras, each possessing a single skill in weaponry.
And thereafter, there will be exactly nine kings in Kosala.
But the Naiṣadhas are indeed those very same [people].
In Magadha, however, one known as Viśvasphaṭika will establish other castes.
He will establish fishermen, students, forest-dwellers, and Brahmins upon the throne.
Having exterminated the entire kṣatriya race, nine Nāgas will enjoy the protected Magadha kingdom in the city named Padmavatī, from the Gaṅgā to Prayāga and from Gayā.
Devarakṣita was the protector of Kośala, Andhra, Puṇḍra, Tāmralipta, Samataṭa, and the city of Purī.
They will occupy the caves of Kaliṅga, Māhiṣa, and Mahendra.
The Maṇidhānyaka Vaṃśas shall not rule over the countries of Naiṣa, Naimiṣaka, Kālakośa, and Kāñcana.
He will rule over the three kingdoms, the country of Muṣika, and the region called Kanaka.
The Vratyas, twice-born men, Abhiras, Shudras, and others will consume the territories of Saurashtra, Avanti, Shudra, Abhira, the Narmada, and the Marubhu region.
In the regions of Sindhutaṭa, Dāvikorvī, Candrabhāgā, and Kaśmīra, people will take pleasure in the ways of outcasts (vrātyas); they will be killers of women, children, and cows;

they will delight in seizing the property of others; they will be of little substance, dominated by darkness, and for the most part rise only to set again; they will be short-lived, full of great desires, possessing little dharma, and greedy.
And all these kings on earth shall be contemporaries.

Having little faith and great anger, always delighting in falsehood and unrighteousness, they will be perpetrators of violence against women, children, and cattle; they will take pleasure in seizing the property of others, possess little substance, be mostly shrouded in darkness, rise and fall as if by fits, have short lifespans, be full of great desires, deficient in dharma, and greedy.

And mixed with them will be those who follow their conduct, who depend on kings for their livelihood, and who, though following Mleccha customs, act in a contrary manner; these shall bring the subjects to ruin.
And thereafter, through a gradual and daily diminution and cessation of both dharma and artha, the destruction of the world will come to pass.
Therefore, wealth alone is the cause for noble lineage.
Power alone is the cause of all dharmas without exception.
Mutual affection alone is the cause of the bond of matrimony.
Femaleness itself is the cause for experiencing [the fruits of] enjoyment.
Untruth alone is the cause of victory in legal proceedings.
The earth is indeed the cause of the rising waters.
The sacred thread alone is the cause of Brahminhood.
The very fact of being a treasury of jewels is the cause for its praiseworthiness.
The wearing of the *liṅga* alone is the cause for the stage of life (*āśrama*).
Unrighteousness alone is the cause of one's livelihood.
Weakness alone is the cause of non-return.
The confident articulation [of words] without fear is itself the cause of scholarship.
Lack of wealth itself is the cause of excellence.
Bathing alone is the cause of adornment.
Generosity alone is the cause of Dharma.
Acceptance alone is the cause of marriage.
The vessel was indeed held by one filled with hatred.
Only the water brought from a distant place is the cause for a sacred bathing site (tīrtha).
The wearing of a deceptive disguise alone is the cause of his greatness.
Thus, on this earth which is subject to many such defects, whoever among all the castes is the strongest shall become the sovereign.
And thus, unable to endure kings who are excessively greedy, the subjects will take refuge in the secluded valleys of the forests.
And they will subsist on food consisting of honey, vegetables, roots, fruits, leaves, flowers, and so forth.
Clad in garments made of tree bark, leaves, and rags, they will have very many offspring and will endure cold, wind, heat, and rain.
And no one shall live for twenty-three years; moreover, in this Kali age, constant fear will come upon all these people.

When the Vedic and Smṛti-based dharma had utterly collapsed and the Kali age was nearly exhausted, a portion of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—the creator of the remaining world, the teacher of all moving and unmoving beings, devoid of beginning, middle, or end, and whose nature is Brahman—descended here upon earth in the form of Kalki. Endowed with the eightfold perfections of qualities, he was born in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas, the preeminent Brāhmaṇa of Śambalagrāma; and possessing immeasurable power and majesty, he [will destroy] all those barbarians, robbers, and evil-minded ones.
He will bring about their destruction and will establish everyone firmly in their own respective duties.

And immediately thereafter, at the end of the entire Kali age, the intellects of those very people will become as pure as the clear petals of a flawless crystal, like those who have awakened at the end of the night.
And for all those humans who have become seeds and have reached maturity, there will be the birth of offspring produced at that very time.
And those offspring of his will indeed be in accordance with the Kṛta Yuga.
To this it is replied:
"Just as the moon and the sun, so too Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati shall come together in a single zodiacal sign; at that time, indeed, the Kṛta age shall prevail."
O best of sages, those kings who have passed away, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come, have all been described to you within these lineages.
From the birth of Parīkṣit until the consecration of Nanda,
this period should be known as one thousand and fifty years.
Of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), those two who are seen first as they rise in the sky—
between them, that constellation which is seen level at night [is the marker].
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the Seven Sages remain conjoined with the Maghās for a hundred years of men;
they were so situated during the time of the son of Parīkṣit.
And at that time, Kali, consisting of twelve hundred years, began to proceed.
O twice-born one, as soon as the Lord Viṣṇu,
born from the lineage of Vasudeva, had departed for heaven, Kali arrived here.
As long as he touched this earth with his two lotus-feet,
Kali was not capable of embracing the world.
When that portion of the eternal Viṣṇu had departed from there,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, together with his younger brothers, abandoned the kingdom and went from earth to heaven.
Having observed these inauspicious omens, Parīkṣit, the son of Pāṇḍu,
performed his consecration after Kṛṣṇa had departed.
And when these great sages depart for Pūrvāṣāḍhā, from that time forward,
beginning with Nanda, this [era] will undergo an increase in its duration.
On that very day when Kṛṣṇa ascended to heaven, the Kali Yuga began; learn from me its duration.
O twice-born one, by human calculation, this Kali age will indeed consist of three hundred and sixty thousand years.
When those twelve thousand divine years have passed away without remainder, the Kṛta age shall begin once again.
O best of the twice-born, in age after age, thousands of high-souled Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have passed away.
Because of the great number of names in every family,
and due to both redundancy and similarity, they have not been fully enumerated by me.
Devāpi, the Paurava king, and Puru, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
were both endowed with the power of great yoga and resided at Kalāpagrāma.
In the Kṛta age, having come here, those two will indeed become the initiators of the Kṣatriya order; established as the seeds for the lineage of Manu, they shall exist.
By this sequential process, the son of Manu has enjoyed the earth throughout the three ages of Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara.
O Sage, there will indeed remain some who have become the seeds for the Kali age,
just as Devāpi and Puru are currently established.
This genealogy of kings has been declared by me only in brief;
it cannot be recounted in its entirety even in hundreds of years.
These and other kings,
blinded by delusion, have always maintained a sense of "mine" toward this earthly sphere, even though the body is eternally something to be abandoned.
"How shall this earth remain unshakable for me? How shall it belong to my son?
How shall it belong to my lineage?"—afflicted by such thoughts, these kings met their end.
There were others even earlier than them, and likewise others after them;
there will be those who come in the future, and yet others who follow after them.
Beholding the kings intent on their expeditions and striving for victory over themselves,
the earth seemed to laugh in autumn with the blossoming of flowers.
O Maitreya, learn from me here these verses sung by the Earth,
which the sage Asita spoke to Dharmadhvaja when he was born as a Naga.
The Earth said:
"How is it that this delusion has come upon these lords of men, even though they are wise,
such that they have become exceedingly trusting in heart toward one who shares their very nature?"
Having first achieved victory over themselves, ministers desire to conquer;
thereafter, they seek to conquer their servants, the citizens, and likewise their enemies.
"In this sequence, we shall conquer the earth together with its oceans"—
with such thoughts their minds were attached, and they did not perceive death, which follows immediately after ignorance.
The entire circle of the earth, bounded by the ocean, comes under his control;
how small is this for one who has conquered himself—liberation is the fruit of self-conquest.
"Having abandoned me, my ancestors have departed—the one whom even my father did not take with him when he went;
yet these kings, out of extreme folly, desire to conquer me."
On my account, conflict arises between fathers and sons, and even among brothers,
due to extreme delusion in those whose minds are governed by the sense of "mine-ness."
"This entire earth is mine; it belongs to me and to my lineage forever.
Whosoever else has become king upon the death of another, he did so only because that predecessor was of evil intellect. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.24.134)
Having seen that single person— whose mind was devoted to the sense of "mine"— departing under the power of death while leaving me behind,
how can his follower still maintain in his heart that sense of "mine" which originated from me?

When kings speak through the mouths of their messengers to their own enemies, saying, "This earth is mine; abandon it quickly," I feel great laughter toward them, and furthermore, compassion arises for those fools.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, these verses sung by the Earth, when heard,
cause the sense of "mine-ness" to dissolve, just as the sun causes snow to melt.
Thus has the lineage of Manu been correctly described by me to you,
wherein kings were portions of portions of Viṣṇu established in the course of his manifestation.
Whoever listens to this account of Manu’s lineage with devotion,
all the sins of that pure-souled person are indeed utterly destroyed.
Having heard this entire, praiseworthy lineage of the Moon and the Sun, one whose senses are unimpaired attains incomparable abundance of wealth and grain.
He beheld those lords of men— possessing great strength, great heroism, and infinite stores of wealth—
who had been reduced by powerful Time to nothing but a mere story.
Having heard this, a man of perfected wisdom does not form a sense of "mine" toward his children and wife, nor toward his house, fields, or wealth.

Those heroic men, who with uplifted arms performed austerities for many groups of years and offered excellent sacrifices, were powerful and exceedingly valiant; yet they have been made by Time to remain as nothing more than a mere legend.
Pṛthu, who traversed all the worlds unimpeded and had conquered the circle of his enemies,
was destroyed when struck by the wind of Time, like the cotton-wool of a silk-cotton tree cast into a fire.
Kārtavīrya, who, having subdued all the continents and destroyed the circle of his enemies, enjoyed [the earth],
is mentioned even in the course of casual conversations as the very cause of conceptual construction and mental fluctuation.

Alas for the power of Death! Why did he not reduce to mere ashes in an instant—by a mere contraction of his eyebrows—the descendants of Raghu, whose sovereignty illuminated the quarters of the sky and who had been pierced by the ten-headed Rāvaṇa?
Bhagīratha and others, Sagara, Kakutstha, Daśānana, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, and Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest—these have all truly existed; it is not false, though we do not know where they are now.
Those kings who exist at present and those who will exist in the future, O best of Brahmins, whom I have described as being of formidable prowess—
these and others likewise shall all be known by their respective names, just as were those of old.
Having understood this, a wise man should not entertain a sense of "mine-ness" even toward his own self;
let alone children, wives, fields, and so forth, as well as other embodied beings.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter (24) in the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
The fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa is completed.
Thus ends the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as the *Viṣṇucittīya* and the *Ātmaprakāśa* by Śrīdhara.
Thus begins the fifth book in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa*, accompanied by the two commentaries known as *Viṣṇucittīya* and *Ātmaprakāśa* by Śrīdhara.
Homage to the venerable Rāmānuja.
Maitreya said:

O Brahman-sage, you have related the entire detailed genealogy of kings, and the history of those dynasties has been described by you exactly as it occurred; now tell me of this incarnation from a portion [of the divine] who was born in the Yadu lineage.
I wish to hear that [account] concerning Viṣṇu in detail and according to its true nature.
O Sage, tell me those deeds which the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, performed after descending upon the earth as partial incarnations of his portions.
The venerable Parāśara said: O Maitreya, listen to this which I have been asked by you here—
the account of the manifestation of a portion of a portion of Viṣṇu, which is for the benefit of the world.
O great sage, in former times Vasudeva married Devakī,
the daughter of Devaka, who was highly fortunate and like unto a goddess.
Kaṃsa, the delighter of the Bhojas, commanded his charioteer to drive their excellent chariot to the union of Vasudeva and Devakī.
"O fool, you who carry her who stands upon the chariot with her husband—
her eighth pregnancy shall take away your life."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard this, the mighty Kaṃsa drew his sword and began to strike Devakī; then Vasudeva spoke these words.
"O illustrious and sinless one, Devakī must not be slain by you;
I shall deliver to you all the offspring born from her womb."
Śrī Parāśara said:
"So be it," Kaṃsa then replied to Vasudeva, O best of the twice-born;
and out of respect for his word, he did not have Devakī executed.
At that very time, however, the Earth, oppressed by her great burden,
went to Mount Meru to the assembly of the inhabitants of heaven.
Then, having prostrated before all the gods who were dear to Brahmā, the Earth,
speaking with compassion out of distress, related everything to them.
The Earth said:
"Agni is the preceptor of gold, and the Sun is the supreme preceptor of cows;
likewise, for me and for all the worlds, Kuru Nārāyaṇa is the preceptor."
Brahmā, the Lord of Prajāpatis, is the first-born even of the ancients;
he is Time, whose nature consists of kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas, and who possesses an unmanifest form.
O best of gods, this assembly of you all is composed of portions of that [Supreme Being].
These are the forms of that immeasurable, great-souled Viṣṇu.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, piśācas, uragas, dānavas,
gandharvas, and apsarases— all these are the forms of the high-souled Viṣṇu.
The planets, constellations, and stars; the variegated sky, fire, water, and wind;
myself and the objects of the senses—this entire world is composed of Viṣṇu.
And likewise, for that which possesses manifold forms, its various aspects undergo the state of being the oppressor and the oppressed day and night, like waves in the ocean.
Therefore, at this time, these Daityas, led by Kālanemi,
having invaded the world of mortals, oppress the subjects day and night.
That great asura Kālanemi, who was slain by the powerful Viṣṇu,
has been born as Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena.
Āriṣṭa, Dhenuka, Keśin, Pralamba, Naraka,
as well as the extremely fierce Asura Sunda, and Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
Likewise, there were others of great prowess who were born in the palaces of kings; I do not venture to enumerate those evil-minded ones.
"Here there are numerous Akṣauhiṇīs of gods bearing divine forms,
and [the forces] of the haughty lords of Daityas of great strength are above me."
"O lords of the immortals, afflicted by the pain of that great burden, I am unable to sustain myself;
thus do I inform you."
"O highly fortunate ones, let that which will relieve my burden be performed,
so that I, overwhelmed as I am, do not sink into the subterranean realm."
Having heard these words of the Earth, Brahmā, urged by all the lords of the gods for the sake of removing the burden of the world, spoke.
Brahmā said: "O dwellers of heaven, everything that the Earth has said is indeed true;
I, Bhava, and all of you are essentially Nārāyaṇa."
And whatever manifestations belong to him, among those very ones there exists a mutual relationship of superiority and inferiority,
characterized by the state of the sublated and the sublator.
"Therefore, come, let us go to the excellent shore of the Ocean of Milk;
having propitiated Hari there, we shall indeed inform him of everything."
In every way, for the sake of the world, he who is the soul of all and composed of the universe descends to earth through a portion of his essence and establishes the dharma.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Brahmā) departed from that place together with the gods;
and with a concentrated mind, he praised the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Brahmā said: "O Lord, there are two kinds of knowledge—the higher, which is beyond the Veda, and likewise the lower;
these two indeed constitute your forms, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest."
O Knower of All, you are the two Brahmans— the subtle and the gross Self that pervades everything—
and the Supreme Brahman which is the very essence of the one composed of Brahman.
You are the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda; you are phonetics, ritual procedure, etymology, prosody, and astronomy.
And likewise, O Lord Adhokṣaja, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as grammar,
Mīmāṃsā, the science of logic (Nyāya), and the treatises on Dharma.
O First Lord, that speech which investigates the self, the body, and the qualities as being the self—
that too is not different from the supreme Self, just like the nature of the inner self.
You are unmanifest, indefinable, inconceivable, and without form; you are without hands or feet, pure, eternal, and higher than the highest.
Though earless, you hear; though formless, you see, assuming many forms.
Though without feet or hands, you are swift and a grasper; you know all that is to be known, being the knower of all.

O Supreme Self, for the steadfast one who perceives You—the subtler than the subtle, whose nature is both being and non-being—there arises the foremost cessation of [dualistic] knowledge; such a wise one perceives nothing else apart from Your most excellent form, which transcends even the beyond.
You are the navel of the universe and the protector of the world; all beings are within you.
Whatever has been and whatever is to be, and that which is subtler than the subtle—you alone are the Supreme Person beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Though one, the Blessed One, as the sacrificial fire, you bestow upon the world an abundance of splendor in four ways;
O Creator, you whose form is infinite, you who have eyes on all sides, you establish your station in three ways.
Just as fire, though single and of an unchanging nature, is kindled in many ways through various modifications,
so too do you, O Lord, who are omnipresent and of one form, nourish all forms without exception.
One is Your supreme and foremost state, which the wise perceive as You, visible through the eye of knowledge;
O Supreme Self, there is no other essential nature whatsoever than You—neither what has been nor what is yet to be.
You are the manifest and the unmanifest in essence; you possess both the collective and the individual forms;
you are all-knowing, all-perceiving, and endowed with all power, knowledge, strength, and prosperity.
Neither diminished nor increasing, independent, beginningless, and self-controlled,
he is untouched by fatigue, sloth, fear, anger, desire, and the like.
He is faultless, beyond attainment, without support, and the imperishable sequence;
he is the Lord of all, the supreme substratum, the essence of all abodes, and the undecaying.
O you who have brought all veils to an end through meditation on the supportless,
O you who abide in great majesty, salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
Neither without a cause, nor from a cause, nor from both cause and non-cause, does the assumption of a body occur; it is solely for the sake of protecting dharma.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard this hymn of praise, the unborn Lord,
manifesting his universal form, spoke to Brahmā with a pleased mind.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Brahmā, whatever is desired by you along with the gods from me, let that be stated in its entirety; consider it already accomplished."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then Brahmā, beholding that divine, universal form of Hari,
offered praise once more while the gods stood with their bodies bowed down in awe.
Brahmā said:
Salutations, salutations to you a thousand times, O thousand-armed one, with many faces and feet!
Salutations, salutations to you, the immeasurable one who effects the origin, destruction, and maintenance of the world.

O Supreme Self, who are subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest, and possessed of a weightiness that surpasses even the most weighty; O Blessed One, who are the primordial source like the primary intellect and the senses, be gracious!
O Lord, this earth, whose mountain fastenings are oppressed by the great asuras born of the earth,
approaches you— the ultimate refuge of the worlds and one of boundless strength— for the sake of removing her burden.
Here we are, as well as this enemy of Vṛtra, the two Nāsatyas, Varuṇa likewise,
these Rudras, the Vasus together with Sūrya, and others headed by Samīraṇa and Agni.
"O Lord, all the gods together with me shall perform every task that must be done for the Lord of the Gods;
command us, and we shall remain ever obedient to your command, forever free from fault."
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus being praised, O great sage, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, plucked out two hairs from his own body, one white and one black.
And he said to the gods:
"These two, my sons, having descended upon the surface of the earth, will effect the removal of the burden and the suffering of the world."
And let all the Suras, having descended to the surface of the earth with their own portions,
engage in battle with the great Asuras who were born previously and have become insane.
Then, crushed by the impact of my thunderbolt, all those Daityas will undoubtedly go to their destruction upon the surface of the earth.
O gods, Devakī, who is like a goddess and the wife of Vasudeva—
therein this eighth conception shall be my hair, O Suras.
Having descended there, Hari said, "He shall slay Kaṃsa on this earth;
Kālanemi has arisen," and then he vanished.
Then, O great sage, having prostrated before him who had become invisible,
the gods departed for the summit of Mount Meru and descended to the surface of the earth.
The venerable sage Nārada declared: "The eighth conception of Devakī shall be the bearer of the earth for Kaṃsa."
Having heard that from Nārada, Kaṃsa then became enraged and confined Devakī and Vasudeva in secret within his own home.
O twice-born one, Vasudeva likewise delivered his son to Kaṃsa, exactly as he had been told by him in the past.
The sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were renowned as the Ṣaḍgarbhas;
impelled by Viṣṇu, Nidrā caused those embryos to be joined together in succession.
The Blessed Lord Hari spoke to that Yoganidrā, the Great Māyā of Viṣṇu, by whom the entire world is deluded through ignorance.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Sleep, go at my command to those who take refuge in the depths of Pātāla;
lead the six embryos, one by one, into the womb of Devakī."
When those [enemies] have been slain by Kaṃsa, then my portion known as Śeṣa will arise as her seventh son, born from a portion of a portion out of disregard for her.
"O Goddess, another wife of Vasudeva named Rohiṇī resides in Gokula; you must carry him within your womb until his birth."
"Out of fear of Bhojarāja, the world will say that the seventh embryo of Devakī has been cast away due to confinement and obstruction."
Then, because he draws forth the embryo, that hero, who resembles the peak of a white mountain, shall indeed obtain the name Saṃkarṣaṇa in the world.
Then I shall come into being within the auspicious womb of Devakī;
you must go to Yaśodā without delay to take Bharga [the embryo].
And during the rainy season, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhas, I shall be born at night;
on the ninth day, you shall obtain my birth.
O blameless one, while I am in Yaśodā’s bed and you are in Devakī’s,
Vasudeva— his mind impelled by my power— will carry you away.
And Kaṃsa, O Goddess, having taken you up, will throw you onto the surface of a mountain rock; then you shall attain a station in the mid-air.
Then the hundred-eyed Śakra, bowing out of respect for me with his head bent low in prostration, will accept you as his sister.
And you, having slain Śumbha, Niśumbha, and thousands of other Daityas,
shall adorn the entire earth with many sacred abodes.
You are prosperity, humility, patience, beauty, heaven, earth, and fortitude; you are modesty and nourishment; and whatever other wrathful power there may be, that too is you alone.
Those who address you as Āryā, Durgā, Vedagarbhāmbikā,
Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Kṣemadā, and Bhagyadā— [to them you grant their desires].
In the morning and in the afternoon, they shall offer praise with bodies bowed low;
indeed, by my grace, every desire of theirs shall be fulfilled.
Honored with offerings of wine and meat, and with various kinds of foods and edibles,
you, being well-pleased, shall bestow all the desires of men without exception.
"O auspicious one, by my grace, all of them shall at all times undoubtedly and without doubt attain this; go, O Goddess, as has been told.
Thus ends the first chapter in the fifth book of the Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Just as it was commanded by the God of gods, the Sustainer of the World,
she performed the placement of the six embryos within her womb and the extraction of another.
When Rohiṇī had reached her seventh pregnancy, Hari then entered Devakī’s womb for the benefit of the three worlds.
On that very same day, Yoganidrā likewise entered the womb of Yaśodā,
exactly as had been foretold by the Supreme Lord.
Then, O twice-born one, the host of planets moved correctly in the sky,
and auspicious seasons shone forth once the portion of Viṣṇu had descended to earth.
No one was able to look upon Devakī because of her exceeding splendor;
seeing her blazing so intensely, the minds of all were thrown into agitation.
Unseen by men or women, the hosts of deities praised Devakī day and night as she bore Viṣṇu within her body.
The deities said:
"In ancient times, you were the supreme, subtle Prakṛti, containing Brahman within you;
thereafter, O beautiful one, you became Vāṇī, the mother of the world, containing the Vedas within you."
O Eternal One, you are the threefold Veda— the womb containing the nature of all that is to be created, the very substance of creation, the seed of everything, and the embodiment of sacrifice.
You alone are the sacrifice containing the fruit, and likewise the fire-drill containing the fire;
you are Aditi, the mother of the gods, and likewise Diti, the mother of the Daityas.

You are moonlight containing the essence of day; you are humility containing the essence of knowledge; you are supreme policy containing the essence of statesmanship; and you are modesty, the bearer of reverence.

You are Desire, whose womb is sensual pleasure; you are Contentment, pregnant with satisfaction; you are Intelligence, whose womb is awakening; and you are Fortitude, who bears the womb of steadfastness.
The sky, containing the planets, constellations, and stars, is composed of all these causes;
O Goddess, these are your manifestations, as are thousands of others.

Likewise, O auspicious one, the entire earth— comprising oceans, mountains, rivers, islands, forests, and cities as its ornaments, and abounding in villages, market towns, and hamlets— is currently contained within the womb of you, the mother of the world, who are numbered among the divine mothers.
All the fires, the waters, and all the winds;
likewise the great serpents, as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, and guhyakas.
The expanse of the sky provides space for everything without exception, crowded as it is with hundreds of variegated celestial chariots, planets, constellations, and stars.

The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the world of heaven (svarloka), as well as Maharloka, Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Brahmaloka— O auspicious one, this constitutes the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
In that interval stood the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as the Mahoragas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and Guhyakas.
O illustrious lady, humans, animals, and other living beings—
by being present within them, that infinite one is omnipresent and the creator of all things.
He whose nature as form and action is not within the scope of any means of knowledge— He, O Queen, is Viṣṇu dwelling within your womb.
You are Svāhā; you are Svadhā; you are the sacred knowledge, O Svadhā, the light in the sky.
You have descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of protecting all the worlds.
Be gracious, O Goddess; O auspicious one, bestow welfare upon the entire world!
Out of love, support that Īśāna by whom the whole universe is sustained.
Thus ends the second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Being thus praised by the gods, she conceived the god.
Through his embryo, he [beheld] the lotus-eyed one, the cause of protection for the world.
Then, for the sake of awakening the lotus of the entire world, the high-souled Acyuta, the sun, manifested within Devakī, who was like the morning twilight.
That day of his birth became exceedingly delightful for all the worlds, making the quarters of the sky pure, just like the moonlight of the moon.
When Janārdana was being born, the virtuous attained supreme contentment, the winds became tranquil, and the rivers reached a state of clarity.
The oceans produced enchanting music with their own sounds;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The gods dwelling on earth and in the intermediate space showered rains of flowers,
and the fires blazed forth peacefully as Janārdana was being born.
O twice-born one, as Janārdana was being born at midnight— the support of all— the clouds, shedding showers of flowers, roared with thunder.
Beholding him who had appeared, possessing four arms and the luster of a full-blown blue lotus petal,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, Ānakadundubhi offered praise.
And having praised him with pleasing words, that high-minded one,
O best of the twice-born, then made his request, being afraid of Kaṃsa.
Vasudeva said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you have been born bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
O God, please withdraw this divine form by your grace."
"O Lord, this Kaṃsa is having me killed this very day;
knowing that you have descended into this, my palace. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.3.11)
Devakī said:

"May that God of gods, who possesses infinite forms and whose form is the entire universe— who even while in the womb sustains the worlds with his body— he who has manifested the form of a child through his illusory power— be gracious."
O Soul of All, assume this four-armed form so that this Kaṃsa, born of the sons of Diti, may not recognize you as an incarnation.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Goddess, that which was previously praised by you, desiring a son,
has today become fruitful for you, since I have been born from your womb."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, the Blessed One became silent;
and Vasudeva, taking him with him that night, went outside.
And there, the guards were enchanted by yogic sleep as Ānakadundubhi was departing through the gates of Mathurā.
And as the clouds rained down exceedingly copious water at night, Śeṣa followed Ānakadundubhi, shielding him with his hoods.
Carrying Viṣṇu, Vasudeva crossed the Yamunā, which was exceedingly deep, agitated by hundreds of various whirlpools, and flowing only knee-deep.
Having arrived right there on the bank to pay tribute to Kaṃsa,
he saw Nanda and the other elder cowherds by the Yamunā.
At that time, O Maitreya, Yaśodā too was deluded by yogic sleep; while the people were thus bewildered, she gave birth to that very same girl.
Vasudeva, of immeasurable splendor, having placed the boy [elsewhere] and taken the girl from Yaśodā’s bed, quickly returned.
And having awakened, Yaśodā beheld her newborn son,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and thereupon she attained exceeding joy.
Vasudeva also, having taken the girl to his own residence,
placed her upon Devakī’s bed and remained there as before.
Then, O twice-born one, hearing the sound of the infant's crying, the guards rose up suddenly and informed Kaṃsa of Devakī’s delivery.
Kaṃsa, approaching her quickly, then seized the girl;
he was restrained by Devakī, who, with a choked voice, cried out, "Release her! Release her!"
And she hurled it onto the surface of a rock; once thrown, it remained suspended in the sky and assumed a massive form with eight great arms equipped with weapons.
She laughed loudly in that same manner and, filled with wrath, said to Kaṃsa:
"Kaṃsa, what was the use of throwing me away? For she has been born who shall slay you."
In former times, Death was like one's own self to the gods;
therefore, having reflected upon this, act quickly for your own welfare.
Having spoken thus, the goddess, adorned with divine garlands and perfumes,
departed through the sky while being praised by the Siddhas, even as King Bhoja looked on.
Thus ends the third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then Kaṃsa, with an agitated mind, spoke to all the great Asuras.
He summoned the foremost among the asuras, headed by Pralambakeśin.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Pralamba, O mighty-armed one, Keśin, Dhenuka, Pūtanā,
Ariṣṭa, and likewise the others— listen to my words."
"O Hero, it is said that an effort was made by the wicked immortals to slay me; yet, scorched by my prowess, I do not even count them."
What is to be accomplished by Indra, who possesses little prowess; or by Hara, who wanders alone;
or even by Hari, the slayer of asuras, who strikes only at moments of vulnerability?
What need is there for the Ādityas, what for the Vasus of little prowess, what for the Agnis,
or what for all the other immortals, when they have been conquered by the strength of my arms?
Did I not see that lord of the gods when he came into battle,
retreating with his very back bearing arrows while his chest was turned away?
When the rain was withheld from my kingdom by Śakra, were the waters then released as desired by the clouds pierced by my arrows? ||| ViP_5.4.7 |||
"Are there any kings on earth who fear the strength of my arms?
They have all submitted to me, with the exception of their preceptor, Jarāsaṃdha."
"O foremost of Daityas, contempt for mortals arises within me;
O heroes, I feel laughter even toward them when they are intent on their efforts."
Nevertheless, O lords of the Daityas, I must indeed strive even more to bring harm to those wicked and evil-minded ones.
Therefore, whatever illustrious persons there may be on earth, and those who are performers of sacrifices—
their destruction must be carried out with all one's soul for the sake of harming the gods.
"Death has indeed arisen for me before;
so it is truly said," thus spoke the maiden born from the womb of Devakī.
Therefore, one must exert the greatest effort against the wicked on this earth;
wherever a wicked person possesses superior strength, he must be slain with diligent effort.
Having thus commanded the Asuras, Kaṃsa then quickly entered his palace and released Vasudeva and Devakī from their confinement.
Kaṃsa said:
"These children of yours have now been killed by me in vain;
surely some other embryo has arisen for my destruction."
Therefore, enough with this lamentation; for surely those children of yours were destined by their very nature to be separated from life through the fault of you two.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having thus consoled and released them, Kaṃsa, filled with apprehension,
O best of the twice-born, then entered his own inner apartments.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been released, Vasudeva also went to Nanda’s cart.
He saw Nanda greatly rejoicing, thinking, "A son has indeed been born to me."
Vasudeva also said to him respectfully, "By good fortune! By good fortune!
Even in old age, this son has now been born to you."
"For the entire annual tax has already been paid by you to the king;
