since you have come for that purpose, those who possess great wealth should not remain here."
"The purpose for which you have come has been accomplished; why do you linger?
O Nanda, you should go quickly now to your own Gokula."
My young son there, who is born of Rohiṇī,
must also be protected by you just as this is your own son.
Thus addressed, the mighty cowherds, led by Nandagopa, set out after paying the tax, with their goods loaded upon carts.
While they were dwelling in Gokula, Pūtanā, the slayer of children,
took the sleeping Kṛṣṇa at night and gave him her breast.
To whichever child Pūtanā offers her breast at night,
that child's body is instantly destroyed.
But Kṛṣṇa, filled with rage, seized that breast— which was being pressed hard by her hands— and drank from it along with her very life-breath.
With her great cries of "Atimukta" and the bonds of her life-force severed,
the most terrifying Pūtanā fell to the ground as she died.
Terrified by the sound of that roar, the inhabitants of Vraja woke up and saw Kṛṣṇa in Pūtanā’s lap and her herself cast down.
O best of the twice-born, Yaśodā, filled with terror, took Kṛṣṇa and then dispelled the infant's affliction by whirling him around like the tail of a cow.
Taking cow-dung, Nandagopa also placed it upon Kṛṣṇa’s head, providing protection while reciting this: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.5.13.
Nandagopa said:
"May Hari, the source of all beings without exception, protect you—
he from whose navel-born lotus the universe arose."
May that Lord Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar and by whom the earth, supported by the tip of his tusk, sustains the world, protect you.
May the all-pervading Janārdana, who assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha and tore open the chest of his enemy with the tips of his claws, protect you everywhere.
May Vāmana protect you always— he who in an instant became Trivikrama, having traversed the three worlds with his strides and wielding flashing weapons.
May Govinda protect your head; may Keśava guard your throat; may Viṣṇu protect your private parts and belly; and may Janārdana protect your thighs and feet.
May the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty is unimpeded, protect your face, arms, forearms, mind, and all your senses.
May those *preta*s, *kūṣmāṇḍa*s, and *rākṣasa*s who are hostile to you go to their destruction by the sound of the conch of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace.
May Vaikuṇṭha protect you in the cardinal directions, Madhusūdana in the intermediate directions, Hṛṣīkeśa in the sky, and Mahīdhara protect you upon the earth.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus, having had the rites for auspiciousness performed by Nanda the cowherd,
the infant was laid beneath the cart on the surface of a small cradle.
And those cowherds, seeing the massive corpse of the dead Pūtanā, then experienced supreme terror and amazement.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Once, while Madhusūdana was lying beneath a cart, he spoke.
Desiring milk, she raised her feet upward and wept aloud.
By the blow of his foot, the cart was overturned;
its jars and vessels shattered, it fell indeed upon its side.
Then, O twice-born one, all the people of the cowherd settlement, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", arrived and beheld the boy lying on his back.
"O cowherds, by whom was this cart overturned? "By this boy," the children there replied, "it was cast down. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.6.4)
"While we were crying, we saw a cart overturned, cast down by the stamping of feet; this was surely not the work of anyone else."
Then, once again, the cowherds and cowherdesses were filled with extreme wonder;
Nanda the cowherd also, greatly amazed, took up the child.
Yaśodā, seeing the fragments of the broken jars upon the cart,
honored the cart with curd, flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice.
And Garga, urged by Vasudeva, remained concealed there in Gokula and performed the purificatory rites for the two of them among the cowherds.
The highly intelligent Garga, the best among the wise, gave them their names, calling the elder Rāma and the younger Kṛṣṇa.
O Brahmin, in a very short time, both of those two wrestlers then became worn at their knees and hands from rubbing against the ground.
With their limbs smeared with cow-dung and ashes, wandering here and there,
neither Yaśodā nor Rohiṇī was able to restrain them.
Playing in the middle of the cow-pen, they went again to the calf-pen,
intent on pulling the tails of the calves born that very day.
When Yaśodā was unable to restrain those two boys, who were both moving about together and playing with extreme restlessness, [she bound them].
Then, having bound him by the middle with a rope, she tied the unblemished-acting Kṛṣṇa to a mortar; and being indignant, she spoke this to him.
"If you are able, go, you whose actions are so exceedingly fickle!
Having said this, the housewife then attended to her own household duties.
Then, while she was distracted, that lotus-eyed one dragged the mortar through the middle of the twin arjuna trees and departed.
As he dragged the mortar sideways between the two trees, the lofty tips of their branches were broken;
thus were those twin *arjuna* trees destroyed.
Then, intent on hearing the sound of the rustling leaves,
the people of Vraja arrived and beheld the two great trees.
And he saw the young boy standing between them, with a smile white with the rays of his newly emerged small teeth,
and bound tightly around his belly by a rope.
And then, because of his binding with cords, he attained the state of being within the womb of Tāmasa.
Then all the elder cowherds, led by Nanda Gopa,
being deeply distressed and terrified by the great portents, held a consultation.
"We have no need to remain here; let us go to another great forest, for many portents are seen here that are causes of destruction."
The destruction of Pūtanā, the overturning of the cart,
and likewise the falling of two trees without any defect such as wind or other causes.
"Let us go from this place to Vṛndāvana without delay,
before the fault of these great terrestrial portents overwhelms the cowherd settlement."
Having thus resolved to depart, all those inhabitants of Vraja said to their respective families, "Let us go quickly; do not delay!"
Then, in an instant, the inhabitants of Vraja set out with their wagons and herds of cattle, and the cowherd boys went in groups, driving the calves along.
O Brāhmaṇa, in a mere instant, that cow-pen became cleared of its material parts and was filled with crows and vultures.
Vṛndāvana was meditated upon with a pure mind by the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are untainted, as he desired the perfection of his own cowherd state.
Then, O best of the twice-born, even during that exceedingly harsh summer season,
fresh grass sprang up on all sides as if it were the rainy season.
Then that entire settlement of Vraja was encamped in Vṛndāvana,
extending as far as the wagon-pasture and arranged in the shape of a half-moon.
Thereafter, Rāma and Dāmodara became cowherd boys;
staying together in one place in the cow-pen, they engaged in the play of childhood.
They wore wreaths fashioned from *barhi* grass and ornaments made of wild flowers; they produced sounds with musical instruments fashioned from cowherds' flutes and with the blowing of leaf-pipes.
Wearing side-locks of hair like two young sons of Agni,
they wandered through the great forest, laughing and playing.
Sometimes they wandered about, carrying one another and playing with others,
as well as herding calves together with the sons of the cowherds.
As time passed, those two became seven-year-old cowherd boys in Mahāvraja, acting as protectors of the entire world.
Then the rainy season arrived, with the sky completely shrouded by masses of clouds,
as if making the quarters of the horizon one with the torrents of water.
The earth was rich with lush new grass, covered with *śakragopa* insects,
and appeared as if made of emerald, yet adorned with rubies.
The waters of rivers flowing out of their courses surged everywhere upon reaching Lakṣmī,
as if they were the minds of the ill-behaved encountering new fortune.
The spotless moon, obscured by dark clouds, does not shine;
nor does the doctrine of the virtuous disputant, when confronted by the boastful speeches of fools.
Even though the bow was devoid of qualities, it attained a place in the sky of Śakra through its association with a king who lacked discernment.
Upon the back of the cloud, the pure row of cranes shone like the exceedingly beautiful conduct and behavior of a man of noble birth amidst wickedness.
The cloud has no stability in the sky, and lightning is exceedingly fickle,
like the friendship shown by a wicked person toward an excellent man.
The paths became indistinct, covered with heaps of grass and young shoots,
like the utterances of the dull-witted that have reached a different meaning.
At that time, in that great forest filled with wild peacocks and deer,
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, filled with joy, wandered together with the cowherds.
In some places, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa wandered together with the cows in delightful areas suitable for cattle; in other places, they rested excessively at the foot of cool trees.
In some places they were variegated with garlands of kadamba flowers and adorned with wreaths of peacock feathers; in other places they appeared smeared with various mountain minerals.
In some places they slept soundly upon beds of leaves, seeking intervals of rest;
in other places, when the clouds thundered, they were filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! in their distress.
Elsewhere, two cowherd flute-players, accompanied by the cries of peacocks, were engaged in praising other cowherds who were singing.
Thus, filled with various emotions and joined by supreme affection,
the two of them wandered through that forest, playing with contented minds.
And at the proper time, together with the cows and accompanied by the herd of cowherds,
those two of great strength, having wandered about as was fitting, returned to Vraja.
Accompanied by their peers, the cowherds, they played like two immortals;
thus did those two of great splendor, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, dwell there.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Once, Kṛṣṇa went to Vṛndāvana without Rāma.
Surrounded by cowherds and radiant with garlands of wild flowers, he wandered about.
Then he went to the Kālindī, which was graced by restless waves and seemed to laugh on all sides with masses of foam clinging to her banks.
There he beheld the exceedingly terrifying lake of the serpent Kālīya, its waters infused with the fire of poison and most fearsome to behold.
Its banks were scorched by spreading fires of poison;
its trees were withered by the spray of water driven by the wind, and its birds were consumed by the touch of that spray.
Beholding that exceedingly great and terrible being, like another mouth of Death, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana reflected.
"In this place dwells that evil-minded Kālīya, whose weapon is poison;
he who was defeated by me fled to the ocean, abandoning this spot."
Thus, this entire Yamunā, which flows to the ocean, has been defiled;
it is not utilized by men, nor even by herds of cattle, though they are afflicted by thirst.
Therefore, I must exercise restraint over this king of the *nāgas*,
so that the inhabitants of Vraja may live happily and free from fear.
It is for this purpose that my incarnation has been made in this world:
so that peace may be brought about for these evil-minded ones who stand upon the wrong path.
Therefore, having climbed this large-branched kadamba tree standing not far away,
I shall leap into this lake of the wind-eater.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having reflected thus and firmly girding his loins,
he then plunged with great speed into that lake belonging to the king of the Nāgas.
As he flew over, that great lake was agitated by him;
he thoroughly drenched the trees that had grown at a very great distance.
Sprinkled by water and wind heated by the flames of that wicked poison,
those trees immediately burst into flame, their fire spreading across the quarters of the sky.
Then Kṛṣṇa slapped his arm in the serpent-hole;
and upon hearing that sound, the king of the serpents quickly approached.
With eyes copper-red from rage, he was surrounded by other great venomous serpents who feed on air, their mouths filled with the flames of poison.
And hundreds of Naga wives, adorned with captivating necklaces,
their beauty enhanced by the swaying of their spears as they moved their trembling bodies.
Then, having been encircled by serpents with their coils as bonds,
they bit Kṛṣṇa with mouths filled with the flames of poison.
Seeing him fallen there, crushed by the coils of the serpent,
the cowherds returned to Vraja and cried out, overwhelmed with grief.
The cowherds said: "Kṛṣṇa has fallen into delusion; he is indeed submerged in the pool of Kāliya and is being devoured by the king of serpents. Come, let us go and see him!"
Having heard those words, which were like a thunderbolt,
the cowherds and the cowherd women, led by Yaśodā, went in haste to the lake.
"Alas, alas! Where is he? cried the people, utterly distraught for the cowherd women;
together with Yaśodā, they wandered about and went away with hurried, stumbling steps.
Nandagopa, the cowherds, and Rāma of wondrous prowess,
eager for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, quickly went to the Yamunā.
And there they also saw Kṛṣṇa, who had fallen under the power of the king of serpents, rendered motionless and entwined by the coils of the serpent's body.
O best of sages, Nanda the cowherd also became motionless, fixing his gaze upon the face of his son, and the highly fortunate Yaśodā did likewise.
But the other gopīs, weeping and overwhelmed by grief,
beheld him and spoke with affection to Keśava, their voices faltering from fear and distress.
The Gopīs said:
"O Yaśodā, let us all enter this great lake;
it is not fitting for us to go to Vraja while we are under the power of the king of serpents."
What is a day without the sun? What is night without the moon? What are cows without a bull? And what is Vraja without Kṛṣṇa?
"Deprived of this Kṛṣṇa, we shall not go to Gokula;
it will be like a lake devoid of water—unpleasant and no longer fit for frequenting."
It is a marvel that even by dwelling in that place where this Hari does not possess the bodily luster of a dark-blue lotus, there is still delight.
Not seeing Hari, whose eyes possess the clear beauty of the petals of a full-blown lotus, how will you remain in the cowherd settlement, O wretched ones?
"Without the lotus-eyed one, whose exceedingly sweet speech has captivated all our desires, we shall not go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement."
Behold the face of Kṛṣṇa, beautiful with a smile as he gazes at us, even though he is encircled by the king of serpents, O cowherd girls!
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of the cowherd women, and seeing the cowherds overwhelmed with terror and their eyes fixed in a stare, the mighty son of Rohiṇī spoke.
And he saw Nanda, whose mind was exceedingly dejected and whose gaze was fixed upon his son’s face,
as well as Yaśodā, who was overwhelmed by fainting, yet still perceiving Kṛṣṇa through her own mental conception of him.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, what is this? Why is this human being revealed by you as being so exceedingly yourself? Or is it that you do not know the Infinite? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.7.35)
You alone are the navel of the universe, the support for all things like the hub of spokes;
you are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector of the three worlds, consisting of the triple Veda.
O you of inconceivable nature, you are meditated upon by the Sādhyas, Rudras, Agnis, Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, and Aśvins, as well as by all the yogis.
O Lord of the World, you have descended among mortals for the sake of the world, with the desire to remove its burden; and I, your elder brother, am a portion of yourself.
O Blessed One, as you engage in human pastimes, all the gods together with their consorts imitate those very pastimes of yours.
O Eternal One, having first caused the celestial damsels to descend into Gokula for your own sport, you subsequently descended yourself.
O Kṛṣṇa, for those of us who have descended here, the cowherds alone are indeed our kinsmen, as are the cowherd women; why do you neglect these relatives who are now sinking in despair?
The human nature has been displayed, and the fickleness of a child has been shown;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, let this evil-minded one whose weapons are his fangs now be subdued.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus reminded, Kṛṣṇa, his lips parted with a smile,
slapped his arms and released his body from the bondage of the serpent's coils.
Bending his middle head with both hands,
he of great prowess climbed upon it with his neck curved and danced.
The vital breaths of this Kṛṣṇa remained within his hood despite the trampling of his feet;
yet, whenever he raised it up, his head would bow down.
The serpent fell into a swoon from the confusion caused by Kṛṣṇa’s breaths;
from the impact of the falling staff, he vomited much blood.
Beholding him with his head and neck severed and blood flowing from his mouths, his wives approached Madhusūdana with piteous cries.
The wives of the Nāgas said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you are known; you are the omniscient and unsurpassed one.
You are a portion of that supreme light which is inconceivable, O Supreme Lord."
Even the gods are not capable of praising that all-pervading Lord, who has no other source of existence;
how then could a woman describe his true nature?
How shall we praise him, of whom this entire universe— composed of earth, sky, water, fire, and air— is but a minute fraction of a fraction?
We bow to Him whose true nature the yogis do not know eternally, who is subtler than the ultimate atom and yet vaster than the vastest; to Him we are prostrate.
Salutations ever to Him, for whose birth there is no Creator, for whose end there is no Destroyer,
and for whom there is no other who ordains His duration.
Not even the slightest anger exists in you; your sole purpose is the preservation of stability.
O Kāliya, hear my words regarding the reason for your subduing.
Women are objects of compassion for the virtuous, as are foolish and wretched beings; therefore, O best among the forgiving, let this wretched man be forgiven.
The serpent, who encompasses the entire world and possesses immense power,
would lose his life within half a moment if he were trampled by your foot.
Where is this serpent of little power, and where are you, the refuge of the world?
O Imperishable One, your feelings of affection and aversion pertain equally to the lowly and the exalted.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, show favor to this one who is despondent;
this serpent is giving up his life—grant him the boon requested by his master.
O Lord of the World, O Master of the Universe, O Foremost of Great Beings!
This serpent is giving up his life; grant us the alms of our master's life.
O Lord of Gods, known through the Vedanta, destroyer of wicked Daityas, this serpent is giving up his life; O Master, let alms be granted to him.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When they had spoken thus, the serpent, though his body was exhausted, took heart and spoke these words very slowly: "Be gracious, O God of gods!"
Kāliya said:
O Lord, how shall I praise you, whose supreme sovereignty consists of eightfold qualities, which is innate, and from which all excellence is surpassed?
You are the beyond; you are the first of that which is beyond; O Supreme Self, there is nothing beyond you.
What indeed can I praise of you, who are higher than the highest?
Since Brahmā, Rudra, Candra, Indra, the Maruts, the Aśvins,
and the Vasus along with the Ādityas [are his], I shall praise that Kitra.
I shall praise that Creator, of whom this entire universe is but a minute fraction of a single limb, and who is himself but a fraction of a conceptual limb.
How can I possibly praise him, whose true nature— both existent and non-existent— is not known even by Brahmā and the other lords of the gods?
How could he, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods with perfumes, flowers, and ointments produced in the Nandana grove and elsewhere, be worshipped by me?
How can he, whose forms of incarnation the King of the Gods always worships,
yet does not know his supreme form— how can he be worshipped by me?
Having withdrawn all the senses from their objects,
that yogin whom they worship through meditation— how could he be worshipped by me?
How can that Lord, whose form yogis conceive in their hearts and worship through meditation with the flowers of their own being, be worshipped by me?
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, I am not capable of worship, praise, or the like; my mental state consists solely of compassion for you. Be gracious to me!
"O Keśava, this serpent race is cruel, and it is within this that I was born;
this is my inherent nature here, O Acyuta, and there is no fault of mine."
By you everything is created, and likewise the entire world is withdrawn;
and by you, as the creator, the species, forms, and inherent natures are brought forth.
O Lord, just as I was created by you with my birth, my form,
and my inherent goodness, so too has this deed been performed by me.
O God of gods, if I should act otherwise than this, then the application of punishment would indeed be just toward me, according to your own word.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the World, you have inflicted punishment upon me, though I am ignorant;
this supreme punishment from you is praiseworthy, and no other boon could be better for me than this.
"O Acyuta, my vigor has been destroyed, my poison neutralized, and I have been subdued by you.
Grant me my life for one moment; give me your command—what shall I do?"
The Blessed Lord said: "O serpent, you must never stay here in the waters of the Yamunā;
together with your sons and your retinue, go to the waters of the ocean."
And having seen my footprints upon your head in the ocean, O serpent,
Garuḍa, the enemy of the pannagas, will not strike you.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus to the king of serpents, the Blessed Lord Hari released him;
and he too, having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, departed for the ocean, the reservoir of waters.
While all living beings were looking on, he— along with his servants, sons, kinsmen,
and all his wives— abandoned his own lake.
Embracing the serpent that had returned as if dead,
the cowherds affectionately sprinkled water from their eyes upon its head.
Seeing the river of auspicious waters, other cowherds, their minds filled with wonder, praised Kṛṣṇa of untiring deeds with joyful hearts.
Being sung of by the cowherd women for his virtuous deeds and noble conduct,
and being praised by the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa returned to Vraja.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Furthermore, Balarāma and Keśava, together tending the cows, [proceeded].
Wandering through that forest, they came upon a delightful grove of palm trees.
That divine palm grove is constantly occupied by a Dānava named Dhenuka,
who has the form of a donkey and subsists on a diet of deer meat.
Seeing that palm grove endowed with an abundance of ripe fruit, the cowherds were filled with longing and spoke these words regarding the gathering of the fruit: ||| ViP_5.8.3 |||
The cowherds said:
"O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, since this region of land is always protected by Dhenuka, these fruits here are indeed ripe."
"Behold the fruits of the palmyra trees, which indeed perfume the quarters with their fragrance;
we desire these, so let them be brought down if it pleases you."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard these words of the cowherd boys, Saṃkarṣaṇa said,
"This must be done," and indeed caused them to fall.
And Kṛṣṇa caused those fruits to fall upon the ground.
Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, that evil-minded Daitya donkey, who was very difficult to approach, arrived there in a rage.
Then that powerful one struck Bala on the chest with both his hind feet; and Bala, in turn, seized him with those two.
Having seized him while he was lifeless,
he whirled him around in the air and hurled him with great force right back into that king of trees.
Then, like a fierce wind felling clouds, the donkey, leaping from the tops of the palm trees, caused many fruits to fall upon the earth.
Then Kṛṣṇa and Balabhadra effortlessly tossed other future Daitya-donkeys of their own kind onto the tops of palm trees.
Then, O Maitreya, the earth was adorned in an instant by those ripe palm fruits and by the bodies of the donkey-shaped Daityas; it shone exceedingly.
Then, O twice-born one, the cows roamed happily on fresh grass in that Talavana forest, free from all affliction, such as they had never experienced before.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When that Daitya Rāsabha had been struck down along with his followers, [the gods rejoiced].
That beautiful palm grove of the cowherds and cowherd-maidens shone with a gentle splendor.
Then, having slain the Daitya Dhenuka, both sons of Vasudeva, filled with joy, arrived at the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree.
They were playing, singing aloud, and searching among the trees;
they were driving the cows to a distance and calling them by their names.
With their yoke-straps and halters removed from their shoulders and adorned with forest garlands,
those two great-souled ones shone like two bulls with powerful horns.
Then, their garments were stained with gold and collyrium powder,
appearing like white and black clouds accompanied by a rainbow.
Having descended to earth as the lords of all the lords of the worlds, they played with one another in sports perfected by the inhabitants of the celestial realms.
Delighting in human virtues and honoring their humanity, they roamed the forest with games suited to their kind and qualities.
Then those two of great strength engaged in exercise there by means of swings, wrestling matches, and likewise with projectiles and stones.
While the two were thus enjoying themselves, a demon named Pralamba,
desiring to seize them, arrived there disguised in the dress of a cowherd.
Assuming a human form, that best of Dānavas, Pralamba, plunged fearlessly into their midst as a human being.
Seeking a vulnerability between the two of them, he considered Kṛṣṇa to be invincible; he then set his heart on killing the son of Rohiṇī.
Then, performing the childhood game called "The Deer's Play," they all rose up in pairs simultaneously.
Then Govinda, together with Śrīdāman, and Balarāma with Pralamba,
as well as other cowherds and the rest of the cowherd boys, leaped forward.
Then Kṛṣṇa defeated Śrīdāman, and the son of Rohiṇī defeated Pralamba; the other cowherds on Kṛṣṇa’s side were also victorious.
Driving one another along, they reached the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree; all those who were defeated there returned once more.
Lifting Saṃkarṣaṇa up by the shoulder, the Dānava quickly ascended into the expanse of the sky, like a cloud with the moon.
Unable to bear the burden of the son of Rohiṇī,
that best of Dānavas grew in massive body like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.
But Saṃkarṣaṇa, seeing him with a form like a scorched mountain,
adorned with hanging garlands and ornaments, and with a head crowned by a towering diadem, [was filled with wonder].
With a mind undaunted, that Rākṣasa, whose eyes were like the wheels of a cart and who made the earth tremble with his tread, began to carry away the son of Rohiṇī;
being thus abducted, he spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.9.19.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, I am being carried away by some Daitya in the guise of a cowherd, who has a form as lofty as a mountain; look! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.9.20)
"O slayer of Madhu, tell me what must be done by me here at this moment; for this evil-souled one is departing with extreme haste."
Śrī Parāśara said: Govinda, the Great Soul, whose lips were parted by a smile, spoke to Rāma,
who was filled with pride regarding the measure of his own strength and heroism.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Why is this human condition being so clearly assumed by you,
who are the Self of all and the most secret essence of all secrets?
O you who are born before all causes, remember yourself— the sole cause that is the seed of the entire universe— and likewise that which exists when the world is a single ocean.
Do you not know how both you and I have come to this mortal world as a single cause for the purpose of removing the earth's burden?

The sky is your head, the clouds are your hair, the earth is your feet, and the infinite fire is your mouth; the moon is your mind, the wind is your breath, and the four directions, O Imperishable One, are your arms.
The Blessed One, the Great-Souled One, who possesses a thousand bulls, whose body is distinguished by a thousand hands and feet,
and who is the primordial source born from a thousand lotuses— sages praise you a thousandfold.
For no one other than you knows your divine form, which is the form of your incarnations recognized by all the gods;
do you not know that very form which is worshipped, at the end of which the entire universe attains dissolution within you alone?
Supported by you, O one of infinite form, this earth sustains the entire universe with its moving and unmoving beings;
yet, O Unborn One, appearing as Time through the divisions of the Kṛta age and others, you consume this world at the beginning of a *nimeṣa*.

Just as water, having assumed the nature of ice by contact with the submarine fire, becomes wood upon reaching the Himalayas, yet returns to the state of water again through contact with the rays of the sun; so too does the self. ViP_5.9.30.
Thus, when you withdraw this entire world, it remains entirely subject to you; yet, O Lord, as you prepare for creation once more, the world comes into being through your inconceivable power.
O Soul of the Universe, you and I are the single cause of this world; yet for the sake of the world, we are established in distinct forms.
Therefore, O immeasurable-souled one, remember your true self; slay the Dānava, and by assuming merely human form, bring about the welfare of your kinsmen.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus reminded by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, O Brāhmaṇa, the powerful Balarāma laughed and began to crush Pralamba.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he struck him on the head with his fist;
by that blow, his two eyes were knocked out.
With his brain forced out and vomiting blood from his mouth,
that foremost of Dānavas fell upon the surface of the earth and died.
Seeing Pralamba slain by Balarāma of wondrous deeds, the cowherds were delighted;
they praised him and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
While being praised by the cowherds after the Daitya had been struck down, Rāma,
together with Kṛṣṇa, returned once more to Gokula.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
While Rāma and Keśava were thus sporting in Vraja, [the following occurred].
The rainy season passed away, and autumn arrived with its blossoming lotuses.
Just as a householder, through the sense of "mine" attached to sons, fields, and so forth, suffers extreme distress, even so did the fish suffer in the water of the pond.
In the forest, the peacocks observed silence, having abandoned their pride,
just as yogis do upon realizing the essencelessness of saṃsāra.
Having surrendered their entire essence as water, the clouds— now pure and white in form— abandoned the sky just as men of realized wisdom renounce their homes.
And the lakes, scorched by the rays of the autumn sun, went to desiccation,
like the hearts of embodied beings due to their attachment to many worldly supports.
The waters attained a state of fitness with the water-lilies,
just as the minds of pure-souled beings attain equanimity through spiritual awakenings.
In the sky, stainless with stars, the moon shone with its full orb, like a yogi in his final body within a virtuous lineage.
Gradually, little by little, the reservoirs abandoned their banks,
just as the wise abandon the deep-seated sense of "mine-ness" regarding fields, sons, and other possessions.
Just as swans, having previously abandoned the waters of a lake, regain union with them,
so too do those of failed yoga (kuyogins) regain union with their remaining afflictions (kleśas), like those struck by obstacles.
The ocean became exceedingly tranquil, its waters stilled,
like an ascetic whose self is motionless after having gradually attained great yoga.
The waters everywhere became exceedingly clear,
just as the minds of the wise become so when Viṣṇu, who pervades all, is known.
The sky became stainless, its clouds destroyed by autumn,
like the minds of yogis whose floods of afflictions have been consumed by the fire of yoga.
Just as the moon, the lord of the stars, eternally pacifies the heat produced by the rays of the sun,
so does great discernment pacify the suffering born of egoism.
Autumn removed the clouds from the sky, the mud from the earth, and the turbidity from the waters,
just as withdrawal (pratyāhāra) draws back the senses from their objects.
Like the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), it is practiced daily by the waters of the lakes through the processes of exhalation (recaka) and retention (kuṃbhaka).
When the time had arrived, under the stars of the stainless sky,
Indra beheld those inhabitants of Vraja preparing for a great undertaking.
Seeing those cowherds eager and longing for the festival, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa, out of curiosity, spoke these words to the elders: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.10.17.
"What is this so-called festival of Śakra, because of which joy has come upon you?
Nandagopa replied with great respect to him who was thus inquiring.
Nandagopa said:
"The King of the Gods, Śatakratu, is the lord of the clouds and of the waters;
impelled by him, the clouds rain down this abundant, savory moisture."
Using the crops produced by that rain, we and other embodied beings sustain ourselves,
and we satisfy the deities.
These cows are rich in milk and accompanied by their calves, living in peace;
indeed, they become satisfied and well-nourished by the crops raised by him.
In that place, the earth was not without grain nor without grass, and no person was seen afflicted by hunger; there, only rain-bearing clouds were visible.
That water, milked from the rays of the sun by the clouds as if by cows,
falls upon the earth as rain from Parjanya for the sake of the prosperity of all the worlds.
Therefore, during the rainy season, all kings, filled with joy,
worship Śakra, the lord of the gods, with sacrifices— both we and other men.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard these words of Nanda Gopa regarding the worship of Śakra,
Dāmodara then spoke out of anger toward the Lord of the Thirty-three.
"O father, we are neither farmers nor do we live by trade;
moreover, cows are our deity, for we are forest-dwellers."
Logic, the three Vedas, economics, and likewise the science of government—this is the fourfold group of sciences; now hear from me that which pertains solely to livelihood.
Agriculture, trade, and likewise the third, cattle-rearing—
these, O highly fortunate one, constitute the single science of livelihood (vārtā), which rests upon these three means of subsistence.
Agriculture is the livelihood of farmers, trade for those who live by the marketplace, and cattle are our means of subsistence; thus, this [economy] consists of these three distinct branches of life.
Whichever knowledge a person is endowed with, that alone is his great deity;
it is that which is to be honored and worshipped, and it is that which provides him benefit.
That man who, while enjoying the fruit of one [deity], worships another,
does not obtain what is auspicious either in this world or after death.
The boundary is known to end at the furrow; the forest, in turn, ends at the boundary.
All mountains end at the forest, and they are our ultimate refuge.
Neither by the obstruction of locking doors nor by houses and fields are people so happy in the entire world as those who indeed wander with the wheel [of sovereignty].
It is heard that even the mountains in this forest can assume any form at will; taking on various shapes, they take their pleasure upon their own peaks.
And when these [beings] are oppressed, then the mountain-dwellers, assuming the forms of lions and other such creatures, slaughter them.
"Therefore, let this sacrifice to the mountains and the sacrifice to the cows be performed;
what need have we for Mahendra? The cows and the mountains are our deities."
The Brahmins are devoted to sacrifices performed with mantras, the farmers to sacrifices performed with the plow,
and we, who dwell in the mountains and forests of the Ādris, are habituated to sacrifices of mountain cattle.
Therefore, let Mount Govardhana be honored and worshipped by you with various offerings, having slaughtered pure animals according to the prescribed rites.
"Let the collection of all sounds be received; let it not be deliberated upon.
Let the Brahmins be fed with that, as well as those who have come to seek it."
There, when the worship has been performed, the fire-oblation offered, and the twice-born have been fed,
let the herds of cows, adorned with wreaths of autumn flowers, roam about.
O cowherds, if this which is my opinion is carried out with affection,
then the pleasure of the cows, of the mountain, and likewise of myself will have been accomplished.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard these words of his, those cowherds of Vraja, headed by Vandā, with faces blooming with joy, then exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (ViP 5.10.42).
"Your thought is excellent, my child, that you have spoken thus;
we shall do all of it. Let the mountain sacrifice be commenced."
And so those inhabitants of Vraja performed the mountain sacrifice;
they then offered the mountain-oblation with curd, milk-rice, meat, and other foods.
And they fed the twice-born by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Then those cows, having been honored, circumambulated the mountain;
and the bulls bellowed loudly, like water-laden clouds.
O twice-born one, on the mountain peak, Kṛṣṇa too, assuming a physical form as a mountain,
ate a great deal of food brought by the best of cowherds.
In his own dark form, Kṛṣṇa, having ascended the summit of the mountain together with the cowherds,
worshipped his own second body.
When he had vanished, the cowherds, having received those boons, performed the Girima sacrifice and returned once more to their own cow-pen.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, when the sacrifice was thwarted, Śakra was filled with extreme rage.
Then he spoke to the host of clouds named Saṃvartaka.
O Medhā, listen to these words as I speak them; immediately after my command, let it be carried out swiftly and without hesitation.
The foolish Nandagopa, supported by other cowherds and emboldened by his reliance on Kṛṣṇa, brought about the destruction of the sacrifice.
Their livelihood depends entirely upon those cows, and they are the cause of his [the king's] power;
by my word, let those cows be afflicted by a downpour of rain.
I too, having mounted a lofty elephant that resembles a mountain peak,
shall provide you assistance by discharging wind and water.
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus commanded by him,
O twice-born one, those clouds released a most terrifying wind and rain for the destruction of the cows.
Then, O Sage, in an instant the earth, the quarters, and the sky itself became one through the flood of that great downpour of rain.
As if terrified by the lash-strokes of the lightning-vines, the clouds,
filling the circle of the quarters with their roar, let fall a torrential downpour.
When the world was enveloped in darkness by clouds raining incessantly,
the universe— below, above, and across— seemed as if it were submerged in water.
But the cows, shaken by that falling rain-wind which was like a violent gust,
gave up their lives, their flanks, thighs, and necks collapsing.
O great sage, some cows stood having trampled their calves with their chests,
while others were deprived of their calves by the flood of water.
And the calves, with dejected faces and necks trembling from the wind, cried out in distress to Kṛṣṇa as if saying "Save us! Save us! in faint voices.
Then, O Maitreya, seeing that entire Gokula crowded with cows, cowherd women, and cowherds, Hari became deeply distressed and reflected thus.
This was done by Mahendra, who acted in opposition to the breaking of his friend's [vow];
therefore, this entire cow-pen must now be protected by me.
With fortitude, I shall uproot this mountain, whose peaks are like massive clouds,
and hold it over the cow-pen like a broad umbrella.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having formed this resolve, Kṛṣṇa uprooted Mount Govardhana with a single hand and held it up effortlessly as if in play.
And Śauri, laughing as he lifted up the mountain, said to the cowherds:
"Enter here quickly; the obstruction of the rain has been accomplished."
"Stay here as you please in places sheltered from the wind; enter without fear, being free from dread even of the falling of mountains."
Having been addressed thus by him, those cowherds entered along with their herds of cattle,
while the cowherd women, oppressed by the downpour, entered with their goods loaded upon carts.
Kṛṣṇa also held that mountain perfectly motionless,
while he was gazed upon by the inhabitants of Vraja with eyes wide with joy and wonder.
While his deeds were being praised by the joyful cowherds and cowherd girls, whose eyes were wide with affection, Kṛṣṇa supported the mountain.
O Brahmin, urged by Indra, who intended to bring about the destruction of the cowherds, great clouds rained down for seven nights upon Nanda’s cow-pen.
Then, once the great mountain had been held up and Gokula had been saved, Indra,
the slayer of Bala, having failed in his vow, caused those clouds to cease.
Then, while the lord of the gods stood in a cloudless sky with his words proven false, the joyful Gokula departed and returned once more to its own place.
Then Kṛṣṇa also released the great mountain Govardhana back to its own place,
while he was watched by those inhabitants of Vraja with faces full of wonder.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When Mount Govardhana had been held up and Gokula had been protected, [the people were filled with joy].
The subduer of Pāka (Indra) caused Kṛṣṇa to behold him.
Having mounted the great elephant Airāvata, that conqueror of enemies,
the lord of the gods, beheld Kṛṣṇa on Mount Govardhana.
He was tending the cows with great vigor, assuming the form of a cowherd;
he was the protector of the entire world, surrounded by cowherd boys.
And he saw the Garuda, the preeminent among birds, who had become invisible and remained high above, O twice-born one,
casting a shadow over the head of Hari with his two wings.
Having descended from the king of serpents, Śakra, his eyes wide with joy, spoke these words with a smile to Madhusūdana in a secluded spot.
Indra said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, listen to this for which purpose I have come to your presence, O mighty-armed one; you should not think otherwise of this."
O support of all, O Supreme Lord, you alone have descended upon the surface of the earth for the purpose of relieving the burden of the world.
In order to frustrate the sacrifice, I commanded great clouds capable of destroying Gokula; by them, this slaughter was wrought.
And those cows were rescued by you after you uprooted the mountain;
therefore, I am pleased with this most wonderful heroic deed of yours.
O Kṛṣṇa, I consider the purpose of the gods to have been accomplished,
since this best of mountains has been held by you with a single hand.
Urged by the cows, O Kṛṣṇa, I have come here into your presence;
I have been exceedingly protected by you for the sake of honoring you.
Impelled by the words of the Cow, he shall consecrate you as Kṛṣṇa;
as the Indra of the cows in the state of Upendra, you shall become Govinda.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, taking the bell from his mount, the elephant Airāvata,
he performed the consecration for her with that vessel filled with sacred water.
While the consecration was being performed, at that very moment, the cows made the earth instantly moist with the milk flowing from their udders.
Having consecrated Upendra Janārdana according to the words of the cows,
the Lord of Śacī spoke these words again with affection and humility.
O illustrious one, listen to these words spoken by the cows, as well as others that I shall speak out of a desire to remove the burden of the earth.
O tiger among men, O upholder of the earth, my own portion has descended upon the earth under the name of Arjuna; he must always be protected by you.
O Madhusūdana, that hero will provide you assistance in removing the burden; he must be protected by you as you would yourself.
The Blessed Lord said: "I know that Pārtha, born in the lineage of Bhārata, is from a portion of you;
I shall protect him as long as I remain upon the earth."
O Śakra, O subduer of enemies, as long as I remain upon the surface of the earth,
no one, O Lord of the Gods, shall defeat Arjuna in battle.
The mighty-armed Daitya named Kaṃsa, as well as the Asura Ariṣṭa,
Keśin, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Naraka, and others besides.
O Lord of the Gods, when those [Asuras] are slain, there will be a great battle;
know, O Thousand-eyed One, that in that moment the removal of the burden shall be accomplished.
Therefore, go; you ought not to feel distress on account of your son.
No enemy of Arjuna shall prevail against me.
But for the sake of Arjuna, I shall give all those led by Yudhiṣṭhira to Kuntī, unscarred, once the Bhārata war has concluded.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the king of the gods embraced Janārdana and,
mounting the elephant Airāvata, returned once more to heaven.
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the cows and the cowherds,
returned to Vraja by a path purified by the glances of the gopīs.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When Śakra had departed, the cowherds [approached] Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds.
Seeing that Govardhana mountain held up by him, they spoke with affection.
O illustrious one, O Blessed One, we and the cows have been rescued from this great danger by your deed of supporting the mountain.
"This childhood play is incomparable, yet your state as a cowherd is contemptible;
and yet your deeds are divine—O Father, tell me what this is."
Kālīya was subdued in the water, Dhenuka was struck down, and this Govardhana was held up; our minds are filled with apprehension.
"Truly, truly, O you of immeasurable prowess, we swear by the feet of Hari that,
having observed your true heroism, we do not consider you a mere man."
O Keśava, the people of Vraja, including their women and children, have affection for you;
yet this deed is impossible even for all the gods combined.
O Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is immeasurable, even our childhood, our extreme vigor, and our birth appear beautiful when reflected upon, yet they give rise to doubt.
Whether you are a god, a dānava, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva—what need have we for inquiry? You are our kinsman; homage be to you!
Śrī Parāśara said: Having remained silent for a moment, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa, feeling a slight touch of affectionate anger at being addressed in this manner by those cowherds, spoke as follows.
The Blessed One said:
"O cowherds, if you feel no shame because of my association with you, then I am indeed praiseworthy; what need have you for further deliberation?"
If you have affection for me, and if I am worthy of your praise,
then let your mind toward me be as it would be toward your own kinsman.
I am neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor a dānava;
I have been born as your kinsman, and this should not be considered otherwise.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard these words of Hari, O highly fortunate one, the cowherds then departed for the forest in silence, while he remained in a state of affectionate anger.
Kṛṣṇa, however, saw the stainless sky, the moonlight of the autumn moon,
and the blossoming night-lily that perfumed the quarters of space.
Beholding the forest grove, enchanting with its rows of bees humming their songs, he, together with the cowherd girls, set his mind upon amorous delight.
Without Rāma, Śauri sang a sweet song, exceedingly pleasing to women, with melodious words and a rhythmic progression of high and low notes.
Then, hearing the delightful sound of singing, the cowherd women abandoned their dwellings and came in haste to where Madhusūdana was staying.
One cowherd girl sang very softly in accordance with his rhythm,
while another, having fixed her attention, remembered him alone with her mind.
One girl, having cried out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!", was overcome with shame;
another, blinded by love, went to his side without delay.
And another, standing at the edge of the dwelling and seeing her guru outside,
meditated upon Govinda with closed eyes, being completely absorbed in him.
Thus, her store of merit was exhausted by the stainless joy of that mind,
and all her sins were dissolved by the great suffering of not attaining it.
Another cowherd girl, meditating upon the source of the universe who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman,
attained liberation through the cessation of her breath.
Surrounded by the gopīs, Govinda, eager for the pleasure of beginning the rāsa dance, honored the night that was as enchanting as the autumn moon.
And the cowherd women, their very bodies surrendered to the movements of Kṛṣṇa,
wandered within the interior of Vṛndāvana when Kṛṣṇa had gone to another region.
With their hearts bound to Kṛṣṇa, they spoke thus to one another:
"I am Kṛṣṇa; here I go gracefully—behold my gait! Others say: "Listen to the song of me, Kṛṣṇa! *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 5.13.26.
"Evil Kāliya, stay here! I am Kṛṣṇa!"—saying this, another [gopī] slapped her arms and playfully seized everything belonging to Kṛṣṇa.
Another said, "O cowherds, remain without fear;
there is no need for concern about the rain here, for Govardhana has been held up by me."
"This Dhenuka has been cast out by me; let the cows roam as they please," said another cow, following the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, amidst those various kinds of dark deeds,
the gopīs, though distracted, wandered together through the beautiful interior of Vṛndāvana.
Beholding the earth, one cowherd woman, a most excellent lady among the gopīs, spoke,
her entire body bristling with horripilation and her lotus-eyes wide open.
O friends, behold these footprints of Kṛṣṇa, who moves with playful grace, marked by lines bearing the signs of a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus bud.
A certain woman of great merit, languid with passion, has arrived here with him;
these are her footprints, both deep and shallow.
Dāmodara certainly gathered flowers here on high,
for here are the footprints of that great-souled one, marked by his toes slightly pressed down.
Having sat down there, she was indeed adorned with flowers by him;
for in another birth, Viṣṇu, the Soul of All, had been worshipped by her.
"Behold! Having cast aside her, who had been honored with gifts of flowers and marks of respect, the son of Nanda the cowherd has departed by this very path."
Another woman here, slow-moving due to the weight of her hips, follows him;
she moves quickly when she ought to go, because her feet are placed unevenly on the ground.
With her hand grasping the tip of her friend's hand, she moves in such a manner;
her trail of footprints appears as if her steps were not under her own control.
By the mere touch of his hand, this woman was insulted by the rogue;
her footsteps are seen to have turned back as she walks slowly out of despair.
"Surely she said, 'I am in haste; I shall return to his presence,' by that Kṛṣṇa for whom this hurried trail of footprints was made."
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the dense thicket; his footprints cannot be seen here.
Turn back; he is no longer within the range of the moon's rays."
Then those gopīs, having returned from the banks of the Yamunā and being despondent at the sight of Kṛṣṇa, sang of his deeds in that manner.
Then the cowherd girls beheld Kṛṣṇa, whose lotus-like face was blooming, the protector of the three worlds, whose actions are effortless.
Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman was filled with exceeding joy;
she cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else.
One woman, having made her forehead furrowed by a contraction of her eyebrows and gazing at Hari with her bee-like eyes, drank in the lotus of his face.
Upon seeing Govinda, one woman closed her eyes;
meditating on his very form, she shone like one who had ascended to the heights of yoga.
Then Mādhava brought one woman to submission with affectionate words, another with glances and the knitting of his brows, and yet another by the touch of his hand.
Together with those cowherd women whose hearts were filled with devotion, Hari, whose conduct is noble, joyfully engaged in the rāsa dance assemblies with great respect.
Even while performing the circular dance formation (*rāsamaṇḍalabandha*), the group of cowherd girls did not leave Kṛṣṇa’s side, their minds remaining fixed on a single point.
Taking each of the cowherd girls by the hand within the circle of the rāsa dance,
Hari caused their eyes to close at the touch of his hand.
Then the *rāsa* dance commenced, accompanied by the tinkling of moving bracelets and the successive songs of cowherds whose voices were inspired by autumnal poetry.
Kṛṣṇa sang of the autumn moon, the moonlight, and the bed of night-lotuses; but the multitude of gopīs sang only the name of Kṛṣṇa again and again.
Out of the fatigue of her constant turning, one cowherd girl placed her vine-like arm— jangling with its moving bracelets— upon the shoulder of the slayer of Madhu.
One clever cowherd girl, embracing Madhusūdana by his outstretched arm, kissed him under the pretext of singing praises in a song.
Having come into contact with the cheeks of the gopīs, Hari’s two arms became like clouds of perspiration-water for the sake of the harvest of rising horripilation.
As Kṛṣṇa sang the Rāsa-song with a voice of increasing pitch, they sang "Well done, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! with twice that intensity.
The cowherd women followed Hari as he went, moved in circles around him, and went before his face; they attended upon Hari by moving both against and with the current.
He sported with those cowherd girls in such a way that his sweet voice seemed like ten million years to them when he was away from them.
Though being restrained by their husbands, fathers, and brothers,
those cowherd women, who were fond of pleasure, took delight with Kṛṣṇa at night.
Honoring his youthful age, Madhusūdana,
whose soul is immeasurable and who has destroyed all enemies, took delight with them throughout the nights that pass away.
Likewise, among their husbands and among those women, as well as in all beings,
this Lord exists pervading them like the wind, having the nature of the self.
Just as ether, fire, earth, water,
and air exist within all beings, so too does that Self abide, pervading everything.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter (13) in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa. Śrī Parāśara said: Once, at the beginning of the evening twilight, while Janārdana was absorbed in the Rāsa dance, a certain woman... [text continues]... said: "O Lord, O Supreme Soul, you have abandoned me, who am devoted to you. Thus addressed by her, the Lord spoke these words: "O beautiful one, I have not abandoned you; I am here before you. Look at me with your divine vision. Having spoken thus, he showed her his universal form, which is difficult even for the gods to behold. Seeing that form, she was filled with wonder and spoke: "O Lord of the World, I wish to see your own natural form. Then the Lord, having shown her his own form, spoke again: "O fortunate one, go now to the city of Dvārakā; there you shall dwell in my abode. She, having obtained his grace, went to Dvārakā and lived there in the company of other women. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Chapter Fourteen. Śrī Parāśara said: Now hear the account of the birth of Pradyumna, which bestows great merit upon those who listen to it. When the Lord of the world had gone to the city of Dvārakā, Rukmiṇī gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks. At that time, the demon Sambara, having learned of this through his spies, seized the infant while he was still in the womb and cast him into the ocean. There, the child was swallowed by a large fish. That fish was later caught by fishermen and brought to the city of Sambara. When the fish was opened, the child was seen by the demon's wife, Mayāvatī, who was skilled in the arts. She raised the boy with great care, and as he grew, he became known as Pradyumna. When he reached youth, he desired to obtain Rukmiṇī’s daughter, Rukmavatī, as his wife. He then challenged the king of Vidarbha to battle and, having defeated him, carried off the maiden. Upon hearing of this, the demon Sambara sent his son, Aniruddha, to seize Pradyumna. A fierce battle ensued between them, in which Pradyumna slew Aniruddha. Then Sambara himself came forth to fight, but Pradyumna, having overcome him, released his father-in-law from bondage and returned to Dvārakā with his bride. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Chapter Fifteen. Śrī Parāśara said: Now hear the story of the birth of Aniruddha, which destroys all sins. While Pradyumna was dwelling in Dvārakā, Rukmiṇī, desiring a grandson, performed various rites. Through the grace of the gods, she conceived and gave birth to a son named Aniruddha. When he grew up, he desired to marry Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa. Bāṇa, however, refused to give her to him. Aniruddha then entered Bāṇa’s palace by night and enjoyed Uṣā’s company. Bāṇa’s guards discovered him and reported it to their master. Bāṇa, enraged, set out with his army to capture Aniruddha. A great battle took place between the armies of Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, Pradyumna, and Gada fought against Bāṇa and his hosts. Finally, Kṛṣṇa slew Bāṇa in combat. Having liberated Aniruddha and won Uṣā for him, they returned to Dvārakā. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Chapter Sixteen.
Śrī Parāśara said: Now hear the account of the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa as Kalki, which occurs at the end of the Kali age.
When the world is filled with wickedness and the Vedic path is obscured, the Lord will appear as Kalki, the son of
Terrifying the herd, the bull Ariṣṭa approached the cow-pen.
Having the luster of water-laden clouds, with sharp horns for his weapons and the sun for his eye,
he tore up the surface of the earth excessively with the blows of his hooves.
Licking his lips repeatedly with his tongue while making a grinding sound,
his tail bristling with fury, and the muscles of his shoulders hardened.
Equal in size to the expanse of a towering hump, difficult to overcome,
with his back covered in excrement and urine, he causes distress even to the cattle.
With a long neck, an oversized mouth, and a face marked by tree-stumps,
that Daitya, assuming the form of a bull, caused the cow to miscarry her fetus.
He who, fierce as a forest-dweller, constantly roams through the woods, destroying the ascetics.
Then, beholding him of such exceedingly terrible eyes, the cowherds and the cowherd women, overcome with great fear, cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"
Then Keśava let out a lion’s roar and made a sound by clapping his hands;
upon hearing that sound, he [Akrūra] approached Dāmodara.
With the tip of his horn thrust forward and his gaze fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s belly,
the evil-minded bull-demon rushed toward Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the bull among the Daityas approaching, the mighty Kṛṣṇa did not stir from his seat, maintaining a playful air of disdainful smiles.
Madhusūdana seized him as he drew near, like a crocodile;
he struck him in the flank with his knee, though he was as immovable as a mountain due to his grip upon the horns.
Having shattered his pride and strength, he seized Ariṣṭa by the two horns and squeezed his throat as if it were a piece of wet cloth.
Then, having uprooted one of his horns, he struck him with it;
that great Daitya died, vomiting blood from his mouth.
When that Daitya had been slain, the cowherds praised Janārdana,
just as the hosts of gods once praised the Thousand-eyed One when Jambha was killed.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter (14) in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: When Kakudmin had been slain and Ariṣṭa and Dhenuka had been struck down, [...]
When Pralamba had been brought to his end and Mount Govardhana was held up, [the people were relieved].
When the serpent Kāliya was subdued, when the pair of lofty trees were broken, when Pūtanā was slain, and when the cart was overturned; ||| ViP_5.15.2 |||
Nārada related to Kaṃsa everything exactly as it had happened in due order,
including the complete exchange of the fetuses of Yaśodā and Devakī.
Having heard all that from Nārada, the seer who beholds the gods,
the evil-minded Kaṃsa then directed his wrath toward Vasudeva.
Having reproached him with harsh words in the assembly of all the Yādavas,
he roared at the Yādavas and reflected upon this matter.
"As long as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are still very young boys and have not yet attained full strength, they must be slain by me; once they have reached their youth, they will be invincible."
"Cāṇūra here is of great heroism, and Muṣṭika is of great strength;
through a wrestling match with these two, we shall kill that evil-minded one."
"Under the pretext of the great festival of archery, I shall bring those two from Vraja;
I will strive in such a way that they both shall go to their destruction."
I shall dispatch [Akrūra] to Gokula for the purpose of bringing back those two— the heroic Akrūra, son of Śvaphaḷpa, and the foremost of the Yadus.
I shall also command the terrible Keśin, who wanders in the Vṛndā forest;
there he, possessed of great strength, will slay both of them.
The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, having come here to my presence,
will slay both these cowherds, the sons of Vasudeva.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having reflected thus, the evil-minded Kaṃsa spoke these words to Akrūra, who was skilled in action, in order to slay Rāma and Janārdana.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Lord of Generosity, let my words be carried out for my pleasure;
mounting a chariot from here, go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement."
The two sons of Vasudeva there, born from portions of Viṣṇu, have indeed arisen for my destruction; those two wicked ones are growing in power.
"The Dhanurmaha festival shall also take place for me here on the fourteenth day;
you must go there and bring those two for a wrestling match."
"The two wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika are skilled in hand-to-hand combat;
let all the world here witness the battle between them and these two."
"The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, urged on by his mahout,
shall slay those two wicked sons of Vasudeva while they are still infants."
Having killed both Vasudeva and the wicked-minded Nandagopa,
I shall also slay this father of mine, the very evil-minded Ugrasena.
Then I shall seize all the cattle-wealth and the property of all the cowherds, those wicked men who desire my death.
"O Lord of Gifts, without you these Yādavas are my enemies;
therefore, I shall strive to slay them one after another in due order."
"Then I shall rule this entire kingdom, free from thorns and devoid of enemies, with your assistance; therefore, O hero, go for my pleasure."
And you must tell them: "Let the cowherds quickly bring buffalo ghee and curd as offerings."
Śrī Parāśara said: O twice-born one, having been thus commanded,
the highly devoted Akrūra became joyful and, eager to see Kṛṣṇa, thought, "I shall see him tomorrow."
Having said "So be it" to the king, Madhupriya mounted a splendid chariot and departed from the city of Mathurā.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
And Keśin, fierce in his strength, was dispatched as a messenger by Kaṃsa.
Desiring the death of Kṛṣṇa, he arrived at Vṛndāvana.
With his hooves scarred by the surface of the earth, shaking the clouds with the tossing of his mane,
and traversing the paths of the sun and moon with swift strides, he rushed toward the cowherds.
At the sound of that neighing, the cowherds, the horses of the Daityas,
and the cowherd girls, agitated by fear, went to Govinda for refuge.
Hearing those words of theirs, Govinda then spoke these words, as deep as the roar of a water-laden cloud: "Save us! Save us! *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 5.16.4.
Enough with this fear, O cowherds! Why are you so overcome by dread, you who belong to the cowherd caste yet destroy the prowess of heroes?
What is the use of this wicked horse, which possesses little substance, causes joy and arrogance,
is driven by the strength of the Daityas, and prances about?
"Come, come, you wicked one! I am Kṛṣṇa; just as the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva] did to Pūṣan, I shall knock all the teeth from your mouth."
Having spoken thus and slapping his arms, Govinda went toward Keśin; and that horse of the Daitya, with its mouth wide open, rushed at him.
Then Janārdana, having extended his arm,
thrust it into the mouth of that wicked horse Keśin during the sacrifice.
As that arm of Kṛṣṇa entered Keśin’s mouth,
his teeth were shattered and fell out like fragments of white clouds.
O twice-born one, Kṛṣṇa’s arm that had entered Keśin’s body grew,
like a disease neglected until its onset that leads to destruction.
With his lips torn apart, he vomited much blood mixed with foam;
his two eyes were wide open, their lids cast loose from their fastenings.
He struck the earth with his feet, discharging excrement and urine;
with his limbs moist with sweat and now exhausted, he became motionless.
With his great maw wide open, that asura was struck down by Kṛṣṇa’s arm upon the ground in two pieces, like a tree felled by a bolt of lightning.
On the two-footed [being], the back, half the tail, one ear, one eye, and one nostril—
those parts possessed of hair— shone forth as two fragments when it was divided in two.
Having slain Keśin, Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the joyful cowherds,
remained right there, his body unwearied and at ease, smiling.
Then, Keśin having been slain, the cowherd women and the cowherds were filled with wonder;
they praised the lotus-eyed one, who was enchanting through his affection.
Then, having seen Keśin slain, the brahmin Nārada, his mind overflowing with joy, spoke from his place within the cloud while remaining invisible.
Excellent, excellent, O Jagannātha! That this Keśin, the bringer of affliction to the inhabitants of heaven, has been slain by you, O Acyuta, through mere sport.
Eager for battle, I have come here from heaven to witness this unprecedented great conflict between men and horses, such as has never occurred elsewhere.
O Madhusūdana, those deeds performed by you in this incarnation have filled my heart with wonder, and through them, I have attained satisfaction.
O Kṛṣṇa, even Śakra and the gods are terrified of this horse when he whinnies while looking toward the clouds, his mane bristling like a mass of filaments.
"O Janārdana, because this evil-souled Keśin has been slain by you,
you shall therefore become renowned in the world by the name Keśava."
"May it be well with you; I shall now depart for the battle with Kaṃsa.
O slayer of Keśin, I will return with you again the day after tomorrow."
O Supporter of the Earth, you have brought about the removal of the earth's burden by striking down Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, along with his followers.
"In that regard, O Janārdana, I must witness the various kinds of battles of the rulers of the earth conducted by you."
Therefore, O Govinda, I shall depart; the great task for the gods has been accomplished.
Everything is already known to you; may it be well with you, I am going now.
When Nārada had departed, Kṛṣṇa, honored by the cowherds,
entered Gokula— the sole vessel for the drinking-glances of the gopīs.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Akrūra also, having set out in his swift-moving chariot, departed.
Desiring a vision of Kṛṣṇa, he set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
And Akrūra reflected: "There is no one more fortunate than I, who shall behold the face of the Discus-wielder descended as a partial incarnation."
Today my birth has become fruitful and the night has turned into a beautiful dawn,
since I shall behold the face of Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like the petals of a full-blown lotus.
I shall behold that lotus-eyed face of Viṣṇu, which, when remembered or even merely conceived in thought, removes the sins of men.
"From which the Vedas and all the Vedāṅgas emerged—
that supreme abode of lights, the face of the Blessed One, I shall behold."
In sacrifices, that Supreme Person, the support of all, who is worshipped by men as the Lord of Sacrifice— I shall behold that Lord of the World.
I shall behold that Keśava, the one without beginning or end, whom Indra worshipped with a hundred sacrifices and thereby attained the sovereignty over the immortals.
Neither Brahmā, nor Indra, Rudra, Aśvin, Vasu, Āditya, nor the hosts of Maruts know His true nature; yet Hari comes directly before my eyes.
The Self of all, the knower of all, the All, who dwells within all beings—
he who is inconceivable, immutable, and all-pervading, shall speak together with me.
He who, as the unborn (aja), established the stability of the world through forms such as the fish, tortoise, boar, horse, and lion— he, the unborn, will today speak to me.
And now the Lord of the World, the imperishable one who assumes a body by his own will, has attained human form in order to accomplish the task residing within his heart.
He who supports the earth from within, established in the state of the crest-jewel, has descended for the sake of the world; he will say to me, "Do not be cruel."
Salutations again and again to Him, by whose māyā— consisting of fathers, sons, friends, brothers, mothers, and kinsmen— the world is unable to cross over.
Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, the immeasurable, by whose being established in the heart one crosses over the vast ignorance consisting of the power of yoga (yogamāyā).
I bow to Him who is called Yajñapuruṣa by the performers of sacrifice, Vāsudeva by the Sāttvatas, and Viṣṇu by the knowers of the Vedānta.
Just as this world, both existent and non-existent, is established in that Sustainer who is the abode of the universe— by that truth, may he be gracious toward me.
I go for refuge to that unborn and eternal Hari, by the mere remembrance of whom a person becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus meditating upon Viṣṇu, his mind and soul bowed down with devotion,
Akrūra reached Gokula while the sun was still shining slightly.
Then he saw Kṛṣṇa at the very beginning, by the milking shed of the cows,
standing amidst the calves, with the complexion of a blooming blue lotus petal.
His eyes were like the petals of a full-blown lotus; his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa;
he had long arms, a broad and high chest, and a prominent nose.
He bore a lotus-face that was the locus of a playful smile,
and he stood firmly established upon the earth with his feet, whose nails were as red as the *juṅga* flower.
Wearing two yellow garments and adorned with wild flowers,
he possessed the luster of a blue mountain topped by the moon, and had a white lotus as his crest-ornament.
O twice-born one, he then beheld the joy of the Yadus, Balabhadra, who was as white as a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and who wore blue garments.
Tall, with long arms and high shoulders, and with a lotus-face in full bloom,
he was like another Mount Kailāsa surrounded by a garland of clouds.
O Sage, seeing them, that high-minded Akrūra’s lotus-like face blossomed and his entire body was covered in horripilation; he then said to the Sustainer of the World: "Welcome! (ViP 5.17.25)
This is that supreme abode; this is that supreme state—the portion of the Blessed Vāsudeva which is established here in two forms.
The success of this pair of eyes has been fully attained by beholding the Creator of the universe;
may this body of mine also become fruitful through contact with his limbs by the grace of the Blessed One.
Will this one of infinite forms, endowed with glory, place his lotus-hand upon my back—
he by the touch of whose fingers all sins are destroyed and perfection, free from defects, is attained?
By him, with his wheel— terrible and exceedingly fierce, wreathed in garlands of flames like fire and lightning, and devoid of spokes—
the collyrium from the eyes of the wives of the Daitya lord was destroyed as he struck down the Daityas.
Where Bali, having offered water, obtained delightful enjoyments while dwelling upon the surface of the earth,
as well as immortality and the lordship of the thirty gods for a full manvantara, free from all enemies.
"Will he indeed make me, who am free from fault yet defiled by fault through my association with Kaṃsa, one struck down by pride? Fie on that birth which is cast out by the virtuous!"
What indeed in this world remains unknown to all men regarding him who consists of wisdom, who is a mass of pure being, who is free from defect, and who is ever manifest, dwelling within the heart?
Therefore, with a mind bowed in devotion, I go to the one who is the Lord of all lords,
the partial incarnation of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, who is unborn and without beginning, middle, or end.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having approached Govinda while thus reflecting, that Yādava [spoke].
Thinking, "I am Akrūra," he bowed his head at the feet of Hari.
He too, having touched him with a hand marked by the signs of the banner, the thunderbolt, and the lotus,
and having drawn him near, embraced him very firmly out of affection.
Having been duly saluted by him, Balarāma and Keśava then entered his own palace, joyful and carrying him with them.
Then Akrūra, having performed the salutations and other rites together with them and having eaten his meal according to custom, spoke to the two of them accordingly.
Just as Ānakadundubhi was rebuked by that Kaṃsa,
and just as the lady Devakī [was treated] by the evil-minded Dānava.
O Ugrasena, [tell us] how that evil-minded Kaṃsa conducts himself,
and for what purpose he was indeed dispatched by Kaṃsa.
Having heard all that in detail, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, said: "O lord of gifts, I have understood all of this."
"O highly fortunate one, I shall do whatever is considered appropriate in this matter;
know that you must not think otherwise, for Kaṃsa has already been slain by me."
"Tomorrow Rama and I shall go to Mathurā along with you;
the elder cowherds will also go, taking many offerings."
"O hero, let this night pass; you should not give way to anxiety. Within three nights, I shall slay Kaṃsa along with his followers."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having thus instructed the cowherds, Akrūra, Keśava,
and Balabhadra then slept in the house of Nanda Gopa.
Then, at the clear dawn, the two of great splendor, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma,
prepared together with Akrūra to go to the city of Mathurā.
Seeing him, the cowherd women, with tears in their eyes and bracelets slipping from their arms,
sighed deeply, afflicted by extreme sorrow, and spoke to one another.
Having reached Mathurā, how will Govinda return to Gokula?
He will drink with his ears the honey of the artful chatter of the city women.
Having found its home in the drinking of the playful words of city-dwelling women,
how could his heart ever again turn toward rustic cowherd girls?
By the cruel and evil-minded one who, according to his design, carried off Hari— the very essence of the entire cow-pen— a blow has been struck against the cowherd women.
Speech infused with the essence of emotion, a gait graceful with charm,
and even the side-long glances of city women— all these were exceedingly present there.
This rustic Hari is bound by the fetters of their charms;
by what means, then, will he come back to your side?
"Here is Keśava, having mounted his chariot, proceeding toward Mathurā,
deceived here by the cruel and pitiless Akrūra."
Does this cruel man not know that people are devoted to him,
such that he leads Hari away from our eyes to another place?
"This utterly merciless Govinda is departing together with Rāma, mounted upon his chariot; let haste be made to restrain him."
"We do not venture to speak before our gurus;
what can the gurus do for us who have been consumed by the fire of separation? (ViP 5.18.22)
These cowherds, who are like the guardians of the quarters, are prepared to depart;
not one among them makes an effort to turn Govinda back.
Today the night has dawned beautifully for the women residing in Mathurā,
whose rows of eyes, like swarms of bees, shall drink from the lotus-face of Acyuta.
Blessed are those on the path who go hence toward Kṛṣṇa unhindered;
for as they behold him, they shall carry their own bodies with hair standing on end in rapture.
Today there will be a great festival for the eyes of the citizens of the city of Mathurā,
as they behold the limbs of Govinda.
Who indeed has been seen by those ill-fated women as they gaze upon Adhokṣaja?
For those with wide eyes shall behold him without being obstructed.
"Aha! Having shown this great treasure to these cowherd women, the compassionate Creator has plucked out their eyes right here!"
When Hari departed from us with his affection slackened,
even the bracelets on our hands quickly fell away in their loosening.
"Akrūra, cruel-hearted as he is, swiftly urges on the horses;
at a sight such as this, in women who are so distressed, in whom would compassion not arise?"
Behold this high cloud of dust from the wheels of Kṛṣṇa’s chariot;
by it, Hari has become distant, and even that dust is no longer visible.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus beheld by the cowherd women with such great affection,
Keśava, together with Rāma, departed from the region of Vraja.
Traveling by chariot drawn by swift horses,
Rāma, Akrūra, and Janārdana reached the bank of the Yamunā at the time of midday.
Then Kṛṣṇa said, "O Akrūra, please remain here for a moment while I perform my daily ablutions in the waters of the Yamunā."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having replied, "So be it," that high-minded sage, having bathed and sipped water according to the rules,
entered the waters of the Yamunā and meditated upon the supreme Brahman, O Brāhmaṇa.
He beheld Balabhadra, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods,
his body like a cluster of kunda flowers, and his eyes as long as the petals of a full-blown lotus.
He was surrounded by great serpent-chiefs such as Vāsuki and Rambha, who were like moving banners;
he was being praised by them and adorned with a fragrant forest garland.
Wearing dark garments,
adorned with beautiful earrings and a lovely crest-ornament, he shone as he stood within the depths of the water.
In his lap [he saw] one who was dark as a rain-cloud, with large copper-red eyes,
four arms, and noble limbs, adorned with weapons such as the discus.
Clad in two yellow garments and adorned with variegated garlands,
