he was like a rain-cloud made beautiful by the bow of Indra and the rows of streaks across the sky.
He beheld the unassailable Kṛṣṇa, whose chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark, who wore beautiful, shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings, and who had a lotus as his ear-ornament.
He was being meditated upon there by the stainless sages, such as Sanandana and others, who were perfected in yoga and whose eyes were fixed on the tips of their noses.
Recognizing Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, Akrūra was struck with wonder and thought quickly from his chariot, "How have they come here?"
Janārdana paralyzed the speech of him who desired to speak;
then, emerging from the water, he returned once more to his chariot.
And there he saw both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa seated upon the chariot, endowed with human bodies just as before.
And having plunged back into the water, he saw those two exactly as before,
being praised by Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and great serpents.
Then, having realized his true nature, that lord of donors praised the infallible Lord, who consists of all knowledge.
Akrūra said:
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure existence, whose greatness is inconceivable, who is all-pervading, and whose singular essential nature is manifold yet one.
Salutations to you who are all forms; salutations to you who have become the inconceivable oblation.
Salutations to the Lord who is beyond primordial nature, the supreme one, and the further shore of consciousness.
You are the self of the elements, the self of the senses, and likewise the self of primordial matter;
you alone exist as the fivefold self, including the individual self and the supreme self.
Be gracious, O All, O Soul of all, O Lord composed of the perishable and the imperishable,
who art proclaimed through the conceptual designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is ineffable, whose purpose is ineffable,
I bow to you who are designated by an ineffable name.
O Protector, that wherein no conceptual constructions of name, genus, and so forth exist—that is the supreme Brahman, eternal, unchanging, and unborn; you are that.
Since the realization of every object does not occur apart from conceptual construction,
he is praised by names such as Kṛṣṇa, Cyuta, Ananta, and Viṣṇu.
O Unborn One, you are the goal of all through these conceptualizations by means of which this infinite universe exists;
you are the soul of the universe, devoid of modification, for there is nothing else whatsoever that exists apart from you in all things.
You are Brahmā, Paśupati, Yama, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, the Lord of the Thirty-three, Vāyu, and Agni;
you are the Lord of Waters, the Lord of Wealth, and Ratakas—you alone protect the world through various powers manifested as distinct entities.
O Lord of the Universe, you create the universe in the form of the rays of the sun; therefore, this phenomenal world consists of your qualities.
I bow down to that Imperishable One, whose nature is knowledge, who is the supreme reality signified by the word "Sat" (Being), and who is both being and non-being.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa as well;
salutations to you, Pradyumna; salutations to you, Aniruddha.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having thus praised Viṣṇu while within the water, that Yādava—
He worshipped the Lord of All with mental incense and flowers.
Having withdrawn his mind from all other objects and fixed it upon that [Brahman],
he remained for a long time established in the state of Brahman and then desisted from his meditative absorption.
Considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose, the high-minded one emerged once more from the waters of the Yamunā and returned to his chariot.
Akrūra, his eyes wide with wonder, beheld Rāma and Kṛṣṇa standing exactly as they had been before; then Kṛṣṇa addressed him.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Akrūra, you have surely seen a marvel in the waters of the Yamunā,
since you are observed with eyes wide open in wonder."
Akrūra said:
"O Acyuta, that wonder which was seen by me there within the water,
I now behold here as well, standing before me in embodied form."
O Kṛṣṇa, I have been united with you, that Great Soul by whom this world—which is of such a wondrous nature—is sustained; I am thus joined with one who is the very embodiment of marvels.
"So what is the use of this? We shall go to Mathurā, O Madhusūdana;
I am afraid of Kaṃsa, fie on the life of those who subsist on alms!"
Having spoken thus, he urged on the horses, swift as the wind;
and in the evening, Akrūra arrived at the city of Mathurā.
Beholding Mathurā, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma, that Yādava said:
"O great heroes, proceed on foot; I shall enter alone by chariot."
"You two must likewise go to the house of Vasudeva;
for it is on account of you two that the old man is being cast out by Kaṃsa."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, Akrūra then entered the city of Mathurā;
and Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, having entered, reached the royal highway.
Gazed upon joyfully by women and men with longing eyes,
the two heroes proceeded with playful ease like two elephants in rut.
Then, seeing a washerman who was a dyer wandering there,
the two of them spoke to him regarding beautiful and radiant garments.
Then Kaṃsa’s washerman, his pride mounted by the favor he had received,
shouted many insulting words at Rāma and Keśava.
Then, with a blow of his palm, Kṛṣṇa, out of rage, struck off the head of that wicked-minded washerman onto the ground.
Then, having killed [the cowherd] and taken his garments, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, dressed in yellow and blue robes, went joyfully to the house of a florist.
With his pair of eyes wide open, the garland-maker was greatly astonished and then thought: "Whose two sons are these who have come here?"—thus he reflected, O Maitreya.
Seeing those two, wearing yellow and blue garments and exceedingly beautiful,
he then reflected that two gods had arrived upon the earth.
Requested for flowers by those two, whose lotus-faces were in full bloom,
he supported himself with his hands and touched the earth with his head.
"The two Lords, supreme in their grace, have come to my home; I am blessed! I shall worship them," said the garland-maker to them.
Then, with a joyful countenance, he began to entice them by offering them flowers according to their desire, saying, "These are beautiful; take these."
Bowing again and again to those two best of men,
the gardener offered beautiful, fragrant, and stainless flowers.
Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with the garland-maker, granted him boons:
"O blessed one, Śrī, who rests upon me, shall never forsake you."
"O gentle one, there shall be no loss of strength for you, nor even a loss of wealth;
and as long as the days endure, your progeny shall not perish."
And having enjoyed abundant pleasures, at the end, by my grace and through the remembrance of me, you shall attain the divine world.
O auspicious one, your mind shall always be fixed upon the Dharma;
and for those born in your lineage, there shall be long life.
O highly fortunate ones, no misfortune such as calamities or the like shall befall one born in your lineage, for as long as the sun shall exist.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva and honored by the garland-maker, departed from that house.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, on the royal highway, Kṛṣṇa [encountered] a woman carrying a vessel of fragrant ointment.
He beheld Kubjā approaching, in the bloom of fresh youth.
Kṛṣṇa said to her playfully: "Whose ointment is this that you are carrying, O lotus-eyed one? Tell me the truth."
As if filled with desire herself, that Kubjā, overcome by the power of beholding him, spoke affectionately toward Hari and addressed her with charming words.
"O beloved, why do you not know her who was appointed by Kaṃsa,
renowned as Naikavakrā in the art of applying unguents?"
Indeed, no unguent ground by anyone else brings such pleasure to Kaṃsa;
for I am the supreme recipient of his favor and wealth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O lady of beautiful countenance, let this fragrant, lovely unguent, worthy of a king and suited to our bodies, be applied."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard this, the hunchbacked woman respectfully said, "Let it be taken," and then she gave both of them unguents suitable for their bodies.
Then those two bulls among men, their limbs smeared with streaks of pigment,
shone like white and black clouds accompanied by Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Then Śauri, who was skilled in the methods of enchantment,
lifted her by the chin with his two fingers of the right hand and held her up.
Then Keśava pulled her with his feet and brought her to a state of straightness;
having thus attained rectitude, she became an excellent woman.
Seizing Govinda by his garment, she spoke with playful grace, languid from the weight of her heart's overflowing love: "Come, let us go to my home."
Thus addressed by her, Śauri, having looked at the face of Rāma,
laughed and spoke to that faultless Kubjā, who possessed many crooked features.
"I shall come to your house," Hari said to her with a smile;
looking at Rāma's face, he dismissed her and laughed aloud.
With their limbs overcome by the various forms of devotion, dressed in blue and yellow garments and adorned with wonderful garlands, the two of them then went to the bow-hall.
When the guards questioned them, they reported that the bow was a sacrificial gift; thereupon Kṛṣṇa suddenly seized that jewel of a bow and drew it to its full extent.
Then, as he drew the bow to its full extent, it broke with force,
producing a tremendous sound by which Mathurā was filled.
Then, when their bows were broken by the guards,
the two of them, having slain the army of guards, emerged from that abode of archers.
Having learned the news of Akrūra’s arrival and hearing that the great bow had been broken, Kaṃsa spoke to Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Kaṃsa said:
"These two cowherd boys have arrived before me through you;
they must be killed by wrestling, for they are the stealers of my life."
"Indeed, I shall be gratified by you two through their destruction in a wrestling match;
I will grant your desired boons, for these two are of great strength, and not otherwise."
Whether by right or even by wrong means, those two have become my enemies;
they must be slain, and through their destruction, the kingdom shall belong to you both in common.
Having thus instructed those two wrestlers, he then summoned the elephant-keeper and spoke loudly:
"By you, at the gate of the wrestling arena, an elephant [must be stationed]."
Kuvalayāpīḍa was stationed by him [to guard] those two cowherd boys;
they were to be killed when they arrived at the entrance of the arena for the wrestling match.
Having issued that command and seen all the platforms prepared,
Kaṃsa, whose death was imminent, awaited the rising of the sun.
Then the citizens ascended all the platforms,
and the kings, along with their attendants, ascended the royal platforms.
And Kaṃsa had the group of wrestlers and prize-fighters stationed near the center of the arena;
Kaṃsa himself, however, was seated upon a lofty throne.
Platforms were likewise prepared for the women of the inner apartments,
as well as others for the chief courtesans, and still others for the women of the city.
The cowherds, headed by Nanda, were seated on other couches,
while Akrūra and Vasudeva were stationed at the edge of the couch.
In the midst of the women of Nāgarī, she who longed for the son of Devakī remained standing,
thinking, "I shall see my son's face even at the time of his end."
While the musical instruments were being played, as Cāṇūra leaped about excessively, while the world was crying out "Alas! Alas! and Muṣṭika was slapping his arms, [the Lord acted].
Smiling slightly, those two heroes, Balabhadra and Janārdana,
appearing as young boys dressed in cowherd attire, approached the entrance of the arena.
Then Kuvalayāpīḍa, urged on by his mahout,
rushed with great speed to slay the two cowherd boys.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the midst of the arena, O best of the twice-born;
and seeing his younger brother, Baladeva spoke these words: ||| ViP_5.20.33 |||
"O illustrious one, this serpent, incited by our enemies, must indeed be slain."
O twice-born one, having been thus addressed by his elder brother Baladeva,
Mādhava, the slayer of enemy heroes, then let out a lion’s roar.
Drawing one hand with the other, the slayer of Keśin whirled him around on the ground like Airāvata in his strength.
Even Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all the worlds, having played for a very long time in accordance with the play of a child, entered into the space between the two feet of Kaḍi.
Having uprooted his left tooth with his right hand alone, he struck the charioteer;
the latter's head was split into a hundred pieces.
Having uprooted the right tusk, Balabhadra also, in that very instant,
furiously crushed the elephant-keepers standing nearby with it.
Then, leaping up with speed, the mighty son of Rohiṇī struck the elephant on the head with his left foot in a fit of rage.
Slain by that Balabhadra with effortless ease,
he fell like a mountain struck by the thunderbolt of the thousand-eyed Indra.
Having slain Kuvalayāpīḍa, who had been urged on by his elephant-driver,
the two of them— whose limbs were smeared with ichor and blood and whose excellent weapons were the tusks of an elephant— [stood there].
Like two lions among a herd of deer, gazing with prideful playfulness,
Balabhadra and Janārdana entered the vast arena.
Immediately thereafter, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on the vast arena, and the people were filled with wonder, exclaiming, "This is Kṛṣṇa! This is Balabhadra!"
He is the one by whom the terrible Pūtanā, the slayer of children, was slain;
by whom the cart was overturned; and by whom the twin Yamalārjuna trees were shattered.
This is he who, as a child, mounted and crushed the serpent Kāliya;
by him the great mountain Govardhana was held up for seven nights.
Behold this Acyuta, by whom the wicked Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, and Keśin were slain with effortless ease by that Great-Souled One.
And this mighty-armed Balabhadra, his elder brother,
goes before him with playful grace, delighting the minds and eyes of women.
This is he who is described by the wise, those experts in the meaning of the Purāṇas:
Gopāla, who will lift up the Yādava lineage that has sunk down.
For he is surely a portion of Viṣṇu, whose birth is universal, descended to the earth as the remover of the world's burden.
When Rāma and Kṛṣṇa had been thus described by the citizens, at that very moment Devakī’s chest burned with emotion, her breasts overflowing with milk from maternal affection.
Having beheld the face of his son, Vasudeva felt as if he had attained a great festival; casting off the old age that had come upon him, he became young once more.
With their pairs of eyes wide open, the women of the royal harem and the multitude of women from the city did not cease looking at him.
"Friends, look at Kṛṣṇa’s face, with its exceedingly reddened eyes,
covered with droplets of perspiration from the exertion of the elephant fight."
We beheld a blooming autumn lotus sprinkled with water;
let it stand as something surpassed, and let your sight be made fruitful.
O beautiful lady, behold this great splendor of the child, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa,
which destroys his enemies, and his pair of arms.
Do you not see this Balabhadra approaching, his form white as milk, the moon, or a lotus stalk, and clad in blue garments?
O friend, behold the laughter of Hari and Balabhadra as they play with Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, who are leaping about.
"Friends, look! Here is Hari approaching Cāṇūra for the sake of wrestling.
Are there no elders here who can stop this improper act?"
Where is Hari, whose delicate body is just beginning to reach its youth;
and where is this great asura, whose expansive body is as hard as a diamond?
These two, possessing limbs of exquisite grace, are in the bloom of youth;
meanwhile, the Daitya wrestlers, headed by Cāṇūra, are exceedingly fierce.
This is a great transgression on the part of the judges of wrestling,
that they allow a combat between a child and a strong man to be overlooked by those acting as umpires.
Śrī Parāśara said: While the women of the city were speaking thus, the Blessed Lord Hari, tightening his girdle, leaped about within the crowd, shaking the very earth.
Balabhadra too, having slapped his arms, roared with such grace that it was a marvel how the earth did not shatter at every step.
Then Kṛṣṇa, of immeasurable prowess, fought with Cāṇūra, while Muṣṭika,
skilled in wrestling, fought with Balabhadra against the two Daityas.
Then Hari, with collisions,
shakings, throws, fist-blows, and strikes like falling stakes and thunderbolts, fought with Cāṇūra.
With dust raised by their feet and scattered about, a great battle took place between the two of them.
That battle between the two was weaponless yet exceedingly fierce and most terrible,
accomplished through sheer strength and vital energy in the presence of a festive assembly.
And for as long as Cāṇūra fought with Hari, he suffered a supreme loss, bit by bit,
morsel by morsel.
Kṛṣṇa, who is identical with the universe, also fought with him as if in mere play;
out of weariness and anger, he shook his own mane-like crest.
Seeing the exhaustion of Cāṇūra and the increasing strength of Kṛṣṇa,
Kaṃsa, overcome with anger, had the musical instruments silenced.
As soon as the drums and other musical instruments were forbidden,
numerous divine instruments gathered in the sky and were sounded.
"Victory to you, O Govinda! Slay the Dānava Cāṇūra, O Keśava!
Thus spoke the gods, who had become invisible, being exceedingly joyful.
After Cāṇūra had tormented Madhusūdana for a long time,
he uprooted him and whirled him around, making an effort to kill him.
Having whirled the Daitya wrestler around a hundred times,
the conqueror of enemies dashed him against the ground, lifeless, as he rose into the sky.
He struck the ground with his hand, and by that blow, Cāṇūra was split into a hundred pieces;
he then turned the world into a great mire of flowing blood.
At that time, the mighty Baladeva also fought with the Daitya wrestler Muṣṭika, just as Hari had fought with Cāṇūra.
He too, having struck him on the head and chest with his fist and with his knee,
threw him down upon the surface of the earth and crushed him whose life had departed.
Kṛṣṇa then struck the exceedingly powerful Mallarāja with a blow from his left fist and felled him to the ground.
When Cāṇūra was slain, the wrestler Muṣṭika was struck down,
and the Tośalaka host was brought to destruction, all the wrestlers fled in every direction.
Then both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, filled with joy, leaped about in the arena, forcibly dragging along cowherds of their own age.
Kaṃsa, his eyes red with rage, spoke loudly to the tall men:
"Let these two cowherds be forcibly removed from this assembly by force."
"Let the wicked Nanda also be seized here with iron chains,
and let Vasudeva too be bound with a punishment that does not spare the aged."
The cowherds who were formerly joined with Kṛṣṇa leap about;
having seized their cows and whatever wealth they possess, he takes it from them.
But Madhusūdana, laughing at those who were thus commanding him,
leapt up, ascended that dais, and seized Kaṃsa with great force.
Having dragged Kaṃsa by his hair so that his crown was falling off, he threw him down upon the surface of the earth and fell upon him.
By Kṛṣṇa, the teacher who supports the entire world without exception, as he flew overhead, the king Ugrasena’s son was made to give up his life.
Then, seizing the hair of the dead man, the mighty Madhusūdana dragged Kaṃsa’s body into the middle of the arena.
By the weight of his body as he fell, by his impact,
and by his being dragged along, Kaṃsa’s corpse was made to resemble the force of a great flood.
When Kaṃsa had been seized by Kṛṣṇa, his brother Sunāman arrived in a rage,
but he was felled with effortless ease by Balabhadra.
Then the entire arena was filled with cries of "Alas!
Alas! upon seeing the Lord of Mathurā slain by Kṛṣṇa out of contempt.
The mighty-armed one, accompanied by Baladeva, quickly grasped the feet of both Vasudeva and Devakī, even as Kṛṣṇa was born.
Having raised up Janārdana, both Vasudeva and Devakī stood bowed before him, remembering the words spoken at the time of his birth.
Śrī Vasudeva said: "Be gracious, O Lord Keśava! That boon which was granted by you to the gods who were sinking in distress has likewise been fulfilled for us through your favor."
Since the Blessed One, having been propitiated, descended into my home for the purpose of destroying the wicked, our lineage has been purified by him.
You abide within all beings, existing as the essence of all beings; O Soul of All, the past and the future proceed from you.
O inconceivable Acyuta, you who consist of all the gods, you are worshipped through sacrifices;
you alone are the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the supreme lord of those who perform sacrifices.
O Janārdana, you are the source of the entire world.
That this mind of mine, which conceals its true nature, should feel such affection for you is a supreme mockery, even compared to Devakī’s maternal love for her own son.
You are the creator of all beings, you who are without beginning or end;
whose tongue among men, O son, will speak such words against you?
O Lord of the World, since this entire world has arisen from him,
by what logic could he have come into being from us without the power of Māyā?
How can he, in whom the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— is established,
be born as a human being lying on the lap of a womb?
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, be gracious and protect the universe through your various incarnations; you are not merely my son.
O Lord, this entire world, beginning with Brahmā, is [sustained] by you; why then, O Puruṣottama, do you delude us?

With a vision deluded by Māyā, you were brought to Gokula by my family out of intense fear of Kaṃsa, though you yourself are free from fear; there you grew up, yet, O Lord, I have no sense of "mine" regarding you.

"O Lord of the worlds, you are Viṣṇu; for the sake of benefiting us, you have arrived, and our delusion has indeed vanished. For the deeds of Rudra, the Maruts, the Aśvins, and Śatakratu, when observed by you, do not become things that need to be accomplished."
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having attained spiritual wisdom through the observation of the Lord’s deeds, those two—
Seeing Devakī and Vasudeva in such a state, Hari once again spread his Vaiṣṇava illusion for the purpose of deluding the Yadu clan.
And he said, "O mother, O father, after a long time I, who have been yearning and terrified by Kaṃsa, have finally seen you both along with Saṃkarṣaṇa."
The time spent by those who fail to honor their mother and father passes away;
indeed, for the wicked, that portion of their lifespan becomes utterly futile.
O dear one, for embodied beings who perform the worship of their guru, the gods, the twice-born, and their mother and father,
time becomes fruitful.
"O father, all this transgression committed by us must be forgiven,
for we were under the control of Kaṃsa’s power and prowess."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus and having bowed down to both elders of the Yadu clan in due order,
they honored them appropriately and then paid their respects to the citizens.
Then Kaṃsa’s wives, surrounding the slain Kaṃsa on the ground,
along with his mothers, wailed, overwhelmed by pain and grief.
Distressed in many ways and tormented by remorse, Hari himself,
his eyes clouded with tears, consoled them.
Then Madhusūdana released Ugrasena from his bonds and immediately consecrated him, whose son had been slain, in his own kingdom.
Consecrated in the kingdom by Kṛṣṇa, that lion of the Yadus performed the funeral rites for his son and for the others who had been slain there.
After he had performed the funeral rites for him, Hari spoke to him as he sat upon the lion-throne:
"O Lord, command without hesitation whatever task is to be done."
Due to the curse of Yayāti, this lineage is currently unworthy of sovereignty;
since I stand here as your servant, O Lord, what need have you for kings? Please give your command.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, he called to mind Vāyu, who arrived at that very moment;
and the Blessed Keśava, appearing in human form, spoke to him regarding his task.
"Go, O Vāyu, and say this: 'O Vāsava, enough with your pride!
Let the Sudharmā assembly hall be given by you to Ugrasena.'"
Kṛṣṇa says: "This unsurpassed jewel, worthy of a king, is joined with the assembly hall named Sudharmā; it is for the Yadus to sit within it."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been thus addressed, Pavana went and told everything to the Lord of Śacī; Purandara, for his part, gave the assembly hall named Sudharmā to Vāyu.
And those leaders of the Yadus, relying on the strength of Govinda’s arms, enjoyed that divine assembly hall, rich in every kind of jewel, which had been brought by the wind.
Though they had mastered all branches of knowledge and were composed of universal wisdom,
those two heroes and supreme beings demonstrated the traditional succession between disciple and teacher.
Then, having performed the rites of initiation, the two boys went to Sāndīpani, a native of Kāśī residing in the city of Avanti, for the sake of learning.
Those two heroes, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Janārdana, who took delight in the study of the Vedas, approached him as disciples; indeed, being intent on the proper conduct toward their teacher,
they displayed exemplary speech and behavior among all people.
O twice-born one, having studied the science of archery (dhanurveda) along with its secret doctrines and its compendiums within sixty-four days and nights, that [skill] became truly marvelous.
Reflecting upon that superhuman deed of theirs, which was beyond all belief, Sāndīpani then thought that the moon and the sun had arrived there.
Having acquired merely upon being told the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, all the scriptures, and the entire collection of weapons, those two—
They both said, "Let that which must be given by you as a teacher's fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) be chosen."
Having perceived with his super-sensory knowledge the deed of those two, O high-minded one,
he requested Sūta as a son from Prabhāsa on the salt ocean.
Then, having received their weapons, the Great Ocean, with the guest-offering (arghya) in his hand, said:
"I have not carried off the son of Sāndīpani."
O destroyer of asuras, that Daitya named Pañcajana, who was in the form of a conch shell, seized the boy within my very waters.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa went beneath the water, slew that Pañcajana,
and took from his bones an excellent conch shell.
By his roar, the strength of the Daityas was diminished;
the splendor of the gods increased, and unrighteousness went to its destruction.
Having filled that Pāñcajanya conch and proceeded to the city of Yama,
Hari and the powerful Baladeva conquered Vaivasvata, the god of death.
Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the best among the strong, restored that boy— who was situated in torment and possessed his former body— to his father.
Then both Rāma and Janārdana returned to Mathurā, which was protected by Ugrasena and filled with joyful men and women.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Jarāsaṃdha’s son, the exceedingly powerful Kasa, married...
O Maitreya, there were also Asti and Prāpti, who killed their husbands, and Hari.
Accompanied by a vast army, the powerful Jarāsandha, lord of Magadha, advanced in anger to slay Yadu along with his followers.
Then, having approached Mathurā, that lord of Magadha besieged it,
surrounded by twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs of his army.
Having gone forth with only a small retinue, both Rāma and Janārdana,
being powerful, fought equally against his mighty soldiers.
Then, O best of sages, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa quickly resolved to take up their ancient weapons.
Immediately thereafter, O Brahmin, Hari’s Śārṅga bow, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
and the Kaumodakī mace arrived from the sky.
O Brahmin, the great plow of Balabhadra and likewise the joyous club— both desired by his mind— descended from the sky.
Then, having defeated the lord of Magadha along with his army in battle,
both heroes, Rāma and Janārdana, entered the city.
O great sage, when that wicked Jarāsandha had been defeated but was still alive, Kṛṣṇa considered him as not yet conquered.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Jarāsaṃdha, accompanied by his army, returned once more; though he had been defeated by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, he had previously escaped.
Thus, the King of Magadha, who was exceedingly arrogant, engaged in eighteen battles with the Yadus, who were led by Kṛṣṇa.
In all these battles, Jarāsaṃdha, though superior in strength, was defeated by the Yādavas with their small forces and fled.
That strength of the Yādavas was not what had been conquered many times over;
rather, it was the majesty of the presence of Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, who is a portion [of the Supreme].
That he discharges weapons of many forms against his enemies is but the sport of that Lord of the World, whose nature is the dharma of a human being.
For him who performs the creation and dissolution of the universe by mind alone,
how great an effort is required to destroy even his own partisan?
Nevertheless, he follows the way of men;
making peace with the powerful, he wages war against the weak.
Displaying conciliation, bribery, and likewise sowing dissension, he inflicts punishment and sometimes even resorts to flight.
The activity of those embodied as humans follows this very course;
it is the sport of that Lord of the World, proceeding according to His will.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: O twice-born one, in a gathering, a brother-in-law called a certain Brāhmaṇa named Gārgya a "eunuch."
Then, in the presence of the Yadus, all those Yādavas abandoned [their lives].
Then, his soul overcome with anger, he went to the Deccan and performed austerities,
desiring a son who would bring fear to the Yadu dynasty.
Worshipping Mahādeva, he consumed iron filings;
and at the end of the twelfth year, Hara, being pleased, granted him a boon.
The childless Yavana king indeed gratified him,
and from his union with that woman, a son was born to him who resembled a bee.
Having consecrated that Kālayavana, whose chest was as hard as a diamond-pointed weapon, as the lord of the Yavanas over his own kingdom, he departed for the forest.
Intoxicated by the pride of his prowess, he questioned the powerful kings on earth,
and Nārada told him about the Yādavas.
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of millions of Mlecchas,
well-equipped with elephants, horses, and chariots, he exerted the greatest effort.
O Maitreya, with his chariot broken and his progress severed day by day, he set out toward the city of Mathurā against the Yādavas, filled with resentment.
Kṛṣṇa also reflected: "The Yādava army has been destroyed;
the Māgadha king will now have to face the Yavana in battle."
The power of the Magadhan king has been exhausted; that powerful Kālayavana shall slay him.
Thus has this twofold calamity come upon the Yadus.
Therefore, I shall construct a fortress that will be difficult for enemies to conquer even for the Yadus;
there, even women could fight, let alone the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis.
Whether I am intoxicated, heedless, asleep, or even away on a journey,
let not the wicked and overweening ones bring about the subjugation of the Yādavas.
Having reflected thus, Govinda requested twelve yojanas of land from the great ocean; there he constructed the city of Dvārakā.
With its great gardens and massive ramparts, adorned with hundreds of lakes,
and crowded with palaces and houses, it was like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Having brought the people residing in Mathurā there, Janārdana himself went to Mathurā while Kālayavana was nearby.
When the army had been encamped outside, Govinda went forth from Mathurā unarmed,
and the Yavana beheld him.
Having recognized that Vāsudeva, whose weapon is his own arms, the king followed him—
that great yogi who cannot be reached even by minds.
Followed by him, Kṛṣṇa also entered the great cave where the immensely powerful King Mucukunda was lying asleep.
That wicked Yavana, having entered and seeing the king lying on his bed,
mistook him for Kṛṣṇa and struck him with his foot.
Having risen, King Mucukunda also beheld the Yavana.
As soon as he was seen by him, O Maitreya, that Yavana blazed up with the fire born of his wrath and was reduced to ashes in that very instant.
For he, having gone to the war between the gods and asuras and slain the great asuras,
being afflicted by sleep, chose from the gods the boon of a very long slumber.
And it was declared by the gods: "He who shall awaken you while you are fast asleep shall instantly be reduced to ashes by the fire born from your own body."
Having thus burned that wicked one and beheld Madhusūdana, he asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am born in the lineage of the Moon;
I am the son of Vasudeva, originating from the race of Yadu."
Mucukunda, for his part, remembered there the words of the aged Gārgya.
Having recollected and prostrated before him, Hari, the Lord of all, he said:
"O Supreme Lord, you are known to me; you are a portion of Viṣṇu."
Long ago, Gārgya declared that in the twenty-eighth yuga,
at the end of the Dvāpara age, the birth of Hari will take place in the lineage of Yadu.
There is no doubt that you have arrived here as one who brings benefit to mortals.
For indeed, I am not able to endure your exceedingly great splendor;
for indeed, your speech is more formidable than the roar of a water-laden cloud, and the earth itself bows down, pressed by your feet.
In the great battle between the gods and the asuras, the mighty warriors of the Daitya army could not endure my splendor; yet I cannot endure your splendor.
For a living being fallen into saṃsāra, you alone are the supreme refuge.
Be gracious, O remover of the distress of those who have sought your protection, and destroy my inauspiciousness.
You are the oceans, the mountains, and the rivers; you are the forests, the earth, the sky, the wind, the water, and the fire, as well as the mind.
Intellect, the unmanifest, the vital breaths, you as the lord of the vital breaths, and likewise the person (puruṣa);
and that which is higher than the person, pervading all that is subject to birth and transformation.
That Brahman is devoid of sound and other qualities, undecaying, immeasurable, free from destruction, without increase or decay, and devoid of beginning and end— you are that.
From you come the immortals, along with the ancestors, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
from you come the siddhas and apsarases, as well as humans, animals, and birds.
All reptiles, all wild animals, and all trees— whatever being exists here, whether past or future, moving or stationary— all these [proceed] from you.
Whether manifest or unmanifest, gross or even more subtle—all that you are the creator of the world; there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from you.
O Blessed One, as I was wandering in this wheel of saṃsāra,
overwhelmed by the three types of suffering, I did not attain peace anywhere at that time.
"O Lord, I mistook sufferings for pleasures, like pools of water in a mirage; those things I grasped have resulted only in my torment."
O Lord, [there are] sovereignty, the earth, the army, the treasury, the faction of allies, as well as sons,
wife, the circle of servants, and the objects of the senses such as sound.
"Out of the notion that it was happiness, I grasped all of this imperishable [wealth];
yet in its ultimate consequence, O Lord, it became for me nothing but suffering."
For even the host of gods, O Lord, having reached the celestial realm, became desirous of my assistance; where, then, is eternal bliss?
O Supreme Lord, without propitiating you— the source and abode of all worlds—
who could attain eternal bliss?
Those whose minds are deluded by your māyā, having experienced the afflictions of birth, death, old age, and so forth,
behold the King of the Dead immediately thereafter.
Consequently, those men who do not know Your true nature experience most terrible suffering in the hells produced by their own actions.
O Supreme Lord, I am utterly deluded by Your Māyā and have become its object; I wander within the pit of possessiveness and pride.

Thus, with a mind scorched by the heat of wandering through the cycle of existence, I have come to you for refuge— you who are the shoreless, the immeasurable, the supreme state beyond which nothing exists— and I yearn for nirvāṇa, the abode of perfected splendor.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been thus praised at that time by the wise Mucukunda, [the Lord spoke].
Hari, the Lord of all beings, who is without beginning or end, spoke.
The Blessed Lord said: "O lord of men, augmented by my grace and possessing unimpeded supreme sovereignty, go to the divine worlds according to your desire."
Having enjoyed great divine pleasures, you will be born into a noble family;
by my grace, you will remember your past lives and thereafter attain liberation.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, O King, the monarch prostrated before the Lord Acyuta, the master of the worlds,
and as he emerged from the mouth of the cave, he beheld men who were diminutive in stature.
Then, considering that the Kali Yuga had arrived, the king went to Gandhamādana, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, in order to perform austerities.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having caused that enemy's army to be destroyed by a stratagem,
arrived at Mathurā and seized it, resplendent with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having brought him, he presented him to Ugrasena at Dvāravatī;
and the clan of Yadu became free from fear of defeat by enemies.
O Maitreya, Baladeva also, with all his hostilities completely pacified and longing to see his kinsmen, set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Then, O conqueror of enemies, he greeted the cowherds and cowherd girls with affection and great respect, just as he had done before.
He was embraced by some, and he embraced others;
he laughed together with some cowherds as well as with the cowherd women.
There, the cowherds spoke many pleasing words to Halāyudha, while the cowherd women,
provoked by love, spoke with jealousy, and others spoke as well.
Other gopīs questioned him, who was beloved by the women of the city:
"Is Kṛṣṇa, whose very essence consists of a fragment of fickle love, dwelling in happiness?"
Does he, whose friendship lasts but a moment, perhaps increase the pride of the city women regarding their own good fortune by mocking our efforts?
Does Kṛṣṇa perhaps remember our sweet recitation following the Gītā?
Will he come even once to see his mother?
Or rather, what is the use of those conversations? Let other stories be told; for whether he is without us, or we are without him, it will be the same.
What was our father, mother, brother, husband, and kinsmen abandoned for his sake? For he is indeed the banner of ingratitude.
Nevertheless, O Rāma, you must tell me the truth: does Kṛṣṇa offer any conversation here concerning his arrival? ViP_5.24.17.
This Dāmodara, this Govinda, whose mind is attached to the women of the city,
appears to us as one from whom we have lost our affection and who is difficult to behold.
And when addressed as "Kṛṣṇa" and again as "Dāmodara," the cowherd girls, their hearts captivated by Hari, laughed aloud.
The cowherd women were comforted by Rāma with messages from Kṛṣṇa that were exceedingly charming, sweet with conciliation, full of love, and free from pride.
And as before, Rāma engaged in charming conversations full of jests with the cowherds, and he took delight with them in the lands of Vraja.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
While that high-souled one was wandering in the forest together with the cowherds,
Of Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth, who had assumed the deceptive form of a human.
Having accomplished his task on earth as a wanderer among men,
Varuṇa spoke at length to Vāruṇī for the sake of her enjoyment.
O auspicious one, go for the delight of that great-souled Ananta, for whom you, O intoxicating goddess, have always been desired for his enjoyment.
Having been addressed thus by him, Vāruṇī then made her presence manifest within the hollow of a kadamba tree growing in Vṛndāvana.
While wandering about, O fair-faced one, Baladeva also smelled that exquisite fragrance of wine and then experienced a longing for liquor.
Then, O Maitreya, seeing a stream of wine suddenly falling from that Kadamba tree, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) attained supreme joy.
Accompanied by cowherds and cowherdesses, he drank [the milk] filled with joy,
while being sung to charmingly by those skilled in song and instrumental music.
Shining with pearl-like droplets of sweat from his intense heat, he spoke in distress: "Come, Yamunā, I wish to bathe."
But that river, disregarding the words spoken by him as if he were intoxicated, did not come; thereupon, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) became enraged and seized his plow.
Seizing her with the end of his plow, he dragged her about, overwhelmed by intoxication:
"O wicked woman, you will not come? You will not come? Go elsewhere as you please!"
Suddenly drawn away by him,
the river abandoned its course and flooded that forest where Balabhadra was staying.
Then Śauri’s sister approached, her eyes overwhelmed with terror, and said to Rāma, "Be gracious; O wielder of the mace, release me!"
Then, having heard her well-spoken words, that wielder of the plow said:
"O river, you disregard my heroism and strength;
I shall carry you away in a thousand directions with the stroke of my plow."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, Balarāma, being greatly terrified by her, appeased the river; once that region of the earth had been flooded, he released the Yamunā.
Then, upon bathing, a radiant luster arose in that great-souled one.
Taking a beautiful blue lotus for an ear-ornament and a single earring,
as well as a garland of unfading lotuses sent by Varuṇa,
Lakṣmī gave him two blue garments resembling the ocean.
Adorned with a crest-ornament and decorated with beautiful earrings,
wearing blue garments and garlands, he shone, endowed with radiant splendor.
Thus adorned, Rāma took his pleasure there in Vraja;
and after two months had passed, he returned once more to the city of Dvārakā.
Bala married the daughter of King Raivata, named Revatī; from her were born Niśitha and Ulmuka.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Bhīṣmaka was the king in Kuṇḍina, in the region of Vidarbha.
Rukmī had a son and a fair-faced daughter named Rukmiṇī.
Kṛṣṇa desired Rukmiṇī, and she, the sweetly smiling one, desired him; yet Rukmin, out of hatred, did not give her to the wielder of the discus even when he entreated her.
And, urged by Jarāsaṃdha, the mighty Bhīṣmaka gave Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla along with Rukmin.
Then, for the sake of the marriage, all the kings headed by Jarāsaṃdha went to the city of Bhīṣmaka, desiring to do what was pleasing to Śiśupāla.
Kṛṣṇa also, surrounded by the Yadus such as Balabhadra and others,
set out for Kuṇḍina to witness the marriage of the King of Cedi.
When the wedding was to take place on the following day, Hari abducted that maiden,
leaving the burden of the opposition upon his kinsmen, Rāma and the others.
And then there were the illustrious Paiṇḍraka, Dantavakra, Vidūratha, and kings such as Śiśupāla, Jarāsaṃdha, Śālva, and others.
Enraged, they made a supreme effort to slay Hari;
however, having come together, they were defeated by Rāma and the other leaders of the Yadu clan.
"I shall not enter Kuṇḍina without having slain Keśava in battle";
having made this vow, Rukmin pursued Kṛṣṇa to kill him.
Having slain the army crowded with elephants, horses, infantry,
and chariots, he was conquered and cast down upon the earth by the wielder of the discus as if in mere sport.
Having completely conquered Rukmin,
Madhusūdana duly married Rukmiṇī, who had been obtained through the Rākṣasa form of marriage.
And from her was born Pradyumna, possessed of great prowess, who was a portion of Madana;
he was indeed carried off by Śambara, and he in turn slew Śambara.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Maitreya said:
O Sage, how was the hero Pradyumna carried away by Saṃbara?
How was that Śambara, possessed of great heroism, slain by Pradyumna?
O Guru, how did he who was previously abducted by him slay him? I wish to hear this in detail and clearly.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Sage, on the sixth day after he was born, Kālaśambara seized Pradyumna from the lying-in chamber, thinking, "He is my slayer."
Having seized him, he threw him into the fierce salt ocean,
that most terrible abode of sea-monsters where whirlpools are produced by the surging waves.
And there, a certain fish swallowed the boy who had fallen;
yet he did not die, even though scorched by the fire within its belly.
And that fish, O twice-born one, was killed by fishermen along with other fish and presented to Śambara, the best of asuras.
His blameless wife, named Māyāvatī, who was the mistress of the entire household,
exercised the authority over the cooks.
When the belly of the fish was torn open, she beheld within it an exceedingly beautiful youth,
like the first sprout of the tree of Love that had been consumed by fire.
"Who is this? How did she enter the belly of the fish?"—thus Nārada spoke to her as she sat upon the ground in distress.
This son of Viṣṇu, the cause of the maintenance and destruction of the entire world, has been carried away from the lying-in chamber by Śambara.
Cast into the ocean, you were swallowed by a fish and have now come home;
O fair-browed one, protect this jewel among men with confidence.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, she protected that infant; from childhood itself, she was infatuated with him due to an excessive passion and his extraordinary beauty.
O Mahāmati, when he was adorned with the fullness of youth,
she too, whose gait was like that of an elephant, became filled with desire for him.
O great sage, Māyāvatī, blinded by passion and with her heart and eyes fixed upon him, bestowed all her magical powers (*māyās*) upon Pradyumna.
To her, who was showing favor, that son of Kṛṣṇa said: "O Kamalebhā, why do you behave so differently today, having abandoned your maternal nature?"
She said to him, "You are indeed not my son;
this Kālaśambara has carried you away, the son of Viṣṇu."
Cast into the ocean, I was obtained by a fish from its belly;
for that mother of mine, so exceedingly affectionate, weeps even now for her beloved.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, Pradyumna, his mind agitated by anger, challenged Śambara to battle and, possessed of great strength, fought with him.
Having slain the entire army of that Daitya, the Yādava bypassed the seventh illusion and employed the eighth.
With that [weapon], she struck the Daitya Kālaśambara through her illusory power (māyā),
and having arisen, she returned with him to her father’s city.
Seeing him fallen in the inner apartments together with Māyāvatī, O Kṛṣṇa, the wives of Kṛṣṇa conceived dark suspicions.
Out of love, the blameless Rukmiṇī, her eyes filled with tears, said:
"Blessed indeed is she whose son exists in the prime of youth."
"At this age, my son Pradyumna—if he be alive—his mother is truly fortunate; O child, what fear can there be for you from her?"
"Or rather, considering the nature of my affection and the appearance of your body,
it is very clear, my child, that you will be the offspring of Hari."
Śrī Parāśara said: In the meantime, Nārada arrived together with Kṛṣṇa and,
gladdening her, spoke to Queen Rukmiṇī, who was staying within the inner apartments.
"O fair-browed one, here is your son who has returned after slaying Śambara;
he is the one by whom your infant was carried away from the lying-in chamber."
"This wife of yours, Māyāvatī, is virtuous;
she is not the wife of Śambara. Hear now the reason for this."
When Manmatha had met his destruction, she who was devoted to his manifestation assumed a form through her illusory power and deluded Śambara.
In the enjoyment of her dwellings and other pleasures, she— this woman with intoxicating eyes— manifested to the Daitya a beautiful form composed of illusion.
"Kāma has descended as your son, and this Rati is his beloved;
O beautiful one, you should have no doubt in this matter—she is your daughter-in-law."
Then Rukmiṇī and Keśava were filled with joy, and that entire city exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu-sādhu).
Seeing Rukmiṇī reunited with her son who had been lost for so long,
all the people in Dvāravatī were then struck with wonder.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: The valiant [Vasudeva] begot Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, and Cārudeha;...
Suṣeṇa, Cārugupta, and likewise Bhadracāru, the supreme.
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons— Cāruvinda, Sucāru, and Cāru, the best among the strong— as well as a daughter named Cārumatī.
And Kṛṣṇa had seven other beautiful wives:
Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyā, and likewise Agnājītī; 3 // ViP_5.28.3 //
And there were also Queen Jāmbavatī, Rohiṇī who could assume any form at will,
and another, Suśīlā, the daughter of the King of Madra, whose ornament was her virtuous character.
Satrājitī Satyabhāmā and the sweetly smiling Lakṣmaṇā were among the sixteen thousand other women who belonged to the wielder of the discus.
Pradyumna, too, of great heroism, took that auspicious daughter of Rukmin at her svayaṃvara,
and she [took] him, the son of Hari.
In that city lived his son by Bhaktā, Aniruddha, who possessed great strength and prowess,
whose ocean of valor was irresistible in battle, and who was a subduer of his enemies.
Keśava chose as his bride the granddaughter of that very Rukmin; though Rukmin was indeed vying with the wielder of the discus, he gave her away to his grandson.
O twice-born one, for the sake of her auspicious marriage, Rāma and the other Yādavas, along with Hari and all the other kings, went from there to the city named Bhojakaṭa, where Rukmiṇī resided.
When that marriage of the high-souled Pradyumna had been completed, the kings headed by the King of Kaliṅga spoke these words to Rukmin: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.28.10.
"Balarama is unskilled at dice; thus his addiction to gambling is great.
Let us defeat him by means of dice—why not, since he is possessed of great strength?"
Śrī Parāśara said:
"So be it," Rukmī, filled with the pride of his own strength, said to those kings;
and then, together with Rāma, he engaged in a game of dice in the assembly hall.
Balarāma was defeated by Rukmin for one thousand gold coins;
at the second throw of the dice, he was likewise defeated by Rukmin for another thousand.
Then Balabhadra staked ten thousand gold coins as a wager; Rukmin, the best among those skilled in gambling, won them.
Then, O twice-born one, the foolish lord of Kaliṅga laughed loudly, baring his teeth; and Rukmin, arrogant with pride, spoke.
"Out of ignorance, I have defeated this Balabhadra at dice; blinded by the arrogance of the dice, I disregarded those who were truly skilled in the game."
Seeing the King of Kaliṅga with his teeth bared in a glare,
and Rukmi as well speaking such wicked words, Halāyudha was filled with wrath.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, Rukmī took up ten million gold pieces as his stake; he accepted the wager and cast the dice for that purpose.
Baladeva defeated him and said loudly, "It has been conquered by me!
Rukmi replied loudly, "By me! "Enough of this false speech, Bala! he cried.
"This stake was proposed by you; it is true that I did not approve of it.
If it has been won by you in this manner, how could it not have been won by me?"
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, a voice resounding deeply from the sky spoke aloud,
increasing the wrath of the high-souled Baladeva.
"Rukmin has spoken falsely that he was conquered by force and by righteousness;
even without saying a word, an action is accomplished through one's deeds."
Then the mighty Balarāma, rising up with eyes bloodshot with anger,
struck Rukmi with a single eight-footed step.
And seizing the King of Kaliṅga as he struggled with force, the powerful one,
enraged, broke his tusks with which he had laughed so loudly.
And having pulled up a great pillar made of gold, Balarāma,
being exceedingly enraged, struck down those kings who were on their side.
Then, O twice-born one, that entire circle of kings became terrified and intent on flight, crying out "Alas! Alas! as the army grew enraged.
O Maitreya, seeing Rukmin slain by Balarāma, Madhusūdana said nothing out of fear for the two brothers, Rukmiṇī, and Bala.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having taken the son who had been born there and having married him off,
Keśava returned to Dvārakā along with the Yadu host.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: While Kṛṣṇa was residing in Dvāravatī, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, [approached him].
Then Maitreya arrived, mounted upon the back of a rutting Airāvata elephant.
Then, having entered Dvārakā and met with Hari,
he related the deeds of the Daitya Naraka.
O Madhusūdana, although you remain in human form, you are the protector of the gods; by you, all sufferings have been brought to peace.
The Asura Dhenuka, who was intent on harming ascetics and brahmins,
as well as Keśin, have all been slain by you.
Kaṃsa, Kuvalayāpīḍa, and Pūtanā, the slayer of infants—
all these and whatever other harassers of the world existed have been brought to destruction by you.
When the three worlds are protected by the power arising from your mighty arms,
the gods attain satisfaction through the receipt of their sacrificial portions from the sacrificers.
Therefore, O Janārdana, you should listen to the purpose for which I have now come and make an effort to provide a remedy for it.
This son of the Earth, named Naraka, the lord of the city of Prāgjyotiṣa,
O subduer of enemies, inflicts injury upon all living beings.
O Janārdana, that asura, having abducted the daughters of the gods, siddhas, asuras, and kings, confined them in his own palace.
He took away the water-shedding umbrella of Pracetas,
as well as the horn of Madaru and the jewel-mountain.
That asura carried off the two divine, nectar-dripping earrings of my mother Diti;
he desired the elephant Airāvata.
"O Govinda, this misconduct has been reported by me to him;
whatever must be done in response to this, let that be considered by you yourself."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having heard this and smiling, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
took Vāsava by the hand and rose from his excellent seat.
Having intentionally summoned the sky-traveling Garuḍa and mounted him,
he placed Satyabhāmā upon his back and departed for the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Having mounted the elephant Airāvata, Śakra also departed for the third heaven;
thereafter, Kṛṣṇa likewise went away while the inhabitants of Dvārakā looked on.
O best of the twice-born, for a hundred yojanas all around the city of Prāgjyotiṣapura, the earth was strewn with the nooses of Mura, which were as sharp as razors.
Hari cut those nooses by hurling his Sudarśana discus;
then Mura rose up, and Keśava struck him down.
Then Hari reduced Muru’s seven thousand sons to ashes with the fire of his discus's edge, like moths consumed by flame.
O twice-born one, having slain the asuras Hayagrīva and Pañcajana,
the wise [Kṛṣṇa] then marched against Tārāvana at the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
There, Govinda— wherein Govinda slew the Daityas by the thousands— had a great battle with Naraka and his vast army.
The powerful wielder of the discus, the slayer of the hosts of Daityas, hurled his discus at Naraka, the son of the Earth, as he was discharging a rain of weapons and missiles, and split him in two.
Then, in the hell named Hate (Dveṣa), the Earth, having taken Ādi and Tiṭibha with her,
approached the Lord of the World and spoke these words.
The Earth said:
"O Lord, when I was uplifted by you in the form of a boar,
this son, born from the touch of you, was then produced within me."
"This very man was given to me by you alone, and by you alone he has been struck down.
Take these two earrings, and protect his lineage."
O Blessed One, for the sake of relieving my burden, you,
the Lord, have come to this world with a portion of yourself, O Master, with a countenance gracious and serene.
You are the creator, the transformer, and the destroyer; you are the origin and the dissolution.
You are the world and the very form of the world; O Acyuta, what more can be praised in you?
Just as the Blessed One is praised as the pervader, the pervaded, the agent of action, and the effect,
so too is he praised for you who have become the self of all beings.
O Lord, you are the Supreme Self, the elemental self, the individual self, and even the dissolution itself; since you are all these, for what purpose does this praise proceed toward you?
Be gracious, O Soul of all beings! Let that which was done by Naraka be forgiven for the sake of his innocence; your son has been struck down by you.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having replied "So be it" to the Earth, O best of sages, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, took the jewels from the abode of Naraka.
O great sage, within the maidens' quarters, he of incomparable prowess beheld more than sixteen thousand maidens.
He beheld four thousand of the foremost elephants with four tusks,
as well as twenty-one hundred thousand horses of the Kāmboja breed.
Govinda caused those maidens, those Nāgas, and those horses to reach the city of Dvārakā instantly by means of Naraka’s servants.
He beheld the umbrella of Varuṇa as well as the mountain of jewels;
Hari then placed them upon Garuḍa, the lord of birds.
And having ascended it himself, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, Kṛṣṇa went to the abode of the gods to give the earrings of Aditi.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Garuḍa [took] the umbrella of Varuṇa, as well as the mountain of jewels.
Carrying Hṛṣīkeśa along with his wife as if in mere play, he proceeded.
Then Hari, having reached the gateway to heaven, blew his conch;
likewise, the gods approached Janārdana with offerings of water and honey-mixture in their hands.
Worshipped by the gods, Kṛṣṇa entered the residence of the mother of the gods,
which resembled the peak of a white cloud, and beheld Aditi.
Having bowed to her, Janārdana gave those two excellent earrings to her along with Śakra,
and he announced to her the destruction of Naraka.
Then Aditi, the mother of the world, being pleased and with her mind composed and directed toward him, praised Hari, the sustainer of the worlds.
Aditi said:
"Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, who grants fearlessness to your devotees;
O eternal Self, universal Self, Self of all beings, creator of all beings!"
O guide of the mind, intellect, and senses; O you whose nature consists of the qualities, yet who transcend the three qualities; O you free from dualities, abiding in the heart with pure being.
It is entirely free from conceptual constructions such as "white" or "long," untouched by birth and the like, and devoid of states such as dreaming.
O Acyuta, you are the twilight, night, and day; the earth, the sky, the wind, and the water;
the fire, the mind, the intellect, and the source of the elements.
O Lord, you are the creator of creation, maintenance, and destruction,
acting as the sovereign agent through your own forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The gods, Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Siddhas, and Pannagas;
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, and likewise human beings.
Domestic animals and wild beasts, winged creatures and reptiles, as well as numerous trees, shrubs, and creepers, and all species of grasses; ||| ViP_5.30.12 |||
Whether they be gross, middling, or subtle, or even subtler than the subtle— all these various types of bodies belonging to you, which depend upon individual souls— [are all subject to this].
This is your illusion, which deludes those who do not know the supreme truth;
by it, the fool is obstructed by the cognition of a self in that which is not-self.
O Lord, that sense of "mine" which arises here toward what is not one's own, and that sense of "I" and "mine" which generally takes birth,
is the activity of this Māyā, who is afflicted by the cycle of worldly existence.
O Lord, those men who, devoted to their own duty, have worshipped you,
cross over this entire illusion for the sake of their own liberation.
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as humans and animals,
are enveloped by the blinding darkness of the great whirlpool of Viṣṇu’s māyā.
"Having propitiated you, these men desire their cherished objects and the destruction of rebirth;
O Blessed One, this very thing is your Māyā."
Desiring a son and for the sake of conquering my enemies' faction, I propitiated you;
it was not for the sake of liberation, for that was merely the play of Māyā.
When even from a wish-fulfilling tree there arises in the unfortunate a desire for little more than a loincloth and a covering, that is a transgression born of one's own faults.
Therefore, O Imperishable One who causes the delusion of Māyā for the entire world, be gracious;
O Lord of Beings, destroy this ignorance which is the very essence of the absence of knowledge.
Salutations to you who hold the discus in hand; salutations to you who hold the Śārṅga bow in hand;
salutations to you, O Viṣṇu, who hold the mace in hand; salutations to you who hold the conch in hand.
I perceive this form of yours, characterized by gross marks;
I do not know what is beyond it. Be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Śrī Parāśara said: Thus praised by Aditi, Viṣṇu smiled and spoke to the source of the gods:
"O Goddess, you are our mother; be gracious and grant us boons."
The Grandfather said:
"So be it; according to your wish, O tiger among men, you shall be invincible by all the gods and asuras in the mortal world."
Śrī Parāśara said: Then Kṛṣṇa’s wife Satyabhāmā, together with Śakra, bowed down to Aditi and said again and again, "Be gracious."
Aditi said:
"By my grace, O fair-browed one, neither old age nor deformity shall befall you;
O lady of faultless limbs, your youth shall remain firm and fresh."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having received permission from Aditi, the king of the gods worshipped Janārdana in the prescribed manner, preceded by great reverence.
And Śacī, considering Satyabhāmā to be a mere mortal woman, did not give her a flower of the Pārijāta tree; she herself adorned herself with the blossoms.
Then, O best of men, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, beheld the charming pleasure gardens, such as Nandana and others.
And he beheld [the tree] rich in fragrance, bearing clusters of blossoms,
providing eternal delight, and adorned with copper-colored young shoots.
While the nectar was being churned,
the Lord of the World, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, produced the Pārijāta tree, which possessed a bark like that of refined gold.
He was gratified with supreme joy at seeing that unsurpassed king of trees.
O best of the twice-born, having seen it, Satyabhāmā said to Govinda:
"O Kṛṣṇa, why is this tree not being taken to Dvārakā?"
If your word is true— that you are exceedingly dear to me—
then let this tree be taken for the sake of my private garden.
"Neither Jāmbavatī nor Rukmiṇī is as dear to me as you are, O Satyā"—this was said by you, O beloved Kṛṣṇa, on many occasions. (ViP 5.30.35)
If this is true, O Govinda, and not merely a polite formality toward me,
then let this Pārijāta tree be the ornament of my home.
"Carrying a cluster of blossoms from the pārijāta tree upon my braid of hair,
may I shine in the midst of my co-wives"— this is what I desire.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, Hari laughed and placed the Pārijāta tree upon Garuḍa; then the guardians of the grove spoke to him.
O Govinda, Śacī is the queen of the king of the gods; you ought not to take away that Pārijāta tree, which is her possession.
O highly fortunate one, he was born and given to the king of the gods; he, in turn, out of curiosity, gave him to his queen, the goddess Śacī.
This was produced by the gods during the churning for nectar for the sake of adorning Śacī;
you will not go safely if you take him with you.
Out of folly, you seek the hand of her who looks to the face of the king of the gods; for who, having taken him [as a husband], would go forth in safety?
O Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gods will certainly seek retribution for this;
and the immortals shall follow Śakra as he raises his thunderbolt in hand.
Therefore, O Acyuta, enough with all these gods and this conflict of yours;
the wise do not praise that karma which is bitter in its ripening.
Śrī Parāśara said:
When they had spoken thus, Satyabhāmā, becoming exceedingly angry, said to them:
"Who is Śacī, and who is Śakra, the lord of the gods, that he possesses the Pārijāta tree?"
If this tree has arisen during the churning for the nectar as common property for all the world, why does Vāsava seize it alone?
Just as wine, the moon, and the goddess Śrī belong to the guardians of the forest,
so too does the Pārijāta tree belong in common to all the world.
Moreover, Śacī restrains him out of great pride in her husband;
therefore, let it be told: enough with patience, for she is causing the tree to lose its essence.
"Go quickly and tell Paulomī my words:
'Satyabhāmā speaks these words with syllables arrogant with pride. (ViP 5.30.49)
"If you are beloved by your husband, and if your husband is under your control,
then cause him to stop my husband as he is cutting down this tree."
I know your husband is Śakra; I know you are the lord of the thirty gods.
Nevertheless, as a mere mortal woman, I shall take this Pārijāta tree from you.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, the guards went and told Śacī exactly what had been said;
and having heard it, Śacī encouraged Cakra, the lord of the gods.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Indra, surrounded by the armies of all the gods, set out to fight Hari for the sake of the Pārijāta tree.
Then, while Śakra stood with the thunderbolt in his hand, the gods became ready for battle, equipped with excellent weapons such as iron clubs, swords, maces, and spears.
Then Govinda, having observed Śakra standing atop the Naga king, surrounded by his divine retinue and prepared for battle, [spoke].
He made a sound like that of a conch shell, filling the quarters with its noise,
and discharged multitudes of sharp arrows by the tens of thousands.
Then, seeing the quarters and the sky covered with hundreds of arrows,
all the gods discharged various missiles and weapons in great numbers.
The Lord Madhusūdana, the master of the worlds, effortlessly cut down each individual missile and weapon discharged by the gods by the thousands.
Having pulled out the noose of the Lord of Waters,
he went back and tore it into pieces with his beak, like the body of a young serpent.
The Blessed One, the son of Devakī, caused the staff sent by Yama to fall upon the earth, shattered by the hurling of his mace.
The all-pervading Śauri reduced the palanquin of the Lord of Wealth to pieces as small as sesame seeds with his discus,
and he rendered the Sun’s splendor powerless before his very eyes.
The fire was brought to coolness by his arrows; the Vasus were driven away in all directions;
and the Rudras, their trident-tips shattered by his discus, were cast down upon the earth.
Then the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts,
and the Gandharvas were struck by arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow and cast into the sky like the cotton-wool of a silk-cotton tree.
Garuḍa, moreover, moved about devouring, striking, and tearing apart the gods with his beak, his two wings, and the tips of his claws.
Then, with hundreds of thousands [of arrows], the Lord of the Gods and Madhusūdana showered each other like two clouds with torrents of rain.
In that tumultuous conflict, Garuḍa fought with Airāvata,
and Janārdana fought with Śakra and all the gods.
When all his arrows, weapons, and missiles had been shattered, Vāsava quickly seized his thunderbolt and Kṛṣṇa took up his Sudarśana discus.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the entire three worlds raised a cry of lamentation upon seeing Janārdana and the king of the gods with the thunderbolt and discus in their hands.
Then the Blessed Lord Hari caught the thunderbolt hurled by Indra;
he did not release his discus at that time, but said to Śakra, "Stay!"
To the heroic lord of gods, whose vajra was lost and whose vehicle had been wounded by Garuḍa,
who was intent on flight, Satyabhāmā spoke:
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, it is not fitting for you, the husband of Śacī, to flee;
Śacī herself, adorned with the full expanse of the Pārijāta garland, will attend upon you."

"O King of the Gods, what kind of divine sovereignty is it for you, if you are free from malice toward Śacī, who has come to you with affection as before, radiant with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers?"
"Enough of this exertion, Śakra; you ought not to feel shame.
Let this Pārijāta tree be taken away; let the gods be free from their distress."
Due to the arrogance and pride born of her great esteem,
Śacī did not receive me with proper hospitality when I went to her house.
"O Śakra, because I am a woman, my mind is lacking in gravity; I was intent on praising my own husband, and for that reason I engaged in a dispute with you."
Therefore, what woman would not be proud because of her beauty, when she has been robbed of her own property, the Pārijāta tree, by my husband? ViP_5.30.76.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by her, O twice-born one, the king of the gods desisted;
and he said to her, "Enough, O fierce woman, with these elaborate words from the mouth of your friend."
Indra said: "Even though he is the creator of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the entire universe,
shame arises in me for having been conquered by him who possesses the form of the cosmos."
Since this entire world has no beginning, middle, or end within Him, and since it shall never cease to exist because He is the soul of all beings,
O Goddess, how can there be shame for one who has been cast out by Him, the cause of its arising, dissolution, and preservation?
Whose form, the source of all worlds, is exceedingly subtle and unknown to all physicians, and which is not known by others—
that unborn, uncreated Lord, eternal, who by his own will became a mortal for the benefit of the world— who is capable of conquering him?
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been praised in this manner by the king of the gods, Keśava, the Blessed One—
Laughing with profound intent, the best of the twice-born spoke to Indra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Lord of the World, you are Indra, the king of the gods, while we are mortals;
therefore, you alone must forgive this offense committed by me."
"And let this Pārijāta tree be taken to its proper place;
O Śakra, it was accepted by me for the sake of fulfilling Satyabhāmā’s word."
"And take this thunderbolt which you have hurled here; O Śakra, this weapon of yours shall indeed be the destroyer of your enemies."
Indra said: "O Lord, why do you delude me by saying, 'I am a mortal'?
We know you as the Blessed One; we are not perceivers of the subtle."
O Lord, you who are who you are, you remain intent upon the activity of protecting the world;
O destroyer of the demon Amura, you extract the thorn from the world.
"O Kṛṣṇa, let this Pārījāta tree be taken to the city of Dvāravatī;
once the mortal world has been abandoned by you, it will no longer remain upon the earth."
O God of gods, Lord of the world, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, O mighty-armed one,
wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace, forgive this transgression.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having replied "So be it" to the Lord of the Gods, Hari descended to the earth,
being praised by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and celestial rishis who followed him with devotion.
Then, O twice-born one, standing above Dvārakā and blowing his conch shell,
he aroused great joy among the inhabitants of Dvārakā.
Then, having descended from Garuḍa accompanied by his attendants, Satyabhāmā planted the great Pārijāta tree in the pleasure garden.
Then all those Yādavas beheld superhuman beings upon that tree, who were performing the observation of the sacrifice.
Then the high-minded Kṛṣṇa divided the wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and other assets brought by his servants, and bestowed it upon his kinsmen.
And Kṛṣṇa took the maidens who were the captives of Naraka.
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, Janārdana married those maidens who had been gathered from all sides by Naraka.
O great sage, at one and the same time, Govinda duly took their hands in marriage according to the sacred law, each in her own separate house.
The Blessed Madhusūdana assumed as many forms as there were sixteen thousand and one hundred women, plus some more.
O Maitreya, Madhusūdana perceived each one of those maidens as thinking, "He has taken my hand in marriage."
O Brahmin, during the nights, Keśava Hari, the creator of the world who assumes the universal form, dwelt in the houses of all those women.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"The sons of Hari beginning with Pradyumna, born of Rukmiṇī, have been described to you."
And Satyabhāmā gave birth to Bhānu, Bhauma, Irā, and others.
Dīptimat, Tāmrapakṣa, and others were said to be born of Rohiṇī from Hari;
and Sāmba and other mighty-armed sons were born of Jāmbavatī.
Bhadravinda and others were the sons of Nāgnajiti, all of great strength;
while Saṃgrāmajit and the other principal sons of Hari were born of Śaibyā.
Vṛka and the others were the sons born to Mādrī; she also obtained sons headed by Gātravat, while Lakṣmaṇā bore sons such as Kālindya and Śruta.
And from his other wives, a hundred thousand and eighty thousand sons were born to the wielder of the discus.
Pradyumna was the first among all of them, the son of Rukmiṇī;
from Pradyumna was born Aniruddha, and from him Vajra was born.
O best of the twice-born, the mighty Aniruddha, unopposed in battle, married Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa and granddaughter of Bali.
Wherein occurred the great and terrible battle between Hari and Śaṅkara,
wherein the thousand arms of Bāṇa were severed by the Discus-wielder.
Maitreya said:
O Brahmin, how did the battle between Hara and Kṛṣṇa come about for the sake of Umā?
And how did Hari bring about the destruction of Bāṇa’s arms?
O highly fortunate one, you ought to relate all of this to me;
a great curiosity has arisen in me to hear this story of Hari.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Brahmin, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, having observed Pārvatī sporting with Śambhu, conceived an intense longing for that state.
Then Gaurī, who knows the minds of all, said to that beautiful woman:
"Enough with this excessive distress; you too shall take delight with your husband."
Having been addressed thus by her, she wondered in her mind, "When [will this happen]? or "Who indeed will be my husband? To her, Pārvatī spoke again.
Pārvatī said:
"O princess, he who shall overcome you in a dream on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha will become your husband."
Śrī Parāśara said: On that lunar day, just as the goddess had described in her dream,
a certain man overpowered her, and she felt passion for him there.
Then, having awakened and not seeing the man, she became anxious; and casting aside her shame, Maitreyī said to her friend, "Where have you gone? *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 5.32.16.
Bāṇa’s minister was Kumbhāṇḍa, and his daughter was Citralekhā;
she became her friend, and she asked: "Who is this being spoken of by you?"
When her friend, overcome with shame, did not tell her this,
she then gained her confidence and related everything to her.
When she had understood the matter, Uṣā spoke to her again as she had been told by the goddess: "Employ that very means which has been described for the attainment of him."
Citralekhā said:
"This is difficult to discern, and it cannot even be attained;
nevertheless, O beloved, I must do something to assist you."
"Wait for that period of time until seven or eight days have passed";
having said this, he went inside and then devised that plan.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then Citralekhā, having drawn the gods, daityas, gandharvas, and humans— preeminent among them— in their respective positions, showed them to her.
Having set aside the Gandharvas, as well as the Uragas, Suras, and Asuras,
she fixed her gaze upon human beings, and among them, specifically upon the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis.
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, that fair-browed woman became as if paralyzed with shame; O twice-born one, at the sight of Pradyumna, she turned her gaze elsewhere out of modesty.
Then, O twice-born one, as soon as her beloved son Pradyumna was seen, the shame of that woman, who was intensely longing for him, was cast away somewhere.
When she said, "This one, this one," Citralekhā, who was skilled in yoga, then spoke to Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa.
Citralekhā said:
"This grandson of Kṛṣṇa, propitiated by the Goddess, is your husband;
he is known as Aniruddha, renowned and of pleasing appearance."
If you obtain this husband who has come to you, then all will be attained;
for formerly, the city of Dvārakā, protected by Kṛṣṇa, was difficult to enter.
Nevertheless, O friend, I shall bring your husband back to you through effort;
this secret must not be told by you to anyone at all.
"I shall return before long; endure my separation.
Having thus consoled her friend Uṣā, he then departed for Dvāravatī.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, Bāṇa also, having prostrated before the Three-eyed Lord, spoke.
"O Lord, with my thousand arms, I am weary of life without battle."
"Will this battle bring fruitfulness to these arms of mine? Without war, what is the use of my arms but a mere burden?"
Śrī Śaṅkara said: "O Bāṇa, when the breaking of your peacock-banner occurs,
you shall then obtain a battle that brings joy to the flesh-eating demons."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, having bowed to Śambhu, the giver of boons, he returned home;
seeing his banner broken, he was filled with joy and experienced even greater delight.
At that very time, however, the excellent Apsaras Citralekhā brought Aniruddha there by the power of her yogic knowledge.
Having discovered that he had entered the maiden's inner apartments and was sporting there with Uṣā,
the guards went and informed the Daitya king.
Taking up a terrible iron club, that slayer of enemy heroes struck down the army of the *kiṅkara*s commanded by that great-souled one.
