While those arrows were being loosed, Bāṇa, standing upon his chariot and intent on slaying him,
was defeated by the hero of the Yadus after fighting to the best of his ability.
Then, impelled by his mantra, he fought with him through illusion;
thereafter, he bound that joy of the Yadus with the serpent-weapon (pannagāstra).
To the Yadus who were lamenting in Dvāravatī, "Where has Aniruddha gone?",
Nārada announced that he had been captured by Bāṇa.
Hearing that he had been led away to Śoṇitapura, the Yādavas gained confidence through the words of a woman who was skilled in the arts of magic.
Then Hari, having mounted Garuḍa— who arrived as soon as he was thought of—
together with Bala and Pradyumna, set out for the city of Bāṇa.
Upon entering the city, there was a battle between the high-souled one and the Pramathas;
Hari led them to their destruction and proceeded to the vicinity of Bāṇa’s city.
Then the great fever of Maheśvara, three-legged and three-headed,
approached for the sake of protecting Bāṇa and fought with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
From contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body, Baladeva also experienced a burning sensation arising from the touch of that ash, and his eyes grew heavy with fatigue.
Then, while fighting with the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
he was quickly expelled from Kṛṣṇa’s body by the Vaiṣṇava fever.
Seeing him overwhelmed by the crushing blow from Nārāyaṇa’s arm, the divine Grandfather said, "Let him be forgiven."
Then, having said "It is forgiven," the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana caused that Vaiṣṇava fever to dissolve back into himself alone.
Jvara said,
"Those men who shall remember my battle with you will become free from fever. Having spoken thus to him, Jvara departed.
Then the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, having conquered the five fires and likewise brought them to destruction, effortlessly crushed the army of the Dānavas.
Then, with his entire army, Bali’s son fought against Śaṅkara, as did Kārttikeya against Śauri.
The battle between Hari and Śaṅkara was exceedingly terrible;
all the worlds were agitated by the heat of the rays from their weapons and missiles.
"In this great battle that was taking place there, the gods thought, 'Surely the dissolution of the entire world has arrived.'"
With the Jṛmbhakāstra, Govinda caused Śaṅkara to yawn;
thereupon the Daityas and the Pramathas prostrated themselves on all sides.
Overcome by yawning, Hara sat down on the seat of his chariot;
he was then unable to fight with Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
With his horses wounded by Garuda and tormented by Pradyumna’s weapon,
Guha, his spear cast away by Kṛṣṇa’s roar of defiance, departed.
Mounted upon a great chariot whose horses were controlled by Nandin,
Bāṇa arrived there to fight with Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and their armies.
The immensely powerful Balabhadra pierced Bāṇa’s army in many ways with his arrows; and having fallen away from righteousness, the army fled.
Bāṇa saw Balarāma quickly drawing back with the tip of his plough and striking with his mace,
while the wielder of the discus (Kṛṣṇa) struck him with arrows and by his own strength.
Then there occurred a most terrible battle between Kṛṣṇa and Bāṇa.
As Bāṇa discharged blazing arrows capable of piercing body armor,
Kṛṣṇa cut those sharp shafts with his own arrows.
Bāṇa pierced Keśava, and the wielder of the discus pierced Bāṇa.
O twice-born one, Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa discharged weapons at each other with the desire for victory, incessantly causing mutual injury through their swiftness of hand.
When all his arrows were exhausted and his weapon was failing,
Hari then set his mind upon killing Bāṇa by means of a great abundance of shafts.
Then Hari, the enemy of the host of Daityas, seized the Sudarśana discus, which possessed a splendor equal to the combined radiance of a hundred suns.
Then, as the enemy of Madhu was about to discharge his discus for the destruction of Bāṇa,
the naked Koṭarī, a magical power of the Daityas, appeared before Hari.
Seeing her before him, Hari closed his eyes and released the Sudarśana [discus],
aiming it at the enemy's forest of arms to cut them down.
Then, by means of his arms, Bāṇa, urged by Acyuta, gradually performed the severing of those weapons,
which had been cast away by the Asura and were intent on consuming him.
When the forest of his arms had been severed, that [spear] remained in the hand of Madhusūdana;
desiring to release it for the destruction of Bāṇa, he was recognized by the enemy of Tripura.
Having approached Govinda, the Lord of Umā,
looking at his left arm which was dripping with a shower of blood from the severed head of Dādaḍa, spoke to him with conciliatory words.
Śaṅkara said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, I know you as the Supreme Person,
the Highest Lord, the Supreme Self, the beginningless and endless Hari.
Among gods, animals, and humans, this play consisting of the assumption of bodies is Your activity, characterized as the movement of You who are the Self of all beings.
Therefore, O Lord, be gracious; protection from fear has been granted by me to this Bāṇa.
You must not consider my spoken word as false.
"O Imperishable One, this Daitya has become arrogant because of his reliance on us; he has committed no offense against you, as he was granted a boon by me. Therefore, I beg your forgiveness."
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, Govinda,
his face becoming serene and his resentment toward the asura having vanished, spoke to the wielder of the trident, the lord of Umā.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Śaṅkara, this Bāṇa shall live, for he has been granted a boon by you;
out of respect for your word, I have withdrawn this discus."
"O Śaṅkara, whatever fearlessness has been granted by you, all that has been granted by me; you ought to perceive yourself as non-different from me."
I am you, and this entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans; there is nothing whatsoever that is other than me—this is the reality that you ought to know here.
O Hara, those whose souls are deluded by ignorance perceive duality;
they speak of difference and behold a distinction between us two.
"I am pleased; I shall depart. You may go, O bull-bannered one."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa departed for where Pradyumna was; the serpents that bound him perished, crushed by Garuḍa as if by a gale.
Then, having placed Aniruddha along with his wife upon Garuḍa,
Rāma, Kārṣṇi, and Dāmodara returned to the city of Dvārakā.
Surrounded there by his sons and grandsons, O Brahmin, Janārdana took delight with the goddesses at all times, desiring to lighten the burden of the earth.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Maitreya said: Śauri, bearing a human body, performed a great deed.
He effortlessly conquered Śakra, Śarva, and all the gods.
O illustrious one, let that other deed which he performed, which thwarted the divine activities, be told; for my curiosity is indeed great.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O brahmin-sage, listen with respect as I relate how Vārāṇasī was consumed by fire by Kṛṣṇa during his incarnation as a man.
But Paiṇḍraka Vāsudeva became known as Vāsudeva on earth,
addressed by people deluded by ignorance as "You have descended."
He thought, "I am Vāsudeva descended upon the surface of the earth," and with his memory thus lost, he then caused all the emblems of Viṣṇu to be fashioned.
And he dispatched a messenger to the great-souled Kṛṣṇa,
instructing him to set aside his own insignia, such as the discus, as well as his own name.
O fool, having completely abandoned everything without exception that consists of Vāsudeva,
bow down to me for the sake of your own life.
Thus addressed, Janārdana laughed and said to that messenger:
"I shall indeed discharge my own emblem, the discus, at you."
And having gone there, O messenger, you must speak these words of mine to Paiṇḍraka: "The true intent of your message has been understood; let that which is to be done be performed."
"Assuming my characteristic attire and emblems, I shall come to your city;
and I will undoubtedly cast down that discus, my own distinctive mark."
"And as for this command of yours, 'Come,' which you have spoken—
having met with you tomorrow, I shall fulfill it without delay."
"O King, having come to you for refuge, I shall act in such a way that no further fear whatsoever shall arise from you."
Śrī Parāśara said: When the messenger had spoken and departed, Hari, remembering that he had arrived,
mounted Garuḍa and went quickly to that city.
Then, having heard of Keśava’s exertion, the Lord of Kāśī,
surrounded by his entire army, approached as an ally from the rear.
Then, with a great force and the army of the King of Kāśī,
that Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva marched toward Keśava.
From afar, Hari beheld him standing in a magnificent chariot,
with the discus in his hand, the mace and the Śārṅga bow in his arms, and a lotus held in his hand.
Hari beheld him wearing a garland and yellow garments, with a banner fashioned by Suparṇa, and the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
Seeing him wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with various jewels, and profound in his inner disposition, he whose banner is Garuḍa laughed.
And he fought with his army, O twice-born one— an army powerful with elephants and horses,
and resplendent with swords, scimitars, maces, spears, javelins, and bows.
In an instant, with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow that tore through his enemies,
and by the falling blows of his mace and discus, he destroyed that army.
Having thus brought the army of the King of Kāśī to destruction, Janārdana spoke to the foolish Pauṇḍraka, who was distinguished by his own insignia: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.34.21.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Paiṇḍraka, as for what was spoken by you to me through the mouth of the messenger—
that 'cast off your insignia'— I shall fulfill that for you."
"This discus has been released; this mace is hurled at you;
and this Garuḍa has been dispatched—may he ascend your banner."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, he was split asunder by the released discus;
his standard was struck down and shattered by the mace and by Garuḍa.
Then, while the world raised cries of "Alas!", the powerful lord of the city of Kāśī,
remaining steadfast in his devotion to his friend, fought with Vāsudeva.
Then, having severed his head with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow,
he hurled it into the city of Kāśī, causing wonder among the people.
Having slain Pauṇḍraka and the King of Kāśī along with his followers, Śauri returned once more to Dvāravatī and rejoiced as if he had gone to heaven.
Seeing that head fallen there in the city of the Lord of Kāśī, the people, filled with wonder, asked, "What is this? By whom was it cut off?"
Having learned that he had been slain by Vāsudeva, his son then,
together with his family priest, propitiated Śaṅkara.
In the great field of Avimukta, Śaṅkara was gratified by him;
he then said to that son of the king, "Choose a boon."
"O Blessed One, O Maheśvara, by your grace, let a *kṛtyā* arise for the sake of slaying Kṛṣṇa, the murderer of my father."
Śrī Parāśara said:
When it was said, "It shall be so," immediately after the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni),
a great Kṛtyā arose from that very fire, destined for his destruction.
Then the enraged Kṛtyā, her face terrifying with flames, her hair and skull-ornaments ablaze, cried out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and went toward the main gate.
Beholding her, O Sage, the people, their eyes trembling with fear,
went for refuge to Madhusūdana, the protector of the worlds.

Then, having understood that this Mahākālī had been produced by the son of the King of Kāśī after propitiating the bull-bannered Lord Śiva for the sake of a great task, the Wielder of the Discus [Viṣṇu] acted accordingly.
Having performed this fierce deed, which was like a mass of flaming fire,
he cast off his discus as if in play, while still intent on gambling with the dice.
Then the Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu swiftly pursued that Kṛtyā, who was exceedingly terrifying due to her emission of flames matted together like a garland of fire.
Then the Kṛtyā of Maheśvara, scorched by the heat of the discus, perished;
and Veginī also followed after her with great speed.
O best of sages, her power having been thwarted by the discus of Viṣṇu, Kṛtyā entered Vārāṇasī itself with great haste.
Then the vast army of Kāśī, as well as the force of the Pramathas,
equipped with all kinds of weapons and missiles, advanced toward the Discus.

Having by his own splendor consumed that army, which was skilled in discharging weapons and missiles, he then reduced the entire city of Vārāṇasī to ashes, including its magical spells and its inhabitants.
But that city, with its mountains, servants, and citizens, along with its horses, elephants, and men,
and including all its cow-pens and treasuries, was difficult to behold even for the gods.
That discus of Hari, with its flames encircling the entire city— including the houses, walls,
and crossroads— consumed that whole city.
With its fury unabated and exceedingly fierce, longing for both the goal to be accomplished and the means to achieve it,
that discus of Viṣṇu, flashing with radiant light, came toward his hand.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Maitreya said: "I desire once again to hear further concerning the wise Balabhadra."
O Brahmin, you ought to relate to me that prowess so that I may hear it.
"O Blessed One, I have heard of such deeds as the dragging of the Yamunā;
O illustrious one, let that which Balarāma performed otherwise be told."
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, hear now the deed which was performed by Rāma,
who is the infinite and immeasurable Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
The hero Sāmba, son of Jāmbavatī, forcibly took the daughter of Suyodhana, who had prepared for her svayaṃvara.
Then Karṇa, Duryodhana, and others, as well as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and their followers— possessing great heroism and filled with rage— bound him after he had been defeated in battle.
Having heard that, O Maitreya, all the Yādavas directed their anger toward Duryodhana and the others, and Kṛṣṇa made a great effort to slay them.
Having restrained them, Balarāma spoke with words faltering from intoxication:
"They shall release you at my word; for I alone shall go to the Kauravas."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then Baladeva, having beheld the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura),
remained in the midst of its outer gardens and did not enter that city.
Perceiving that strength had returned to him, King Duryodhana and the others presented Rāma with a cow, water for honor, and water for refreshment.
Having duly received everything, he then said to those Kauravas:
"Ugrasena commands you: release Sāmba immediately!"
Then, O best of the twice-born, having heard those words, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the other kings, as well as Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the rest, were greatly agitated.
And all the Kauravas, led by Bāhlīka, spoke in anger,
O wielder of the mace, upon seeing that the lineage of Yadu was unworthy of sovereignty.
"O sir! What is this speech uttered by you, O Balabhadra?
Which Yādava shall issue commands to those born of the Kuru lineage?"
If Ugrasena also gives his consent to the Kauravas,
then enough with these white umbrellas, those mockeries fit only for kings.
Therefore, go or do not go, O Bala; we shall release Sāmba despite his unjust conduct, by the command of you and Ugrasena.
"The prostration that was performed by the Kukuras and Andhakas toward us, who are worthy of honor—that indeed has not been performed; what is this command from a servant to a master?"
"You have been elevated to pride by being granted equal seats and food;
what fault is there in your conduct that your duty was not observed with affection?"
"This honor which we have presented to you, O Balarāma, is out of affection;
it is not something appropriate for your family from our own family."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, the Kurus, having firmly resolved, "We shall not release the son of Hari along with Sāmba," quickly entered the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Reeling with anger born from that insult,
Halāyudha rose up and struck the earth with his heel.
Then, by the strike of his heel, the earth was rent asunder;
he then slapped his arms, filling the quarters with the sound.
And he spoke, his eyes exceedingly copper-red and his face contorted with a frown.
Ah, this is the arrogance born of pride belonging to these wicked and worthless Kauravas; they truly believe that their sovereignty over the earth was produced by Time,
such that even today they disregard the command of Ugrasena.
Ugrasena occupies the throne of Sudharmā, not the lord of Śacī;
fie upon these kings whose satisfaction lies in a royal seat that is but the leavings of a hundred men!
The womenfolk of that king wear clusters of blossoms from the *pārijāta* tree; yet even he is not the sovereign of these [servants].
"Let Ugrasena remain as the lord of all kings;
today, having made the earth devoid of Kauravas, I shall go to his city."
Today [he will slay] Karṇa, Duryodhana, Droṇa, Bhīṣma along with Bāhlika,
Duḥśāsana and the others, as well as Bhūri and Bhūriśravas.
Having slain Somadatta and Śala, as well as Bhīma, Arjuna, Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, and other Kauravas, along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
Then, taking that hero Sāmba along with his wife,
I shall go to the city of Dvārakā and see Ugrasena and my other kinsmen.
Or else, together with all the Kurus, I shall quickly cast the city named after the elephant— the abode of the Kauravas— into the Bhāgīrathī.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having spoken thus, the wielder of the mace, his eyes reddened with intoxication, dragged his plow toward the base of the ramparts and walls of the fortress, drawing it downward.
Then, seeing that city of Hastināpura suddenly reeling, all the Kauravas, their hearts agitated, were thrown into turmoil.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, may you forgive me, may you forgive me! Let your anger be withdrawn; be gracious, O wielder of the mace.
This Sāmba, together with his wife, has been forcibly expelled by you from those who do not recognize his power, who are trembling with fear, and who have committed no offense.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then, O bull among sages, having quickly departed from their own city, the Kauravas brought forth Sāmba together with his wife.
To Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others who were bowing and speaking pleasant words, Bala, the best among the powerful, said: "I have already forgiven you."
Even today, O twice-born one, that city is seen to have a reeling appearance;
this is the power of Rāma, characterized by his strength and heroism.
Then the Kauravas, having honored Sāmba along with Bali,
sent them forth accompanied by their wife and the wealth received for the wedding.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"O Maitreya, this is the power of that powerful Bala."
Whatever else was accomplished by him, that too should be heard from you.
Dvivida, the bull among monkeys and possessed of great heroism, became the friend of Naraka, the lord of the asuras who opposes the side of the gods.
Urged by the king of the gods, the powerful Kṛṣṇa slew Naraka and established a persistent enmity toward the gods.
Therefore, I shall perform this counter-action against all the gods,
bringing about the destruction of the sacrifice as well as the ruin of the mortal world.
Then, deluded by ignorance, he destroyed sacrifices;
he violated the boundaries of the virtuous and brought about the ruin of embodied beings.
He burned the sacrificial grounds, the regions, and the interiors of cities and villages;
and in some places, by hurling mountains, he completely pulverized the villages and other settlements.
Having uprooted mountains, he likewise cast them into the waters of the ocean;
then, standing in the midst of the sea, he agitated the ocean once more.
O twice-born one, agitated by him, the ocean overflows its shores with great velocity,
submerging the villages, cities, and other settlements situated on its banks.
Assuming various forms and a massive body, the monkey completely crushes the crops by rolling, wandering, and trampling them.
O Maitreya, this entire world was oppressed by that evil-souled one; it became devoid of Vedic study and sacrificial exclamations, and was deeply afflicted with suffering.
Once, in the Ārāvatya grove, Halāyudha drank wine,
as did the highly fortunate Revatī and other excellent women.
Being celebrated in song and situated in the midst of a circle of radiant women,
the best of the Yadu clan took his pleasure like Kubera in the Nandana grove.
Then that monkey, having approached and seized the plow and the pestle of Balarāma, mocked him by brandishing them before his face.
In the same manner, the monkey laughed in the faces of those women;
and then, striking them, he threw at them drinking vessels filled with wine and water-jars.
Then the wielder of the plow, his soul overcome with anger, rebuked him;
yet even so, disregarding him, he made a "kila-kila" sound.
Then, smiling, Balarāma seized his club in anger;
that best of monkeys also seized a formidable mountain crag.
And he, the best of the Yādavas, shattered that [missile] into a thousand pieces with his mace as it was hurled; it fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then that monkey, leaping over the pestle,
came with great speed and struck him on the chest with his hand in a fit of rage.
Then, struck on the head with a fist by Bala out of anger,
Dvivida fell down, vomiting blood, his life exhausted.
O Maitreya, as that body fell, the mountain peak shattered into a hundred pieces, like when it is split by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the vajra.
Then the gods showered a rain of flowers upon Rāma; approaching him, they praised him, saying, "Excellent! This great deed you have performed is well done."
O Hero, by this wicked monkey who aided the faction of the Daityas, the world was cast into ruin; fortunately, he has now met his destruction.
Having spoken thus, the gods, together with the Guhyakas, departed for heaven, filled with joy.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Such were the many and immeasurable deeds of the wise Baladeva, the protector of the earth who remains in his entirety.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus did Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva as his assistant, carry out the slaughter of the Daityas.
In the same way, he brought about the destruction of wicked kings for the sake of the world.
And the Lord, the omnipresent one, accompanied by Phalguna, caused the burden of the earth to be removed by the slaughter of an entire akṣauhiṇī.
Having relieved the earth of its burden and slain all the kings,
he brought about the destruction of his own lineage under the pretext of a curse from the Brahmins.
O Sage, having abandoned Dvārakā and relinquished his human form, Kṛṣṇa, together with his portions, entered his own abode consisting of Viṣṇu.
Maitreya said:
How did he destroy his own lineage under the pretext of a brahmin’s curse,
and how did Janārdana cast off his human body?
Śrī Parāśara said: Viśvāmitra, Kaṇva, and the great sage Nārada were seen by the young princes of the Yadu lineage at the great sacred site of Piṇḍāraka.
Then, intoxicated by youth and impelled by their future destiny,
they dressed Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, like a woman.
Bowing down before those sages with prostrations, they spoke humbly:
"This woman truly desires a son; tell us, what will she give birth to?"
Śrī Parāśara said: Those sages, endowed with divine knowledge, being thus deceived by the boys, became enraged and declared, "She shall give birth to a pestle."
It was the cause for the destruction of all the Yādavas and was unsurpassed in the world; by it, the extermination of the entire lineage of the Yādavas shall come to pass.
Thus addressed, those princes related the matter exactly as it had happened:
how the club was born from the belly of Sāmba for Ugrasena.
Ugrasena had that club ground into powder;
that powdered dust of the club was then thrown by them into the great ocean.
Then, from the iron club that had been shattered by the Yādavas,
there remained a fragment of the pulverized remnant which was shaped like a lance.
That too was thrown into the ocean and swallowed by a fish caught in a net;
when the fish was killed, a hunter extracted it from the belly, and the courtesans seized it.
Although the Blessed One Madhusūdana understood the ultimate truth,
he did not wish to alter that which had been ordained by destiny.
And Vāyu, dispatched by the gods, having prostrated himself, said to Keśava:
"O Blessed One, I have been sent as a messenger by the deities with this message."
Together with the Vasus, Aśvins, Maruts, Ādityas, Rudras, Sādhyas, and others, Śakra makes this request of you; O All-pervading Lord, let this be heard.
For the sake of relieving the burden of the earth, the Blessed One descended here more than a hundred years ago, impelled by the gods of the thirty-three.
The wicked Daityas have been slain and the burden of the earth has been removed by you;
let the gods, having you as their protector, dwell forever in heaven.
O Lord of the World, more than a hundred years have passed since then;
now, if it pleases you, please proceed to heaven.
"O Lord, it is being requested by the gods that your pleasure remains right here;
therefore, please stay for as long as is appropriate, for dependents must remain at their master's disposal."
The Blessed One said: "O messenger, everything that you have spoken, I too know;
indeed, the destruction of the Yādavas has already been set in motion by me."
"Since this burden of the earth has not yet been removed by the Yādavas,
I shall quickly discharge it within seven nights."
Just as I took [the earth] from the ocean and gave it to the land of Dvārakā,
so shall I withdraw the Yādavas and go to the abode of the gods.
Having cast off this human body, I am to be regarded by the Lord of the Gods and likewise by the immortals as one who has already attained Saṃkarṣaṇa, being without companion.
Jarāsaṃdha and others, who were the causes of the earth's burden and have been slain,
do not diminish the weight of the earth even by a hair’s breadth compared to this prince of the Yadus.
Therefore, having relieved this very great burden of the earth, I shall go for the protection of the world of the immortals; speak to them thus.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, O Maitreya, the messenger of the gods bowed to him and departed for the presence of the king of the gods by means of his divine gait.
Then the Blessed One also beheld, day and night, portents arising from the heavens, the earth, and the intermediate space, foreboding the destruction of the city of Dvārakā.
Seeing them, he said to the Yādavas: "Behold these most terrible great portents! Let us go to Prabhāsa without delay for their pacification."
Śrī Parāśara said: When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, Uddhava, the eminent scion of the Yādavas and a great devotee of the Lord, bowed down and addressed Hari.
"O Blessed One, command now what must be done by me;
I believe that the Blessed One intends to annihilate this entire lineage."
O Acyuta, I perceive the omens that portend the destruction of this lineage.
The Blessed One said:
"Go by means of a divine gait arising from my grace to the meritorious Badarī-āśrama on Mount Gandhamādana."
That sacred place on the surface of the earth is the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
"Fixing your mind on me, you shall attain perfection there through my grace;
for I shall go to heaven, having withdrawn this entire family."
And the ocean shall submerge Dvārakā once it has been abandoned by me;
however, out of fear of me, it shall leave my single palace within that body of water.
There I shall remain present, desiring the welfare of my devotees.
Śrī Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, and being encouraged by Keśava, he prostrated before him and quickly went to the hermitage for penance, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, O twice-born one, all those Yādavas, having mounted swift-moving chariots, set out for Prabhāsa together with Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the others.
Having arrived at Prabhāsa, the Kukuras, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis,
urged by Vāsudeva, indulged there in a great drinking bout.
And as they were drinking there, through their mutual rivalry,
the fire of quarrel— fueled by insults— was kindled, bringing about their destruction.
Maitreya said:
O best of the twice-born, you ought to explain to me what caused the quarrel or the rivalry among them as they were each enjoying their own respective shares.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"Your food is delicious, mine is not," so they argued;
from that dispute over whether it was delicious or not, a quarrel born of rivalry arose.
Then, having approached one another with eyes bloodshot with rage,
they struck each other with weapons, driven by the power of fate.
And their weapons exhausted, they seized the nearby mountain, Aitaka.
Indeed, when the *erakā* grass was grasped, it appeared as if it were a thunderbolt;
with it, they struck one another in that most terrible combat.
O twice-born one, Cāruvarman, Cāruka, and likewise Akrūra and the others,
struck one another with vajras in the form of eraka grass.
Hari tried to restrain those Yādavas, and they [tried to restrain] Keśava;
thinking that their enemy had arrived as an ally, they struck one another down.
Kṛṣṇa, also enraged, took up a handful of erakā grass for their destruction;
that handful then became an iron mace.
With that [weapon], he struck down all the Ādavas who were attacking him without exception;
likewise, others also rushed forward suddenly and slew one another.
Then, O twice-born one, that victorious chariot of the wielder of the discus, drawn by horses, proceeded through the midst of the ocean while Dāruka looked on.
Having circumambulated Hari clockwise— the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the quivers, the conch, and the sword— they departed by the path of the sun.
In an instant, O great sage, there was no one among the Yādavas who had not been slain,
with the exception of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa and Dāruka.
As the two of them were walking about, they saw Rāma seated at the foot of a tree,
and a great serpent emerging from his mouth.
Having emerged from that sacrifice, the serpent of great fortune departed for the ocean,
being honored by the Siddhas as well as by the Uragas.
Then, taking the water-offering (arghya), the Ocean went forward to meet him;
thereafter, honored by the best of the serpents, he entered the waters.
Having seen Bala’s departure, Keśava said to Dāruka:
"Relate all of this to Vasudeva and Ugrasena."
Having witnessed the departure of Balabhadra and likewise the destruction of the Yādavas,
I too, remaining in yoga, shall cast off this body.
And all the people residing in Dvārakā, as well as Āhuka, must be told:
"The ocean will submerge this entire city."
Therefore, all of you must await the arrival of Arjuna;
once the Pāṇḍava has departed from there, you must not remain within Dvārakā.
One must go along with him alone, wherever that Kaurava goes.
And having gone there, speak these words of mine to Arjuna, the son of Kuntī:
"This person, who is under my protection, must be guarded by you to the best of your ability."
Accompanied by Arjuna, you shall likewise take the people from Dvāravatī;
and Vajra shall become the king of the Yadus.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Dāruka prostrated himself before Kṛṣṇa again and again,
and after circumambulating him many times, he departed as instructed.
Having gone there, he reported that matter to Arjuna in Dvārakā;
then the one of great intelligence brought Vajra and likewise installed him as king.

The Blessed One Govinda also, O highly fortunate one, having merged the supreme Vāsudeva-self into the Brahman within his own self, maintained it within all beings; having yoked his self to the Self in that which is free from conceptual proliferation.
And the Supreme Person lay there, sporting in the state of the Fourth (turya).
Honoring the words that Durvāsas had spoken to the twice-born,
O best of men, he became absorbed in yoga, placing his foot upon his knee.
Then that hunter named Jarā arrived there,
carrying a tomara-spear fixed upon a single iron arrow that remained from a broken club.
O best of the twice-born, standing at a distance, he beheld that foot in the form of a deer and pierced its sole with that very same lance.
Then, he saw there a man possessing four arms;
having prostrated before him, he said to him again and again, "Be gracious!"
"This was done by me unknowingly, under the suspicion that it was a deer;
may you forgive me, for you ought to protect me who am consumed by my own sin."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Let there not be even the slightest fear for you;
go, O hunter, to heaven, the abode of the gods, by my grace."
Śrī Parāśara said: Immediately upon those words, a celestial chariot arrived;
having ascended it by her grace, the hunter departed for heaven.

When he had departed, the Blessed One, having united himself with the Self— that immutable, inconceivable, stainless state consisting of Vāsudeva which is identical with Brahman— remained absorbed therein.
In Viṣṇu— the unborn, the immortal, the immeasurable, and the self of all—
he abandoned his human body, having transcended the threefold path of existence.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Arjuna, having then beheld the bodies of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa...
He caused the consecration ceremony to be performed for him, and likewise for the others in due order.
The eight principal queens, headed by Rukmiṇī, who have been described,
embraced the body of Hari and entered the fire.
And Revatī also, the most excellent woman, having embraced the body of Rāma,
entered the blazing fire, which was cooled by the joy of union with him.
Having heard that, Ugrasena as well as Ānakadundubhi,
Devakī, and Rohiṇī entered the fire.
Then Arjuna, having performed the funeral rites for them according to the prescribed rules,
emerged taking all the people and Vajra himself.
The thousands of wives of Kṛṣṇa departed from Dvāravatī;
the son of Kuntī proceeded slowly, protecting both the Vajras and the people.
O Maitreya, when the world of mortals had been abandoned by Kṛṣṇa, the Sudharmā assembly hall and the Pārijāta tree ascended to heaven.
On the very day that Hari departed for heaven, abandoning the earth,
this powerful Kali, whose body is Time itself, descended.
The great ocean flooded that empty Dvārakā,
yet the sea did not flood the single dwelling of Vāsudeva.
O Brahmin, even today the great ocean is not able to overstep its bounds,
because the Blessed Lord Keśava is eternally present there.
That place is exceedingly meritorious and the destroyer of all sins;
by beholding that abode endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from leprosy.
O best of sages, Pārtha made his dwelling in the land of Pañcanada, which was richly endowed with grain and wealth, for the sake of all people.
Then greed arose because of that single archer, Pārtha,
upon seeing the women being led away, their protectors having been slain by the bandits.
Then those Ābhīras, evil-doers whose minds were carried away by greed and who were exceedingly arrogant, gathered together and took counsel.
"This lone archer Arjuna, bypassing us, leads away these women whose lords have been slain; fie on this strength of yours! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.38.15)
Having slain Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the others, he became filled with pride; yet he did not recognize the strength of those who dwell in the villages.
Seeing us with staves in our hands, that evil-minded one, bow in hand, disregards us all, saying: "What use have you for these uplifted arms?"
Then, seizing their staffs as weapons, thousands of robbers carrying clods of earth rushed toward that multitude whose lord had been slain.
Then, having rebuked them, the son of Kuntī spoke to the Ābhīras as if laughing:
"Turn back, O you who are ignorant of dharma, unless you are desirous of death!"
Disregarding his words, O Maitreya, they then seized that wealth, as well as the women's property and the possessions of Viṣvaksena.
Then the heroic Arjuna began to string the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, which is undecaying in battle, but he was unable to do so.
He managed with great difficulty to string it, but it became slack again;
then the Pāṇḍava, though reflecting upon them, could not recall his celestial weapons.
And the son of Pṛthā, provoked to anger, released arrows at these enemies;
those shafts discharged by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow merely pierced their skin.
Even those inexhaustible arrows given by Agni came to an end as Arjuna fought with the cowherds at the time of Bhava’s destruction.
And Kuntī’s son thought: "Indeed, that strength belongs to Kṛṣṇa alone, by which all the mountains were struck down by me with volleys of arrows."
While the son of Pāṇḍu looked on, those excellent women were dragged away by the Ābhīras,
while others fled at will.
Then, O Sage, when his arrows were exhausted, Dhanañjaya struck the bandits with the tip of his bow; but they laughed at his blows.
O best of sages, while Pārtha was looking on, all those Mlecchas departed, taking with them the excellent women of the Puṇḍrakas and Andhakas.
Then Jiṣṇu, deeply distressed, crying out "Alas! Alas!
and saying, "O, I have been robbed by this venerable one," wept indeed.
That bow, those weapons, that chariot, and those horses—
all were destroyed in an instant, like a gift given to one who is not learned in the Vedas.
Oh, how powerful is destiny without that Great-Souled One,
since it bestows victory even upon the lowly who are devoid of capability!
Those two arms, that fist, that position, and I myself am Arjuna;
yet, without that merit alone, everything has become utterly worthless.
"Arjuna's status as Arjuna and Bhīma's status as Bhīma are certainly due to him;
for when he was absent, I, the best of chariot-warriors, was defeated by cowards."
Śrī Parāśara said: Speaking thus, Jiṣṇu went to Indraprastha, the most excellent of cities; there he installed Vajra, the delight of the Yādavas, as king.
Then Phālguna saw Vyāsa dwelling in the forest;
approaching that illustrious one, he saluted him with humility.
Beholding him bowing at his feet for a long time, the Sage, appearing dejected, spoke these words: "Why are you such as this today?"
"Have you followed a woman who has no hero [to protect her], or have you committed the murder of a Brahmin?
For you are now shorn of your luster, as if pained by the crushing of a firm hope."
Or perhaps you have been rejected by those seeking alms for their families and the like,
or else you have taken pleasure in women who should not be approached, whereby you have become shorn of your luster.
Or perhaps you alone eat choice food without giving anything to the Brahmins;
"O Arjuna, have you perhaps come within the range of Śūrpa’s breath, or have you been struck by his evil eye? Otherwise, how could you be so devoid of splendor?"
Have you been touched by water from [another's] nails, or even sprinkled with the water from a jar? Why are you so pale, or have you been defeated in battle by those inferior to you?
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then Pārtha, having sighed, said, "O Blessed One, let it be heard," and related his own defeat to Vyāsa exactly as it had happened.
Arjuna said: "Whatever strength, whatever splendor, whatever heroism, whatever prowess, whatever fortune, and whatever shadow we possessed— all that Hari has departed from us, leaving us behind."
O Sage, even by that great Lord, who addresses others with a smile,
we have been rendered as if made of straw, deprived of our dignity.
That Supreme Person, who was the very embodiment of the essence of my missiles, arrows, and the Gāṇḍīva bow, has departed.
That Govinda, by whose very glance prosperity, victory, wealth, and advancement never left us— that Blessed One has departed, leaving us behind.
He by whose power Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the King of Aṅga, and others, as well as Duryodhana and his followers, were utterly consumed— that Kṛṣṇa has now abandoned the earth.
Deprived of youth and its splendor, the earth appears like a land that has lost its luster;
O Father, I do not shine at all in the absence of that wielder of the discus.
By whose power Bhīṣma and the others acted like moths in the fire that was I;
without that Kṛṣṇa, I have today been defeated by cowherds.
By whose power the Gāṇḍīva bow attained renown throughout the three worlds,
he was now surpassed by mere cowherd staffs in its absence.
O great sage, many thousands of women who had me as their protector were carried off by bandits armed with clubs, even as I was striving to prevent it.
O Kṛṣṇa, the women of Kṛṣṇa’s inner apartments, who were being led away by the Ābhīras,
were seized by them using staffs as weapons, having utterly disregarded my strength.
"It is no wonder that I am bereft of splendor; that I still live is the marvel. O Grandfather, I am shameless, marked by the mire of the insults of the lowly."
Vyāsa said:
Enough of this shame, O Pārtha; you ought not to grieve.
Know that such is the course of Time among all living beings.
Time leads to the existence and the non-existence of all beings, O Pāṇḍava.
Knowing that this world has time as its root, O Arjuna, be devoted to steadfastness.
The rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and the entire earth;
the gods, humans, animals, trees, and reptiles.
Created again and again by time, they shall once more go to their destruction;
knowing that all this is of the nature of time, attain tranquility.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotuses, is the very embodiment of Time;
O Dhanañjaya, that which you have spoken regarding the majesty of Kṛṣṇa is exactly so.
In former times, when he had descended to the earth for the purpose of relieving its burden,
the earth, oppressed by that burden, went to the assembly of the gods.
For that purpose, Janārdana has descended in the form of Time;
and that task having been accomplished, all the kings have been slain without exception.
The entire lineage of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas has likewise been destroyed by Pārtha;
O Lord, there remains nothing further for that master to do upon the surface of the earth.

Therefore, having accomplished his purpose, that Blessed One, the God of gods, has departed as he desired; he performs creation during the period of emanation, sustenance during the period of maintenance, and is capable of bringing about the end during the period of dissolution, just as he has now departed.
Therefore, O King, you should not feel distress over your defeat, since the fortunes of men rise and fall according to the times; this is why there is praise [for you].
O Arjuna, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the others were slain by you alone in battle;
was their defeat at the hands of Time not greater than that?
Just as their defeat was brought about by the power of that Viṣṇu,
so too has this defeat of yours been wrought by the bandits.
That Lord of the Gods, the Master of the World, having entered into bodies, maintains the stability of the world and brings about the destruction of all beings at the end.
O son of Kuntī, Janārdana was your ally at the time of your rise;
likewise, at the end, those who were your adversaries were destroyed by Keśava.
Who would believe that you could slay the Kauravas along with Bhīṣma?
And who would believe in your defeat at the hands of the Ābhīras?
O Pārtha, all this is the playful conduct of Hari, the soul of all beings,
that you have destroyed the Kauravas and that you were defeated by the Ābhīras.
"O Arjuna, I shall relate to you exactly what has happened regarding those women whom you grieve for, and who were carried off by bandits."
In former times, O Pārtha, the brahmin Aṣṭāvakra was devoted to living in the water for many series of years, chanting the eternal Brahman.
When the hosts of asuras had been defeated, a great festival took place on the summit of Mount Meru;
while traveling there, the celestial women beheld it.
Then Rambhā, Tilottamā, and others by the hundreds and thousands praised and extolled that great-souled one, O Pāṇḍava.
Bowing low with humility and intent upon hymns of praise, they prostrated before the sage, who was submerged up to his neck in water and bearing a heavy mass of matted locks.
O best of the Kauravas, as each of them became more and more filled with faith, they praised him— the most excellent among the twice-born— in that same manner.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O highly fortunate ladies, I am pleased with you; whatever is desired from me, ask for it all—I shall grant it, even if it be exceedingly difficult to obtain."
O twice-born one, Rambhā, Tilottamā, and the other celestial nymphs (apsarases) mentioned in the Vedas said to him: "If you are pleased with us, what is insufficient for us? (ViP 5.38.77).
The others, however, said: "O Brahmin, if the Blessed One is pleased, then we wish to obtain Puruṣottama as our husband, O best of Brahmins."
Vyāsa said:
Having said, "So shall it be," the sage emerged from the water;
and they beheld him, having emerged, deformed and with eight mouths.
O descendant of Kuru, seeing them concealing themselves, the sage became enraged and cursed those whose laughter had become manifest.
"Since you have treated me with contempt and derision because you consider my form to be deformed,
therefore I pronounce this curse upon you."
"Having obtained Puruṣottama as your husband through my grace,
you shall all, however, fall victim to the curse of my [son] and come into the hands of bandits."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this spoken, the sage was propitiated by them and spoke again:
"Indeed, you shall go once more to the world of the Lord of the Gods."
Thus, by the curse of that sage Aṣṭāvakra,
those celestial nymphs, having obtained the wielder of the discus as their husband, fell into the hands of bandits.
O Pāṇḍava, not even the slightest grief should be felt here regarding the truth;
for all that has been withdrawn by Him alone, the Lord of All.
And because your own withdrawal was imminent, O Pāṇḍava,
he accordingly withdrew his strength, splendor, heroism, and majesty.
For one who is born, death is certain; likewise, there is a fall following elevation. There is separation from what is united, and depletion following accumulation.
Having understood this, the wise do not succumb to grief or joy;
others, however, emulate their conduct and become like them.
Therefore, O best of men, having understood this together with your brothers,
you must abandon the entire system of governance and go to the forest for asceticism.
Therefore, go and report these words of mine to the King of Dharma,
and act in such a way that you may depart with your brothers on the day after tomorrow.
Having been addressed thus, Arjuna approached the two sons of Pṛthā and the twins,
and related everything exactly as it had been seen and experienced.
Having heard those words of Vyāsa spoken from the mouth of Arjuna,
and having installed Parīkṣit on the throne, all the sons of Pāṇḍu departed for the forest.
Thus, O Maitreya, I have related to you in detail these deeds of Vāsudeva, who was born in the lineage of Yadu.
And whoever shall constantly hear this life-story of that Kṛṣṇa,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus concludes the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as the Viṣṇucittīya-Ātmaprakāśa and the Śrīdharīya.
Now begins the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa, accompanied by the two commentaries known as the Viṣṇucittīya-Ātmaprakāśa and the Śrīdharīya.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Maitreya said:
You have explained the creation, the lineages, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the maintenance of the world.
And the history of the dynasties as well, in detail, O great sage.
O great sage, I wish to hear from you exactly how the withdrawal [of the world] occurs,
as well as that which is known as the great dissolution at the end of a kalpa.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, listen from me to how the withdrawal [of the world] occurs exactly as it is,
and how dissolution arises both at the end of a kalpa and at the time of primordial nature (prakṛti).
A day and night of the ancestors is a month; a year of the inhabitants of heaven is a day and night of the ancestors.
But four thousand such cycles of the four ages, O best of the twice-born, constitute a single day of Brahmā.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga);
it is said that these consist of twelve thousand divine years.
O Maitreya, all the cycles of four ages are identical in their essential nature, with the exception of the first Kṛta-yuga and the final Kali-yuga.
Just as the creation was performed by Brahmā in the first Kṛta age,
so too is the dissolution performed at the end in the Kali age.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, you ought to describe in detail the true nature of Kali,
in which the four-footed Lord Dharma undergoes dissolution.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Maitreya, O great sage, listen briefly to that nature of Kali about which you wish to hear, and how it prevails.
In the Kali age, the conduct of men does not follow the observances of the castes and stages of life;
nor is it motivated by the performance of the duties prescribed in the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas.
In the Kali age, marriages are not righteous, nor is the relationship between disciple and teacher established;
there is no proper conduct for husband and wife, nor indeed the ritual sequence centered on the deity Agni.
In the Kali age, whoever is born into any family whatsoever, if he is powerful and the lord of all,
is fit to take a bride from among all the social classes.
O Maitreya, by whatever means a twice-born man is initiated in the Kali age,
that very same act constitutes the rite of atonement in the Kali age.
O twice-born one, in the Kali age every scripture belongs to whoever practices it;
in the Kali age, every deity is valid, and everyone may belong to any stage of life.
In the Kali age, fasting, physical exertion, the distribution of wealth,
and austerity constitute dharma when they are practiced according to one's own inclination.
In the Kali age, men will become intoxicated with pride by even a small amount of wealth,
and women likewise will become intoxicated with pride by their hair alone.
When gold, gems, jewels, and even clothing have fallen into decay,
women in the Kali age will then be adorned only by their hair.
In the Kali age, women will likewise abandon a husband who is destitute of wealth;
indeed, for women, the husband will be one who possesses wealth alone.
He who indeed gives abundantly of his own is always the master of men;
the basis of mastership is relationship, and not likewise mere lineage.
In the Kali age, accumulations of wealth will end with the household, the intellect will likewise end with material objects, and all things will end with being for one's own personal enjoyment.
In the Kali age, women will become wanton and full of longing for pleasure;
men will be covetous for wealth acquired through unjust means.
Even when entreated by a friend, one looks only to one's own interest;
they will likewise desire even half of half a penny’s worth of debt.
In the Kali age, O Brahmin, the minds of men on earth will indeed be equal in their human nature;
likewise, there will be a respect toward cows associated with the giving of milk.
At that time, all people, mostly beset by the fear of drought and distressed by the fear of hunger,
will have their eyes fixed upon the sky.
Like ascetics subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits,
men will bring about their own destruction, afflicted by the sufferings of drought and other calamities.
In the Kali age, men lacking self-mastery will constantly encounter famine as well as affliction; deprived of happiness and joy, they shall suffer.

When the Kali age has arrived, people will not bathe before eating, nor will they perform worship of the fire-god, the deities, or guests, nor will they perform the rites of offering funeral cakes and water.
In the Kali age, women will be greedy, small-statured, intent on eating large quantities of food, prolific, and possessed of little fortune.
Scratching their heads with both hands, women will disregard and even revile the commands of their elders and husbands.
In the Kali age, women will be devoted solely to nourishing themselves, petty-minded, devoid of bodily refinement, and speakers of harsh and untruthful words.
Women of noble family will become immoral and of evil conduct, constantly harboring a longing for men of wicked character.
Boys who have not yet undertaken their vows will take up the Vedas;
householders will neither offer oblations nor give even what is appropriate.
Forest-dwellers will take up the consumption of village food,
and even monks will be bound by the constraints of affection for friends and others.
When the Kali age has arrived, kings will not be protectors but plunderers under the pretext of taxes, seizing the wealth of the people.
In the Kali age, whoever possesses horses, chariots, and elephants shall become a king; and whoever is weak shall be a servant.
The Vaiśyas, having abandoned their own duties such as agriculture and trade,
will proceed to live by the occupation of Śūdras, subsisting on the work of artisans.
Devoted to the vow of begging for alms, these base Śūdras, wearing the outward marks of renunciation,
will be honored as they resort to the livelihood of heretics.
Greatly oppressed by famine and the burden of taxes,
the distressed people will flee to regions abundant in wheat and barley.
When the path of the Vedas has vanished and people are filled with heresy,
the lifespan of the world will become short due to the increase of unrighteousness.
While men perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures,
death shall occur in childhood due to the fault of the king.
In the Kali age, the birth of women will occur at five, six, or seven years of age;
likewise for men, it will occur at nine, eight, or ten years of age.
And likewise, there will be the appearance of gray hair at twelve years of age;
indeed, in the Kali age, no one lives beyond twenty years.
In the Kali age, men will possess little wisdom, wear external marks in vain, and have corrupt inner natures;
therefore, they shall perish in a short time.
For whenever, Maitreya, a decline of the Dharma is observed,
at that very time an increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
For whenever an increase in wickedness is observed, O Maitreya,
at those very times an increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the great-souled ones.
Whenever there is a decline among the virtuous who follow the path of world-weariness,
at those very times the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.
O Maitreya, when the undertakings of men who uphold dharma come to naught, then the preeminence of the Kali age should be inferred by the wise.
When Puruṣottama, the Lord of sacrifices and the heir of all,
is no longer worshipped by men with sacrifices, then the power of the Kali age should be recognized.
When there is no delight in the declarations of the Vedas and a fondness for heretics,
then the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by wise and discerning men.
In the Kali age, O Maitreya, people afflicted by heresy will no longer worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, the creator of all, and the Supreme Sovereign.
"What is the use of gods? What is the use of twice-born brahmins or the Vedas? What is the use of ritual purity or the lotus-born Brahmā?"—thus will people, afflicted by heresy, speak.
O Brahmin, when the Kali age has arrived, the rain-cloud pours down only a little water, the crops likewise yield little fruit, and even that fruit is of little substance.
In the Kali age, garments will consist mostly of hemp, trees will consist mostly of the *śamī*, and likewise, the social classes (*varṇa*) will consist mostly of *śūdras*.
When the Kali age has arrived, grains will consist mostly of minute seeds, milk will consist mostly of clarified butter, and the only ointment will be that made from uśīra root.

O best of sages, in the Kali age, the elders of men will consist mostly of mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law; likewise, brothers-in-law and others will seize their wives, while kinsmen will become mere friends in name.
"Whose mother is he, whose father is he? For man follows according to his own karma"—thus will men say, following the example of their fathers-in-law.
Overcome again and again by the faults of speech, mind, and body,
men of little intelligence will commit sins day after day.
Whatever brings suffering to men who are devoid of virtue, impure, and shameless— all that will come to pass in the Kali age.
When the Vedic recitation and the *vaṣaṭ* call have ceased, and when the offerings of *svadhā* and *svāhā* are abandoned,
then Dharma will dwell only sparsely in some parts of the world.
In that [Kṛta Yuga], one performs an unsurpassed mass of merit with very little effort; for it is achieved there through austerity alone.
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Regarding this very subject, the highly intelligent Vyāsa spoke as follows.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate ones, as I speak it according to the truth.
At what time does even a small dharma yield a very great fruit? When did the praise of merit arise among the sages, and by whom was it easily practiced?
O Maitreya, those foremost of sages went to the great sage Vedavyāsa in order to resolve their doubts and to ask him about their uncertainty.
O twice-born one, they saw there in the waters of the Jāhnavī my son, the highly fortunate Veda-vyāsa, the sage who had half-completed his bath.
Waiting for the conclusion of his bath, those great seers remained on the bank of the great river, taking refuge in a grove of trees.

Then, rising from the waters of the Gaṅgā, my son said, "The Śūdra is virtuous; Kali is virtuous," while those sages were listening to these words; and having spoken thus, he again submerged himself in the river water.
And rising up, he said, "Excellent, excellent! O Śūdra, you are blessed."
Having submerged himself and then emerged, the great sage spoke again: "Excellent! Blessed are those women; compared to them, I am more blessed."
Then, having bathed according to the rule and performed the ritual acts, those sages approached my illustrious son who had sipped water for purification.
When they had performed their salutations and taken their seats,
the son of Satyavatī asked them, "For what purpose have you come?"
Śrī Parāśara said:
"We have come to you to ask about a doubt;
let that suffice for now. Please tell us something else."
When the Lord said, "Kali is virtuous," and when he said to the women, "The Śūdra is virtuous," he spoke repeatedly, "Excellent! Blessed! 6.2.12.
O Great Sage, if it is not a secret, we wish to hear all of that;
let what is in your heart be told, for we ask you about its purpose.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by the sages, Vyāsa smiled and then spoke these words:
"Listen, O best of sages, to that which was said [by you] as 'Excellent, excellent! (ViP 6.2.14).
Vyāsa said:
That which [is accomplished] in ten years during the Kṛta age is achieved in a single year during the Tretā;
that same [result] in the Dvāpara is attained in a month, and in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day and night.
"O twice-born ones, because a man obtains the fruit of austerity, celibacy, recitation, and so forth, it is said that Kali is virtuous. (ViP 6.2.16)
What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by performing sacrifices in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the name of Keśava.
In this Kali age, a person attains a supreme excellence of dharma with very little effort; O knowers of dharma, because of that, I am pleased with the Kali age.
First, the Vedas should be mastered by the twice-born who are devoted to the practice of vows;
thereafter, having attained righteousness, they should perform sacrifices with wealth according to the prescribed rules.
For the twice-born, idle talk, idle food, and idle sacrifice lead to their downfall;
therefore, they must always remain self-restrained.
O twice-born ones, there is a fault for them in performing anything improperly regarding all objects; even food, drink, and the like do not come to them by their own will.
Since they are indeed dependent upon others in all their undertakings,
those twice-born ones conquer their own worlds only with great hardship.
"By the mere service of the twice-born, this Śūdra becomes entitled to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices; he conquers his own worlds and is therefore more blessed than that [other]. (ViP 6.2.23)
O tigers among sages, because he has no restriction regarding what may or may not be eaten, nor regarding what may or may not be drunk, he is therefore called "Sādhu" (the Good).
Wealth always acquired by men without violating their own dharma should be bestowed upon worthy recipients and offered in sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
O best of the twice-born, there is great hardship in its acquisition and in its preservation;
likewise, through its improper application, the path of men is known to be profound and difficult to navigate.
In this same way, O best of the twice-born, men are likewise overcome by other afflictions and thus conquer their own worlds, beginning with those of Prajāpati, in due order.
O twice-born ones, by serving her husband through action, mind, and speech, and by being devoted to his welfare, a woman attains auspiciousness and, consequently, residence in the same world as him.
Just as a man [approaches] those same women without excessive effort,
so did I, by that third utterance, say "Excellent" to the woman.
"O Brahmins, I have told you this reason why I have come here.
Ask whatever you desire, and I shall explain it all clearly to you."
Then those sages said: "O great sage, that which was to be asked has been explained by you exactly as it is in this very question."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, laughing, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke to those ascetics who had approached him, their eyes wide with wonder.
"This question of yours has been understood by me through my divine eye; therefore, in connection with it, I have uttered to you, 'Excellent! Excellent! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.2.33)
For in the Kali age, dharma is indeed accomplished with very little effort by men who have washed away all their sins with the waters of their own virtues.
And by Śūdras, O best of the twice-born, through being intent on service to the twice-born;
likewise, by women, through service to their husbands alone and without weariness.
Therefore, I consider all three of these to be most blessed;
for the twice-born, there is hardship in the performance of dharma during the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
"O twice-born ones who know the Dharma, that which was intended by you has been told by me, even though unasked; what else should be done? ||| ViP_6.2.37 ||
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, having honored Vyāsa, they praised him again and again;
the twice-born ones, having reached their firm resolve through Vyāsa’s words, departed as they had come.
O illustrious one, this great secret has been told by me even to you:
that this is the sole great merit of the exceedingly wicked Kali age.
Furthermore, regarding that dissolution of the worlds which you asked me about—
both the elemental (prākṛta) and the intermediate (antarāla)— that too I shall now describe to you.
Thus ends the second chapter in the sixth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
For all beings indeed, there is a threefold dissolution.
Dissolution is likewise of three kinds: occasional, elemental, and absolute.
Among these, the *brāhma* dissolution occurs at the end of a kalpa;
the absolute dissolution is called liberation; and the *prākṛta* dissolution lasts for two parārdhas.
Maitreya said: O Blessed One, tell me the calculation of a parārdha, by which—
when doubled— it is to be understood as the dissolution of the primal nature (prākṛta-pratisaṃcara).
Śrī Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, from one place to the next, each successive position is ten times the previous;
thus, in the eighteenth place, the number is designated as a *parārdha*.
O twice-born one, that dissolution which lasts for twice a parārdha is the primary (prākṛta) dissolution;
at that time, the entire manifest universe indeed goes to dissolution within its own cause, the unmanifest.
That which is a human blink is the measure of a *mātrā* according to its duration;
fifteen of those constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* are known as a *kalā*.
In measure, that *nāḍikā* consists of fifteen *kalās*.
By measuring water, that [quantity] is thirteen and a half *palas*;
by the Māgadha measure, it is known as a *prastha* of water,
made with four gold *māṣas* [weighing] four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) and having a hole [of that size].
O best of the twice-born, two nāḍikās constitute one muhūrta;
thirty muhūrtas make up a day and night, and likewise, thirty days make up a month.
Twelve months constitute a day and night in heaven;
three hundred and sixty such years constitute a year for the enemies of the Asuras.
Twelve thousand such [cycles] are declared to be a Caturyuga;
a thousand Caturyugas, however, is said to be a single day of Brahmā.
O great sage, fourteen Manus exist there during that kalpa; and at its conclusion, O Maitreya, occurs the elemental dissolution of Brahmā.
O Maitreya, listen as I describe its exceedingly fierce nature; furthermore, I shall explain to you again the dissolution of the primary elements.
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, when the surface of the earth has almost entirely perished,
an exceedingly fierce drought occurs that lasts for a hundred years.
Then, O best of sages, those beings who possess little essence perish entirely from the constant trampling by earthly creatures.
Then the blessed and imperishable Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Rudra,
strives to bring about the destruction of all beings who abide within himself.
Then, O best of sages, the Blessed Viṣṇu, stationed within the seven rays of the sun, drinks up all waters without exception.
Having drunk all the waters, even those residing upon the earth and within living beings,
O Maitreya, he dries up the entire surface of the earth.
It dries up the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, and the springs,
and it brings to exhaustion all the water that exists within the netherworlds.
Then, by its power, those same seven rays, nourished by the intake of water, arise as seven suns.
Then, O twice-born one, those seven blazing suns, shining both below and above,
burn the entire triple world together with the subterranean realms.
O twice-born one, when the three worlds— including the expanse of mountains, rivers, and oceans— are being consumed by those blazing suns, they become devoid of moisture.
Then, O twice-born one, when the three worlds have been consumed along with their trees and waters,
this earth becomes in appearance like the back of a tortoise.
Then, having become that Rudra of the fire of time,
the all-consuming fire born from the breath of the serpent Śeṣa burns the netherworlds below.
Having burnt all the netherworlds, that great fire reached the earth and devours the entire surface of the world.
Then, that most terrible one, possessing great whirlpools of garlands of flames, revolves right there throughout the entire Bhuvarloka and Svarloka.
Then the entire three worlds shone like a frying pan,
surrounded by a whirling mass of flames, with all moving and stationary beings consumed.
Then, O great sage, those inhabitants of the two worlds who have fulfilled their duties, being overcome by the heat, go to Maharloka.
Therefore, from that world which is scorched by great heat,
those seekers of the highest state proceed further to Janaloka by means of tenfold repetition.
Then, O best of sages, Janārdana, assuming the form of Rudra after having burnt the entire world,
creates clouds born from the breath of his mouth.
Then, like herds of elephants, thundering and flashing with lightning,
the terrible Saṃvartaka clouds rise up in the sky.
Some were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled white water-lilies;
some clouds were smoke-colored, while others were yellow.
Some have the color of a donkey, others resemble lac-dye;
some are like beryl, and in some places they resemble sapphire.
Others resemble conch shells and jasmine flowers; others are like pure gold; some resemble indragopa insects, and others likewise resemble crystals.
Some indeed have the luster of red arsenic, others resemble yellow orpiment;
some, resembling the feathers of a blue jay, arise as massive clouds.
Some have the form of excellent cities, some resemble mountains;
others are like peaked pavilions, and some are dense masses resembling level ground.
With great roars and massive bodies, they fill the expanse of the sky;
raining down those great torrents, O Brahmin, they extinguish that most terrifying fire situated within the three worlds in its entirety.
And when the fire has perished, O best of sages, raining continuously day and night, they flood the entire world with waters.
Having flooded the entire earth with excessive torrents,
O twice-born one, they likewise flood the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) and the worlds above it.
When the world was enveloped in darkness and all things, both stationary and moving, had perished,
those great clouds rained down for more than a hundred years.
Thus, O best of sages, at the end of the kalpa,
everything perishes through the majesty of Vāsudeva, the eternal Supreme Self.
Thus ends the third chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O great sage, when the waters had risen so high that they reached the station of the seven ṛṣis, the Lord remained there.
Then this entire triple world becomes a single ocean.
Then, O Maitreya, the wind born from the breath of Viṣṇu’s mouth blows for another hundred years, destroying those clouds.
The Blessed One, who consists of all beings, is inconceivable and the creator of beings;
he is without beginning and the origin of the universe, having drunk up the wind entirely.
Then, in that single ocean,
the Lord Hari, the primordial creator, the Blessed One, assuming the form of Brahmā, lay upon the bed of Śeṣa.
He was praised by the Siddhas, such as Samaka and others, who had gone to Janaloka,
and was meditated upon by those seeking liberation who had gone to Brahmaloka.
Having entered into his divine yogic sleep, which consists of his own creative power (māyā),
Madhusūdana meditated upon himself under the name of Vāsudeva.
This, Maitreya, is the so-called "occasional" dissolution (pratisaṃcara);
for therein Hari, assuming the form of Brahmā, lies as the causal sign (nimitta).
When the Soul of All awakens, then this world moves;
when Acyuta has gone to the bed of Māyā, all this closes its eyes.
That which is a day of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas,
is considered his night when the world has become a single ocean.
Then, awakened at the end of the night, the Unborn One, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Brahmā, performs creation once again, just as was described to you previously.
Thus, O twice-born one, this dissolution of the kalpa, known as the occasional (naimittika) dissolution, has been described to you; now hear further concerning the elemental (prākṛta) dissolution.
O Sage, when the entire world—including all the heavens and all the netherworlds—had been cleansed through contact with drought and other calamities, [the earth was purified]. ViP_6.4.12.
When that dissolution has commenced, brought about by the will of Kṛṣṇa, there occurs the withdrawal of the entire transformation beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa).
The waters indeed first swallow the quality consisting of smell belonging to the earth;
then, its smell having been taken away, the earth becomes fit for dissolution.
When the subtle element of smell has perished, the earth becomes watery in nature;
then the waters increase, becoming forceful and loud-sounding.
Filling this entire world, they remain and move about everywhere, as far as the limits of light, like a garland of waves upon the water.
That quality which belongs to water is consumed by fire;
consequently, those waters perish due to the destruction of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra).
Then the waters, their essence having been taken away, indeed reach the light;
for when the water remains within the fire, it is enveloped on all sides by radiance.
And that fire, having pervaded everything, likewise consumes that water;
then this entire world is gradually filled with flames.
When that [world] was enveloped by flames extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards,
the wind then devoured even the supreme form of light, the maker of radiance.
Then, when that fire, which is the self of all, has dissolved and become wind,
and the subtle element of form has perished, the fire is deprived of its form.
Then that light subsides and the great wind blows fiercely;
thus it is in both the worldless state and in the world when the fire has reached the state of wind.
Then, having reached its own source, the wind vibrates upward,
downward, and across the ten directions.
Then space swallows the quality of wind, which is touch;
consequently, wind subsides, and space remains unobstructed.
It is without form, taste, touch, or smell, and it is not material;
yet it fills everything and shines forth as the Great One.
When the elements and the senses have indeed become simultaneously established in the primordial matter (bhūtādi),
this [state] is known as the tamasic bhūtādi, which consists of the absence of ego-consciousness (abhimāna).
Furthermore, the Great One, characterized by the intellect (buddhi), devours even fear and the rest.
The earth and the great world-system likewise exist within and without.
Thus, O Great Sage, the seven primary natures are traditionally taught;
yet in the process of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), they all enter into one another.
By this [egg], all this is enveloped— the egg which dissolves into the waters,
including the seven continents and oceans at its edge, the seven worlds, and the mountains.
That which is the obstruction of water is consumed by light;
light goes to dissolution in wind, and wind goes into space.
Space, O twice-born one, devours the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and the Great One (mahat) likewise devours that; Prakṛti devours the Great One along with these [other principles].
O great sage, that which is equal to the gums (the qualities), neither excessive nor deficient,
is called Prakṛti, the Cause, Pradhāna, and the Supreme Source.
Thus, this entire primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
dissolves into the unmanifest, O Maitreya, because its manifest form is [contained] within the unmanifest.
The person (puruṣa) is likewise one, pure, imperishable, eternal, and all-pervading;
he too, O Maitreya, is a portion of the Supreme Self who exists within all beings.

In that Lord of All, who consists of pure existence, who is the object of knowledge, whose nature is consciousness, and who is the Supreme Self, there exist no conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth.
That is Brahman, the supreme abode; he is the Supreme Self and the Lord;
he is Viṣṇu, this entire universe, from whom the ascetic does not return.
The primordial nature (prakṛti) which I have described, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest,
and the person (puruṣa)— both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self.
And the Supreme Self, the support of all,
the Supreme Lord named Viṣṇu, is celebrated in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas.
Vedic action is twofold: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to its cessation;
by means of both of these, He who possesses all forms is worshipped by men.
For he, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person, is worshipped by men through the paths of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas as they engage in ritual action.
When the path has ceased, Viṣṇu— who is the self of knowledge, who is worshipped through the yoga of knowledge, and whose very form is knowledge— bestows the fruit of liberation upon the yogins.
Whatever object is denoted by short, long, or protracted vowels,
and that which is beyond the reach of words— all that is the imperishable Viṣṇu.
He alone is the manifest, and he alone is the unmanifest;
he is the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the Self of the universe, and Hari who assumes the form of the universe.
Within that [Puruṣa], O Maitreya, Prakṛti—consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest—is completely dissolved; and Puruṣa likewise [dissolves] into the all-pervading, unobstructed Self.
O Maitreya, that period of time consisting of two parārdhas which I have described to you is said to be one day of Viṣṇu, the Lord.
O great sage, when the manifest has merged into primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise primordial nature has merged into the Person (puruṣa),
his night remains there for a duration equal to that [day].
For that eternal Supreme Self, there is neither day nor night;
nevertheless, O twice-born one, this metaphorical designation is applied to that Lord.
Thus, O Maitreya, this primary dissolution has been described to you;
now, O Brahmin, learn of the ultimate reabsorption.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, having understood the threefold suffering—namely, that which is internal and the rest—the wise man [should act accordingly].
Having attained knowledge and dispassion that have arisen, he reaches ultimate dissolution.
The internal [self] is also twofold: corporeal and likewise mental. The corporeal is divided into many varieties; hear now about that.
By means of various ailments such as diseases of the head, catarrh, fever, colic, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, swelling, asthma, vomiting, and so forth, in many ways; ViP_6,5.3 //
Likewise, the bodily heat known as eye disease, dysentery, leprosy, and physical ailments is divided; you should now listen to that which is mental.
It is born of desire, anger, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and despondency;
likewise, it consists of grief, envy, humiliation, jealousy, malice, and so forth.
"O best of the twice-born, mental affliction also occurs in many ways;
indeed, through such various distinctions as these, affliction is known as internal (ādhyātmika)."
For humans, the *ādhibhautika* [suffering] arises from beasts, birds, humans, and the like, as well as from *piśācas*, serpents, *rākṣasas*, reptiles, and so forth.
The heat arising from cold, wind, heat, rain, water, lightning, and so forth,
is described by the best of the foremost twice-born as *ādhidevika* (supernatural).
O best of sages, suffering arising from the womb, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and likewise from hell, is divided into thousands of varieties.
Within the womb, the creature with its delicate body is covered by much impurity;
