enveloped by the fetal membrane, the collection of its bones has its back and neck bent.
Due to his mother’s food that was excessively bitter, pungent, sharp, hot, and salty,
and because of extreme heat, he experienced exceedingly increasing pain.
He is no longer master of his own limbs for extending or contracting them;
lying in the great mire of excrement and urine, he is tormented everywhere.
Then, breathless yet conscious, remembering hundreds of previous births,
he remains in the womb in extreme suffering, bound by his own karma.
Being born with a face defiled by excrement, blood, urine, and semen,
his skeletal frame is tormented by the wind of Prajāpati.
Indeed, turned head-downwards by the powerful winds of birth,
the afflicted one emerges from the mother's womb with great difficulty.
Having fallen into a great swoon and being touched by the external air,
O best of sages, he experiences a loss of consciousness upon being reborn.
With his limbs pierced as if by thorns and torn as if by saws,
he fell from the putrid wound onto the earth like a worm.
He is unable even to scratch himself, nor is he master of his own movements;
even for bathing, drinking, and eating, he must depend on the will of others.
Sleeping upon a bed of impurities, even while being bitten by insects, gadflies, and the like, he is utterly incapable of warding them off.

There are manifold sufferings of birth, and that which follows immediately upon birth; for in childhood, one indeed encounters sufferings such as those caused by other beings (ādhibhautika) and so forth.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, with a deluded inner organ,
a man does not know from whence he comes, who he is, where he is going, or what belongs to his self.
By what bond am I bound? What is the cause, and what is not a cause? What is to be done, and what is not to be done? What is to be spoken, and what is not to be spoken? ||| ViP_6.5.22 |||
What is dharma and what is adharma? In what does one abide, and how? What is to be done and what is not to be done? Or what possesses virtue and what possesses fault? (ViP 6.5.23)
Thus, great suffering born of ignorance is experienced by foolish men who are like beasts, who are devoted solely to their heads and bellies.
Ignorance is a state of darkness (tamas); from it arise the undertakings and engagements in action for those who lack knowledge, and consequently, O twice-born one, the neglect of prescribed duties.
The wise say that hell is the fruit resulting from the neglect of one's duties;
therefore, for the ignorant, there is supreme suffering both in this world and in the next.
And a man whose body is worn out by old age, with limbs grown flaccid, with loose and decayed teeth, and covered with wrinkles, sinews, and veins; 6.5.27.
His eyes were lost in the distance, with stars appearing within his sky-like gaze;
a mass of hair emerged from the openings of his nostrils as his body trembled.
The mass of bones in his back was made manifest by every vertebra being bent;
because the fire of his stomach had been extinguished, he took little food and remained motionless.
His movements—walking, rising, lying down, and sitting—become difficult;
his hearing and sight grow dim, and his face is fouled by trickling saliva.
With all his faculties no longer under his control and facing death,
he is unable to remember at that very moment any of the objects he had previously experienced.
When the sentence was uttered just once, a great exhaustion arose;
there was great fatigue and wakefulness produced by panting and coughing.
The aged man is raised up by one person and likewise laid down by another;
he is made an object of contempt for his servants, his own sons, and his wife.
With all his purity exhausted, longing for recreation and food,
he became an object of ridicule even to his own attendants, having become utterly despondent toward all his kinsmen.
As if remembering his own actions in another birth from his youth, he sighs deeply, tormented by distress.
Having indeed experienced such sufferings as these in old age,
hear now also of those sufferings which one encounters at death.
Then, with his neck, feet, and hands drooping, he was violently overcome by trembling;
now fainting and helpless, and now possessed of a mere fragment of consciousness.
"Regarding gold, grain, sons, wife, servants, houses,
and so forth— how will these fare?"— thus he was exceedingly agitated by the sense of "mine-ness."
With his vital points being pierced by terrible, piercing diseases as cruel as saws,
his bonds of life were severed as if by the fierce arrows of Death.
With his pupils rolling and tossing his hands and feet repeatedly,
his palate and lips parched, he gasped with a wheezing sound.
His throat was obstructed by floods of humors, he was oppressed by the upward-moving breath,
pervaded by great heat, and likewise afflicted by thirst and hunger.
Afflicted by the servants of Yama, he undergoes transcendence from his afflictions;
and thereafter, through those very afflictions, he assumes a body of torment.
These and other terrible sufferings await men at the time of death;
now hear of those which are experienced by deceased persons in hell.
The seizing by the nooses and other instruments of Yama’s servants, the beating with staffs, the sight of Yama himself, and the gazing upon the most terrible paths; 6,5.44.
O twice-born one, in each of these hells— which are terrifying with burning sand, fire, machines, and weapons such as swords— the torments endured are unbearable.
Of those being split with saws, or even being burned in crucibles, or being hacked with axes, or even being buried in the ground; ViP_6.5.46.
May they be impaled upon stakes, cast into the mouths of tigers,
devoured by vultures, and eaten by leopards.
They are boiled in the midst of oil, they are made to rot in a mire of alkaline sludge;
they are hurled down from great heights and cast about by mechanical catapults.
O Brahmin, there is no known limit to the number of sufferings arising from sinful causes that are experienced by those in hell.
O best of the twice-born, it is not only in hell that there is a succession of sufferings;
even in heaven, one who fears falling is subject to decay and finds no peace.
Furthermore, it enters the womb and is born again and again;
having dissolved back into the womb, it truly sets as it is being born once more.
One dies as soon as born, or in childhood, or in youth;
death occurs upon reaching middle age, or else in old age.
As long as he lives, he is overwhelmed by various kinds of sufferings;
yet he remains there like a cotton seed amidst a mass of its own causal fibers.
In the loss of wealth, as well as in its acquisition and preservation, men always encounter manifold sufferings; likewise, so it is when their cherished desires fail.
O Maitreya, whatever object arises that brings pleasure to men,
that very thing becomes the seed of the tree of suffering.
Through wife, son, friends, wealth, house, field, riches, and the like,
men do not experience such abundant happiness as that which [is found] in happiness itself.
Thus, for those whose minds are scorched by the heat of the sun of the suffering of saṃsāra,
where is there happiness for human beings except in the shade of the tree of liberation?
Thus, for me, this threefold mass of suffering will indeed prevail throughout the stages of existence beginning with conception, birth, and old age.
The attainment of the Blessed One, characterized solely by the state of bliss consisting of unsurpassed and extraordinary joy, is considered the medicine that is absolute and eternal.
Therefore, wise men should exert effort to attain that;
O Great Sage, it has been taught that both knowledge and action are the means for attaining it.
That knowledge is said to be twofold: arising from scripture and from discernment.
That which consists of scripture is the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman); that which is born of discernment is the Supreme Brahman (parabrahman).
O brahmin sage, ignorance is like blinding darkness, while that which arises from the senses is like a lamp; but the knowledge born of discernment is like the sun.
O best of sages, listen now as I relate here, in this connection, that which Manu also spoke after recollecting the meaning of the Vedas.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman that is sound (śabdabrahman) and that which is the supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman that is sound attains the supreme Brahman.
"There are indeed two sciences to be known," so says the Atharvanic revelation;
by the higher [science] there is the attainment of the Imperishable, while the lower consists of the Ṛgveda and the others.
That which is unmanifest, undecaying, inconceivable, unborn, immutable,
indefinable, formless, and devoid of hands, feet, and other such limbs.
All-pervading, omnipresent, eternal, the source of all beings, and without cause;
that which pervades and is pervaded by everything—this is what the wise truly behold.
That is Brahman, that is the supreme abode; that is to be meditated upon by those desiring liberation.
It is the subtle, supreme state of Viṣṇu, proclaimed by the words of the Vedas.
That very nature of the Supreme Self is what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat";
the word "Bhagavat" is the designator of that primordial, imperishable Self.
Thus, that knowledge by which the true nature of each of these aforementioned objects is known in its reality—that is the supreme knowledge consisting of the three Vedas; all else is different.
O twice-born one, although that Brahman is beyond the range of words,
the term "Bhagavat" is applied to its worship by way of metaphorical designation.
O Maitreya, the word "Bhagavat" is applied to the supreme Brahman, which is called the Great Sovereignty (Mahāvibhūti), the pure one, and the cause of all causes.

O Sage, the letter *bha* possesses a twofold meaning: it signifies "one who nourishes" (*saṃbharta*) and likewise "one who sustains" (*bhartā*). Similarly, the letter *ga* signifies "one who leads" (*netā*), "one who causes to go" (*gamayatā*), and "one who creates" (*sraṣṭā*).
The term *bhaga* is said to denote the six qualities: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, as well as knowledge and detachment.
Beings dwell there within that Self of beings, the soul of all;
and he dwells in all beings without exception—therefore, the meaning of the syllable *va* is the Imperishable.
In this way, O Maitreya, this great sound "Bhagavān" belongs to Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman; it does not apply to anyone else.
In this context, this word is endowed with the technical definition used for denoting objects worthy of worship;
it is not used figuratively here, whereas elsewhere it is indeed used figuratively.
He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings,
and who knows both knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called Bhagavān.
Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— these,
in their entirety and devoid of all qualities and attributes subject to abandonment, are what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat."
All beings dwell there within the Supreme Self, and that Universal Self dwells within all beings; therefore, he is remembered as Vāsudeva.
In former times, when questioned by Khāṇḍikya Janaka, Keśidhvaja spoke of the true nature of Vāsudeva, who is infinite, yet he did not provide a full explanation.
Because He dwells within all beings and because they dwell within Him,
Vāsudeva is therefore the Lord, the Ordainer and Disposer of the worlds.

O Sage, he has transcended the primordial nature of all beings, their transformations, and the defects such as the guṇas; having surpassed all veils, his entire self pervades that which exists within the intermediate spaces of the worlds.

He is the embodiment of all auspicious qualities; by a mere fraction of his own power, he sustains the multitude of beings; assuming whatever vast body he desires at will, he has accomplished every benefit for the entire world.
He is the sole mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, heroism, and power;
he is the highest of the high, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist.
He is the Lord, whose nature is both individual and collective, manifest in form;
he is the Lord of all, the seer of all, the knower of all, possessed of all powers, known as the Supreme Lord.

That by which something is perceived—being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and uniform—is either seen or understood; that is called knowledge, and everything else is said to be ignorance.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said: That Supreme Person is perceived through the study of the Vedas and self-restraint.
Brahman is the cause for attaining that; thus it is recited: "That is this."
One should engage in the practice of yoga through Vedic study, and one should abide in Vedic study through yoga;
by the perfection of both Vedic study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
For the purpose of seeing that [Self], sacred study is the eye, and yoga is likewise supreme;
yet he who has become Brahman cannot be seen by me with the physical eye.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to know that yoga; please describe it, so that once it is known, I may behold the Supreme Lord, the support of all."
Śrī Parāśara said: Just as Keśidhvaja formerly spoke to the high-souled Nakaka, the son of Khāṇḍikya, concerning that Yoga, so shall I relate it to you.
Maitreya said: O Khāṇḍikya, who was that Brahmin, and who was the virtuous Keśidhvaja? And how did their conversation come about on account of their connection through yoga?
Śrī Parāśara said: Janaka was indeed Dharmadhvaja; his son was Amitadhvaja, and there was also a king named Kṛtadhvaja, who was ever devoted to the supreme self.
The son of Kṛtadhvaja was the renowned King Keśidhvaja;
the son of Amitadhvaja was Khāṇḍikya-Janaka.
Through the path of ritual action, Khaṇḍikya became the lord of the earth;
Keśidhvaja, too, was exceedingly proficient in the knowledge of the Self.
Both of them were indeed desirous of conquering one another;
Khāṇḍikya was deposed from his own kingdom by Keśidhvaja.
Then, accompanied by his domestic priest and ministers, he— possessing few resources and expelled from the kingdom— became a wanderer in the difficult forests.
Relying upon knowledge, he too performed very many sacrifices;
having taken his stand in the knowledge of Brahman, he sought to cross over death by means of knowledge.
Once, O best among those who know yoga, while he was performing a sacrifice,
a fierce tiger killed his sacrificial cow in the lonely forest.
Then, having heard from his officiating priests that Dhanu had been killed by a tiger, the king asked what expiation should be performed for this matter.
They also said, "We do not know; let Kaśeru ask.
When Kaśeru was addressed by him in the same manner, he spoke thus to Bhārgava.
"O Indra among kings, ask Śunaka; I do not know, but he will know.
Having gone there, he asked him, and he too said: "Listen, O Sage, to what [he] said."
Neither Keśaru nor I, nor anyone else on earth at present,
knows [this], except for your single enemy, Khāṇḍikya, who was defeated by you.
And he said to him: "O Sage, I am going now to question my own enemy;
for the great sacrifice has already arrived, and if he should slay me."
If he, when questioned, shall speak the atonement in its entirety,
then, O best of sages, the yoga will become complete and unimpaired.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, the king, wearing a black antelope skin, mounted his chariot and went to the forest where the high-minded Khāṇḍikya resided.
Seeing his enemy approaching, Khaṇḍikya, his eyes copper-red with rage and having drawn his bow, spoke: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.6.21.
Khāṇḍikya said:
"By fastening a black antelope skin as armor, you will slay us;
for you believe that one who wears a black antelope skin will not strike at you."
"O fool, why do you not place a black antelope skin upon the backs of the deer, for whom—and for you as well—I have discharged fierce, sharp arrows? (ViP 6.6.23)
I shall slay you; you shall not escape from me alive, O evil-minded one, for you are an assailant and an enemy who has seized my kingdom.
Keśidhvaja said: "O Khāṇḍikya, I have come before you to ask about a doubt;
it was not to kill you that I released this arrow in anger after due reflection."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then the high-minded Khāṇḍikya, together with his ministers and his family priest, deliberated in private with all of them.
The ministers said to him: "This enemy who has fallen into our power must be slain; once he is killed, the entire earth will come under your control. (ViP 6.6.27)
And Khāṇḍikya said to them all, "This is so, without a doubt;
once he is slain, the entire earth shall come under my control."
"The victory over the next world is his, and the entire earth is mine;
if I do not kill him, the victory over the world is mine, and the earth is his."
I do not think that the conquest of the earth could be greater than the conquest of the world;
for the conquest of the next world is infinite, whereas the conquest of the earth is but of short duration.
Therefore, I will not kill him; whatever he asks, that I shall tell him.
Śrī Parāśara said: Then Khāṇḍikya Janaka approached his enemy and said, "Ask me everything that you wish to ask; I shall tell it to you."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then, O twice-born one, having related everything exactly as it had occurred— the slaughter of the cow of virtue— he asked about the expiation pertaining to that act.
And he explained to Keśidhvaja, O twice-born one,
according to the rule that entire expiation which is prescribed for that matter.
Having understood the matter and being permitted by that very high-souled one,
he approached the sacrificial ground and performed all the rites in due order.
Having performed the sacrifice in due order according to the prescribed rites and having bathed at the concluding ablution (avabhṛtha),
the king, feeling his duty fulfilled, then reflected:
All the twice-born ones have been honored by me, as have all the members of the assembly;
likewise, those who came as supplicants have been gratified with the desired wealth that I have acquired.
I have performed every action for this world as was appropriate;
nevertheless, what is it to me that my mind has not yet accomplished its task?
Reflecting thus, that lord of the earth remembered:
"I have indeed not yet given the teacher's fee to Khāṇḍikya."
Then that king, Maitreya Khāṇḍikya, mounting his chariot once more, went to where the impenetrable thicket of Durga was located.
Khāṇḍikya, seeing him approaching again with weapon raised, stood ready to kill him; then the king spoke to him once more.
"O Khāṇḍikya, I have not come to do you harm; do not be angry.
Know that I have arrived here for the purpose of purchasing my preceptor."
"The sacrifice has been completed by me through your excellent instruction;
as such, I wish to give you a gift—choose a teacher's fee."
Śrī Parāśara said: Once again, the king deliberated with his ministers,
desiring to provide a fee for his preceptor, thinking, "What should be requested by me?"
The ministers said to him: "Let this kingdom be requested;
for the kingdom is sought by enemies who have exhausted their armies."
Laughing, that high-minded King Khāṇḍikya said to them:
"How can the guardianship of the earth, which lasts for such a short time, be desired by those like me?"
"It is thus, O sirs, for you here are ministers who accomplish worldly ends;
what is the ultimate truth here, and how so? You are not discerning in this matter."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, that king approached Keśidhvaja and said,
"Will you certainly give me the teacher's fee?"
Having been told "So be it" by him, Khāṇḍikya then said to him:
"You are today one who is discerning regarding the supreme truth of the knowledge of the Self."
"If you would grant me the price for my preceptor,
then declare that deed which is sufficient for the pacification of my afflictions."
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Keśidhvaja said:
"Why did you not request our kingdom, which is now free from all thorns?"
Nothing else is as dear to Kṣatriyas as the acquisition of a kingdom.
Khāṇḍikya said:
O Keśidhvaja, understand this from me: I did not request this entire kingdom of yours, for which the unwise feel such greed.
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas:
the protection of their subjects and the execution, through righteous war, of those who oppose their own sovereignty.
In this matter, there is no fault on my part, as you have carried it away;
for even ignorance, when deprived of its proper sequence, leads only to bondage.
"This desire for sovereignty of mine is for the sake of obtaining a small amount of enjoyment;
that same desire, when arising from the faults of others, does not indeed conform to righteousness."
"Entreaty is not the way for those of the kṣatriya lineage; this is the view of the virtuous according to dharma.
Therefore, you did not ask for the kingdom, which was within the reach of your ignorance."
It is the ignorant who, their minds captivated by the sense of "mine," covet sovereignty;
those like me do not, being intoxicated by the great draught of the pride of "I."
Śrī Parāśara said:
Then King Keśidhvaja, greatly delighted, said "Excellent! to Khāṇḍikya Janaka; out of affection he said, "Listen to my words."
Keśidhvaja said: "Indeed,
desiring to cross over death through ignorance,
I perform kingship, various sacrifices, and likewise the destruction of merit through ritual means."
Therefore, by good fortune, this mind of yours has attained the sovereignty of discernment;
listen, O delighter of your lineage, to the true nature of ignorance.
The notion of a self in what is not-self, and the thought of "mine" in what is not one's own—
this twofold state is the seed for the growth of the tree of saṃsāra.

In this body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul, enveloped by the darkness of delusion and possessed of poor intellect, loudly forms the notion: "I am this; this is mine. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.12)
When the self exists as something distinct from ether, air, fire, water, and earth,
who can produce a sense of "self" within the body?
For who, when the Self is wise and bodiless, would think "this is mine" regarding houses, fields, and so forth, which are merely objects of enjoyment for the physical body?
And thus, regarding sons and grandsons produced from his own body, what wise man would claim ownership over this selfless physical frame?
A human being performs every action for the sake of the enjoyment of the body;
yet when that body is different from the person, then that [action] leads to further bondage.
Just as a house made of clay is plastered with clay and water,
so too this earthly body is maintained by the application of clay and water.
If the body, which consists of the five elements, is nourished by enjoyments that also consist of the five elements,
then what enjoyment has been produced for the person here?
Traversing the path of saṃsāra through many thousands of births,
he has fallen into the exhaustion of delusion, obstructed by the thorns of latent impressions (vāsanā).
When that dust of his is washed away by the hot water of knowledge,
then the fatigue of delusion of this traveler through saṃsāra comes to rest.
When the exhaustion of delusion has come to rest,
the person whose inner organ is composed attains the supreme nirvāṇa, which is unsurpassed and unimpeded.
This self consists entirely of nirvāṇa; it is composed of knowledge and is stainless.
Phenomena, however, consist of suffering and ignorance; they arise from primordial nature (prakṛti), but not from the self.

O King, although there is no direct contact with fire in the water due to its association with the cooking pot, it nevertheless produces properties such as the intensification of sound; even so is this case.

In the same way, the Self, through its attachment to primordial nature (prakṛti), becomes defiled by egoism and other such traits, and thus partakes in the qualities of nature; for it is indeed distinct from them and immutable.
Thus, I have explained to you this seed of ignorance;
there exists nothing other than yoga that brings about the destruction of the afflictions.
Khāṇḍikya said:
"O illustrious one, best among those who know yoga, tell me that yoga;
for you have mastered the meaning of the science of yoga within this lineage of Nimi."
Keśidhvaja said: O Khāṇḍikya, listen as I describe the true nature of yoga,
established in which the sage, having attained absorption into Brahman, does not fall away.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage, while free from sense objects, the mind leads to liberation.
Having withdrawn the mind, whose essence is consciousness, from the sense objects,
the sage should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who is Brahman, for the sake of liberation.
Just as a magnet draws iron toward itself by its own power, so does that external [object] draw the meditating sage toward its own form, subjecting him to transformation.
The union of that distinguished movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort, with Brahman is designated as *yoga*.
Thus, he whose yoga is characterized by qualities endowed with such absolute distinction is indeed called a yogin seeking liberation.
A yogi who is engaged in yoga is indeed called a "practitioner" (yuñjāna) at the outset;
but one whose samādhi is perfected is one who has attained the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
Even if his mind is defiled by the fault of obstacles,
liberation arises for the former [person] through practice over successive births.
But the yogin whose concentration is fully perfected, having burned away the accumulation of karma by the fire of yoga, attains liberation in that very birth without delay.
Leading his own mind toward fitness, the desireless yogi should practice celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness. (ViP 6.7.36)
One who has restrained the self should perform study of the sacred texts, purity, contentment, and austerity,
while likewise directing the mind toward the supreme Brahman.
These five restraints (yamas) and five observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed;
they grant distinguished fruits when practiced with desire, and liberation for those free from desire.
Seated upon one of the auspicious seats (bhadrāsana) and endowed with virtuous qualities,
the disciplined ascetic (yati) should practice yoga through those known as restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
That which brings the vital air called *prāṇa* under control through practice is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*; it is both with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*abīja*).
Just as the prāṇa and apāna breaths mutually overcome one another like two winds,
the third [state] arises through the proper regulation of those two by means of restraint.
O best of the twice-born, for that yogin who possesses an object of focus and practices meditation, the gross form is traditionally taught as the object of the Infinite One.
Restraining the senses that are attached to sound and other objects, the knower of yoga,
devoted to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), should make them follow the lead of the mind.
By that [means], supreme mastery over the fickle senses is born;
for one who has not mastered those senses, the yogi is not an achiever of yoga.
Once the vital breath has been brought under control through breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) and the senses through withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
one should then cause the mind to abide in a virtuous object of focus.
Khāṇḍikya said: "O highly fortunate one, let that auspicious support of the mind be told to me—
that foundation which destroys the entirety of the impurities arising from defects."
Keśidhvāja said: O King, Brahman is the support of the mind; by its very nature, it is twofold:
manifest and unmanifest, as well as supreme and non-supreme.
O King, understand that this entire universe consists of a threefold cultivation:
that called Brahman, that known as Karma, and likewise that which is of the nature of both.
For the cultivation of existence (bhāvabhāvanā) is threefold: one consists of the nature of karma, another of the nature of Brahman, and likewise yet another consists of both. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.49)
Those such as Sanandana and others who are endowed with the contemplation of Brahman,
while others, from the gods downward to the lowest immobile beings, are characterized by the contemplation of karma.
And among those such as Hiraṇyagarbha, who are endowed with awakening and the authority [to act], there exists a twofold cultivation of being consisting of both Brahman and action.
As long as all the specific cognitions and karmas remain undiminished,
this entire universe and that which is beyond it appear divided by the perception of those men who see through the lens of duality.
That knowledge which has all distinctions subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the self— this is designated as Brahman.
And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu, known as the formless, unsurpassed,
characterized by being the opposite of the nature of the universe, belonging to the Supreme Self.
O King, since it is not possible for one engaged in yoga to contemplate that [subtle form],
one should therefore contemplate the gross form of Hari, which is the object of the entire universe.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsudeva, Prajāpati, the Maruts, the Vasus, the Rudras, the suns, the stars, and the planets; ViP_6.7.56.
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and all other divine lineages;
human beings, animals, mountains, oceans, rivers, and trees.
O King, all beings without exception, as well as the causes of beings—
everything from primordial matter (pradhāna) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa), consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious— [are his].
This embodied form of Hari, consisting of three types of contemplation, is one-footed, two-footed, many-footed, and footless.
All this entire universe, this world with its moving and non-moving beings,
is endowed with the power of Viṣṇu, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
The power of Viṣṇu is declared to be supreme (parā), while that called the individual soul (kṣetrajña) is the subordinate (aparā);
another power, known as ignorance and karma, is held to be the third.
Enveloped by that [māyā], O King, the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field undergoes the entirety of the most continuous torments of saṃsāra.
And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is perceived in all beings according to their relative degrees of excellence.
Among those without breath, that [power] is very slight; it is greater among stationary beings, and even greater than among them in reptiles, and indeed with exceeding force in winged creatures.
From the winged creatures came the deer; from them, by their power, the domestic animals were superior;
and from the domestic animals, humans were manifested through even greater power.
O King, even from them [the Pitṛs] come the deities such as the Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others.
Śakra is superior to all the gods; from him, Prajāpati;
from him, Hiraṇyagarbha; and from him, the Puruṣa characterized by Śakti.
O King, all these forms without exception are his very forms,
because they are joined with his power, just as they are with the ether.
O Great-minded One, the second form of Viṣṇu is that which is to be meditated upon by yogis;
it is the formless aspect of Brahman, which is called "Being" (sat) by the wise.
O King, that other great form of Hari, in which all these powers are established, is both identical with and different from the universal form.
O Lord of Men, He performs by His own play all forms of power, including those possessing the activities of gods, animals, humans, and others.
For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the immeasurable one is not born of karma; it is all-pervading and characterized by being unimpeded.
O King, that form of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) should be meditated upon by one engaged in yoga for the sake of purifying the self and for the destruction of all sins.
Just as fire with its flames raised burns dry wood when fanned by the wind,
so does Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, burn away all the impurities of yogis.
Therefore, one should establish the mind there, in that which is the support of all powers; that indeed should be known as pure concentration (śuddha-dhāraṇā).
O King, for the yogin whose mind has a pure basis, who is all-pervading and of an immovable nature, liberation comes from transcending the manifestation of the three states of existence.
But others, O tiger among men, whose minds are dependent on external objects, are entirely impure; these include the gods and other beings who are born of their past actions.
The embodied form of the Blessed One, which is free from desire for any support—
this indeed is declared to be *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is held steady.
O King, hear now what form of Hari, which is material, should be meditated upon;
for that which is without support cannot logically serve as a support.
With a serene countenance and eyes resembling the petals of a beautiful lotus,
he had handsome cheeks and shone with a broad, expansive forehead.
His beautiful earrings were placed as far as his ears,
his neck was like a conch shell, and his broad chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa.
With a belly possessing three folds and a sunken navel,
he should be Viṣṇu with eight long arms, or else with four arms.
One should meditate upon Him who has become Brahman, whose thighs and shanks are symmetrical, whose excellent lotus-feet are well-placed, and who is clad in pure yellow garments.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
He was equipped with the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, the sword, the discus, and a rosary;
his hands displayed the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he was adorned with jewels and rings.
The yogi, having concentrated his own mind, should contemplate [the object] with total absorption until, O King, the dhāraṇā becomes firmly established in that very state.
Whether one is walking, standing, or performing any other action according to one's own will,
when the mind does not depart [from its object], then one should consider that state to be perfected.
Then, the wise one should contemplate the form of the Blessed One as peaceful, devoid of the conch, mace, discus, and Śārṅga bow, yet holding a rosary.
When that meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) has likewise become stable,
one should then remember [the deity] devoid of ornaments such as crowns and armlets.

Then, O King, the wise man should first contemplate that deity with his mind as consisting of a single limb; thereafter, he should become intent upon meditating upon the whole composed of those limbs.
And that mental continuum, having that as its object and free from longing for anything else,
is accomplished through those first six factors of dhyāna, O King.
Indeed, the grasping of its very own nature, free from conceptual construction,
which is to be accomplished by the mind through meditation— that is designated as *samādhi*.
O King, consciousness is that which attains the supreme Brahman as its object;
likewise, the Self, in whom all latent impressions have been utterly extinguished, is that which is to be attained.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the agent, and knowledge is his instrument;
having accomplished the task of liberation by means of that [knowledge], he indeed ceases once his purpose has been fulfilled.
Having attained the state of being that very essence, he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
any difference, moreover, would be caused by ignorance.
When the knowledge that produces the sense of duality has gone to absolute destruction,
who will bring about the unreal distinction between the self and Brahman?
Thus has Yoga been explained by me to you, O Khāṇḍikya, as you requested;
both in brief and in detail. What else shall be done for you?
Khāṇḍikya said:
"Now that the true essence of Yoga has been explained, everything has indeed been accomplished for me;
for by your instruction, the impurity of my mind has been destroyed without remainder."
O Lord of Men, that which I have stated as "mine" is not false, nor can it be otherwise; even by those who know what is to be known, it cannot be spoken differently.
"This is I" and "this is mine"—this is ignorance, and conventional usage proceeds in this way regarding these two;
but the ultimate truth is beyond discourse, that which is not within the range of words.
Therefore, depart for your own welfare; all this has been done by you for me, since you have proclaimed the imperishable Yoga of Keśidhvaja, which bestows liberation.
Śrī Parāśara said: O Brahmin,
having been honored by that Khāṇḍikya according to his merit,
King Keśidhvaja then returned to his city.
Khāṇḍikya also, having made his son king for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga,
went to the forest with his mind fully devoted to Govinda.
There, having attained one-pointed concentration and being endowed with virtues such as self-restraint (yama), the king attained absorption into the stainless Brahman known as Viṣṇu.
Keśidhvaja, intent on the exhaustion of his own karma for the sake of liberation,
enjoyed sense objects while performing actions without attachment to their results.

O twice-born one, having exhausted his evil through the enjoyment of non-virtuous things, he likewise became stainless and attained ultimate perfection, the fruit of which is the destruction of all suffering.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the sixth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Parāśara said:
Thus has this third dissolution been fully described.
Absolute liberation is that which is absorption into the eternal Brahman.
Primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties have all been recounted by me to you.
This Purāṇa of Viṣṇu destroys all sins;
it is superior to all scriptures and brings about the goals of human existence.
O Maitreya, that imperishable [teaching] has been declared to you exactly as it was requested;
whatever else remains to be said, ask now and I shall tell it to you.
Maitreya said: "O Blessed One, O Sage, everything that you were asked by me has been told;
this has been heard by me with devotion, and there is nothing else remaining for me to ask."
All doubts have been severed and my mind has attained purity;
through your grace, I have understood the origin, the maintenance, and the dissolution [of all things].
O Guru, the threefold aggregate has been known, as well as the threefold power;
and that threefold cultivation of states has been understood by you in its entirety.
"O twice-born one, by your grace I have understood that which is to be known; enough with others!
For this entire world is not distinct from Viṣṇu."
O great sage, by your grace I have undoubtedly achieved my purpose,
since the duties of the social classes and other such dharmas have been understood by me in their entirety.
All knowledge, whether pertaining to worldly engagement or renunciation, consists entirely of karma.
Be gracious, O best of Brahmins; there is nothing else remaining for me to ask.
O Guru, whatever merit has been earned by me through the fatigue of speaking to you, let that be forgiven; for among the virtuous, there is no distinction between a son and a disciple.
Śrī Parāśara said: This Purāṇa, which I have narrated to you, is in accord with the Vedas;
upon hearing it, the heap of sins arising from all defects is destroyed.
The primary creation, the secondary creation, the genealogies,
the periods of the Manvantaras, and the complete history of the dynasties have all been recounted by me here to you.
In this regard, the gods, as well as the Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas,
Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and likewise the Apsarases, are described.
Sages whose selves are cultivated and who are endowed with austerity are so described;
likewise, the fourfold order of society and the distinguished conducts of men [are explained].
The holy regions of the earth, the sacred rivers and oceans, the most meritorious mountains, and the deeds of the wise; ViP_6.8.16.
The duties of the castes and other such dharmas, as well as the Vedas and Śāstras in their entirety—
by the mere recollection of these, one is instantly liberated from all sins.
He who is the immutable cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the world—
that Lord Hari is said to be all beings and the self of all.
Even by one who is powerless, when his name is uttered, a man is instantly freed from all sins,
like deer terrified by a lion.
O Maitreya, the chanting of the names [of the Lord] with devotion is the unsurpassed dissolution of all sins, just as fire is for the elements.
The most fierce impurity of the Kali age, which brings the agony of hell to men,
goes to immediate dissolution as soon as this [name] is remembered even once.
By Hiraṇyagarbha, Indra, Rudra, the Ādityas, the Aśvins, and Vāyu;
by the Pāvakas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and other such gods.
By yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas; by siddhas, daityas, gandharvas, and dānavas; likewise by apsarases, as well as by all the stars, lunar mansions, and planets.
Likewise by the seven ṛṣis, by the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya) and their presiding deities,
by humans beginning with Brahmā, and similarly by domestic animals and wild beasts.
With reptiles and birds, with trees such as the *palāśa*, with forest fires, oceans, rivers, and the netherworlds (*pātāla*), together with the gods and the sacrificial fires; 6.8.25.
O twice-born one, this entire cosmic egg, together with its sound and other qualities, is like an atom compared to him;
and it is composed of that very essence, O best of the twice-born.
He is all, the knower of all, the embodiment of all yet devoid of form;
the Blessed One Viṣṇu is celebrated here as the destroyer of sins.
O best of sages, by hearing this, a human being obtains that very fruit which one attains when bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
A man who observes a fast at Prayāga, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and likewise at the ocean, obtains that same merit simply by hearing this.
O Brahmin, whatever great fruit of merit a person obtains through a year of well-performed Agnihotra sacrifices, he obtains that very same fruit by hearing this [account] but once.
Having bathed in the waters of the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha and having beheld Hari in Mathurā, a person attains that fruit.
O brahmin-sage, he who listens properly to this entire chapter of this Purāṇa with his mind offered to Keśava indeed attains all that.
O best of sages, a man who has bathed in the waters of the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, having fasted, [attains the highest goal].
Having properly worshipped Acyuta in Mathurā with a concentrated mind,
one obtains the complete fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Then, observing the prosperity of others who had been elevated by their own descendants,
even their fathers and grandfathers reportedly said this:
I hope that one born in our family, having fasted and bathed in the waters of the Kālindī,
will worship Govinda in Mathurā.
"In the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭhāmūla, by what means shall we too attain supreme prosperity, delivered by those born of our own lineage? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.8.37)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having duly worshipped Janārdana,
one born into a family of the fortunate will offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the Yamunā.
At that time, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa there with a concentrated mind and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, he bathed in the waters of the Yamunā.
Whatever merit a man attains by delivering his ancestors,
he obtains that same merit by listening to this chapter of the Purāṇa according to his ability.
This is the unsurpassed protection for those who fear saṃsāra;
it is the supreme thing to be heard among all that is worth hearing, and the highest among all purifying things.
It destroys the evil dreams of men, subdues all that is wicked,
is the most auspicious of auspicious things, and bestows the attainment of sons.
In ancient times, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] spoke this to Ṛbhu;
Ṛbhu spoke it to Priyavrata, and he, in turn, declared it to Bhāguri.
Bhāguri taught it to Staṃbhamitra, and he [in turn] spoke it to Dadhīca;
he spoke it to Sārasvata, and Bhṛgu received it from Sārasvata.
Bhṛgu told it to Purukutsa, and he in turn told it to Narmadā;
Narmadā told it to the Nāga Dhṛtarāṣṭra and to Āpūraṇa.
And those two spoke it to Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, O twice-born one;
Vāsuki spoke it to his son, and the son indeed to Aśvatara.
And he spoke to Kambala, and he indeed to Elāputra.
Then the sage Vedaśiras reached Pātāla;
having obtained all this, he gave it to Pramati.
This was told by Pramati to the wise Jātukarṇa,
and it was likewise spoken by Jātukarṇa to others who perform meritorious deeds.
Through the granting of a boon by Pulastya, this has come to my memory as well;
and thus, O Maitreya, I have related this to you exactly as it is.
You too, O Śinī, shall speak this at the end of the Kali age.
This is the supreme secret that destroys the impurities of the Kali age;
the man who hears this with devotion is liberated from all sins.
He who listens to this day by day has performed all ritual baths at sacred fords and has offered praise to all the immortals.
Having heard these ten chapters, one undoubtedly attains that merit born of the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā), which is extremely difficult to obtain. (ViP 6.8.54)
But that person who hears all of this in its entirety, having fixed in his mind Acyuta— the All, who consists of all, the support of all worlds, whose refuge is the Self,

who is knowledge and the object of knowledge, without beginning or end, and the benefactor of all the immortals— he attains, without a doubt, the complete fruit that is obtained from a horse sacrifice.

In which [text] the Blessed One—the teacher of the moving and the unmoving—is present at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end; he who consists of the knowledge of Brahman, the infallible Lord of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe;
by hearing, reciting, or causing others to read that [text], a person attains everything pure and stainless. There is no fruit in the three worlds equal to that, for Hari is the singular perfection.

When the sun of one's life is set upon Him, one does not go to hell; even heaven is a hindrance when He is meditated upon; and for one whose mind and intellect are absorbed in Him, even the world of Brahmā seems insignificant.
Since that Imperishable One, when established in the hearts of men of impure intellect, bestows liberation itself, what wonder is there that sin dissolves away when Acyuta is glorified?

Those who know the sacrifice constantly worship Him with sacrifices as the Lord of Sacrifice; and the men of knowledge meditate upon Him who consists of Brahman and who comprises both the high and the low.
Having contemplated Him, one is not born, nor does one die, nor does one grow, nor does one decay; He is neither non-existent nor existent. What more than this can be heard of Hari? Listen.

He who, assuming the form of the ancestors, consumes the *kavya* offered by the ritual rules, and as the Lord, the beginningless and endless one, consumes the *havya* offering in his divine state—He who is designated as *svāhā* and *svadhā*, in whom all powers reside as the Abode of Brahman, and for whom the measures of the proud do not suffice for His vastness; that Hari has entered our ears and destroys our impurity.
I bow to that Supreme Person, the Lord worthy of praise, who has no end and no origin, who has no growth and is devoid of transformation, and who never undergoes decay, being the unchanging Reality.
To that very Puruṣa, who alone, though one, enjoys the womb and the earth in many ways, and who, though pure, appears as if impure through various forms;
who is endowed with knowledge and is the creator of the glory of all beings—to that eternally imperishable One, let there be salutation.
I bow to the one who consists of the unity of the rule governing the operation of knowledge, who is capable of bestowing experience upon the person, who is composed of the three qualities (guṇas),
who is unmanifest, who is the cause of the manifestation of worldly existence, who is the abode of his own essential nature, and who is eternally free from old age.

I bow to the Manifested One, who consists of the arrangement of ether, air, fire, water, and earth; who is capable of bringing forth the objects of enjoyment such as sound and the rest; who assists the person through all the sense organs; and who possesses a subtle yet vast self.

May Lord Hari grant to all beings that perfection which is free from birth, old age, and the like— the manifold eternal form of the unborn one, consisting of both primordial nature and the supreme self.
Thus ends the eighth chapter (8) in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa;
the sixth book is completed.
Thus the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa is finished.
